0.title: Remember and Obey: The Book of Deuteronomy
0.overview:
The message. Deuteronomy is Moses’ farewell to a people about to enter the promised land without him. It says that the God who rescued Israel from slavery, chose them for no reason but his own love, and carried them through the wilderness asks for one thing in return: their whole heart. “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (6:4–5). Grace comes first, and obedience is love’s answer to it; to remember what God has done is to want to do what he says. Yet the book is honest that Israel’s heart cannot rise to this, and it ends with a promise that God himself will change it (30:6).

Background: the speaker. The book is a set of farewell addresses by Moses, now a hundred and twenty years old (31:2), the man who led Israel out of Egypt and met God at Sinai (which Deuteronomy calls Horeb). Knowing he must die on this side of the Jordan (3:23–27), he does what a dying father does: he gathers his family and tells them what matters most. Our title comes from the Greek translation of a phrase in 17:18, “a second law”, yet this is not a new law but the Sinai law preached to a new generation: “Moses undertook to explain this law” (1:5). The Hebrew title, Debarim, “Words”, fits it better.

When and where. Moses speaks “in the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month” after the exodus (1:3), on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho. If the exodus was about 1446 BC (1 Kings 6:1), this was about 1406 BC; many date it about two centuries later, and this commentary, as in Exodus, leaves the date open. The generation that left Egypt has died in the desert for refusing to enter the land at Kadesh (1:19–46); their children now stand at the border. East of the Jordan the Amorite kings Sihon and Og have already fallen (2:24–3:11). West of it lies Canaan, whose people “even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods” (12:31).

The kind of writing. Deuteronomy is preaching: three sermons, then a song, a blessing and Moses’ death. Its shape follows the covenant treaties of the ancient world: what the great king has done, his requirements, blessings and curses, witnesses, and arrangements for the treaty to be kept and read aloud. A covenant is a bond sealed by oath, and here the LORD binds himself to Israel and Israel to him. Its laws are moral, ceremonial (worship, sacrifice and purity) and civil (Israel’s life as a nation). This commentary holds that the moral law remains the rule of life for Christians, as the shape of love and never a way to earn salvation, while the ceremonial and civil laws are fulfilled in Christ.

How the book makes its case. The first address (1:1–4:43) looks back: the failure at Kadesh, the forty years, the victories God gave, and the God who spoke from the fire with no form to be copied (4:12). The second and longest (4:44–28:68) begins with the Ten Commandments (chapter 5) and the call to love (chapter 6), then insists that God chose Israel “because the LORD loves you” (7:8), not because they were good, “for you are a stubborn people” (9:6). Only then come the detailed laws (chapters 12–26): worship at the place God chooses, justice in the courts, open hands for the poor and the stranger, a king under the law, and a prophet like Moses. Blessings and curses follow (chapters 27–28). The third address (chapters 29–30) renews the covenant, looks past Israel’s coming failure and exile to restoration, and ends, “Therefore choose life” (30:19). The last chapters (31–34) pass the leadership to Joshua and the written law to the priests, give the Song of Moses as a witness, bless the tribes, and tell of Moses’ death on Mount Nebo. The order itself preaches: grace is told before a single command is given.

Did Moses write it? Many scholars hold that Deuteronomy was written in the seventh century BC, the book found in the temple under King Josiah (2 Kings 22), composed to support his reforms. They point to its likenesses with Assyrian treaties of that age. Others find its shape at least as close to Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC, so that argument settles nothing. The book itself says, “Moses wrote this law” (31:9), and Jesus spoke of its commands as what Moses wrote (Mark 10:3–5). The account of Moses’ death (chapter 34) and a few explanatory notes, such as 2:10–12, were added by a later inspired hand; Jewish tradition named Joshua. This commentary’s view is that the substance is Moses’ own, as the book and our Lord say, and that what Josiah’s men found was a neglected copy of an old book, which is why its words made the king tear his clothes (2 Kings 22:11–13).

The hard commands. Readers are rightly troubled by the command to destroy the nations of Canaan (7:1–5; 20:16–18). The book gives the reason: “Not because of your righteousness … but because of the wickedness of these nations” (9:5), a wickedness God had borne with for centuries (Genesis 15:16). This commentary holds that these were God’s unique judgments on persistent wickedness, given once, to one people, at one moment, and never a pattern or licence for violence since. The same book warns Israel that if it goes after other gods it will perish “like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you” (8:20).

Where it leads: to Christ. Deuteronomy leads to Christ by promise, by the need it exposes, and in his own life. By promise: Moses said God would raise up “a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers” (18:15), and the book closes admitting none had yet come (34:10); Peter and Stephen announce that he has come in Jesus (Acts 3:22–26; 7:37). By need: the book’s own verdict is that “the LORD has not given you a heart to understand” (29:4). The law commands, “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (10:16), but cannot make it happen, so God promises, “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (30:6), the new covenant Christ brings by his Spirit. The curse the law pronounces on all who break it (27:26), Christ bore: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13, citing 21:23). And Jesus was the true Israel. Tested in the wilderness, as Israel was for forty years, he answered the devil three times from this book: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4, from 8:3). Asked for the greatest commandment, he answered from the Shema (Matthew 22:37–38), and kept it to the cross. Moses could only bring Israel to the border; Joshua, whose Hebrew name is the name Jesus, took them in, yet “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). The true rest is in the greater Joshua.

For us. Deuteronomy teaches Christians to remember. Its commands rest on what God has done, and so does the Christian life: we obey not to be loved, but because we already are. It warns that comfort breeds forgetfulness (8:11–18). Above all it humbles us: we are the stubborn people, and Christ is the obedient Son who loved God with all his heart in our place and bore the curse we earned. Through him the promise Moses gave Israel (31:6) is ours: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

1.title: Looking Back: The God Who Was Faithful Though We Failed
1.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.<sup>2</sup>It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea.<sup>3</sup>In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel according to all that the LORD had given him in commandment to them,<sup>4</sup>after he had defeated Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei.<sup>5</sup>Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, saying,<sup>6</sup>"The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, 'You have stayed long enough at this mountain.<sup>7</sup>Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all their neighbors in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negeb and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates.<sup>8</sup>See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their offspring after them.'<sup>9</sup>"At that time I said to you, 'I am not able to bear you by myself.<sup>10</sup>The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven.<sup>11</sup>May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you!<sup>12</sup>How can I bear by myself the weight and burden of you and your strife?<sup>13</sup>Choose for your tribes wise, understanding, and experienced men, and I will appoint them as your heads.'<sup>14</sup>And you answered me, 'The thing that you have spoken is good for us to do.'<sup>15</sup>So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers, throughout your tribes.<sup>16</sup>And I charged your judges at that time, 'Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him.<sup>17</sup>You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God's. And the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.'<sup>18</sup>And I commanded you at that time all the things that you should do.<sup>19</sup>"Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God commanded us. And we came to Kadesh-barnea.<sup>20</sup>And I said to you, 'You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us.<sup>21</sup>See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not fear or be dismayed.'<sup>22</sup>Then all of you came near me and said, 'Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us and bring us word again of the way by which we must go up and the cities into which we shall come.'<sup>23</sup>The thing seemed good to me, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe.<sup>24</sup>And they turned and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied it out.<sup>25</sup>And they took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, 'It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.'<sup>26</sup>"Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God.<sup>27</sup>And you murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us.<sup>28</sup>Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. And besides, we have seen the sons of the Anakim there."'<sup>29</sup>Then I said to you, 'Do not be in dread or afraid of them.<sup>30</sup>The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes,<sup>31</sup>and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.'<sup>32</sup>Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God,<sup>33</sup>who went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents, in fire by night and in the cloud by day, to show you by what way you should go.<sup>34</sup>"And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore,<sup>35</sup>'Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers,<sup>36</sup>except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his children I will give the land on which he has trodden, because he has wholly followed the LORD!'<sup>37</sup>Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there.<sup>38</sup>Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter. Encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it.<sup>39</sup>And as for your little ones, who you said would become a prey, and your children, who today have no knowledge of good or evil, they shall go in there. And to them I will give it, and they shall possess it.<sup>40</sup>But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea.'<sup>41</sup>"Then you answered me, 'We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us.' And every one of you fastened on his weapons of war and thought it easy to go up into the hill country.<sup>42</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Say to them, Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, lest you be defeated before your enemies.'<sup>43</sup>So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country.<sup>44</sup>Then the Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you as bees do and beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah.<sup>45</sup>And you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice or give ear to you.<sup>46</sup>So you remained at Kadesh many days, the days that you remained there.
1.overview:
Where we are. Deuteronomy opens on the plains of Moab in the fortieth year after the exodus. The generation that left Egypt has died in the wilderness, and Moses, forbidden to cross the Jordan, begins his farewell. Before giving a single command he tells the story, starting at the nation’s deepest wound.

The message. Israel was kept out of the land not by giants but by unbelief. God had given them everything, even the fruit in their hands, and they decided he hated them. Yet his promise outlived their failure, and the door their fathers would not walk through stands open again for their children. Do not repeat your fathers’ sin: trust the God who carried you.

Why it was said. The listeners are the children of the Kadesh generation, standing at the same kind of border and facing the same kind of enemies (see the introduction). Moses fears they will lose heart the same way, so he tells them plainly why their fathers’ graves are in the desert.

How the chapter makes its case. An eleven-day journey took forty years (vv. 1–5). At Horeb God told Israel to go and take the land sworn to their fathers (vv. 6–8), and as the people multiplied, Moses shared the burden with judges who were to fear no one, because the judgment is God’s (vv. 9–18). At Kadesh the spies called it a good land, and the people refused, murmuring that the LORD hated them, though he had carried them “as a man carries his son” (vv. 19–33). So God swore that this generation would not see the land, except Caleb and Joshua and the children (vv. 34–40). Then, told to turn back, they charged up the hill without him and were routed (vv. 41–46).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by pattern. Hebrews reads Kadesh as the standing warning to the church: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19). Only one Israelite ever trusted his Father all the way through the wilderness, the Son who was tested there forty days and did not doubt his Father’s heart. Moses, the lawgiver, does not take the people in; Joshua, whose name is the name Jesus, does, and Hebrews points beyond him to the greater rest that Jesus gives (Hebrews 4:8–10). And the suspicion that God hates us is answered at the cross, where the Father did not spare his own Son.

For us. Unbelief is not only doubting that God can help; it is suspecting that he does not mean us well. The cure Moses prescribes is memory: look at how he has carried you, and above all look at Calvary. “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Word at Horeb: ‘Go, Take Possession’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word at Horeb was a command to move: leave the mountain and take the land already given. The narrator sets the scene on the plains of Moab, on the far side of forty years, and measures the tragedy in one line: eleven days’ journey, forty years (vv. 1–3). Moses, with Sihon and Og already defeated, sets out to explain the law to a new generation, beginning with what God has done (vv. 4–5). Then he recalls the word that ended the year at Sinai: you have stayed long enough, go in and possess the land the LORD swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (vv. 6–8). The gift was given before a step was taken.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s promises are grounded in his oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The land is a gift, secured by covenant and not earned by merit.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel stood on the threshold of an inheritance already sworn to them. Every believer stands before promises God has already sworn to give in Christ, and the call is the same: go forward in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are Moses’ last words to the whole nation, spoken on the edge of the promised land. Deuteronomy is a farewell sermon, and every Israelite was meant to hear it.

These are the words. The Hebrew Bible names its books from their opening line, and this one is Debarim, “Words”. Our title comes by a longer road: the Greek translators rendered a phrase in 17:18 as deuteronomion, a second law. That is a little misleading. This is not a second law but the first law preached, the same commandments pressed home to a congregation, which is why Deuteronomy reads more like a sermon than anything else in the Pentateuch.

The preacher. A hundred and twenty years old, knowing his death is near, he speaks to the children of the people he began with, almost none of whom remember Egypt. He might settle scores, secure a legacy, or go quiet. Instead the whole book is one old man trying to get the truth into a generation he will not see again.

To all Israel. Not only the elders or the men who could read, but the whole people. God means his word to be heard by all his people, and that has never changed.

A greater farewell. Moses could only urge Israel to keep the covenant without him. In the upper room another leader said farewell, “having loved his own who were in the world” (John 13:1), then went to his death to seal a new covenant, and promised not to leave his people as orphans.

Uncertain wording. Several place names here cannot be located with confidence. Suph may be short for the Red Sea (in Hebrew the “Sea of Suph”) or a separate place; Tophel, Laban and Dizahab are not certainly identified, though Hazeroth was a wilderness camp (Numbers 11:35). The likely meaning: the verse sets Moses’ words east of the Jordan and recalls, through names on the route, the long road that brought Israel there.
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ farewell sermons, given on the plains of Moab in the fortieth year (1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea. In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel according to all that the LORD had given him in commandment to them, after he had defeated Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei. Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A journey of eleven days took forty years, and now, at its end, Moses explains God’s law to the new generation.

It is eleven days’ journey. The narrator leans in before the sermon starts. Eleven days: something like a hundred and fifty miles, a fortnight’s march for a family with animals, from the mountain of the law to the border of the promise. Then verse 3: “In the fortieth year.” Set the figures side by side and you have Deuteronomy in miniature. Nothing was wrong with the route, the provisions or the God leading. A fortnight’s journey took four decades, and every year has a grave in it.

Moses undertook to explain this law. Not new revelation, but what God has already said, made plain to a new generation. He begins where ancient covenant treaties began, with what the great king had already done before a single demand was laid on his people (see the introduction), so the commands of chapters 5 to 26 reach a people just reminded that they owe the LORD everything.

In everyday life. Most lives have an eleven-day journey that has been taking years: a conversation that should have happened, a sin that should have been confessed, a step of obedience put off until putting it off became a way of life. The distance never grows; only the years do. But this sermon is preached to people on the far side of such years, and the door is still open. The way out of a forty-year delay is not a grand resolution but to confess it to the God who has not given up on you, and take the next step he shows.
verseByVerse.note: Horeb is Sinai; Kadesh-barnea was the oasis on Canaan’s southern border. The years from leaving Kadesh to crossing the brook Zered were thirty-eight (2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, 'You have stayed long enough at this mountain. Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all their neighbors in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negeb and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates. See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their offspring after them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God moved his people on from the mountain of glory, because the land was already given and they had only to go in and take it.

You have stayed long enough at this mountain. They had been at Sinai about eleven months: the mountain burning, God speaking to a whole nation, the covenant made, the glory filling the tabernacle. If any place deserved permanent settlement, it was that one. And God says: enough. Break camp.

See, I have set the land before you. The grammar repays attention: “I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession.” The first verb speaks of something already done; the second is a command. The land is already given and still has to be walked into. Grace does not cancel effort; without grace, effort would achieve nothing.

The land that the LORD swore to your fathers. Underneath stands an oath older than anyone present. Centuries earlier God bound himself to a childless man, Abraham. Nothing Israel did at Kadesh put that oath at risk. It never rested on them. Paul says the promise to Abraham’s offspring finds its fulfilment in Christ (Galatians 3:16).

Moving on from the mountaintop. Some Christians want to live at the site of their best experience of God, the conversion or the year everything was clear, and measure every later season against it. But the mountain was never the destination. It was where they were made ready to go somewhere.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — Leaders Appointed: Sharing the Burden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s blessing created the burden, and God provided men to share it. Israel had become as many as the stars, just as God promised Abraham, and Moses could no longer carry them alone; yet he prays that God will make them a thousand times more (vv. 9–12). He asks the tribes to choose wise, understanding and experienced men, and appoints them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (vv. 13–15). His charge to the judges is the heart of the section: hear every case fairly, the alien as well as the brother, the small as well as the great; fear no one, for the judgment is God’s; and bring the hardest cases to him (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: God multiplies his people and provides leaders to care for them. Because justice belongs to God, judges act in his name and must show no partiality.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel grew too numerous for one man, and the load was shared. Christ gives shepherds and elders to his church (Eph 4) in the same way: leadership is shared stewardship under the Chief Shepherd, not one person carrying everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time I said to you, 'I am not able to bear you by myself. The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you! How can I bear by myself the weight and burden of you and your strife? Choose for your tribes wise, understanding, and experienced men, and I will appoint them as your heads.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The burden that was too heavy for Moses was the fruit of God’s kept promise, and he met it by sharing the work with wise men.

I am not able to bear you by myself. Moses is candid about the day the work became too big, and in the same breath says why: Israel is now “as numerous as the stars of heaven”, as God promised a childless Abraham (Genesis 15:5). The weight crushing Moses is answered prayer.

A thousand times as many. Flattened by the size of this nation, he asks God to multiply it by a thousand. Most of us can pray for relief. Praying for more of the very thing that is breaking you is possible only if you believe it is good and God gave it, which is exactly what Moses believed.

Wise, understanding, and experienced men. His solution is not to work harder but to share the load, with men chosen for character and judgment, not force of personality. The apostles reached for the same remedy when the church outgrew them (Acts 6:2–4). On leadership and order in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

A burden that is blessing. The ministry that has outgrown you, the family bigger than your energy: not every burden means something has gone wrong. Some are what blessing feels like from underneath. Nor need anyone carry them alone; only one man ever bore the full weight of God’s people by himself, and he did it on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And you answered me, 'The thing that you have spoken is good for us to do.' So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers, throughout your tribes. And I charged your judges at that time, 'Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him. You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God's. And the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.' And I commanded you at that time all the things that you should do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s judges were to judge every case fairly and fearlessly, because they gave judgment on God’s behalf.

I charged your judges. The charge is short, and every clause has teeth. “The alien who is with him” gets the same court as a man with a tribe behind him.

You shall not be partial in judgment. The Hebrew idiom is not to recognise faces. In the ancient world law bent toward wealth as water runs downhill; this forbids leaning either way, towards the rich or towards the poor, as Leviticus says outright: “You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great” (Leviticus 19:15). Sympathy can corrupt a verdict as surely as a bribe.

For the judgment is God’s. A judge afraid of the man in front of him cannot do justice, and the cure for that fear is this clause. The judge administers a verdict that belongs to someone else and will answer for it. That is why he need not fear the powerful, and why he dare not favour them.

The case that is too hard for you. Easily missed: the hardest case is brought to Moses. Even the appointed men are allowed a limit. There is no shame in a man in authority saying this one is beyond me, and considerable danger in a man who never does.

The Judge who sees no faces. Every judge in Israel fell short. The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), who “shall not judge by what his eyes see” (Isaiah 11:3). He cannot be flattered or frightened, and those who trust him need not fear his verdict, because he has borne their sentence himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–33 — Kadesh-barnea: The Tragedy of Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel refused the land because they would not believe God. They came through the terrifying wilderness to Kadesh-barnea, where Moses told them the land lay before them and they need not fear (vv. 19–21). The spies they asked for brought back fruit and one verdict: it is a good land (vv. 22–25). Yet the people rebelled, murmuring in their tents that the LORD had brought them out because he hated them, and their fear made the cities reach to heaven (vv. 26–28). Moses answered with evidence: the LORD fights for you, as in Egypt, and he carried you through the wilderness as a father carries his son. Still they did not believe the God who went ahead of them to find their camping places (vv. 29–33).
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief is the root sin: it calls God a liar and recasts his love as hatred, even while he is carrying his people like a father.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel saw the giants and forgot the God who split the sea. We do the same when we let our obstacles grow larger in our minds than the God who has already carried us through worse.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God commanded us. And we came to Kadesh-barnea. And I said to you, 'You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us. See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not fear or be dismayed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the terrifying wilderness, God brought Israel to the border, set the land before them and told them not to fear.

That great and terrifying wilderness. Moses does not tidy the journey up. They went through that and came out the other side, and the wilderness they survived is the evidence he will hold up against their fear.

Do not fear or be dismayed. The moment at the border is packed into two verses: a gift already given, a command to act, and a word about their emotions, spoken before anybody had said they were afraid. God addressed the fear in advance rather than waiting to rebuke it. Everything they needed to know, Moses told them that morning; whatever happens next cannot be blamed on insufficient information.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all of you came near me and said, 'Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us and bring us word again of the way by which we must go up and the cities into which we shall come.' The thing seemed good to me, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe. And they turned and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied it out. And they took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, 'It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses recalls the spies, and of their report he gives only the heart of it: the land God was giving was good.

Let us send men before us. In Numbers the command to send spies comes from God (Numbers 13:1–2); here the people asked. Both are true: the request came from below and God permitted it. And Moses does not shelter behind that: “The thing seemed good to me.” Forty years later he puts his own judgment on the record.

It is a good land. The report as he gives it: the fruit in their hands and “It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.” No giants, no fortified cities, no ten against two. Moses knows what else was said (he quotes the fear in verse 28), but here he gives the good land and stops. He is not misremembering; he is preaching. The land was good, God was giving it, they had the fruit in their hands, and they would not go. Strip out the excuse and the refusal stands with nothing in front of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. And you murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us. Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. And besides, we have seen the sons of the Anakim there."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel refused to go in, and their unbelief turned into slander: they said God had rescued them only because he hated them.

You murmured in your tents. Not at the tabernacle or to Moses’ face, where it could be answered, but in the dark, at home, to the family, which is where grumbling against God always grows, because it needs privacy and dies in daylight.

Because the LORD hated us. The God who broke Egypt for them, opened a sea, drowned an army, fed them every morning and stood over their camp in fire every night had, they said, done all of it to get them somewhere quiet enough to kill them.

What unbelief does. Unbelief cannot leave God’s character alone. It never stops at “I am not sure this will work”; it goes on to “he does not mean me well”, because if God is both good and able, there is no excuse for refusing him. It is the serpent’s oldest lie, that God is keeping something from you: “God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5).

Fortified up to heaven. See what fear does to measurement. Cities “fortified up to heaven” is not a report but a feeling with numbers on it. Nobody had measured a wall.

When the thought forms. If you have lain awake after a diagnosis or a bereavement and felt the thought forming that God is against you, that thought has a history, and this is where it is recorded. It is answered much later: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). You cannot hold that sentence and the whisper in the tent at the same time.

What if God is holding out on me? The whisper in the tents has become the air we breathe. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur called Marx, Nietzsche and Freud the masters of suspicion, because each taught us to look behind what people say for the interest it hides. The habit has its uses, but it is easily turned on God: his commands must be about control, his no a proof that he does not want us to flourish. It is the oldest suspicion there is, and it always leaves the suspicious person alone, with nobody left to trust. The gospel answers it with an act. The serpent said God was grasping. Then the Son of God, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped”, emptied himself and went to a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). Suspicion can explain away a great deal. It has never managed to explain away that.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to you, 'Do not be in dread or afraid of them. The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes, and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.' Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God, who went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents, in fire by night and in the cloud by day, to show you by what way you should go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses answered their fear with evidence of God’s care, yet they would not believe the God who had carried them like a son.

Do not be in dread or afraid of them. Moses answers their terror not with encouragement but with evidence, in three pieces: the God who goes before them now, what he did “in Egypt before your eyes”, and, deepest, the wilderness, where “the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son”.

As a man carries his son. It is one of the tenderest images in the Old Testament, placed here on purpose. A father at the end of a long walk with a child who cannot go another step: the child up on his shoulder, asleep, arms round his neck, contributing nothing whatever and getting there anyway. That is what the forty years had been. The people who said “the LORD hated us” had been carried the whole way by the one they accused.

You did not believe the LORD your God. Then verse 32 falls like a stone. Not “you were outnumbered”, not “the giants were real”: they did not believe him. Hebrews hands this to the church as the standing warning: “So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19).

To seek you out a place to pitch your tents. Verse 33 adds the last, quietly devastating piece. While they decided he meant to destroy them, he was out ahead of them, in the dark, looking for somewhere they could sleep.

The Son who trusted. Israel was God’s son (Exodus 4:22), carried yet distrustful. The true Son, hungry and alone in the wilderness, answered every temptation from this book and never suspected his Father’s heart (Matthew 4:1–11). He went ahead of us to the cross and through it, and still goes ahead: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–46 — The Sentence and the Stubborn Presumption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unbelief brought judgment, and presumption was no cure for it. God heard and swore that none of that evil generation would see the good land, except Caleb, who had followed him fully (vv. 34–36). Moses himself would not enter; Joshua would lead Israel in, and the little ones the people had said would become prey would possess it (vv. 37–39). Told to turn back into the wilderness, the people suddenly decided to fight, against God’s word and without his presence. The Amorites chased them like bees, God did not listen to their weeping, and they stayed at Kadesh many days (vv. 40–46).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s discipline is real and his oath is sure. Presumption is as deadly as cowardice, and true faith waits on God’s timing rather than acting on its own remorse.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel wept too late and fought without God. Religion that ignores God’s word, however zealous it feels, ends in defeat; only faith that listens to him, worked in us by the Spirit, prevails.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore, 'Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his children I will give the land on which he has trodden, because he has wholly followed the LORD!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God heard their unbelief and swore that their whole generation would not see the land, except Caleb, who followed him fully.

The LORD heard your words. The murmuring in the tents was private only from Moses. And God answers with an oath, the same form by which he bound himself to Abraham; this second oath shuts these men out of the land that the first oath had promised.

And was angered. Resist the modern instinct to explain God’s anger away. It is not a loss of temper or disproportionate. It is what holy love looks like when told, by people it carried through a desert, that it is hatred.

Except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Then, mid-sentence, one name: Caleb, “because he has wholly followed the LORD”. The Hebrew is more concrete: he filled up after the LORD, went all the way behind him, left no gap. The rest followed partially and stopped where it got frightening.

Faithful in a faithless generation. Caleb, with Joshua, had seen the same walls and stood before a crowd that wanted to stone them (Numbers 14:6–10). His stand changed nobody’s mind, yet God took his name out of the general sentence and wrote it into the promise. Faithfulness in a faithless generation is seldom noticed except by God, which turns out to be enough. Yet only one man ever followed his Father with no gap at all, and those joined to Christ share his inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there. Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter. Encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it. And as for your little ones, who you said would become a prey, and your children, who today have no knowledge of good or evil, they shall go in there. And to them I will give it, and they shall possess it. But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses too was shut out, but Joshua would lead Israel in, and the children their parents feared for would inherit the land.

Even with me the LORD was angry on your account. Moses says this three times (1:37; 3:26; 4:21), yet Numbers is specific that Moses lost the land for his own failure at Meribah, striking the rock in temper (Numbers 20:10–12). Both are true. The sin was his, and God named it. The provocation was theirs: forty years of being ground down, in an argument they started, about water they blamed him for. Anyone who has snapped after years of provocation knows both can be true at once, and that the second does not excuse the first, which is why Moses, though he pleaded to cross (3:23–25), never disputes that the sin was his.

Joshua the son of Nun. The name Joshua is Yehoshua, which comes into Greek as Iesous, Jesus. The lawgiver dies outside the land; the man who bears the name of Jesus takes the people in. Hebrews makes the point and leaves it hanging on purpose: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). One Joshua brought them into Canaan, but Canaan was never the final rest. A greater Joshua brings his people into that.

Encourage him. A small instruction. The man God has chosen still needs strengthening from those he leads. Nobody is so appointed that he can do without that.

Your little ones. The children their fathers said would “become a prey” are the very ones God brings in.

Does “no knowledge of good or evil” teach an age of accountability? It means children too young to share the guilt of Kadesh, and so they inherited the land. Scripture does not set an age. But it gives hope for little ones who die, that God deals with them in mercy (2 Samuel 12:23), and grieving parents may rest them in the hands of the Judge who does right.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you answered me, 'We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us.' And every one of you fastened on his weapons of war and thought it easy to go up into the hill country. And the LORD said to me, 'Say to them, Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, lest you be defeated before your enemies.' So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country. Then the Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you as bees do and beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah. And you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice or give ear to you. So you remained at Kadesh many days, the days that you remained there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Told the door was shut, Israel charged up the hill without God and were routed: presumption is as much a refusal of God as fear.

Thought it easy to go up. The strangest turn comes last. Told the door is shut, Israel suddenly wants to go in. It sounds like repentance and is not. Yesterday God said go and they would not. Today he says “Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst”, and they go. They have changed direction, but their hearts have not changed at all. Both times they set aside what God said.

Chased you as bees do. Then the humiliation: a rout, men running from something small and furious and everywhere at once. And the saddest line: they “wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen”. That was grief at the consequences, not repentance, and God can tell the difference.

Two ways to refuse God. A man can disobey by hanging back or by charging ahead, and the second is more dangerous because it feels like courage and can be mistaken for faith by everyone watching, including himself. “I am not in your midst” is the only difference that matters, and it is invisible until the fighting starts.

What, then, should they have done? Exactly what they were told in verse 40: “turn, and journey into the wilderness.” Accept the discipline and wait for God to open the door again. And he did: Deuteronomy is preached at the foot of that reopened door, to the children of the men chased down that hill. If you have missed a window God opened, the answer is not a self-willed charge at it, but to submit to the wilderness and wait for him to speak again.

Uncertain wording. “The days that you remained there” is an idiom of indefinite length. It is not clear whether Israel stayed at Kadesh for much of the thirty-eight years or a shorter time before circling Mount Seir (2:1, 14). The likely meaning is simply a long, wasted stay.

1.theology:
Unbelief as the root sin. Israel’s catastrophe was not military but spiritual (1:32), and Hebrews 3–4 makes it the great warning for the church. Unbelief always slanders God’s character, recasting his love as hatred (1:27).

The faithfulness of God to his oath. He swore the land to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (1:8), and though a generation perishes, the promise passes to their children. Against Israel’s failure, God’s faithfulness to his covenant shines out: his grace outlasts human sin.

The mediator who cannot bring them in. Moses is barred from the land (1:37), and Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, is appointed to lead Israel in (1:38). The law can show us the land, but only the Saviour can bring us into its rest.
1.examples:
Then: at Kadesh-barnea, with the fruit of the land in their hands, Israel looked at the giants instead of God, grumbled in their tents and turned a fortnight’s journey into forty years of graves.

Now: we do the same whenever we magnify our obstacles and shrink our God, or rush into self-willed action when he says wait. The cure is remembrance, rehearsing how God has carried us (1:31), and resting in Christ, who believed where we failed, entered the rest on our behalf, and by his Spirit leads us through death into the everlasting land.

keyVerse.quote: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.
keyVerse.note: The chapter turns on the contrast between this verse and the next. The people who said “the LORD hated us” had been carried every step by a Father, and still they “did not believe” him (v. 32). Unbelief forgets how it has been carried; faith remembers, and at the cross sees the Father’s heart most clearly of all.

1.reflection:
Israel took forty years over an eleven-day journey (vv. 2–3). Is there a step of obedience you have been postponing so long that the delay has become a way of life? What would the next step be?

The people murmured in their tents that “the LORD hated us” (v. 27). When hard things happen, how does suspicion of God’s heart creep in, and how does the cross answer it (Romans 8:32)?

Moses reminded Israel that God had carried them “as a man carries his son” (v. 31). Where can you look back and see that God carried you when you could not walk? How does remembering it help you trust him now?

Israel first refused to go when God said go, then went when he said stop (vv. 41–43). Why is presumption as dangerous as fear, and how can we tell the difference between bold faith and self-will?

2.title: The Journey Around Edom and Moab: The Sovereign Lord of All Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea, as the LORD told me. And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir.<sup>2</sup>Then the LORD said to me,<sup>3</sup>'You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward<sup>4</sup>and command the people, "You are about to pass through the territory of your brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you. So be very careful.<sup>5</sup>Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.<sup>6</sup>You shall purchase food from them with money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them with money, that you may drink.<sup>7</sup>For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing."'<sup>8</sup>So we went on, away from our brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-geber. "And we turned and went in the direction of the wilderness of Moab.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.'<sup>10</sup>(The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim.<sup>11</sup>Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim, but the Moabites call them Emim.<sup>12</sup>The Horites also lived in Seir formerly, but the people of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place, as Israel did to the land of their possession, which the LORD gave to them.)<sup>13</sup>'Now rise up and go over the brook Zered.' So we went over the brook Zered.<sup>14</sup>And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.<sup>15</sup>For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.<sup>16</sup>"So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people,<sup>17</sup>the LORD said to me,<sup>18</sup>'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar.<sup>19</sup>And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.'<sup>20</sup>(It is also counted as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly lived there—but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim—<sup>21</sup>a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and settled in their place,<sup>22</sup>as he did for the people of Esau, who live in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them and they dispossessed them and settled in their place even to this day.<sup>23</sup>As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.)<sup>24</sup>'Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle.<sup>25</sup>This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you.'<sup>26</sup>"So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon the king of Heshbon, with words of peace, saying,<sup>27</sup>'Let me pass through your land. I will go only by the road; I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left.<sup>28</sup>You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot,<sup>29</sup>as the sons of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I go over the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving to us.'<sup>30</sup>But Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand, as he is this day.<sup>31</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land over to you. Begin to take possession, that you may occupy his land.'<sup>32</sup>Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz.<sup>33</sup>And the LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people.<sup>34</sup>And we captured all his cities at that time and devoted to destruction every city, men, women, and children. We left no survivors.<sup>35</sup>Only the livestock we took as spoil for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities that we captured.<sup>36</sup>From Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God gave all into our hands.<sup>37</sup>Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near, that is, to all the banks of the river Jabbok and the cities of the hill country, whatever the LORD our God had forbidden us.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with Israel turned back from Kadesh into the wilderness. Chapter 2 covers thirty-eight years in a few sentences, then resumes the march north past Edom, Moab and Ammon to the first battle of the conquest.

The message. The LORD is not a tribal god but the Lord of every nation, who gives each people its land and sets its times. So Israel must not take an inch he has given to others, and must take without fear what he has given to her. The God who disciplined a generation also supplied them every day, and he hands the first enemy over before a sword is drawn.

Why it was said. The listeners have just defeated Sihon and Og and are about to cross into Canaan (see the introduction). They need to know that the war ahead is not a licence to seize whatever they can reach, and that the giants who terrified their fathers are nothing to the God who leads them.

How the chapter makes its case. God ends the years of circling Mount Seir and forbids Israel to touch Edom, the land he gave to Esau; they are to pay for food and water, for they have lacked nothing (vv. 1–8). Moab, given to Lot’s descendants, is likewise out of bounds, and an aside shows God had long ago cleared giants out of it (vv. 9–12). At the brook Zered the thirty-eight years end with the last of the old generation dead (vv. 13–15). Ammon is spared too, with another note on peoples God displaced (vv. 16–23). Then the order changes: cross the Arnon, for I have given Sihon into your hand (vv. 24–25). Moses offers Sihon peace; God hardens Sihon’s heart; Israel defeats him and takes his land, and still does not touch Ammon (vv. 26–37).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him and by promise. The God who cared for Edom, Moab and Ammon had a purpose for them beyond borders: Ruth the Moabitess became an ancestor of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), and Amos foresaw “all the nations who are called by my name”, which James saw fulfilled as Gentiles turned to Christ (Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16–17). And the order of verse 24, “I have given” before “begin to take”, is the shape of the gospel: Christ has won the victory, and his people go out to take up what is already theirs.

For us. God’s discipline is real, and so is his daily provision through it; no season he appoints lasts a day longer than he intends. Hold what he has given you with gratitude, do not covet what he has given others, and face what frightens you by remembering what he has already done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Passing By Edom: Land You May Not Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God ends a season of discipline in his own time, and he defends even the land of a brother who refused Israel. After many years circling Mount Seir, God says, “long enough”, and turns them north (vv. 1–3). They must pass Edom, the people of Esau, without provoking them, for God has given Seir to Esau and will not give Israel so much as a footprint of it (vv. 4–5). They are to buy their food and water, for God has blessed them and been with them every one of the forty years: “You have lacked nothing” (vv. 6–7). So they go on, past their brothers, toward Moab (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s rule extends to all nations. He grants lands even to peoples outside the covenant line, and holds his own people to respecting them.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel paid for Edom’s food and water rather than seizing them. God’s people still honour boundaries and deal fairly with those they could overpower.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea, as the LORD told me. And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir. Then the LORD said to me, 'You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward
verseByVerse.commentary:
After thirty-eight years of circling Mount Seir, God said “long enough” and turned his people north again. The wandering had an end God had fixed from the start.

Traveled around Mount Seir. Thirty-eight years in a sentence, and “around” is exactly right: they circled a mountain while a generation died.

Long enough. In 1:6 God had said “You have stayed long enough at this mountain” of Sinai, the place of glory. Here almost the same words are spoken over a wilderness of failure. He will not let his people settle permanently on their highest day, and he will not leave them permanently in their worst one.

Turn northward. From inside, nobody could have said how much longer. But God knew the day he would say it. Anyone in a season that seems to have no end should notice that this verse exists. The circling was not aimless to God, even when it looked aimless to them.

verseByVerse.quote: and command the people, "You are about to pass through the territory of your brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you. So be very careful. Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession. You shall purchase food from them with money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them with money, that you may drink. For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing."' So we went on, away from our brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-geber. "And we turned and went in the direction of the wilderness of Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must pass Edom without taking an inch, for God gave it to Esau, and pay its way, for God had supplied them for forty years.

Do not contend with them. The first order to the newly turned nation is a restraint: not “so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on”. Six hundred thousand fighting men may not take a single pace of Edomite ground. And they pay for food and water: the nation on its way to conquer Canaan walks past the brother who had refused them the road (Numbers 20:18–21) and buys its dinner at the going rate.

Your brothers, the people of Esau. Esau despised his birthright (Hebrews 12:16), yet God gave him a country and defends his right to it even against his own covenant people. The Lord who chooses is not careless of those he did not choose. He “made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place” (Acts 17:26). Every people holds its land from God, and answers to him for it.

You have lacked nothing. Forty years of judgment, and he says they lacked nothing. That is a hard thing to say over a generation of funerals, and it is true. The discipline was real; so was the daily bread, all the way through. The manna pointed to the one who said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

The nation is not a god. Few idols are as respectable as the nation. The historian Benedict Anderson observed that modern nationalism has taken over much of religion’s work: it tells people what they belong to and gives a death meaning, which is why nations speak of sacred soil. Loving your own country is right. But it turns into worship when it claims what belongs to God alone: the right to decide who counts, and to sacrifice anyone for its sake. Verse 5 cuts that off at the root. Even Israel held her land as a gift; no people owns its ground, every people is a tenant. And the King of this book is gathering a people “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9), so a Christian can love his country without worshipping it, because his deepest citizenship is held where no border can reach.
verseByVerse.note: Edom, Moab and Ammon were Israel’s relatives, descended from Esau and Lot; Israel was not to take their land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Passing By Moab: The Old Giants Displaced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The giants that terrified Israel had never troubled God. Israel must not harass Moab, for God has given Ar to Lot’s descendants (v. 9). An aside explains that the Emim, giants like the Anakim, once lived there, and that Esau’s people likewise dispossessed the Horites, as Israel would later do in Canaan (vv. 10–12). Then God sends Israel over the brook Zered, and the narrator marks the moment: thirty-eight years since Kadesh, and the whole generation of fighting men has died, because the hand of the LORD was against them, as he had sworn (vv. 13–15). The discipline has ended exactly where God said it would.
verseByVerse.theology: God displaces one people to settle another according to purposes he does not always explain, and the death of the wilderness generation keeps his solemn oath (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.examples: God moved the old giants out to make room for nations that had no covenant with him. When the movements of nations bewilder us, we can trust the same God to be ruling them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.' (The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim. Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim, but the Moabites call them Emim. The Horites also lived in Seir formerly, but the people of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place, as Israel did to the land of their possession, which the LORD gave to them.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Moab to Lot’s descendants and long ago cleared giants out of it for them: Israel must not touch it, and need not fear giants.

Do not harass Moab. Moab was the people of Lot: Abraham’s nephew, who chose the well-watered plain and ended in Sodom, and whose line came out of a cave and a drunken night that Scripture reports without approval (Genesis 19:30–38). That family gets a country too, and God will not have it touched. Centuries later a Moabite widow, Ruth, would become an ancestor of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

The Emim formerly lived there. The Emim were giants, of the same stock as the Anakim whose name made the spies at Kadesh go to pieces, and God cleared them out of Moab for Lot’s descendants. While Israel’s fathers stood at Kadesh saying the giants were too big, God had been dispossessing giants for centuries, in that very neighbourhood, for nations with no covenant and no promise. The thing that paralysed the people of God had never once given him any trouble.

As Israel did. Verse 12 looks back on Israel’s conquest as already done. It is one of the few explanatory notes added to Moses’ words by a later inspired hand (see the introduction).

Were these literally giants? They were peoples remembered as unusually tall and strong, like the Anakim (compare Goliath, 1 Samuel 17:4). The text describes men, not monsters, and names such as Emim and Zamzummim were what their neighbours called them.

Uncertain wording. Emim may mean “terrors”. Rephaim here names an ancient people of great size, but elsewhere the same word is used of the dead (Isaiah 26:14), and how the uses connect is unclear. The Horites are often linked with the Hurrians of ancient records, though this is disputed. The point does not depend on any of it: these were strong, feared peoples whom God removed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now rise up and go over the brook Zered.' So we went over the brook Zered. And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them. For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty-eight years after Kadesh, at a small brook, God’s sentence on the unbelieving generation was complete.

Go over the brook Zered. A brook, not a river: a seasonal stream a man steps over. That is the boundary God set for the end of a generation, and it took thirty-eight years to reach it.

The hand of the LORD was against them. Verse 15 should not be softened. Every funeral in that camp was the hand of God, and Moses says so to their children’s faces. It should stand, because Scripture never treats God’s judgments as an embarrassment to be managed.

Kindness and severity. But look who is being told. The listeners are the boys who dug those graves, now told what it meant. God buried a generation of redeemed people who would not trust him, and then walked their sons across the stream. Both halves are the same God, and the New Testament puts them in one sentence: “Note then the kindness and the severity of God” (Romans 11:22). At the cross they meet: the severity fell on the Son, so that the kindness could reach those who deserved the sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — The Command to Begin: Ammon Spared, Sihon Devoted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God governs the movements of every nation, and when he gives, Israel may go forward without fear. As soon as the old generation has died, God sends Israel past Moab and forbids them to touch Ammon, another gift to Lot’s sons (vv. 16–19). A second aside lists more peoples God displaced: Rephaim called Zamzummim, Horites, and Avvim driven out by the Caphtorim (vv. 20–23). Then the word changes: cross the Arnon, for I have given Sihon and his land into your hand; begin to take possession. And God promises to put the dread of Israel on the peoples who hear of them (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: God alone sets the time for judgment and conquest. He goes before his people, and the fear of him reaches the nations before they do.
verseByVerse.examples: God said, This day I will begin (v. 25). His kingdom still advances on his timetable, not ours, and he still goes ahead of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people, the LORD said to me, 'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar. And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God placed Ammon out of Israel’s reach as well: Israel was to take only the land God gave, and walk past what he had given to others.

Do not harass them. A third nation placed out of reach: Edom, Moab, Ammon. Each time God says: this is not yours; I gave it to somebody else. Israel is about to be told to take a country by force, and God first establishes that this is no licence to take whatever she can. A land-grab does not begin by ruling out three softer targets.

Assigned to somebody else. Much of a Christian’s life consists of walking past things good and obtainable, because they were assigned to somebody else. The tenth commandment exists for this. So does contentment, which is not the belief that others’ portions are worthless but the settled conviction that God has allotted them on purpose, and has given us in Christ more than any field. Paul learned it as a secret, through the one “who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: (It is also counted as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly lived there—but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim— a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and settled in their place, as he did for the people of Esau, who live in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them and they dispossessed them and settled in their place even to this day. As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long before Israel came, God had displaced people after people: he redraws the map, and great powers are moved by him.

Rephaim and Zamzummim. Another parenthesis, the same drumbeat: Rephaim, Zamzummim, Horites, Avvim, Caphtorim, people after people displaced in four verses, none of it Israel’s doing. The map that looked permanent was being redrawn constantly by a God most of those nations had never heard of. Empires think they are the ones who act. In Scripture God acts, and they are moved.

For any century. That steadies any century: “It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers… who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness” (Isaiah 40:22–23). The Zamzummim were the great power of their valley, and we cannot even pronounce their name with confidence.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Zamzummim is unknown, and the Avvim are otherwise almost unknown. Caphtor is usually identified with Crete or the Aegean, from which the Philistines came (Amos 9:7), so the Caphtorim are probably early Philistines settling the coast near Gaza.
verseByVerse.note: The Rephaim were a people remembered for their great height.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle. This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Sihon into Israel’s hand before the battle began, and sent his people to take what was already theirs.

Begin to take possession. After all the restraint, and forty years of not beginning, the first real order to advance.

I have given into your hand. The order of the clauses governs everything that follows: “I have given” comes before “Begin to take possession”. The gift is announced in the past tense before a sword is drawn. One army fights in hope of winning; this one goes to collect what is already its own.

God’s gift first. The same order runs through the New Testament: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). The working out is real and strenuous, but it is never the means of getting what God has not already given, and the power for it is his. Behind it stands the victory Christ has already won: “thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

The dread and fear of you. God fights this war in the minds of Canaan before Israel arrives, and Rahab will soon describe it from the inside: “our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you” (Joshua 2:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–37 — The Defeat of Sihon: The First Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first victory was God’s gift and God’s judgment, carried out within the limits he set. Moses offers Sihon peace and asks only to pass along the road and buy food, as Edom and Moab had allowed (vv. 26–29). Sihon refuses, because God hardened his spirit to give him into Israel’s hand (v. 30). God says he has begun to give Sihon over; Sihon attacks at Jahaz and is defeated (vv. 31–33). His cities are devoted to destruction and not one is too high for Israel, because the LORD gave them all; yet Israel does not go near the land of Ammon, as God had forbidden (vv. 34–37).
verseByVerse.theology: God offers terms of peace and also hardens hearts to carry out his judgment; how the two fit together is taken up at verses 26–30.
verseByVerse.examples: Sihon’s refusal of peace sealed his doom. The gospel goes out with a genuine offer of peace, and it is the refusal of that offer, not any lack of welcome in it, that ripens into judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon the king of Heshbon, with words of peace, saying, 'Let me pass through your land. I will go only by the road; I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left. You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot, as the sons of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I go over the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving to us.' But Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand, as he is this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel offered Sihon peace, but he refused because God hardened his already hostile heart, so that God might give him into Israel’s hand.

With words of peace. Israel’s first war opens with a genuine offer of peace, the same modest request Edom refused. Judgment comes only after peace is refused, as the gospel of peace is still preached before the day of judgment (Ephesians 2:17; Acts 17:30–31).

As the sons of Esau… did for me. Verse 29 says Edom sold Israel food, while Numbers says Edom refused passage (Numbers 20:14–21). Both are true: Edom refused the main road through its land, so Israel went round its borders, and along the edge Edom and Moab sold them food and water.

The LORD your God hardened his spirit. Here Deuteronomy first raises the hardest question about the will of God and the will of man. Begin with what Scripture does not say: it never says God put a desire for evil into a good man. Sihon was an Amorite warlord who had taken Heshbon by conquest (Numbers 21:26) and marched out to attack a nation that had asked to use a road. What God hardened was already there.

The parallel case. Of Pharaoh, Exodus says God will harden his heart (Exodus 4:21), Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15), and God hardened it (Exodus 9:12): Scripture states both without explaining how they fit. Paul sharpens it rather than smoothing it: “So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills”, and voices our objection, “Why does he still find fault?” (Romans 9:18–19).

Two truths that stand. God never makes a man sin; every man hardened is hardened in what he already wanted. And God is no spectator of wickedness; he governs it, and it serves his purposes. Both truths stand, and the line where they meet is not shown us. The supreme case is the cross, where wicked men did what they chose and yet did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, 'Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land over to you. Begin to take possession, that you may occupy his land.' Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz. And the LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people. And we captured all his cities at that time and devoted to destruction every city, men, women, and children. We left no survivors. Only the livestock we took as spoil for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities that we captured. From Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God gave all into our hands. Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near, that is, to all the banks of the river Jabbok and the cities of the hill country, whatever the LORD our God had forbidden us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Sihon and his cities to Israel in a single judgment, and even in victory Israel kept to the limits God had set.

We defeated him. The battle is over in a verse. Israel fought, and the credit is placed with God in the same sentence: “the LORD our God gave him over to us.” Not one city was “too high for us”, the very fear that had broken their fathers (1:28).

Devoted to destruction. Deuteronomy sets out the grounds in chapters 7 and 20. The judgment is God’s, executed through Israel at a fixed moment for a stated reason: four centuries of Amorite wickedness, which God had borne with while it ripened (Genesis 15:16). And it is no pattern for anybody: no nation since has held that commission, and the New Testament rules it out, for “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near. In the flush of a first victory the restraint holds. An army that has tasted success and can still be told “not that” is a nation under orders, not a nation out for whatever it can get.

But women and children? The judgment fell on a whole people, as the flood and Sodom did, and the Judge of all the earth has the right to take any life (Genesis 18:25). Those who turned to the LORD, like Rahab, were spared (Joshua 6:25). This was a unique command for that moment, never a pattern: the law itself forbids punishing children for their fathers’ crimes in human courts (24:16).
