And the Judge at last bore judgment himself, in his Son, so that people from every nation might be spared.
verseByVerse.note: “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

2.theology:
The sovereignty of God over all nations. Three times God forbids Israel to seize the lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon, because he himself allotted them (2:5, 9, 19). The God of Israel rules the boundaries of every people (Acts 17:26), raising up and casting down, displacing giants to settle nations according to his hidden counsel.

Divine hardening and human responsibility. Sihon refuses peace of his own pride, yet “the LORD your God hardened his spirit” (2:30). Scripture holds both together, as with Pharaoh: God’s righteous judgment is accomplished even through the free rebellion of the wicked (see vv. 26–30).

The faithful provision of God. Through forty years in “this great wilderness,” God was with his people and “you have lacked nothing” (2:7). The Lord of history is also the shepherd who counts every need of his children.
2.examples:
Then: Israel marched north under restraint, buying food from Edom and sparing Moab and Ammon, until the appointed hour came for Sihon.

Now: We serve the Lord of all nations, whose kingdom advances on his timetable with a genuine offer of peace in the gospel. His people go forward certain that every enemy is already “given over” in Christ, who has disarmed the powers and goes before us to the final victory.

keyVerse.quote: For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing.
keyVerse.note: Spoken over thirty-eight years of discipline and a generation of graves, this verse shows that God’s judgment and his care ran side by side the whole way. He knew every step, was present in every year, and supplied every day. It is the confidence of the chapter, and of every believer in a wilderness season.

2.reflection:
God told Israel “long enough” after thirty-eight years of circling Mount Seir (v. 3). How does it help to know that God sets the end of hard seasons as well as their beginning?

Israel was forbidden to take any land God had given to Edom, Moab or Ammon (vv. 5, 9, 19). Where are you tempted to want what God has assigned to somebody else, and what does contentment in Christ look like there?

Moses says that through forty years of discipline “you have lacked nothing” (v. 7). Looking back on a hard time in your life, what did God supply that you did not notice then?

God says “I have given” before he says “begin to take possession” (v. 24). How does knowing that Christ has already won the victory change the way you face temptation, fear or difficult service?

3.title: Victories East of the Jordan: ‘It Is Enough for You’
3.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.<sup>2</sup>But the LORD said to me, 'Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.'<sup>3</sup>So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people, and we struck him down until he had no survivor left.<sup>4</sup>And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.<sup>5</sup>All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, besides very many unwalled villages.<sup>6</sup>And we devoted them to destruction, as we did to Sihon the king of Heshbon, devoting to destruction every city, men, women, and children.<sup>7</sup>But all the livestock and the spoil of the cities we took as our plunder.<sup>8</sup>So we took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon<sup>9</sup>(the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir),<sup>10</sup>all the cities of the tableland and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.<sup>11</sup>(For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its breadth, according to the common cubit.)<sup>12</sup>"When we took possession of this land at that time, I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites the territory beginning at Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and half the hill country of Gilead with its cities.<sup>13</sup>The rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, that is, all the region of Argob, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh. (All that portion of Bashan is called the land of Rephaim.<sup>14</sup>Jair the Manassite took all the region of Argob, that is, Bashan, as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called the villages after his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day.)<sup>15</sup>To Machir I gave Gilead,<sup>16</sup>and to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead as far as the Valley of the Arnon, with the middle of the valley as a border, as far over as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites;<sup>17</sup>the Arabah also, with the Jordan as the border, from Chinnereth as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah on the east.<sup>18</sup>"And I commanded you at that time, saying, 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>Only your wives, your little ones, and your livestock (I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in the cities that I have given you,<sup>20</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also occupy the land that the LORD your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then each of you may return to his possession which I have given you.'<sup>21</sup>And I commanded Joshua at that time, 'Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing.<sup>22</sup>You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.'<sup>23</sup>"And I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying,<sup>24</sup>'O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand. For what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do such works and mighty acts as yours?<sup>25</sup>Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.'<sup>26</sup>But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.<sup>27</sup>Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes, for you shall not go over this Jordan.<sup>28</sup>But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.'<sup>29</sup>So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor.
3.overview:
Where we are. Sihon has fallen (chapter 2), and Moses completes the story of the victories east of the Jordan. Then, before the sermon turns to its great appeal in chapter 4, he tells of the prayer God refused him.

The message. The LORD fights for his people, so they need not fear even the strongest enemy; what he has already done is the pledge of what he will do. Yet the man who led them cannot lead them in. God answers Moses’ longing to cross the Jordan with a firm no, and even that no is surrounded by kindness and points beyond itself.

Why it was said. The listeners are about to cross into Canaan under a new leader, against cities like those that broke their fathers’ nerve (see the introduction). They need the evidence of Og’s defeat, the example of tribes who will fight for their brothers, and the sobering sight of Moses, who must stay behind.

How the chapter makes its case. Og of Bashan, the last of the giants, comes out to battle, and God says, “Do not fear him”; sixty fortified cities fall, and Og’s great bed becomes a curiosity (vv. 1–11). Moses divides the conquered land among Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh (vv. 12–17), but their fighting men must cross armed ahead of their brothers until all Israel has rest (vv. 18–20). Moses charges Joshua to reason from what his eyes have seen: the LORD fights for you (vv. 21–22). Then Moses pleads to go over and see the good land; God refuses, tells him to look from Pisgah and to strengthen Joshua, and the people stay in the valley opposite Beth-peor (vv. 23–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The mediator of the law cannot bring the people into the inheritance; Joshua, whose name is the name Jesus, will, and even his rest pointed beyond itself (Hebrews 4:8). The tribes who cross over to fight for brothers whose land they do not need are a small picture of the elder Brother who did that for us. And Moses’ refused prayer is not the end of his story: centuries later he stood in the land, on the mountain of transfiguration, talking with Jesus about the departure he would accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30–31).

For us. Fear is met by remembering what God has done, above all at the cross and the empty tomb. Do not rest while your brothers and sisters still struggle. And when God says no to a good prayer, trust that his no is never his last word to those who are his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Defeat of Og: The Last of the Giants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who defeated Sihon will defeat the strongest enemy too, so Israel need not fear. Og king of Bashan comes out to battle at Edrei, and God tells Moses not to fear him, for he has already given him into Israel’s hand, as he did Sihon (vv. 1–3). Israel takes all sixty of Og’s cities, fortified with high walls, gates and bars, and devotes them to destruction as before (vv. 4–7). So the whole land east of the Jordan, from the Arnon to Mount Hermon, is taken from the two Amorite kings (vv. 8–10). A closing note marks Og as the last of the Rephaim and points to his enormous iron bed, still to be seen at Rabbah (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: No enemy, however great, can stand before the LORD who fights for his people; the giants of legend fall before him.
verseByVerse.examples: The fear that broke the fathers was overcome by their sons. What once terrified us, and what God has since brought us through, is evidence to hold up against the next fear.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. But the LORD said to me, 'Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.' So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people, and we struck him down until he had no survivor left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Og, the most fearsome king Israel could meet, came out to fight, and God said, “Do not fear him”, for he had already given him into their hand.

Og the king of Bashan. Of all the enemies Israel could have met so early, this is the worst. Og was the last of the Rephaim (v. 11), the giant stock that made the spies at Kadesh say “we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:33). The terror that destroyed their parents comes down the road at them in the first campaign of their lives. Bashan was the rich, well-walled tableland east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its cattle and oaks (Psalm 22:12; Isaiah 2:13).

As you did to Sihon. Look at God’s argument. Not “he is smaller than he looks”, not “you are stronger than you think”, but: you have just seen me do this to Sihon. The cure for fear is not to measure the enemy again but to remember what God has done. And it worked. The fathers ran from giants they had only heard described; their sons defeated one. Nothing had changed about the giants.

The greater victory. Christians face enemies no army can defeat: sin, the devil and death. The answer is the same argument on a larger scale: Christ has already “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, besides very many unwalled villages. And we devoted them to destruction, as we did to Sihon the king of Heshbon, devoting to destruction every city, men, women, and children. But all the livestock and the spoil of the cities we took as our plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel took all sixty of Og’s fortified cities: the walls their fathers called unconquerable fell when this generation went up at God’s word.

Fortified with high walls, gates, and bars. Read 1:28 beside this. The report that broke the nation at Kadesh was “The cities are great and fortified up to heaven.” Here are sixty of them, and not one left untaken. What their fathers called insurmountable their sons list like an inventory.

The walls had not got lower. The text insists on how strong Bashan’s cities were. What changed was that this generation went up when God said go. Most Christians spend much of life in front of some wall, and the question is almost never whether the obstacle is real. Israel’s fathers were right about the walls and wrong about God, and being right about the walls did not save them.

As with Sihon. As with Sihon (2:34), this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened, carried out once through Israel. Those who turned to the LORD were spared, and it is no pattern for any later war.

verseByVerse.quote: So we took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon (the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir), all the cities of the tableland and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. (For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its breadth, according to the common cubit.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole land east of the Jordan was taken, and all that remained of the last giant was his bed, a curiosity for anyone to see.

His bed was a bed of iron. The narrator stops for a museum note. Nine cubits by four, by the ordinary cubit something over thirteen feet by six, and of iron, rare and costly in that age. And the aside is almost conversational: “Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites?” You can go and look at it.

What became of them. Before long the only thing left of the last of the Rephaim was a piece of furniture for tourists to stare at. The man who came out at Edrei with an army had become an exhibit. Scripture does this with what frightens people: it tells you what became of them. Pharaoh’s chariots are on the sea floor. Og’s bed is in a museum. And the last enemy, death, is spoken of in the same way: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “bed” usually means a bed or couch, but some think it here means a coffin, perhaps of the dark, iron-rich basalt common in Bashan. Either way the point is the same: the object was huge, and its owner was gone.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbah was the Ammonite capital, on the site of modern Amman.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — The Land Allotted; ‘The LORD Fights for You’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s gifts are measured out and received, and those who have received must fight for those who have not. Moses gives the land from the Arnon to Gilead to Reuben and Gad, and the rest of Gilead and Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh, with notes on Jair and Machir and the borders (vv. 12–17). But the fighting men of these tribes must cross the Jordan armed, ahead of their brothers, leaving their families and herds behind, until the LORD gives rest to all Israel (vv. 18–20). Then Moses charges Joshua: you have seen what God did to these two kings, so he will do to every kingdom; do not fear, for the LORD fights for you (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The people of God are one body: no tribe may rest in its own inheritance while its brothers still fight for theirs.
verseByVerse.examples: The eastern tribes had to fight for their brothers before enjoying their own land. Christians cannot settle into private comfort while the rest of the body still labours.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we took possession of this land at that time, I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites the territory beginning at Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and half the hill country of Gilead with its cities. The rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, that is, all the region of Argob, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh. (All that portion of Bashan is called the land of Rephaim. Jair the Manassite took all the region of Argob, that is, Bashan, as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called the villages after his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day.) To Machir I gave Gilead, and to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead as far as the Valley of the Arnon, with the middle of the valley as a border, as far over as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites; the Arabah also, with the Jordan as the border, from Chinnereth as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah on the east.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses gave the conquered land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, the first instalment of the promise.

When we took possession of this land. Six verses of surveying, because this is the first land any Israelite has owned since Egypt: four centuries there, forty years of tents, and now somebody has a deed. God’s gifts are not received in a heap but measured out and written down.

The first instalment. Moses is about to ask them to trust God for a country across a river, and they can walk out of the assembly and stand on the first instalment. The full inheritance is still across the water, but something is already in hand as a pledge. Paul calls the Holy Spirit exactly that: “the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it” (Ephesians 1:14).

As it is to this day. The notes in verses 13–14, like 2:10–12, read as explanations added by a later inspired hand (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. The region of Argob and the extent of Havvoth-jair, “the villages of Jair”, cannot now be mapped precisely (compare Numbers 32:39–42). The general picture is clear: the south went to Reuben and Gad, and northern Gilead and Bashan to Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I commanded you at that time, saying, 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel. Only your wives, your little ones, and your livestock (I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in the cities that I have given you, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also occupy the land that the LORD your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then each of you may return to his possession which I have given you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes had their land, but their fighting men must cross and fight ahead of their brothers until all Israel had rest.

Cross over armed before your brothers. Their fighting men go over in the front rank, into a war they have nothing to gain from.

Until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you. Rest is one of the great words of this book: not merely the end of fighting but a people settled at home, everyone on his own ground. And nobody gets it early; that is the force of “as to you”. In God’s reckoning rest is one thing belonging to one people, not a private arrangement each family reaches separately.

A Sabbath rest. Hebrews builds a whole argument on the word, “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), and keeps it a rest shared by the whole people. No Christian arrives home alone. You do not sit down while your brothers are still fighting. And the pattern is Christ’s before it is ours. He who had every right to rest crossed over for brothers who could not win their own inheritance, and his Spirit now makes his people willing to do the same for one another.

verseByVerse.quote: And I commanded Joshua at that time, 'Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing. You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua need not fear, because what God did to Sihon and Og he would do in Canaan: the LORD fights for his people.

Your eyes have seen. The charge to Joshua makes three moves, and the order matters. First, what he has seen with his own eyes, not been told. Second, the inference: “So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing.” Third, the conclusion for the heart: “You shall not fear them.” Scripture does not tell a man to feel braver; it reasons forward from what God has done. Faith here is not a mood.

It is the LORD your God who fights for you. The last clause takes the weight off Joshua entirely. He is handed a nation and a war and told the outcome does not finally rest on him. Every leader who has lain awake over something too big should notice that this is the last thing Moses says to his successor before he prays about his own death. For Christians the great evidence is Easter: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Moses’ Plea Denied: ‘It Is Enough for You’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God can say no to his most faithful servant, and his no comes wrapped in grace. Moses pleads to cross and see the good land, praising a God who has only begun to show his greatness (vv. 23–25). God refuses, angry with Moses on Israel’s account, and tells him not to raise the matter again (v. 26). Instead Moses may see the land from the top of Pisgah, and he is to charge, encourage and strengthen Joshua, who will lead the people in (vv. 27–28). The chapter ends quietly with Israel encamped in the valley opposite Beth-peor (v. 29), where Moses will preach the rest of the book.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the greatest mediator of the old covenant cannot bring God’s people into the inheritance, and God’s refusal of his servant is not the end of his kindness to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses saw the land but could not enter it. When our own prayers meet a closed door we are not abandoned, and the One who brings God’s people home is greater than Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying, 'O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand. For what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do such works and mighty acts as yours? Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses, still hungry to see more of God’s greatness, begged to be allowed to cross the Jordan and see the good land.

I pleaded with the LORD. One of the most affecting prayers in the Old Testament. The verb is the one used for asking for grace: the plea of a man with no claim who asks anyway.

You have only begun. Moses has seen the bush burn, the sea open, the mountain shake, bread fall from the sky for forty years, and has spoken with God as a man with his friend. And he calls it “only begun”. Long acquaintance with God has not dulled the appetite. The old man is the hungriest believer in the camp.

Let me go over and see the good land. The request is almost childlike. He does not ask to lead the conquest or have Meribah removed from the record. He asks to cross a river and look at some hills. Forty years of carrying this nation, and what he wants is to see the place he has been walking toward.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refused Moses and told him not to ask again: his refusals are real, but never his last word to his people.

Enough from you. God says no, and tells Moses to stop asking. There is no making that comfortable: the friend of God prays a humble, good request, and the door is closed. On why Moses says it was “because of you”, see on 1:37.

When prayer is refused. Scripture does not hide such cases. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). David fasted for a child who died (2 Samuel 12:16–18). And the Lord Jesus in Gethsemane asked three times for a cup to pass, and drank it (Matthew 26:39–44). No one is exempt, including him; and because he drank that cup, no refusal his people receive is a sign that God is against them.

Real refusals. Two things must be held together. God’s refusals are real refusals, and pretending otherwise wrecks faith when the answer comes back no. And God’s refusals are not the last word about the person refused.

Moses in the land. The end of this is not on the far side of the Jordan. Centuries later, three disciples on a mountain in that country saw two men talking with Jesus, and one was Moses (Luke 9:30–31). He got into the land, in glory, in company with the Christ he had served: not because the no was reversed, but because it was never the whole account. What God refused him was a walk among some hills. What God had in mind was standing next to his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes, for you shall not go over this Jordan. But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.' So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s no came with gifts: a view of the whole land from Pisgah, and the task of strengthening Joshua.

Look at it with your eyes. First, a sight. God will not let Moses enter, and will not let him die without seeing. That kindness cost nothing to withhold, and God gives it anyway.

Charge Joshua. Second, a task: to strengthen Joshua, who will do the very thing Moses has just been forbidden, in “the land that you shall see”. There is no hint that he resented it. His last months are spent making his successor braver.

Opposite Beth-peor. Third, easily missed, the location: the place of Numbers 25, where twenty-four thousand died over Baal of Peor. Deuteronomy is preached from a valley facing Israel’s worst failure, and the whole book pleads with them not to do it again. When Moses dies, God buries him there (34:6). In sight of the place where his people betrayed their God, Moses is buried by the God who never once betrayed them.
verseByVerse.note: Pisgah is the ridge of Mount Nebo, overlooking the Jordan valley.

3.theology:
The LORD fights for his people. The defeat of Og and the charge to Joshua rest on one truth: it is the LORD your God who fights for you (3:22). Faith for the future is built on God’s remembered faithfulness in the past; the giants behind us assure us of victory over the giants ahead.

The mediator who cannot bring them in. Moses pleads to enter the land and is refused (3:26). The greatest prophet of the old covenant dies outside, for the law cannot carry anyone into the rest; that is left to the One the law points to.

God’s refusals. God’s no to Moses was real, and Scripture does not soften it. But it was not cruelty, and it was not the last word: Moses would yet stand in the land beside Christ (see v. 26). A believer whose prayer has been refused may grieve honestly and still trust the One who sees what we cannot.
3.examples:
Then: Israel watched the last giant fall and the eastern land divided, while Moses climbed Pisgah to see a land he would never enter and handed the work to Joshua.

Now: we face our own giants knowing the Lord fights for us, and remembering what he has already brought us through. We pray boldly, and when the answer is no, we may grieve it, as Moses did, without letting go of God. And we rest our hope not in the law that brings us to the border but in Jesus, who carries us across into the everlasting inheritance.

keyVerse.quote: You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.
keyVerse.note: Moses’ last charge to Joshua before his own prayer is refused sums up the chapter’s argument: Og is defeated, the eastern land is given, and the same God will do the same across the Jordan. The weight of the battle rests on the LORD, not on his servant, and in Christ’s finished victory it still does.

3.reflection:
God answered Israel’s fear of Og with a reminder of what he had done to Sihon (v. 2). What has God already done, in Scripture and in your own life, that you can reason from when you are afraid?

The eastern tribes had to fight for their brothers before they could rest (vv. 18–20). Who in your church family is still in the battle, and how could you stand with them?

Moses, after a lifetime with God, said, “you have only begun to show your servant your greatness” (v. 24). How can we keep that kind of hunger for God as we grow older in faith?

God said no to Moses’ prayer but gave him a view from Pisgah and a task to do (vv. 26–28), and later brought him into the land with Christ (Luke 9:30–31). How might this help someone living with an unanswered or refused prayer?

4.title: The God Who Speaks: ‘What Great Nation Has a God So Near?’
4.text: <sup>1</sup>"And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you.<sup>2</sup>You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.<sup>3</sup>Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor.<sup>4</sup>But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.<sup>5</sup>See, I have taught you statutes and rules, as the LORD my God commanded me, that you should do them in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>6</sup>Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.'<sup>7</sup>For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him?<sup>8</sup>And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?<sup>9</sup>"Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children's children—<sup>10</sup>how on the day that you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, 'Gather the people to me, that I may let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so.'<sup>11</sup>And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.<sup>13</sup>And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone.<sup>14</sup>And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules, that you might do them in the land that you are going over to possess.<sup>15</sup>"Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire,<sup>16</sup>beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female,<sup>17</sup>the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the air,<sup>18</sup>the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water under the earth.<sup>19</sup>And beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven.<sup>20</sup>But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day.<sup>21</sup>Furthermore, the LORD was angry with me because of you, and he swore that I should not cross the Jordan, and that I should not enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.<sup>22</sup>For I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan. But you shall go over and take possession of that good land.<sup>23</sup>Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make a carved image, the form of anything that the LORD your God has forbidden you.<sup>24</sup>For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.<sup>25</sup>"When you father children and children's children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image in the form of anything, and by doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, so as to provoke him to anger,<sup>26</sup>I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will soon utterly perish from the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess. You will not live long in it, but will be utterly destroyed.<sup>27</sup>And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations where the LORD will drive you.<sup>28</sup>And there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.<sup>29</sup>But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>30</sup>When you are in tribulation, and all these things come upon you in the latter days, you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice.<sup>31</sup>For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.<sup>32</sup>"For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of.<sup>33</sup>Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?<sup>34</sup>Or has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great deeds of terror, all of which the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?<sup>35</sup>To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him.<sup>36</sup>Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire.<sup>37</sup>And because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power,<sup>38</sup>driving out before you nations greater and mightier than you, to bring you in, to give you their land for an inheritance, as it is this day,<sup>39</sup>know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.<sup>40</sup>Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments, which I command you today, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."<sup>41</sup>Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan,<sup>42</sup>that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past; he may flee to one of these cities and save his life:<sup>43</sup>Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.<sup>44</sup>This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel.<sup>45</sup>These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt,<sup>46</sup>beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt.<sup>47</sup>And they took possession of his land and the land of Og, the king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who lived to the east beyond the Jordan;<sup>48</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, as far as Mount Sirion (that is, Hermon),<sup>49</sup>together with all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under the slopes of Pisgah.
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 is the climax of Moses’ first address. Three chapters of history, from Horeb through Kadesh to the victories over Sihon and Og, now turn into an appeal: “And now, O Israel, listen” (v. 1).

The message. The LORD is the only God, and he has come near to Israel as no god ever came near to any nation: he spoke to them from the fire and rescued them from Egypt. So hold fast to him, keep his word as given, and never reduce him to an image, for he showed no form and is a consuming fire. And if you fall into idolatry and exile, seek him from there and you will find him, because he is merciful.

Why it was said. Israel is about to enter a land full of idols, and has just seen the cost of idolatry at Baal-peor (see the introduction). Moses knows that comfort in the land will tempt the coming generations to forget, and that the sin which will finally undo them is the worship of other gods.

How the chapter makes its case. Keep God’s statutes without adding or subtracting: remember Baal-peor, and the privilege of a God so near and laws so righteous (vv. 1–8). Remember Horeb and teach it to your children: you heard a voice but saw no form (vv. 9–14). So make no image and worship no star, for the LORD is a consuming fire, a jealous God (vv. 15–24). Idolatry will bring exile, yet from exile they will seek him and find him (vv. 25–31). No people has ever heard God speak and lived, or been taken by a god out of another nation; so know that the LORD is God and there is no other, and obey him (vv. 32–40). Three cities of refuge follow (vv. 41–43), and a heading introduces the law (vv. 44–49).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him and by promise. At Horeb there was a voice and no form; in Christ “the Word became flesh” and the God no one has seen was made known (John 1:14, 18). The nearness Israel boasted of is surpassed in him, for those far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). And the promise that the scattered would seek and find him (vv. 29–31) is kept in the gospel, where the Son of Man comes to seek the lost.

For us. Guard your memory of what God has done, and pass it on. Refuse every image of God, carved or imagined, that he has not given. And if you have wandered far, do not wait until you are tidy: seek him from where you are, for the merciful God has promised to be found.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Privilege of God’s Law and Nearness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Obeying God’s word, exactly as given, is Israel’s life and her witness to the world. Moses turns from history to appeal: hear and do the statutes, that you may live and enter the land, and do not add to the word or take from it (vv. 1–2). The graves of Baal-peor show the difference between following other gods and holding fast to the LORD (vv. 3–4). Keeping these laws will be Israel’s wisdom before the nations, who will call them a wise and understanding people (vv. 5–6). For no great nation has a god so near whenever they call on him, or laws so righteous as this (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law is a gift and a privilege, not a burden. Obeying it displays his wisdom and the nearness of a God unlike any other.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s obedience was meant to make the nations marvel at her God. The church’s holy life still commends the gospel to those who are watching.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you. You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having told what God has done, Moses calls Israel to hear and do his word, the way of life for a redeemed people, without adding to it or taking from it.

And now, O Israel. Three chapters of history end, and the sermon turns. Moses has shown what God did; from here he shows what Israel is to do about it, and Scripture never reverses that order. Grace first, then the response.

That you may live. Obedience is not the price of life; they are already redeemed, already carried, already on the border. It is the way that life is lived. A man does not obey in order to be brought out of Egypt. He obeys because he has been. And the Old Testament itself promises where the power will come from: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey my rules” (Ezekiel 36:27).

You shall not add to the word. A sentence that has shaped the doctrine of Scripture. We usually fear only one direction. Taking away is the obvious sin, but adding is named first, and it is the one religious people commit. The Pharisees did not delete the law; they fenced it until the fence was heavier than what it protected, and Jesus told them the result: “You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8). Every generation adds something and then requires it, and the addition ends up obscuring what it was meant to guard. The last book of the Bible closes with the same double warning (Revelation 22:18–19). God’s word is sufficient, and the reverence that will not subtract from it must also refuse to improve it.

Does this forbid the rest of the Bible? No. It forbids human additions or subtractions; God himself added his word through the prophets and apostles, and the canon (the list of books that are Scripture) closed with them. It also forbids raising church traditions to the level of God’s commands (Mark 7:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor. But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baal-peor showed that life and death depend on what you hold on to: those who followed Baal died, and those who held fast to the LORD were alive.

What the LORD did at Baal-peor. Moses is not arguing from theory; he is pointing across the valley. Beth-peor is in sight, the graves are recent, and every man listening knows somebody in them (Numbers 25:9).

You who held fast. Two verbs divide the living from the dead: some followed the Baal of Peor; others held fast to the LORD. The second is dabaq, to cling, to be glued to, what a man does to his wife when the two become one flesh (Genesis 2:24). It describes not an opinion but a grip.

What separated them. Not intelligence, courage, upbringing or knowledge of the law. They grew up in the same camp and ate the same manna. What separated them was what they were holding on to when the invitation came. Anyone who has watched someone he respected fall a long way should notice: it was seldom because he did not know enough. And the grip itself is a gift: those who held fast were held first by the God who had carried them for forty years, as Christ says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.quote: See, I have taught you statutes and rules, as the LORD my God commanded me, that you should do them in the land that you are entering to take possession of it. Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s obedience would be her wisdom before the nations, who would look at how she lived and call her wise.

In the sight of the peoples. Israel’s obedience is not private. It is evidence, and the nations are the jury.

A wise and understanding people. What would the watching world see? Not a temple, an army, art or a great city, but how these people treated their poor, slaves, foreigners, debtors, animals and enemies. In the ancient world greatness was measured by what a nation could take. Moses says the peoples will look at a code that protects the widow, cancels debts every seventh year and orders you to return your enemy’s stray ox, and conclude that these people know how to live.

The same for the church. “Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Nobody is asked to argue the world into the kingdom. They are asked to live in a way that raises the question. And the wisdom the nations glimpsed in Israel’s law is found whole in Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him? And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s only boasts were a God who is near whenever they call and a law more righteous than any other.

What great nation is there? Two questions to the nations of the earth, never answered, and two boasts, the only ones Israel had: not size or power, but nearness and righteousness.

So near to it. The gods of the ancient world were far off by definition: up a mountain, inside a temple only a priest could enter, reachable through ritual if you knew the procedure and could pay. Nobody expected a god to be near “whenever we call upon him”, with no conditions on the hour or the mood or the man. And look who says it: former brick-makers in a valley with no country, capital, king or temple. By every Moabite measure they had nothing. The claim is not that God had made them comfortable, but that he was close.

Brought near. Centuries later a church of Gentiles was told, “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13), and invited, “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). Israel could call whenever she liked, and God was near. The church is nearer still, and the distance was closed from his side, at his cost. Most religions are about man’s climb up to God; the gospel is about God’s coming down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Remember Horeb: The God You Heard but Did Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God made himself known at Horeb by his voice, and Israel must never forget it. Moses urges them to guard their souls, lest the things they saw slip from their hearts, and to teach their children and grandchildren how God gathered them to hear his words and learn to fear him (vv. 9–10). The mountain burned to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, and God spoke out of the fire: they heard words but saw no form (vv. 11–12). He declared his covenant, the Ten Commandments, writing them on two tablets, and commanded Moses to teach them the rest of his statutes (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: God makes himself known by his word rather than by any visible form, which is why hearing comes before seeing in true worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was to tell her children what she had heard at the mountain. Christian parents still pass on the faith mostly by talking: about what God has said and what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children's children— how on the day that you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, 'Gather the people to me, that I may let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must guard the memory of what God did at Horeb and pass it on to their children and grandchildren, so that each generation learns to fear him.

Keep your soul diligently. The great enemy in Deuteronomy is not persecution but forgetting, and Moses treats it as something to be actively guarded against, in the language of a watchman on a wall. Memory does not fail suddenly. It thins. The story gets shorter, the wonder becomes information, and one day a man finds he can recite what God did for him without any of it touching him. Nobody decides to forget; it is what happens to everything not deliberately kept.

Your children and your children’s children. The timescale is two handovers, to people not yet born. The exodus generation saw the sea; their children saw the wilderness; their grandchildren would see only a settled country and hear what they were told. Israel’s knowledge of God depended on whether ordinary parents kept talking.

That they may learn to fear me. The purpose is not merely to pass on facts but reverent awe, and the proof that it has taken root is that the next generation passes it on. Parents who have failed at this, as all have in part, should hear that the God of this book keeps his covenant “to a thousand generations” (7:9); the telling is ours, but the giving of faith is his.

verseByVerse.quote: And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom. Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Horeb God made himself known not by a shape but by his voice: Israel heard words and saw no form. This is the theological centre of the chapter.

The mountain burned with fire. Everything about the scene overwhelms the eye: a mountain on fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud and gloom, three words piled up. One of the most spectacular events in religious history, and the deliberate effect of the darkness is that there was nothing to look at.

There was only a voice. God revealed himself by speaking: not by a shape or a vision with edges, but by words, the way one person makes himself known to another. That fact grounds the second commandment, explains why Israel’s worship had no image at its centre when every other nation’s did, and why the Christian faith has been carried by preaching rather than spectacle. “Faith comes from hearing” (Romans 10:17), because of Horeb.

In Bethlehem the voice took a form. The New Testament does something with this no one at Sinai could have anticipated: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18); “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). At the mountain there was a voice and no form. In Bethlehem the voice took a form. The God who would not be represented by anything he had made represented himself, in a body, once, and men who had eaten fish with him wrote of what “we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands” (1 John 1:1).

Why a culture of images struggles to hear this God. We live surrounded by pictures: screens, feeds, faces, every message turned into something to look at. In Amusing Ourselves to Death the critic Neil Postman paused over this very commandment. A people who worship a God known by words and not by pictures, he argued, must learn to listen, follow a thought through and hold on to what cannot be seen; a culture formed by images finds that harder, and so finds this God harder. When faith seems thin, the trouble may not be that God has gone quiet but that we have lost the habit of listening to anything for long. Yet the voice at Horeb is no cold abstraction. A picture can be looked at without your being known in return, but a voice addresses you and waits for an answer. The God who would not be seen at the mountain wanted to be heard, and that was the most personal thing he could have done, until he took flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone. And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules, that you might do them in the land that you are going over to possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Ten Commandments were the heart of God’s covenant, spoken by God himself to the whole nation and written by his own hand; the other statutes came through Moses.

He declared to you his covenant. These are not ten pieces of advice or a moral system detached from a relationship. They are the terms of a bond between a God who had already rescued this people and a people who now belonged to him, which is why the first thing the fire said was not a command but a reminder: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (5:6).

The Ten Commandments. Two details mark them off from the rest of the law. God spoke them directly to the whole nation; and he wrote them himself, on stone (Exodus 31:18), while Moses wrote the rest in a book (31:9, 24). Whatever else they are, they are the part of God’s law that he took the trouble to say out loud to everybody and to carve in rock. Verse 14 marks the distinction from the other side: the statutes and rules came through Moses. Both are God’s word; the manner of their giving differs. This is one reason Christians have long seen the Ten Commandments as the summary of the moral law that still binds us, as the shape of love and never a way to earn salvation, while the ceremonial and civil laws are fulfilled in Christ (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: “The Ten Commandments” is literally “the ten words” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Warning Against Idolatry: A Consuming Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God showed no form, Israel must never give him one, and must worship nothing he has made. They must make no image of man or woman, beast, bird, creeping thing or fish, and must not bow to sun, moon and stars, which God gave to all peoples (vv. 15–19). The LORD brought them out of the iron furnace of Egypt to be his own inheritance (v. 20). Moses himself will die outside the land, a sobering reminder of God’s anger (vv. 21–22). So they must not forget the covenant and make an image, for the LORD is a consuming fire, a jealous God (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Because God showed no form, any image of him is a lie about him, and turning to idols is unfaithfulness to the God who has bound himself to his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Few of us are tempted by carved images, but every heart makes idols of its own: good things loved in God’s place, and false pictures of God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female, the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the air, the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water under the earth. And beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God showed no form, to make an image of him, or to worship anything he has made, is to tell a lie about him.

Since you saw no form. The argument hangs on one word: since. Because God showed no shape, to give him a shape is to say something false about him. That is what an idol is: not primarily a rival to God but a lie about him, a statement in wood or stone that he is like this, when he never said so.

The form of any figure. The catalogue runs male or female, beast, bird, creeping thing, fish, roughly reversing Genesis 1. Moses walks back down the ladder of creation, ruling out every rung, because every idol is a created thing put in the Creator’s place. Then he raises his eyes to sun, moon and stars, the cleanest things in the visible world and worshipped by nearly every ancient civilisation. They too are on the wrong side of the line; they were made on the fourth day.

The image in the head. Almost nobody reading this owns a carved image. But the commandment also reaches the picture of God a man carries in his head, assembled from his father, temperament, culture and preferences, and then treated as the real thing. That is a carved image, carved where you cannot see it. The test is the same as at Horeb: has God said he is like that, or have you decided it? The only true image of God is the one God gave: Christ, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), known through his word.

Does this forbid religious art? It forbids any image made to represent God or to be used in worship, since Israel “saw no form” (v. 15). God himself commanded art for the tabernacle, including cherubim (Exodus 25:18), so art as such is not forbidden.

Where Christians differ: pictures of Christ. Many Christians hold that since he took a real body he may be depicted, especially for teaching, and Orthodox and Roman Catholic Christians venerate icons and images. The Reformed confessions (for example the Westminster Larger Catechism, question 109) answer that no image can show the person who is God and man, and that images used in worship break this commandment. This commentary’s view: the Reformed caution is the safer course: no image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer (see on 5:8–10).

Uncertain wording. What it means that the sun, moon and stars are “allotted to all the peoples” is not certain. The most natural sense is that God gave the heavenly lights to all mankind for light and seasons (Genesis 1:14), as lamps, not gods. Others take it to mean that God, in judgment, left the other nations to the worship of the heavenly bodies, while taking Israel for himself (v. 20; compare Romans 1:24–25). Either way, Israel must not follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day. Furthermore, the LORD was angry with me because of you, and he swore that I should not cross the Jordan, and that I should not enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance. For I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan. But you shall go over and take possession of that good land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brought Israel out of the furnace of Egypt to be his own treasured inheritance, and Moses, who must die outside the land, is living proof that sin has consequences.

The iron furnace. A smelting furnace, the fierce enclosed heat in which ore is melted: a brutal image for four hundred years. Egypt was not merely captivity; it was a fire. The chapter is organised around fire: the fire of Egypt, which was slavery; the fire on the mountain, which was revelation; and, three verses on, the fire that God himself is (v. 24). He brought his people out of one into the presence of another.

A people of his own inheritance. An inheritance is the thing of lasting value that is properly a man’s own. Israel was not God’s workforce but his portion. Paul prays Christians would grasp the same: “the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:18). The inheritance is us, bought by the blood of his Son.

I must die in this land. Moses mentions his own exclusion a third time (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). It is not self-pity; each time it comes in the middle of a warning about sin, as the nearest and costliest illustration he has. His last sermon uses his own funeral as an argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make a carved image, the form of anything that the LORD your God has forbidden you. For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must not forget the covenant and make an idol, because the LORD is a consuming fire and a jealous God who will not share his people with a rival. Both words need explaining rather than softening.

A consuming fire. Not a warm hearth. It is the fire that spoke from the mountain, and it will not tolerate a rival in the camp. God’s holiness is not passive; the presence that gives light and warmth to those who belong to him burns what is set up against him. The New Testament quotes this at Christians, not pagans: “for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). Only one place is safe near that fire: where it has already fallen, on the Son who bore it for us.

A jealous God. Jealousy in Scripture is not envy, which wants what belongs to someone else. It is a husband’s rightful refusal to share his wife, the opposite of indifference. A man who watches his wife leave with somebody else and feels nothing does not love her. God had married this nation at that mountain; covenant language is marriage language, and idolatry in the prophets is adultery. So when Moses says God is jealous, he is telling them how much they are loved, and what it will cost to treat that love as though it did not matter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will punish idolatry with exile, but even in exile he will be found by those who seek him. Moses foresees that, after they have grown old in the land, Israel will make idols, and he calls heaven and earth to witness that they will perish from the land (vv. 25–26). God will scatter them among the nations, where they will serve lifeless gods of wood and stone (vv. 27–28). Yet from there they will seek the LORD and find him, if they search with all their heart; in distress, in the latter days, they will return and obey (vv. 29–30). For he is a merciful God, who will not forget the covenant he swore to their fathers (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s judgment on idolatry is certain, but his covenant mercy is greater: he disciplines his people and will not abandon them.
verseByVerse.examples: Exile and return were foretold before Israel had even entered the land. A believer who has wandered far can still come back, for God meets the seeking heart with mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you father children and children's children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image in the form of anything, and by doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, so as to provoke him to anger, I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will soon utterly perish from the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess. You will not live long in it, but will be utterly destroyed. And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations where the LORD will drive you. And there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses foresees that, once settled and comfortable, Israel will turn to idols, and God will scatter them among the nations to serve the lifeless gods they chose.

Grown old in the land. Moses looks down the centuries and describes exactly how this will go wrong. Not the first generation, nor a crisis, but when they have grown old in the land, after the vineyards are producing and nobody remembers a tent. Prosperity, not persecution, is what he expects to undo them. That is the pattern of the Bible and of most Christian lives: few people are argued out of faith, and many are made comfortable out of it.

I call heaven and earth to witness. Courtroom language. Ancient treaties named the gods of both parties as witnesses; Israel has no such gods, so Moses calls creation itself.

That neither see, nor hear. The punishment fits the crime with terrible precision. You wanted a god you could see, so you will get gods that neither see nor hear. The Psalms name what this does over time: “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). Whatever a man worships he grows to resemble, whether wood, or money, or Christ, as those who behold his glory are “being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18), which is the only reason any of us has hope of becoming anything worth being.

Was this written after the exile happened? Scholars who date Deuteronomy late read these verses as written after the event. But exile was a familiar threat long before Babylon: ancient treaties threatened it, and the empires of the region deported conquered peoples as a matter of policy. The verses name no Babylon and give no date. And for a reader who believes the God of this chapter speaks, his “declaring the end from the beginning” is no difficulty (Isaiah 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul. When you are in tribulation, and all these things come upon you in the latter days, you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice. For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even from exile, those who seek the LORD with all their heart will find him, because he is merciful and will not forget his covenant.

From there you will seek the LORD. Out of the middle of the worst thing Moses has said comes this. From there: not from the land, nor after they have got themselves back, but from exile, from the middle of the consequences, surrounded by the wooden gods they chose. God names the place in the promise, so that nobody can claim to be too far away.

With all your heart. Not a sacrifice, pilgrimage or temple; there will be no temple. Only the whole heart, which was nothing they could not give in Babylon.

You will return. Verse 30 shifts from condition to prediction. Not “you may”: the God who foresees the falling away foresees the homecoming, and says so before either has happened.

A merciful God. The ground is not in them. The word rachum is the tender compassion Scripture compares to a mother’s for the child she carried (Isaiah 49:15), not a response to anything the child has done. The security is an oath sworn to men centuries dead. Israel’s way home did not depend on Israel’s performance in exile. It rested on a promise made to Abraham and on a mercy that is simply what God is like. This is the comfort for every reader who knows he has broken the commands of this chapter: the way back is to turn and seek, and the welcome rests on God’s faithfulness, which Christ has sealed by keeping the covenant perfectly in our place.

Christ’s story of the son. Jesus told a story with the same shape. A son took everything, went to a far country, ended up feeding pigs, and “when he came to himself” went home, and his father saw him a long way off and ran (Luke 15:17–20). The road home runs along the line verse 29 had already drawn. And the seeking was never only ours: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

How do I seek him from there? “There” may be years of drift, or a mess you made yourself. You do not have to tidy it before you come; God named the far country in the promise. Start today, in words. Tell him plainly what you went after and what it cost: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5). Put the wooden god down. Name the specific thing you turned to, the habit, the relationship, the second job that swallowed Sunday, and take one concrete step away from it this week. Open the word again. A Gospel, a chapter a day, read to meet him rather than to catch up. Go back to his people. Turn up on Sunday and tell one Christian you are coming home. Seeking with all your heart is not a level of feeling to reach first; it is ceasing to keep a foot in both camps. Whoever sets out from “there” finds he was being looked for before he started.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–40 — There Is No Other: The Incomparable God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD alone is God, proved by what he has done, and so he alone must be obeyed. Moses challenges Israel to search all history and all the world for anything like it: a people who heard God speak from the fire and lived, a nation taken by a god out of another nation by signs and wonders (vv. 32–34). It was shown to them so that they would know there is no other (vv. 35–36). Because he loved their fathers he chose them and brought them out with his own presence, to give them the land (vv. 37–38). So they must know it and lay it to heart, and keep his commands, that it may go well with them (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s unrepeatable acts of revelation and rescue show that he alone is God, and so he alone is to be worshipped.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s history was her proof that the LORD alone is God. For the Christian the greatest proof is the resurrection of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of. Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live? Or has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great deeds of terror, all of which the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing in all history compares with what God did for Israel: he spoke to a people from the fire and they lived, and he went into another nation to take them for himself.

Ask now of the days that are past. A challenge with no limits: search all of time, back to the creation of man, and all of space, and find a parallel.

To take a nation for himself. The second question is the more staggering. Gods belonged to nations; a god of Egypt was for Egyptians, and his fortunes rose and fell with theirs. A god crossing a border into the strongest empire on earth to extract a slave population, the lowest thing in that society, and make them his own, is not a variation on ancient religion. There is no category for it. And has any god even attempted it? The gods of the nations did not go and get anybody. They stayed where they were and waited to be fed.

The God who came to get them. That is the God of the Bible from beginning to end, and supremely when the Son of God became man. He came down into a foreign country and took people out of it at his own cost: the Father “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him. Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire. And because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power, driving out before you nations greater and mightier than you, to bring you in, to give you their land for an inheritance, as it is this day,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All God’s mighty acts were meant to teach Israel that the LORD alone is God, and he did them for one reason: he loved their fathers.

That you might know. The plagues, the sea, the fire, the voice, the forty years had one aim: that they should know. God taught a nation of slaves, by means of an entire national history, one fact, and that it took so much teaching shows how hard the lesson is to learn.

That he might discipline you. Verse 36 puts a voice from heaven and the fire on earth side by side. The verb yasar is to train, what a father does to a son he means to make into something. Sinai was a classroom with the roof off.

Because he loved your fathers. Why them? Not because they were numerous or good; three chapters have just established the opposite. Deuteronomy will say it more bluntly: “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you… but it is because the LORD loves you” (7:7–8). The love is its own explanation, with nothing underneath it. So it is with every believer, chosen in Christ “before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4).

With his own presence. Literally, with his face. He did not send. He came.

verseByVerse.quote: know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other. Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments, which I command you today, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing that the LORD alone rules heaven and earth must move from the head to the heart, and from there into glad obedience.

Lay it to your heart. Two commands, and the second is harder. Know: settle it as fact. Then lay it to your heart: bring it from the head to where decisions are made. Moses did not think the first would produce the second automatically, and he was right. A man can hold without hesitation that God rules heaven and earth, and still lie awake at three in the morning managing the universe on God’s behalf, or decide out of fear of someone who will be dead in forty years. Laying it to heart is the work of a lifetime, and it is the Spirit’s work in us more than ours, done through the word and prayer.

In heaven above and on the earth beneath. There is nowhere he does not rule, which is precisely what no other god of that world ever claimed, and precisely why an Israelite in exile, under Babylon’s gods in Babylon’s land, could still pray.

Therefore you shall keep his statutes. That therefore is the logic of Deuteronomy. Obedience is not the foundation; it is the roof. First know who he is, then lay it to heart, then keep his commandments, because a command obeyed without the first two is mere compliance, and it never lasts a generation. And when the roof leaks, as in every life it does, the foundation does not move: we are accepted not for our keeping but for Christ’s, whose obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

How do I lay it to heart? Not by learning more, but by bringing what you already know to the place where you actually decide and worry. Take one truth slowly. Read verse 39 in the morning and say it back to God as a prayer: you are God over this meeting, this diagnosis, this child. Use it at three in the morning. When the mind starts managing tomorrow, name the thing you are carrying, say who rules it, hand it over, and lie still. Ask what it changes. If he rules heaven and earth, what would I do differently today: the honest answer to the client, the apology I have been avoiding? Then do it. Ask him to do it. Paul prays for this very thing: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know” (Ephesians 1:18). Christ laid the Father’s rule to heart where it cost most: “nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). Because he did, the God who rules heaven and earth is your Father, and his rule is the safest thing in the world to rest on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — The Cities of Refuge East of the Jordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Belief in the one true God comes down to practical mercy. Having finished his first address, Moses sets apart three cities east of the Jordan where a person who has killed someone by accident, without previous hatred, can flee and save his life (vv. 41–42). They are named and placed, one for each of the eastern tribes: Bezer on the tableland for Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead for Gad, and Golan in Bashan for Manasseh (v. 43). The God who is a consuming fire also provides a refuge for the guilty, and these cities anticipate the fuller law of chapter 19.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides refuge for one who has killed without malice, a picture of Christ as the refuge to whom sinners flee.
verseByVerse.examples: The manslayer fled to a city of refuge; sinners flee to Christ, who shelters them from the judgment they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan, that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past; he may flee to one of these cities and save his life: Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses set apart three cities east of the Jordan where someone who had killed by accident could flee and live: the God who is a consuming fire provides refuge for the guilty.
