Three cities in the east. The strangest paragraph in the chapter. Moses has just finished some of the highest theology in the Pentateuch, and the next thing he does is administration: three towns, named, mapped, allocated.

A stranger’s worst day. These cities are for a man who has not yet killed anybody, who may not yet be born, whose axe head will fly off a handle some afternoon decades from now (19:5). Moses is arranging a stranger’s worst day in a future he has no part in. That is what the theology of verses 32–40 is for. A man who truly believes there is no other God will find himself doing small concrete kindnesses for people he will never meet. Doctrine that does not come down into three named towns on a map has not yet been laid to the heart.

Shelter for the guilty. It is truly mercy: not a reward for the innocent but shelter for a man who has really taken a life. The avenger of blood was the dead man’s nearest kinsman, who had the duty of executing justice on a murderer (see 19:4–6). The chapter that establishes God as a consuming fire ends by building somewhere for the guilty to run. Hebrews uses the same picture for the gospel: “we who have fled for refuge” to the hope set before us, anchored in Jesus (Hebrews 6:18–20).
verseByVerse.note: Bezer served Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead served Gad, and Golan in Bashan served the half-tribe of Manasseh (v. 43).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–49 — The Setting of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law is given to a people standing on God’s past gifts and facing their future inheritance. A heading introduces the second address, the body of law that begins in chapter 5: the testimonies, statutes and rules Moses gave after Israel came out of Egypt (vv. 44–45). The setting is given with care: beyond the Jordan, in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon, whom Israel had defeated (v. 46). The land of Sihon and Og, from the Arnon to Mount Hermon and down the Jordan valley to the Dead Sea, is already theirs (vv. 47–49), a pledge that God will keep the rest of his promise.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law is given in real history to a redeemed people, at a real time and place.
verseByVerse.examples: The law was set before Israel on land taken from defeated kings. God’s word still comes to us as history, not as abstract philosophy.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel. These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt, beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt. And they took possession of his land and the land of Og, the king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who lived to the east beyond the Jordan; from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, as far as Mount Sirion (that is, Hermon), together with all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under the slopes of Pisgah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A heading introduces the law, given to a people camped between their worst failure and their promised inheritance, on land that proved God keeps his word.

This is the law. A heading and a hinge: the first address is over, and from chapter 5 the law itself begins.

The testimonies, the statutes, and the rules. The three words are not synonyms piled up. Testimonies are what God has borne witness to; statutes are fixed; rules are a judge’s decisions applied to cases. Together: what God has declared, what he has fixed, and how it works out in ordinary disputes.

In the valley opposite Beth-peor. Every detail of the location preaches. Beyond the Jordan: still on the wrong bank. Opposite Beth-peor: facing the nation’s latest and most shameful collapse. In the land of Sihon: standing on ground God had already given.

Where the church stands. That describes where the church stands whenever Scripture is opened: our failures behind us and in plain view, the promise ahead and not yet possessed, and enough already given, above all an empty tomb, to make it unreasonable to doubt the rest.

4.theology:
The God who reveals himself by his word. At Horeb Israel heard but did not see (4:12). This is why images are forbidden and why hearing God’s word comes first in worship, and the speaking God is fully revealed in the Word made flesh (John 1; Heb 1:1–2).

A consuming fire, a jealous God. God’s holiness burns against every rival, and his jealousy is a husband’s love (4:24; Heb 12:29). Yet this same fire fell on Christ at Calvary, so that the redeemed are embraced rather than consumed.

There is no other. The whole sermon aims at one confession (4:35, 39). God’s acts in history prove that he alone is God, supremely now in the resurrection of Christ, and they call for undivided devotion.
4.examples:
Then: Israel was the most privileged nation on earth, and Moses pleaded with her to remember, to shun idols, and to know that the LORD alone is God.

Now: We who have a God nearer than our breath, who hears us “whenever we call upon him”, must still guard our hearts, which are always making idols, and teach God’s mighty acts to our children, and we do it in the power of his Spirit, not our own. The consuming fire is our Father; the jealous God is our faithful husband; and the merciful God meets every seeking heart, however far it has wandered, with the welcome of grace.

keyVerse.quote: know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter, the voice from the fire, the rescue from Egypt, the warning against idols and the promise of mercy in exile, serves this one confession. Moses wants it not only known but laid to heart, where it governs fear and choice, and the obedience of verse 40 flows from it. In Christ the one God has made himself known, and laying this to heart means trusting him as Father.

4.reflection:
Moses says that what separated the living from the dead at Baal-peor was holding fast to the LORD (vv. 3–4). What are you holding on to most tightly, and what helps you cling to Christ when other things invite you away?

Israel heard a voice but saw no form (v. 12). What pictures of God do people carve in their minds today, and how does God’s word, and above all Christ, correct them?

Moses expected comfort, not persecution, to make Israel forget (vv. 9, 25). Where might comfort be thinning your memory of what God has done, and how can you pass that memory on to the next generation?

God promised that even from exile, “you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him” (v. 29). How would you explain this promise to someone who feels too far gone to come back?

5.title: The Ten Commandments Repeated: Grace Before Law
5.text: <sup>1</sup>And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today, and you shall learn them and be careful to do them.<sup>2</sup>The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb.<sup>3</sup>Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.<sup>4</sup>The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire,<sup>5</sup>while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain. He said:<sup>6</sup>"'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>7</sup>"'You shall have no other gods before me.<sup>8</sup>"'You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.<sup>9</sup>You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,<sup>10</sup>but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.<sup>11</sup>"'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.<sup>12</sup>"'Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you.<sup>13</sup>Six days you shall labor and do all your work,<sup>14</sup>but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you.<sup>15</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.<sup>16</sup>"'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>17</sup>"'You shall not murder.<sup>18</sup>"'And you shall not commit adultery.<sup>19</sup>"'And you shall not steal.<sup>20</sup>"'And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.<sup>21</sup>"'And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.'<sup>22</sup>"These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me.<sup>23</sup>And as soon as you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, you came near to me, all the heads of your tribes, and your elders.<sup>24</sup>And you said, 'Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die.<sup>26</sup>For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived?<sup>27</sup>Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.'<sup>28</sup>"And the LORD heard your words, when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, 'I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken.<sup>29</sup>Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!<sup>30</sup>Go and say to them, "Return to your tents."<sup>31</sup>But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules that you shall teach them, that they may do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.'<sup>32</sup>You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.<sup>33</sup>You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land that you shall possess.
5.overview:
Where we are. Moses has finished his first address (chapters 1–4), a long look back that ended with the call to hold fast to the one God who spoke from the fire. Now his second and longest address begins, and it begins where Israel’s covenant began: with the Ten Commandments spoken at Horeb.

The message. The God who rescued Israel from slavery speaks to every generation as though it stood at the mountain itself, and what he asks of a freed people is summed up in ten words: love him alone, and love your neighbour. Grace comes first, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out” (v. 6), and the commands describe the life of the rescued, never the price of rescue. Yet sinners cannot stand before this holy voice without a mediator, and even with one they need a new heart, which God longs for them to have (v. 29).

Why it was said. A new generation, children at Horeb or not yet born, was about to enter a land full of other gods (see the introduction). They might think Horeb was their parents’ story; Moses insists it is theirs, today.

How the chapter makes its case. The covenant binds the living (vv. 1–5). The ten words are then restated, opening with God’s act of rescue (v. 6). The first table concerns God: no other gods, no images, the honour of his name and the keeping of his rest, which Deuteronomy grounds in Israel’s release from slavery (vv. 7–15). The second concerns the neighbour: parents, life, marriage, property, truth, and finally the heart’s desire (vv. 16–21). Last, Moses recalls the people’s terror at the voice, their plea for him to stand between, God’s approval and his longing for a heart that would always fear him, and the charge to walk in his way (vv. 22–33).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by pattern. The tenth commandment reaches the heart, and no one but Christ has kept these words inside and out; he kept them in our place, so that “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Moses standing between the fire and the people is a pattern of the “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), who does not merely carry God’s word but is the Word. And God’s “Oh that they had such a heart” (v. 29) is answered in the new covenant, where he writes his law on the heart by his Spirit.

For us. Read the commandments from verse 6, not verse 7: they are the shape of a freed life, not a ladder to God. Let them show you your heart, run to the Mediator who kept them for you, and ask for the new heart God longs to give.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Covenant Is Ours Today
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant God made at Horeb is not a family heirloom but a present bond with everyone alive to hear it. Moses gathers the whole nation and tells them to hear, learn and do (v. 1). Then he says something startling: the LORD made this covenant not with their fathers but with them, all who are alive today (vv. 2–3), though most of them were children or unborn at the mountain. God spoke there face to face, out of the fire, yet the people were afraid, and Moses stood between them and God to carry his word across (vv. 4–5). Those two facts, a God who comes near and a people who need a mediator, frame the whole chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant is present and personal. Each generation has to own it as made with them, rather than leave it in the history books.
verseByVerse.examples: The children of the wilderness generation were told that Horeb was their covenant too. Faith cannot be inherited second-hand: every believer has to receive the gospel for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today, and you shall learn them and be careful to do them. The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant made at Horeb is not the story of a past generation but a bond with everyone alive to hear it today.

Hear, O Israel. The phrase reaches its summit in the next chapter (6:4) and sets the posture of the whole book: before Israel does anything, she listens. Then come three verbs: hear, learn, do.

Not with our fathers. Strictly, the covenant was made with their fathers, now dead in the wilderness, and Moses has just spent three chapters on those graves. He is making a preaching point, one of the most important in Scripture: the covenant is not a title deed handed down from somebody else. It binds the living, and every generation stands at Sinai for itself.

Third-generation faith. It is possible to be the third generation in a Christian family, to know the language, hold the doctrines, keep the habits, and never once to have dealt with God personally. That is to treat the covenant as made with our fathers and not with us. Moses will not permit it, and today, one of the great words of this book, sounds through it dozens of times, as it does in the gospel: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain. He said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spoke to the whole people directly, yet they were too afraid to come near, so Moses stood between them and God to carry his word.

Face to face. Two things are said in one breath, and they pull against each other. God spoke face to face, directly and in person, to the whole people; and Moses stood between. That tension is the whole situation of fallen people before God. God came near enough to be heard by everybody, without priest or temple, and they could not bear it, so a man stood in the gap and carried the words across.

The one mediator. The Old Testament is arranged around such men: Moses at the mountain, Aaron with a censer in a plague (Numbers 16:46–48), the high priest behind the curtain once a year. Each was temporary, and each died. The New Testament names the office and adds one word: “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). One, not a succession. The man between the fire and the people at Horeb did for a day what Christ does permanently, and unlike Moses he does not merely carry the words: he is himself the Word of God (John 1:1).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a single command, God says who he is and what he has done. The Ten Commandments open not with a demand but with a rescue: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” Everything that follows rests on this sentence. The commands are addressed to people already freed, and they describe how freed people live; they are not the terms on which God will free them. Grace comes before law, and this verse is the key to reading all ten.
verseByVerse.theology: God saves first and commands second, and this order runs through the whole Bible.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians obey, as Israel was meant to, out of thankfulness for a rescue already finished, never to earn it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single command, God says who he is and what he has done: he rescued them first, so the commandments describe the life of a freed people, never the price of their freedom.

Before any command. This is the most important structural fact about the Ten Commandments, and it is missed almost every time they are quoted. Read from verse 7, they sound like entrance conditions for getting in with God; read from verse 6, they are the way a rescued people now live. God does not say, “Keep these and I will bring you out of Egypt.” They are already out. Every one of the ten is addressed to ex-slaves by the God who unlocked the door: not new chains, but a description of what free people look like, written by the one who paid to make them free.

Grace before law. This is the shape of the whole Bible: what God has done before what we must do, as Romans spends eleven chapters on God’s mercy before chapter 12 calls for obedience. The difference between earning God’s favour and the gospel is not in the commandments, which are the same, but in what they are for. “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14).

The LORD your God. The capital letters in LORD mark God’s own name, Yahweh, which Jews out of reverence stopped saying aloud and English Bibles print as LORD (see Lord). God explained it to Moses at the bush: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). He simply is, and leans on nothing. Yet the name never stands alone here. It comes with “your God”, and with a date in history, “who brought you out”. The God who needs nothing has bound himself to a nation of former slaves. That matters, because everything else we lean on needs us to keep it going. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a career or someone’s approval will punish you when you let it down, while Jesus is the one Lord who, when you fail him, forgives you. And Jesus is this LORD come near. He said, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and they picked up stones, because they knew which name he had claimed. So when you pray this week, begin where the commandments begin: not with what you must do, but with who he is, and whose he has made you.
verseByVerse.note: Why lists of the Ten differ: Jewish tradition counts this verse as the first of the ten words; Roman Catholics and Lutherans join the images commandment to the first and divide the coveting commandment in two. This commentary follows the numbering used by most Protestant churches.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — The First Table: Loving God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first four commandments concern Israel’s life with God himself. He alone is to be their God, with no rival in his presence (v. 7). He is to be worshipped as he has revealed himself, never through an image, for he is a jealous God whose mercy runs far beyond his judgment (vv. 8–10). His name, which reveals who he is, must never be used emptily (v. 11). And one day in seven is to be his, a rest shared even with servants and animals, which Deuteronomy grounds in Israel’s rescue from slavery (vv. 12–15). Together they say: love the LORD as the only God, in the way he has given.
verseByVerse.theology: God is to have no rival, no image, no careless use of his name, and his people are to stop and rest because he has set them free.
verseByVerse.examples: These commandments reach past carved idols to the idols of the heart, and past swearing to every way of using God’s name for our own ends.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall have no other gods before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD alone is to be Israel’s God: no rival may stand in his presence, and his presence is everywhere.

You shall have. The sentence does not say “there are no other gods”, although Deuteronomy says that plainly enough (4:35, 39). The issue is possession: what you actually rely on and live for. A person’s real god is not the one he would name if asked but the one he consults when frightened, obeys when the two conflict, and cannot imagine living without. Grieving a real loss is not idolatry; making something the ground of life in God’s place is.

Before me. Literally, before my face. It is not about ranking, as though lesser gods were permitted underneath; it means in his presence, and his presence is everywhere. No one may keep other gods in the back of the house.

Why he forbids rivals. The command comes from the God who has just rescued his people (v. 6): he forbids rivals because he offers himself as the one they can lean their whole weight on. Jesus kept this first word perfectly: offered all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, he answered from this book: “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10, from 6:13).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew phrase translated “before me” can mean in my presence, besides me (the ESV margin) or even in opposition to me. Each leaves the command the same in substance: no other god at all alongside the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God must be worshipped as he has revealed himself, never through an image; he is jealous for his people’s love, and his mercy outruns his judgment beyond counting.

How, not whom. The first commandment governs whom Israel worships; the second governs how. A man may aim at the true God and still worship falsely, if he has made an image and put it in the way. Israel “saw no form” at Horeb (4:15), and any image of God makes him smaller than he is and puts him in our hands. And he is “a jealous God”, not with the jealousy of insecurity but with a husband’s right jealousy for his wife’s faithfulness.

Of those who hate me. The threat attached troubles many readers; three things make it clearer. First, the limiting words: the children in view have taken up their fathers’ hatred and continued in it, for Scripture insists, “The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20). Second, what is described is observable: sin runs in families, the drinking, the temper, the coldness, each generation learning it from the last. Third, the arithmetic: three or four generations set against thousands. His mercy outweighs his judgment beyond counting, and the line can be broken: anyone who turns to the Lord steps out of “those who hate me” into the thousands who are loved. So he described himself to Moses: “keeping steadfast love for thousands” (Exodus 34:7).

The image God gave. God forbade every image of himself because he meant to give one. Christ “is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and he said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). We do not need to carve a likeness of God; we need to look at his Son.

Where Christians differ: may Christ be pictured? The commandment does not forbid art as such, for God commanded carved cherubim for the tabernacle (Exodus 25:18); it forbids any image made to represent God or to serve in worship. Many hold that because he took a real body he may be depicted, especially in teaching, and Orthodox and Roman Catholic Christians venerate icons and images. The Reformed confessions reply that no picture can show the one person who is both God and man, and that images used in worship break this commandment. This commentary’s view: the Reformed caution is the safer course: no image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer.

Uncertain wording. “To thousands” may mean thousands of people or, matching “the third and fourth generation”, thousands of generations (compare 7:9, “to a thousand generations”).

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s name reveals who he is, so to use it emptily, in oaths, prayers or claims he has not made, is to treat God himself as worth nothing.

In vain. The verb is lift up or carry, and “in vain” means emptily, for nothing. Profanity is the least of it. The commandment covers the false oath, which makes God the guarantor of a lie; the prayer that uses his name as a formula; and most searchingly, claiming God’s authority for what he has not said, attaching his name to our preferences, our politics, our certainty about somebody else’s motives. That is done most often by people who would never swear.

The LORD will not hold him guiltless. Only this commandment carries the clause, because his name is the revelation of who he is. To handle it carelessly is to handle him carelessly.

Wearing the name. Israel had the name of God put upon her (Numbers 6:27); Christians are baptised into “the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). To wear that name and live emptily is to take it in vain without a word. So Jesus taught us to begin our prayers, “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "'Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day in seven belongs to the LORD as a day of rest for the whole household, servants and animals included, because rest is what freedom looks like for a people brought out of slavery.

Observe the Sabbath day. Exodus says “Remember”; Deuteronomy says “Observe”, and it gives a different reason. It is a deliberate second lesson, not a discrepancy. Exodus grounds the Sabbath in creation (Exodus 20:11); Deuteronomy grounds it in redemption. Creation says rest is woven into the structure of the world, and someone who never stops is working against the way he was made.

You shall remember that you were a slave. Redemption says rest is what freedom looks like. Slaves in Egypt got no seventh day; every time Israel stopped, she said with her body, “I am not a slave any more.”

That your male servant and your female servant may rest. Deuteronomy names the servants’ rest as a purpose of the day. A man who had been a slave is forbidden to turn his own household into what he came out of, and even the ox gets its day off, a real cost in a farming economy. A Christian who employs others has every reason to see that they get their rest too.

The rest itself is a Person. Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27), and he is what it was pointing at: “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:9–10). Entering that rest means giving up the exhausting business of justifying yourself.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath bind Christians today? The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession of Faith (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, because the pattern of one day in seven goes back to creation; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), because the New Testament repeats and deepens the other nine commandments but names the Sabbath among the shadows, and it leaves the believer free (Romans 14:5): no one may bind another’s conscience about a day. The Lord’s Day is a gift. Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a law with rules about work.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus 20:8 begins “Remember the Sabbath day”; Deuteronomy begins “Observe the Sabbath day” and keeps the word remember for the slavery in Egypt (5:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — The Second Table: Loving Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last six commandments turn to the neighbour, and they protect everything a neighbour cannot live without. Honour for parents comes first, the hinge between the two tables, with a promise attached (v. 16). Then four short lines guard a neighbour’s life, marriage, property and good name (vv. 17–20). The tenth goes where no court can follow, into the heart’s desire for what belongs to someone else (v. 21). Love for God shows itself in how we treat the people he has made, and the last command shows that he looks for that love on the inside, not only in what we do.
verseByVerse.theology: Love for God overflows into love for neighbour. The second table protects a neighbour’s life, marriage, property and good name, and then reaches into the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord Jesus did not loosen these commands; he took them inward, so that they govern anger, desire and envy as well as deeds.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parents are to be treated with weight and respect all their lives, and God attaches a promise to this command: that it may go well with his people in the land.

Honor your father and your mother. This commandment stands at the hinge of the two tables. Parents are the first authority anyone meets, and a child learns submission or defiance long before he thinks about God.

What honour means. The Hebrew word elsewhere means heavy: to treat as weighty. It is not agreement, nor affection, which cannot be commanded, but a settled way of treating a person that outlasts childhood and survives a parent’s failures. Not everybody had honourable parents, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise; the command is not “obey” but “honor”, and it is possible to honour a parent who failed badly.

What this looks like. For a child at home, honour usually means doing what you are asked without the sigh and the slammed door. For grown children it changes shape but does not end. Keep in touch: ring, visit, and ask about their lives, not only report on yours. Ask their counsel, even when you decide otherwise. Speak of them well; do not make them a running joke in front of your spouse or your own children, who are learning from you how parents are treated. Carry them when they grow old. Paul calls it making “some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God” (1 Timothy 5:4): the hospital appointments, the hard conversation about care, money where it is needed. Forgive the ordinary failures. They were sinners raising a sinner.

The Son who honoured his mother. The Son of God honoured his mother from the cross, giving her into John’s keeping: “Behold, your mother!” (John 19:27). He kept this commandment perfectly in our place, and we honour our parents as children who already have a Father who will never fail us.

That it may go well with you. Deuteronomy adds these words to the commandment as Exodus gives it (Exodus 20:12), and Paul quotes them: “‘Honor your father and mother’ (this is the first commandment with a promise), ‘that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land’” (Ephesians 6:2–3).

What it does not mean. Honouring a parent who was abusive never means staying within reach of harm. It can mean speaking of them truthfully and without revenge, praying for them, and caring for them from a safe distance. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and anyone in danger should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not murder. "'And you shall not commit adultery. "'And you shall not steal. "'And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four short commands guard what a neighbour cannot live without: his life, his marriage, his property and his good name.

You shall not murder. The command does not cover warfare or judicial execution, which the same law regulates. Its ground is that “God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6): human beings are not merely useful; they bear God’s likeness.

Adultery, stealing, false witness. Marriage is placed immediately after life, which is its own statement of how seriously God treats it. The ban on stealing assumes that property is real and that a person may rightly own things. And false witness belongs first to the courtroom: where testimony cannot be trusted, the weak are the first to suffer.

Driven inward. All four can be kept outwardly by a thoroughly bad man, which is why the Lord Jesus drove them inward: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:21–22). He was not adding to Moses. He refused to let the commandments be reduced to a list of things a man has not done, and he did the same with adultery, tracing it back to the lustful look (Matthew 5:27–28). Then, while men broke all four against him by false witness and a cross, he kept them perfectly and prayed for those who did it.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for “murder” also covers causing death by negligence (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tenth commandment reaches the heart’s desire, where no court can follow, and so shows that no one but Christ has truly kept any of the ten.

You shall not covet. The tenth is unlike the other nine, and that is why it is last. Every other commandment can be broken visibly. A man could keep the first nine outwardly for sixty years with a heart like a sewer, and no court could touch him. The tenth takes hold of what nobody can see, and once the heart is counted, nobody has kept the other nine either.

Your neighbor’s wife. Deuteronomy puts the wife first, where Exodus 20:17 begins with the house, and uses a different verb for her (“covet”) than for the property (“desire”): she is set apart from a man’s goods.

A mirror. This commandment broke Paul’s confidence in himself. He had kept the visible law and counted himself blameless (Philippians 3:6), and then: “I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7). The law was never a ladder to climb up to God. It is a mirror that shows you what you are, not only what you have done: “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20).

What Christ did. The mirror is not the end. What no one has done, Christ did: he kept all ten, inside and out, in our place, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). So the believer whom the tenth commandment still exposes is not cast off; he confesses and is forgiven (1 John 1:9), and the Spirit who now lives in him writes this law on his heart (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:27).

An economy that needs you to covet. The tenth commandment may be the one our culture finds strangest, because so much of modern life runs on breaking it. Early in the twentieth century Edward Bernays, a nephew of Sigmund Freud and one of the founders of public relations, showed that goods could be sold by attaching them to deeper longings: status, freedom, being admired. A contented customer buys very little, so we are surrounded all day by skilled efforts to make us want our neighbour’s house, car, body and holiday, and covetousness is no longer felt as a sin. It is called aspiration.

The cure. God’s word calls the restless wanting a sickness of the heart, and getting more cannot cure it, because the wanting simply moves on to the next thing. It is cured by having something better. Someone who knows that in Christ he is a child of the Father, with an inheritance nobody can take, can look over the fence and be glad for his neighbour. Contentment is not wanting less. It is finding that you already have the One you were wanting all along.

What it does not mean. Not every desire is coveting: to want a home, a spouse or good work is no sin. Coveting wants what belongs to someone else, or wants anything so much that God is no longer enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–33 — The People’s Fear and God’s Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The voice from the fire was too much for sinful people, and God agreed. Moses recalls that the LORD spoke the ten words himself and wrote them on stone (v. 22). The people, astonished to be alive, begged Moses to go near and listen for them, promising to obey (vv. 23–27). God said they were right, and then voiced a longing: “Oh that they had such a heart as this always” (vv. 28–29). The people went home and the mediator stayed with God to receive the rest of the law (vv. 30–31), and Moses charges Israel to walk in it without turning aside (vv. 32–33). The chapter ends where the gospel begins: a holy God, a needed mediator, and a heart only God can give.
verseByVerse.theology: Sinners cannot bear the presence of a holy God with no one to stand between. The law shows the need both for a mediator and for a new heart, and only grace can supply either.
verseByVerse.examples: We draw near through Christ, the greater Mediator, who does what Moses could not: he removes our sin and gives the new heart the law could only ask for.

verseByVerse.quote: "These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me. And as soon as you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, you came near to me, all the heads of your tribes, and your elders. And you said, 'Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spoke the ten words himself, aloud, to the whole nation and wrote them with his own hand, and the people were astonished to have heard his voice and lived.

He added no more. Everything else in the law came through Moses. These ten God spoke himself to the whole nation, and then wrote on stone. The rest of Scripture is no less inspired, but this manner of delivery is why the Ten Commandments have always held a place of their own.

And man still live. Their astonishment is not that God spoke but that they were still standing afterwards, a fear we have almost entirely lost. Our difficulty with God is that we cannot hear him; theirs was that they had, and were somehow not dead.

A different mountain. Hebrews sets this scene beside the Christian’s: “you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest”, but “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:18, 24). The same holy God speaks, now through his Son; the reverence remains, but the terror of standing before him with no one between is gone.

Uncertain wording. “He added no more” most likely means that God spoke only these ten words to the whole people; the rest came through Moses. An old Jewish reading took the Hebrew as “and he did not cease”, his voice still speaking. The first fits the context best.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die. For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived? Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrified that God’s voice would kill them, the people asked Moses to go near and listen for them, and promised to do all that God said.

Why should we die? The terror catches up with them. It is neither superstition nor cowardice but an accurate reading of their situation: sinful people cannot stand before a holy God with no one between, and they were right.

Go near and hear. So they ask for a go-between. Not less of God, nor a lower standard, but a man who can survive the fire to bring them what is said in it. It is one of the most spiritually intelligent things this nation ever says, the request every human being has once he understands the problem. Israel asked God for the solution instead of inventing one, and the next verses record what he thought of that.

We will hear and do it. They meant it, but within weeks they were bowing to a golden calf (9:8–21). They needed not only a mediator to carry the words but a heart to keep them (v. 29). Christ is the Mediator who also kept the words in their place, “for I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "And the LORD heard your words, when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, 'I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken. Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God approves the people’s fear and their request, and then voices his longing that they would always have such a heart, to fear him and keep his commands.

They are right in all that they have spoken. God endorses their fear. Not “they should be braver”, not “they have misunderstood me”: their judgment of what it would cost to hear his voice directly was correct, and he says so.

Oh that they had such a heart. The Hebrew is an exclamation of wish, literally who will give that they had such a heart: longing. The God who needs nothing says: if only. This is not a defect in his knowledge, as though he did not see what was coming; this book has already foretold the exile (4:25–28). It shows his heart: he genuinely delights in the obedience of his people and grieves at its absence, and he wants us to know it. Ezekiel says the same in the same tone: “For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone” (Ezekiel 18:32).

Such a heart. He wishes not for better behaviour but for a different heart. The problem is not in the commandments or the mediator but in the people. Twenty-five chapters on comes the answer to God’s own wish: “And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live” (30:6). That is the gospel in the space of one book: God asks for what we cannot produce, and then produces it in us himself. That is the new covenant Christ sealed with his blood (Luke 22:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Go and say to them, "Return to your tents." But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules that you shall teach them, that they may do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.' You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land that you shall possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people go home while Moses stays with God to receive the rest of the law, and Israel is charged to walk in it without turning aside, that they may live.

But you, stand here by me. Two destinations in one sentence: the people go home; the mediator stays with God. A crowd walks down to the cooking fires and the children, and one man is left on a burning mountain in the dark, being given the rest of the law. Somebody has to remain in the fire so that everybody else can go home; that is what a mediator is for.

The Mediator who brings us in. Christ stood in the fire of God’s judgment in our place and then did what Moses could not: he brings his people with him into the Father’s presence, for “through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). And he still says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Neither right nor left. There are two ways off a road: someone can leave God’s way by being too lax or too strict, by loosening what God tied or tying what God left free, and Deuteronomy worries about both, which is why it forbade addition as well as subtraction (4:2). The road runs straight, and the God who brought his people out walks it with them.

5.theology:
Grace before law. The commandments open with what God has done (5:6), so obedience is the grateful answer of a freed people, never the price of freedom. That order governs all of Scripture and reaches its fullness in the cross.

Rest for the redeemed. Deuteronomy ties the Sabbath to the rescue from slavery (5:15), and the rest it promised is found in Christ (Heb 4), entered by faith.

A new heart. God’s own wish in 5:29 exposes the central problem: the law commands a heart it cannot create. What he longs for here he supplies in the new covenant, writing his law on hearts of flesh by the Spirit (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26).
5.examples:
For Israel, this chapter was a new generation taking the Horeb covenant as its own: trembling at God’s voice and asking for a man to stand between them and him.

For us it means owning the covenant of grace personally, obeying out of gratitude for a redemption already accomplished, and drawing near through Jesus, who not only brings us God’s word but takes away our sin.

keyVerse.quote: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
keyVerse.note: Every one of the ten commandments rests on this sentence. God names himself and his act of rescue before he gives a single command, so the law is the way of life of a freed people, not the price of their freedom. In Christ the greater exodus has been accomplished, and we obey as the rescued, never in order to be rescued.

5.reflection:
Moses tells a generation that was not at Horeb that the covenant was made “with us, who are all of us here alive today” (v. 3). What is the difference between inheriting a family’s faith and dealing with God for yourself, and how would you know which is true of you?

The commandments begin with what God has done (v. 6) before what we must do. How does reading them from verse 6 rather than verse 7 change the way you hear them, and the way you would explain them to a child or a sceptical friend?

Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath in Israel’s release from slavery and in rest for servants (vv. 14–15). What would it look like for your week to say, “I am not a slave any more”, and for those who depend on you to share that rest?

The tenth commandment exposes the heart (v. 21), and God longs for his people to have “such a heart” (v. 29). Where do you see covetousness at work in your own heart, and how do Christ’s obedience in your place and the promise of a new heart give you hope?

6.title: The Shema and the Great Commandment: Love the LORD with All Your Heart
6.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now this is the commandment—the statutes and the rules —that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, that you may do them in the land to which you are going over, to possess it,<sup>2</sup>that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son's son, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be long.<sup>3</sup>Hear therefore, O Israel, and be careful to do them, that it may go well with you, and that you may multiply greatly, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you, in a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>4</sup>"Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.<sup>5</sup>You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.<sup>6</sup>And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart.<sup>7</sup>You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.<sup>8</sup>You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.<sup>9</sup>You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.<sup>10</sup>"And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you—with great and good cities that you did not build,<sup>11</sup>and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant—and when you eat and are full,<sup>12</sup>then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>13</sup>It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear.<sup>14</sup>You shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who are around you—<sup>15</sup>for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God— lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.<sup>16</sup>"You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.<sup>17</sup>You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes, which he has commanded you.<sup>18</sup>And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers<sup>19</sup>by thrusting out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has promised.<sup>20</sup>"When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?'<sup>21</sup>then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt and against Pharaoh and all his household, before our eyes.<sup>23</sup>And he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in and give us the land that he swore to give to our fathers.<sup>24</sup>And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are this day.<sup>25</sup>And it will be righteousness for us, if we are careful to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.'
6.overview:
Where we are. Moses has restated the Ten Commandments and recalled how Israel begged him to stand between them and God (chapter 5). Now he begins to teach “the commandment” he received on the mountain (5:31), and he begins with its heart.

The message. The LORD alone is God, and what he wants from his people is not grudging compliance but love with everything they are. That love lives first on the heart, then fills the home and is passed to the children. It is endangered less by hardship than by comfort, which tempts the rescued to forget their Rescuer. And when children ask why we live this way, the answer is a story of rescue.

Why it was said. Israel was about to move from tents and manna into cities it did not build, and from a desert where God was plainly needed into a land of many gods (see the introduction). Moses knew that the next generation would ask why, and that full stomachs forget.

How the chapter makes its case. The commandments are given for life across the generations (vv. 1–3). At their centre stands the Shema: the LORD is one, so love him with all your heart, soul and might (vv. 4–5). These words must be on the heart and spoken of in every part of the day, at home and in public (vv. 6–9). In a land full of gifts they did not earn, Israel must not forget the LORD but fear and serve him alone (vv. 10–15), and must not put him to the test as at Massah (vv. 16–19). When a son asks what it all means, the answer is the exodus: we were slaves, and the LORD brought us out (vv. 20–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and in his own life. Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus quoted verses 4–5 (Mark 12:29–30), and in the wilderness he answered the devil from this chapter twice (Matthew 4:7, 10). He is the one Israelite who loved God with all his heart every hour, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him. Paul even names Jesus inside the Shema’s confession of the one God (1 Corinthians 8:6). And the love no one can produce on command, God gives: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

For us. Love for God grows where we look long at his love for us. Speak of him in the ordinary hours of home, thank him most when life is easy, and when your children ask why, tell them the story of your rescue in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Purpose of the Law: Life and Multiplication
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commandments are given for life, not as a burden. Before the great confession, Moses says what the law is for: that Israel may fear the LORD, not for a moment but “you and your son and your son’s son”, across the generations (vv. 1–2), and that it may go well with them in a land flowing with milk and honey (v. 3). God’s commands aim at the good of a people he has already rescued. The fear of the LORD meant here is not dread but reverent trust, the root from which the love of the next verses grows.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s commands are given for our good. Obedience grows out of the fear of the Lord and leads to life.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was shown the good life in the land God was giving. The redeemed still walk in his ways as the path of life, not the price of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is the commandment—the statutes and the rules —that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, that you may do them in the land to which you are going over, to possess it, that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son's son, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be long. Hear therefore, O Israel, and be careful to do them, that it may go well with you, and that you may multiply greatly, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you, in a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s commands are given so that his people, generation after generation, may fear him and flourish: they are aimed at life.

You and your son and your son’s son. Before the great confession, Moses states what the commands are for: the fear of the LORD, across three generations in one verse. Nothing here is aimed only at the people in front of him.

That it may go well with you. The law is said to bring not merit or a standing with God but life and good. Every command in this book is aimed at the good of a people God has already rescued, which the human heart has doubted since the serpent suggested otherwise in Eden (Genesis 3:1–5).

That you may fear the LORD your God. Fear does not mean terror of a God who might turn on you. Deuteronomy always sets it alongside loving him, serving him and holding fast to him (10:12, 20). It is the awe of a creature taking the living God seriously, the opposite of treating him as someone to be used. Whoever fears God in this sense is the freest person alive, because nothing else can frighten him (Matthew 10:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — The Shema: The Great Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the centre of Israel’s faith, the Shema. The LORD is one: the only God, and one in himself, undivided and consistent (v. 4). And what this one God asks of his people is love, with all the heart, all the soul and all the strength, everything they are (v. 5). Jesus called this the greatest commandment. It exposes every heart, because no one has kept it for a single day, and it points to the one man who did and to the God who promises to give the love he commands (30:6).
verseByVerse.theology: Because God is one, he asks for undivided love. True religion is more than ritual or right doctrine: it is love for him with the whole self, which Christ alone has given perfectly and the Spirit now works in us.
verseByVerse.examples: This is still the first and greatest commandment, the measure of every other love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD alone is God, and he is one: undivided, consistent, the same in all he is and does, and so his people belong wholly to him.

The Shema. These six Hebrew words, named from their first word, shema (“hear”), are probably the most repeated sentence in Jewish history: said morning and evening, taught to children before they can read, and on the lips of countless Jews as they died. The whole faith of Israel is compressed into one line.

Hear, O Israel. It opens with a command to listen. Faith begins with somebody speaking and somebody attending: “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17).

The LORD is one. The line carries two truths. There is only one God, against a world with a god for every city, crop and crisis. And he is one: undivided, consistent, not at war with himself. The gods of the nations were a committee with rival interests, and a worshipper could never know where he stood. Israel’s God has one will and one character, and he is the same on Tuesday as he was on the mountain.

Does this deny the Trinity? Jewish objectors have always raised this verse against the Trinity, and it should be answered. The word itself does not settle it: the same Hebrew word for one describes a man and wife who become “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), a oneness that is not solitary. The doctrine of the Trinity rests on how the New Testament speaks of Father, Son and Spirit, and it confesses exactly what this verse says: there is one God. Paul even names Jesus within the Shema’s own words: “yet for us there is one God, the Father … and one Lord, Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6). Paul did not abandon the Shema. He recited it with the name of Jesus in it.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew has no verb (literally “the LORD our God the LORD one”), so it can be rendered several ways; the ESV margin offers “The LORD our God is one LORD”, “The LORD is our God, the LORD is one” and “The LORD is our God, the LORD alone”. Some stress that he alone is Israel’s God, others that he is one in himself. Both are taught elsewhere (4:35, 39).
verseByVerse.note: Shema is the Hebrew for “Hear,” the first word of verse 4. In Jewish prayer the name covers 6:4–9 together with 11:13–21 and Numbers 15:37–41, recited as one.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the one God asks first is love, with the whole person and all he has; and because no one has given it, the command drives us to the one man who did and to the God who gives what he commands.

You shall love the LORD your God. Of everything God might have required first, sacrifice, obedience, worship, he asks for love. Asked for the greatest commandment (the rabbis later counted six hundred and thirteen), the Lord Jesus quoted this verse (Mark 12:29–30).

Heart, soul, might. The three terms are not compartments but a way of saying “everything” three times. Heart in Hebrew is the whole inner person, above all the thinking and the will. Soul (nephesh) is the whole living self. Might translates a word that normally means “very” or “much”, so Israel is to love God with all its “muchness”; the rabbis took it to include a man’s property, energy and abilities.

Can love be commanded? To modern ears it sounds like a contradiction: love, we assume, is a feeling that happens to us, and love given because you were told to is not really love. Søren Kierkegaard turned this round in his Works of Love. Love that rests only on feeling, he argued, lasts only as long as the feeling does; only when love has become a duty, something the will is bound to, is it secure against the moods and seasons that would otherwise end it. The command does not replace delight; it carries love through the days when delight is absent, so that delight can return. And God may command love of this kind because his own love is of exactly this kind. His “steadfast love” (7:9) did not rise and fall with how Israel felt or behaved; it held through Kadesh and the years of complaint, and at the cross it held when it cost him everything.

Who has ever done this? Not one of us, for a single morning. That is not a reason to lower the command; it is the reason the rest of the book exists. Deuteronomy states the problem plainly, “Oh that they had such a heart” (5:29), and then announces the solution: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart … so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart” (30:6). The commandment that exposes us is answered by a promise that God will do in us what he requires of us.

The one who loved like this. One man has loved God like this every hour of his life: “I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father” (John 14:31). His obedience is counted to us, and his Spirit teaches cold hearts to love. So John, who had leaned against the chest of the Son of God, tells us where such love begins: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

How do I love God with all my heart? Love for God is not first a feeling to manufacture but a response to being loved, so it grows where you look at his love long enough. With the heart: read Scripture to know him, not only to collect facts, and talk to him as a person, telling him what you enjoyed today and what you fear. With the soul: bring your whole self, grief and anger included, rather than a tidied version for church. With your might: look at the diary and the bank statement; love for God shows in what gets the first of your time, money and best abilities, not what is left over. When it is cold, ask, as the psalmist did: “unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — These Words on the Heart: Passing Faith to Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s words must be on the heart first, and from there they fill the whole of life. Parents are to press them into their children, not in a lesson slot but in the ordinary rhythm of the day: at home and on the road, at bedtime and on waking (vv. 6–7). They are to be bound on the hand and before the eyes and written on doorposts and gates, so that work, thought, private life and public life all come under God’s word (vv. 8–9). Faith is handed on by a household where God is genuinely loved and talked about.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is meant to fill the whole of ordinary life and to be handed on deliberately to the next generation.
verseByVerse.examples: Discipleship happens at the kitchen table and in the car as much as in church.

verseByVerse.quote: And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s words must live on the parents’ own hearts first, and then be pressed into the children through the ordinary conversation of every day.

On your heart. The order cannot be reversed: first on your heart, then teach them. A parent cannot hand on what he does not have, and children are extraordinarily good at telling what their father believes from what he merely says on Sundays.

Teach them diligently. The verb is used of sharpening a blade: repeatedly, with pressure, until an edge forms. And the method is the least formal thing imaginable: sitting, walking, lying down, getting up, the whole of an ordinary day. There is no lesson slot. The faith is passed on the way a family’s accent is, by constant, unremarkable exposure.

A relief and a rebuke. A relief, because a parent who is no teacher can still do it: the qualification is presence and honesty, not eloquence. A rebuke, because it cannot be handed over to a church or school, and the times listed are the ones most of us have handed to a screen. Moses describes a household where God comes up in conversation because he is genuinely on the mind of the people who live there; and the God who first put his words on our hearts is the one who keeps them there.

How do I teach them diligently? Start small, and keep going. One meal a week: read a short passage at the table and ask one question: what does this show us about God? Children notice whether the adults are actually interested. Pray aloud at bedtime: bring their worries to God by name, the friend who was unkind, the test tomorrow, so that they learn he is someone you talk to about real things. Take their questions seriously: when a child asks why God let the dog die, answer honestly, and when you do not know, say, “I don’t know; let’s look.” Tell them your own story: where God has helped you, and where you have failed and been forgiven. Say sorry to them: a parent who says, “I was wrong to shout; will you forgive me?” teaches the gospel better than many lessons.

A promise, not a guarantee. None of this saves a child; faith is God’s gift, and he loves to give it in families: “For the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39). We teach in the hope of a promise, not under the weight of guaranteeing the outcome, and parents whose grown children have wandered can keep praying to the God who seeks the lost.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s words are to shape everything: what we do, what we look at and think about, our private life at home and our public life at work.

As a sign on your hand. Devout Jews have taken these words literally for over two thousand years: small leather boxes of Scripture (phylacteries) bound to arm and forehead for prayer, and the mezuzah, a small case of Scripture on the doorframe. Whatever Moses intended, the four places are clear. On your hand: what you do. Between your eyes: what you look at and think about. On the doorposts: private life, where nobody is watching. On your gates, where the town’s cases were tried and deals struck (see the city gate): public life and work. No area of life is left over.

Was it meant literally? The same language in Proverbs is plainly figurative, “bind them on your fingers” (Proverbs 7:3), and the purpose is that God’s words shape what we do and how we see. Christians are not bound to wear them.

Broad phylacteries. Jesus remarked that some “make their phylacteries broad” (Matthew 23:5), enlarging the boxes so everybody could see. The commandment can be obeyed to the letter and turned into its opposite. The word was meant to go on the hand to shape the hand, not so that people would look at the strap.

Uncertain wording. “Frontlets” translates a rare Hebrew word of unknown origin; it probably means a band or mark on the forehead.
verseByVerse.note: The boxes are called tefillin in Hebrew; phylacteries is the Greek word used in Matthew 23:5.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — The Danger of Prosperity: Do Not Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s greatest danger lies not behind it in the desert but ahead of it in comfort. The LORD is about to give them cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards and olive groves that they did not build, fill, dig or plant (vv. 10–11). When they eat and are full, they must take care not to forget the God who brought them out of slavery (v. 12). He alone is to be feared, served and sworn by; no other god may share his people, for he is a jealous God living in their midst (vv. 13–15). Gratitude is how faith survives prosperity.
verseByVerse.theology: Plenty is a particular danger to faith: comfort breeds forgetfulness, and forgetfulness breeds idolatry.
verseByVerse.examples: Affluence still dulls the soul, and the cure is to remember the Giver behind each gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you—with great and good cities that you did not build, and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant—and when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel will receive a land full of good things it did not build or plant, and the danger then will be to eat, be full and forget the LORD who rescued them.

That you did not build. Four times Moses hammers the phrase: did not build, did not fill, did not dig, did not plant. Everything Israel is about to own will be second-hand mercy: finished houses, cisterns somebody else cut through rock, olive trees that had taken years to bear before Israel arrived.

When you eat and are full. Then the great warning of this book: the danger is not adversity but comfort. This nation survived slavery, plagues, desert, serpents and forty years of funerals with its faith more or less intact. Moses warns them about full stomachs, and he is right: within a generation of settling they are worshipping the Baals (Judges 2:10–13).

How comfort works. Hardship drives people to God; comfort quietly persuades them they never needed him. It happens not by rebellion but by forgetting, which requires no decision at all. Someone who prayed daily through an illness stops when he recovers, not because he has changed his mind about God but because the pressure has gone. So giving thanks is not mere good manners; it is how faith stays alive. Every good thing in your house was given, and most of it was dug by somebody else: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

A house we did not build. So does every Christian: Christ did the work, and his obedience, suffering and victory are given to us finished, “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9).

verseByVerse.quote: It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear. You shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who are around you— for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God— lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD alone is to be feared, served and sworn by, for he lives among his people as a jealous God who will not share them with other gods.

Him you shall serve. Some fourteen centuries later, in a wilderness, a starving man quoted this verse to the devil. Offered all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, Jesus answered: “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve’” (Matthew 4:10). His other two answers came from 6:16 and 8:3: under the greatest pressure, with no food and no company, what came out of the Son of God was Deuteronomy, quoted and not argued. He used the weapon available to any believer, and it was enough. Where Israel failed in its wilderness, the true Son stood firm, for us. Anyone who thinks memorising Scripture a schoolroom exercise should remember that desert.

A jealous God. Verse 15 gives the reason he alone must be worshipped, in the language of marriage: he lives among them, and like a husband he will not share his wife with the gods of the neighbours.

Where Christians differ: may Christians swear oaths? Quakers and many Anabaptists take Jesus’ “Do not take an oath at all” (Matthew 5:34) as forbidding every oath, and will only affirm. This commentary’s view: Jesus forbids the evasive swearing that dodged obligations (Matthew 5:33–37); his point is plain honesty. He does not forbid solemn oaths before God: he answered under oath at his trial (Matthew 26:63–64), Paul called God to witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), and God swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17). Marriage vows and oaths in court are lawful; what a Christian promises, he must keep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Do Not Put the LORD to the Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not put the LORD to the test as their fathers did at Massah, when they demanded water and asked whether he was among them at all (v. 16). Testing God means demanding that he prove himself on our terms before we will trust him. The alternative is simple trust shown in obedience: keep his commandments and do what is right and good in his sight, and he will keep his promise to bring them into the land and drive out their enemies (vv. 17–19). Jesus answered the devil with this verse when he was tempted to force his Father’s hand.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith trusts God rather than demanding proof. To test him is to doubt his goodness and faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Faith rests on God’s promises instead of asking for signs, and Christ in the wilderness shows what perfect trust looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah. You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes, which he has commanded you. And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers by thrusting out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must not demand that God prove himself, as their fathers did at Massah, but trust him and show it by doing what is right in his sight.

As you tested him at Massah. At Massah, whose name means testing, there was no water, and the people quarrelled and asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7).

What testing is. Testing is not honest doubt. Scripture is full of hard questions put to God, and lament is never rebuked; the Psalms are largely made of it. Testing demands that God prove himself on our terms, at our moment, by a sign of our choosing, before we will trust him. It puts God on trial and makes us his judge. And Israel asked this after the sea had opened, so her question was really a verdict that none of it counted.

Jesus and the tempter. Jesus used this verse when the devil quoted Scripture at him and urged him to throw himself from the temple: “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test’” (Matthew 4:7). A verse can be quoted accurately and used wickedly, and the defence is not less Scripture but more of it, each verse read in the light of the rest. The devil knows the Bible. He does not know it whole.

What counts as testing God? Demanding that he prove himself before we trust him, or forcing his hand, as Satan urged Jesus to do. Gideon’s fleece was weak faith that God bore with, not a model for guidance (Judges 6:36–40). Malachi’s “put me to the test” (Malachi 3:10) is God’s own invitation to obey and see his faithfulness, which is different from setting the terms ourselves.
