verseByVerse.note: Massah means “testing”; the same place was also called Meribah, “quarrelling” (Exod 17:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Tell the Story to Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with a child’s question and a parent’s answer. When a son asks what all the commands mean, the answer is not a list of reasons but a story: we were Pharaoh’s slaves, and the LORD brought us out with signs and wonders, to bring us into the land he promised (vv. 20–23). Only then come the commands, given for our good, to keep us alive (v. 24), and the life of obedience they describe is the righteousness of a rescued people (v. 25). Every generation tells the rescue in the first person: “we were slaves”.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is handed on by retelling what God has done. Obedience answers his saving acts; it never causes them.
verseByVerse.examples: Christian parents tell the gospel story, so that their children’s faith rests on what God has done in Christ and not on family rules.

verseByVerse.quote: "When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?' then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand. And the LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt and against Pharaoh and all his household, before our eyes. And he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in and give us the land that he swore to give to our fathers. And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are this day. And it will be righteousness for us, if we are careful to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When children ask why we live as we do, the answer is a story of rescue: we were slaves, the LORD brought us out, and his commands are for our good.

When your son asks you. The chapter ends where the whole book is aimed: at a child’s question. A boy grows up inside habits he did not choose, and one day he asks why. The answer decides whether faith survives a generation, and Moses gives it: not philosophy, not a defence of each statute, but a story. Why do we live like this? Because we were slaves and we were rescued, and everything in this house follows from that one fact.

We were Pharaoh’s slaves. The pronoun is “we”, said by a man whose parents came out of Egypt to a boy two generations further removed. The rescue of Pharaoh’s slaves is not commemorated from a distance; each generation is taught to tell it in the first person.

That he might bring us in. Rescue has a destination (v. 23). So Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).

In a Christian family. A Christian family answers the same question the same way: not “these are our standards” or “this is how we were raised”, but “we were slaves and were bought, at a price, by somebody who came for us.” Any answer without the rescue at the centre has turned the faith into house rules, and house rules do not survive a child leaving home.

Does this teach salvation by works? The obedience comes after redemption: “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out” (v. 21). Righteousness here is the faithful living of a people already redeemed, not a way of earning rescue. As a way to earn life, the law demands a perfect obedience no sinner can give (Galatians 3:10–12); Christ gave it, and his righteousness is counted to all who believe (Romans 10:4–5).

6.theology:
One God, loved with everything. Because the LORD is one, he claims undivided love (6:4–5). Jesus named this the greatest commandment (Mark 12:30); he alone has kept it, and by his Spirit the love of God is poured into our hearts (Rom 5:5).

Faith handed on. God’s words go on the heart and into the rhythms of the day (6:6–9), anchored in the retold story of redemption (6:20–25). Faith is always one generation from being lost, and the remedy is deliberate, gospel-centred teaching in the home.

The danger of plenty. Moses fears full stomachs more than hunger (6:10–12). Deliberate remembrance and the fear of the Lord guard the heart in prosperity.
6.examples:
Israel was given the Shema as the heart of her faith: love the one God with everything, teach that love to the children, and do not forget him among the gifts of the land.

Christians love God only because he first loved us in Christ, who loved the Father perfectly in our place. So we fill ordinary life with his Word, tell our children the gospel before the rules, resist the dulling pull of affluence, and remember the greater exodus by which Christ brought us out of slavery to sin.

keyVerse.quote: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.
keyVerse.note: Jesus called this the greatest commandment, and it gathers the whole law into one word: love. It asks for everything we are, and so it shows that no one but Christ has kept it. Yet it is also the love God promises to create in his people (30:6), for “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

6.reflection:
God commands love “with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (v. 5). Why do you think love, rather than obedience or worship, is what he asks for first? What would it look like for you to love God with your time, money and abilities?

Moses expects God’s words to come up “when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way” (v. 7). What one change could make God a natural part of the conversation in your home or friendships this week?

The great danger, Moses says, comes “when you eat and are full” (v. 11). Where has comfort made you forget God, and what habits of thanksgiving could help you remember?

When a child asks what the commands mean, the answer is a story: “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt” (v. 21). How would you tell your own story of rescue in Christ to a child or a friend who asks why you live as you do?

7.title: A Holy Nation: Chosen Not Because You Were Great, but Because He Loved You
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, and clears away many nations before you, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and mightier than you,<sup>2</sup>and when the LORD your God gives them over to you, and you defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.<sup>3</sup>You shall not intermarry with them, giving your daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for your sons,<sup>4</sup>for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly.<sup>5</sup>But thus shall you deal with them: you shall break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire.<sup>6</sup>"For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.<sup>7</sup>It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples,<sup>8</sup>but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations,<sup>10</sup>and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face.<sup>11</sup>You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today.<sup>12</sup>"And because you listen to these rules and keep and do them, the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the steadfast love that he swore to your fathers.<sup>13</sup>He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. He will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, in the land that he swore to your fathers to give you.<sup>14</sup>You shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall not be male or female barren among you or among your livestock.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD will take away from you all sickness, and none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew, will he inflict on you, but he will lay them on all who hate you.<sup>16</sup>And you shall consume all the peoples that the LORD your God will give over to you. Your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.<sup>17</sup>"If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?'<sup>18</sup>you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt,<sup>19</sup>the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm, by which the LORD your God brought you out. So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.<sup>20</sup>Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>You shall not be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God.<sup>22</sup>The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you.<sup>23</sup>But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed.<sup>24</sup>And he will give their kings into your hand, and you shall make their name perish from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand against you until you have destroyed them.<sup>25</sup>The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>26</sup>And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.
7.overview:
Where we are. Moses has called Israel to love the one LORD with all their heart and warned them against forgetting him in the comfort of the land (chapter 6). Now he turns to the nations already living in that land, and to the question beneath Israel’s whole existence: why did God choose them?

The message. God chose Israel for no reason in Israel, not their size and not their goodness, but “because the LORD loves you” (v. 8). A people loved like that must belong to him without rivals: no peace with Canaan’s gods, no marriages that would turn their children away, no gold kept back from the idols. And a people loved like that need not fear the nations, because the faithful God who brought them out of Egypt is in their midst.

Why it was said. Israel was about to face nations “more numerous and mightier” than themselves (v. 1), whose religion included burning their children (see the introduction). They would be tempted both to fear these peoples and to imitate them, and Moses answers both temptations.

How the chapter makes its case. The seven nations of Canaan are under God’s sentence: Israel is to destroy them, make no covenant or marriage with them, and break down their altars (vv. 1–5). What makes Israel different is not in Israel: they are holy and treasured because the LORD chose them in love and keeps his oath (vv. 6–8), so they must know him as the faithful God who keeps covenant for a thousand generations and repays those who hate him (vv. 9–11). Obedience will meet his blessing in family, field and flock (vv. 12–16). When they are afraid, they must remember what he did to Egypt and trust the God in their midst, who will clear the land little by little (vv. 17–24); and they must burn the idols and keep none of their gold (vv. 25–26).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by pattern. The love that chose Israel for nothing in her is the love shown supremely at the cross: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Peter gives the words of verse 6 to the church (1 Peter 2:9). And the judgment on Canaan is a small preview of the judgment of the whole world, whose Judge will be Jesus (Acts 17:31), who is also the refuge from it: Rahab, a Canaanite under this very sentence, believed and was spared, and every sinner who comes to Christ finds the same mercy.

For us. If you belong to Christ, you were not chosen for anything in you, so you can neither boast nor despair. Remember what God has done when you are afraid, deal ruthlessly with the sins that would ensnare you, and be patient with his “little by little”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nations of Canaan are under God’s sentence, and Israel must make no peace with their gods. When the LORD gives Israel victory over the seven nations, they are to devote them to destruction, his judgment on wickedness long borne with, and make no covenant with them (vv. 1–2). They must not intermarry, because foreign wives would turn their sons to other gods (vv. 3–4), and they must destroy every altar, pillar, Asherah and image (v. 5). The real danger is not military but religious: that Israel would end up worshipping what it was sent to judge. This was a unique command for one moment, never a pattern for violence since.
verseByVerse.theology: God asks for a clean break with idolatry, because compromise with other gods corrupts the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The church fights no such war, but believers still refuse to be shaped by the idols of their age.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, and clears away many nations before you, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and mightier than you, and when the LORD your God gives them over to you, and you defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God gives Israel victory over the seven nations of Canaan, they are to carry out his sentence on those nations’ long-ripened wickedness and make no covenant with them. These are among the hardest verses in the Bible, and they should be neither softened nor hurried past.

Devote them to complete destruction. The Hebrew word is herem: to devote something to God so completely that it is put beyond any human use. Applied to plunder it means burnt rather than kept. Applied to a people it means they are put to death.

Seven nations. The command is limited to seven named nations in one territory. It is not a policy toward foreigners; the same book commands Israel to love the sojourner (10:19) and forbids her to abhor an Egyptian (23:7). It is bounded by geography, by a list, and by a moment.

The reason. Deuteronomy states it repeatedly, and in full at 9:4–5: this is God’s judgment on sin. “Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you” (9:5). God had told Abraham centuries earlier that his descendants would wait, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16): he delayed judgment for four hundred years while their wickedness grew to its full. What it grew into is described in 12:31: they burned their children.

What remains hard. What remains after all that is still hard, and Scripture does not remove it: whether God has the right to judge, and when. He does, and he exercises it in every generation without consulting us; what is unusual here is only that we are allowed to watch. “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). Abraham asked that while pleading with God for Sodom, sure that the answer was yes.

But women and children? The judgment fell on a whole people, as the flood and Sodom did. Yet even here the door stood open: those who turned to the LORD were spared with their households (Joshua 6:25). And the law itself forbids punishing children for their fathers’ crimes in human courts (24:16): this command was unique.

The Judge is also the refuge. The Judge does not stand outside the story. Canaan was a small, local preview of a judgment the whole world will face, and the New Testament says the Judge on that day will be Jesus (Acts 17:31). The same Jesus is the refuge from it. Rahab, a Canaanite living under this very sentence, believed and was spared (Joshua 2:9–11; Hebrews 11:31), and every sinner who comes over to him finds the same mercy, because on the cross he bore the judgment himself.

A model for nobody. This must be said plainly: no nation, church or individual since has held this commission, and the New Testament closes the door explicitly. “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting” (John 18:36); “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Every use of this chapter to justify violence has been a misuse.

Where Christians differ: how literally was the command meant? A careful reader notices a tension inside the chapter: Israel is told to destroy these nations (v. 2), in the next breath not to marry them (v. 3), and God will clear them away “little by little” (v. 22); Judges 1 shows Canaanites still living in the land. Many evangelical scholars think the language of total destruction is partly the stock idiom of ancient war reports, which spoke of complete victory where many survived. Others take the command more literally. This commentary’s view: it was a real sentence of judgment, as 9:5 presents it, while the reports of its execution use the sweeping idiom of their day. Either way, its aim was to break Canaan’s religion and its hold on the land, and the door stood open to any Canaanite who turned to Israel’s God.
verseByVerse.note: The rule is given again in 20:16–18, with the reason this chapter gives in verse 4: that these nations would teach Israel their abominable practices.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not intermarry with them, giving your daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for your sons, for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly. But thus shall you deal with them: you shall break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must not marry into the Canaanite nations, because their gods would turn the next generation away from the LORD; the real war is against their altars and idols.

You shall not intermarry with them. God gives the reason himself: “they would turn away your sons from following me”. The danger is not military, and the prohibition is not racial. Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and is in the genealogy of Christ; Ruth was a Moabite and King David’s great-grandmother. Both married Israelites, and Scripture celebrates it, because they had come over to the God of Israel: “your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

Turn away your sons. The danger is religious, and it is specific: not only that the husband will be drawn from his faith, but that his sons will be raised by a mother who worships something else. Solomon, the wisest of kings, proved it: “his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). Paul applies the same principle to the church, for the same reason, faith and not race: a widow may remarry whom she wishes, “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39).

What it does not mean. It does not tell a Christian already married to an unbeliever to leave; Paul says the opposite (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

Break down their altars. Verse 5 shows what the real war was: altars, pillars, Asherim (wooden poles for the goddess Asherah) and images are to be destroyed, not looted. Every time Israel left a shrine standing, she ended up kneeling at it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Chosen in Love: The Heart of Election
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the heart of the chapter: why God chose Israel. They are holy, set apart to him, and his treasured possession out of all the peoples (v. 6). Not because they were many, for they were the fewest, but simply because the LORD loves them and keeps his oath to their fathers; that is why he redeemed them from Egypt (vv. 7–8). So they must know him as he is: faithful, keeping covenant and steadfast love to a thousand generations of those who love him, and repaying those who hate him (vv. 9–10). The response follows the love: therefore be careful to obey (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Election rests on God’s free love alone, not on anything in the chosen, and they are kept by his faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: The church is God’s treasured people in the same way, saved not by works but by love it did nothing to earn.

verseByVerse.quote: "For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is set apart for God and is his own treasured possession, chosen out of all the peoples of the earth.

A people holy to the LORD. Holy (qadosh) does not first mean morally pure but set apart for a particular use. A holy pot in the tabernacle was not a better-behaved pot, only one kept for God’s service. Israel is holy because God has taken her out of ordinary use to be his own.

His treasured possession. The word (segullah) means a king’s personal treasure, kept apart from the wealth of his kingdom. Everything belongs to God by creation (Psalm 24:1); Israel is his the way a man’s own treasured things are his.

Handed to the church. Peter gives the verse to mostly Gentile congregations: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession”, and names the purpose, “that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). And the treasure was bought with blood: Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God did not choose Israel for their size or their goodness, but simply because he loved them and keeps his promises: his love has no cause outside himself.

Not because you were more in number. Moses answers the question every chosen person eventually asks: why me? Not size: Israel was “the fewest of all peoples”, and says so in its own Scriptures, which is not how nations write about themselves. Nor goodness: two chapters on, “you are a stubborn people” (9:6).

Because the LORD loves you. So what is left? He set his love on them because he loves them. Ask why he loves them, and the answer is that he loves them; there is no further reason underneath. God’s love for his people has no cause outside himself, which is precisely why nothing outside himself can end it. And it is held in place by an oath, the one he swore to their fathers.

Why this matters. If God had chosen Israel for something in her, that thing would have to be maintained, and the day it failed the choosing would fail with it. Every believer who has lain awake wondering whether God has finally had enough of him is asking whether the ground of his acceptance is in himself. This verse says it never was. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8): not when we were improving, but when there was nothing in us to explain it.

Doesn’t being chosen make people proud? To many modern readers a chosen people sounds like the root of every ugly nationalism: we are special, and you are not. It is a fair worry, because human beings turn every advantage into a reason to look down on others. But Israel was chosen for nothing in her, and that is the one ground on which nobody can boast. If you are chosen for your merits, you will be proud of them and contemptuous of those who lack them. If you are chosen for no reason in you at all, pride has nothing left to stand on, and the outsider is simply someone God has not yet brought in, as he once brought you. Paul says the same to Gentile Christians: salvation “is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). People who know they were loved for no reason are the very people who can love others the same way.

Where Christians differ: does God choose individuals in the same free way? Arminians hold that God chooses individuals for salvation on the basis of their foreseen faith. This commentary’s view: the New Testament applies this same free love to the choosing of individuals in Christ before the world began; faith is the fruit of election, not its ground (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face. You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who chose Israel is faithful: he keeps covenant love to a thousand generations of those who love him and repays those who hate him, so his people must obey him.

The faithful God. The great covenant words gather here. Faithful, from the root that gives us amen: something you can put your weight on. Steadfast love (chesed): loyal covenant love that keeps going when the other party has given every reason to stop. And the contrast of the second commandment appears again (5:9–10): a thousand generations of love against judgment within a lifetime. A thousand generations at even twenty-five years apiece is twenty-five thousand years, a Hebrew way of saying for ever, past any horizon you can see.

Repays to their face. Verse 10 will not let the picture be sentimental. He repays those who hate him directly and personally, and is not slack. A reader who takes only one half has not got the God of the Bible. Both halves meet at the cross, where God kept his promise and judged sin together, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

You shall therefore be careful. The “therefore” is always in the same place. Because he chose you, loves you and is faithful, therefore obey. Never the other way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — The Blessings of Covenant Faithfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Obedience is the path on which God’s covenant blessing meets his people. If Israel keeps his rules, he will keep the covenant and steadfast love he swore to their fathers (v. 12). The blessings are the stuff of ordinary life in that land: children, grain, wine and oil, herds and flocks, no barrenness, and freedom from the diseases of Egypt (vv. 13–15). These are promises to a nation under the Sinai covenant, not guarantees of health and wealth to individuals today. The section ends by returning to the warning: Israel must not pity the nations or serve their gods, for that would be a snare (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God delights to bless the people he has made his own, and his blessings were always meant to reach beyond them.
verseByVerse.examples: The believer’s lasting blessings are secured in Christ, the offspring of Abraham, rather than promised as health and harvests.

verseByVerse.quote: "And because you listen to these rules and keep and do them, the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the steadfast love that he swore to your fathers. He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. He will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, in the land that he swore to your fathers to give you. You shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall not be male or female barren among you or among your livestock. And the LORD will take away from you all sickness, and none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew, will he inflict on you, but he will lay them on all who hate you. And you shall consume all the peoples that the LORD your God will give over to you. Your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel keeps God’s commands, he will keep his covenant love and bless them above all peoples, in family, field, flock and health.

He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. The blessings are farm blessings: children, crops, cattle, health, and freedom from “the evil diseases of Egypt”. He is not offering a religious experience; he is offering rain and babies and a healthy flock. Obedience does not buy his love, which was given first (vv. 7–8); the blessing follows it.

Promises to a nation. Two cautions belong here. First, these promises are made to a nation, under a specific covenant, in a specific land, and the New Testament does not simply transfer them to individuals. Job’s friends assumed that health and prosperity always follow righteousness, and God rebuked them (Job 42:7); a Christian who reads verse 15 as a guarantee of health has forgotten to whom it was made. God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them rich or always healthy, and childlessness or illness in a believer is no proof of disobedience.

Blessed above all peoples. Second, the blessings were meant to flow through Israel to others, not to stop with her, because of what Abraham’s family was called for: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).

The blessing in Christ. The fuller fulfilment is in Christ, in whom God “has blessed us … with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3), and who will one day take away all sickness and pain for good (Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — Do Not Be Afraid: Remember What God Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s fear is real, and God answers it with memory. If they say in their hearts that the nations are too strong, they must remember what the LORD did to Pharaoh and to Egypt, and reason forward: he will do the same again (vv. 17–19). He will send hornets; he is in their midst, a great and awesome God; and he will give them victory, though little by little, so that the land does not go wild (vv. 20–24). Finally the idols must be burned and their silver and gold not kept, lest Israel be ensnared by what God has devoted to destruction (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: Faith overcomes fear by remembering what God has already done. He works gradually, but surely.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians facing odds they cannot meet look back to the cross and the empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?' you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt, the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm, by which the LORD your God brought you out. So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel fears that the nations are too strong, the answer is to remember what the LORD did to Egypt and to reason forward: he will do the same again.

In your heart. God says aloud the thing Israel has not said aloud: the private thought at three in the morning that the nations are too great. He quotes it back before they have said it, which is its own comfort. And the fear is accurate; verse 1 called these nations “more numerous and mightier than you”. God never argues that the odds are better than they look.

You shall remember. His answer is a discipline of memory: remember Pharaoh, the signs, the mighty hand, and reason forward from it. That is not positive thinking. Nobody is told to feel differently or to shrink the enemy; they are directed to what God did, which they saw. Faith here reasons from evidence.

Better evidence. The Christian has better evidence still, and Paul draws the same inference: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

How do I remember when I am afraid? Say the fear out loud to God. He has already quoted it back; you will not shock him. Name it plainly: the redundancy, the scan, the child who has stopped speaking to you. Rehearse what he has done. Moses lists the plagues by name. Make your own list: what God has done in Scripture, above all at the cross, and the specific times he has carried you; write it down and read it when the fear comes back. Reason forward: if he did that, will he drop me here? Do the next obedient thing. Israel was not told to wait until the fear left but to go in; make the phone call, keep the appointment, with the fear still there. Remember who is in the camp: “the LORD your God is in your midst” (v. 21), and in Christ that became a promise to every disciple: “And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Fear that will not lift, or panic that disrupts daily life, is worth bringing to a pastor or biblical counsellor and to a doctor; medicine is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed. You shall not be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God. The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you. But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed. And he will give their kings into your hand, and you shall make their name perish from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand against you until you have destroyed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD in Israel’s midst will fight for them and give them victory, but little by little, so that the land is not left empty and wild.

Hornets. God promises to fight, even with hornets, an image of panic and rout, and gives the ground: “the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God”. Not watching from a distance. In the camp.

Little by little. God, who could have emptied Canaan in a week, chooses not to, and the reason is practical: a land emptied faster than Israel can occupy it goes back to wilderness, and the wild beasts move in. The slow victory is a kindness.

When sin will not die. Anyone who has prayed for years about a sin that will not die should hold on to verse 22. God’s usual method with his people is little by little, not for lack of power but because sudden deliverance would give us ground we are not yet mature enough to hold. Sanctification is slow for the same reason, and it is God’s own work: the Spirit who lives in his people goes on clearing the land (Galatians 5:16–17), and “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “hornets” is rare (also Exodus 23:28; Joshua 24:12). It may mean literal hornets, or picture the panic God sends on an enemy (compare v. 23). Either way, the victory is the LORD’s.

verseByVerse.quote: The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God. And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idols must be burned and their silver and gold not kept, because what God has devoted to destruction will ensnare whoever holds on to it.

The silver or the gold. The temptation is precisely calculated. Nobody in that army would be converted to Baal by a statue, but the statues were plated in silver and gold, and Israel was poor.

Lest you be ensnared. A snare is not a wall; it lets you walk in freely and then holds you. Someone who kept one piece would find years later that he had kept a thread back to the whole thing. So verse 26 is deliberately extreme: utterly detest and abhor it, not admire it as an antique. Achan would take a cloak and some silver at Jericho, bury it under his tent, and destroy his family (Joshua 7:21).

Besetting sin. That is how a besetting sin survives in a Christian life. Few people keep the idol; many keep something that came with it: the friendship, the taste for it, the door left unlocked. “If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away” (Matthew 5:30) is the same instruction, given by the gentlest man who ever lived, to people he had come to save. He asks us to let go of the gold, and he let go of far more for us: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

7.theology:
Election rests on love. God did not choose Israel for her size or goodness but because he loved her (7:7–8). That is the bedrock of assurance: if he chose us for no reason in us, nothing in us can unchoose us.

The faithful God. The security of the chosen rests not on their shaky faithfulness but on God’s chesed, his loyal love (7:9), whose every promise is kept in Christ (2 Cor 1:20).

A clean break with idols. Holiness is not a polite distance from sin but the renouncing of it (7:25–26). The believer puts sin to death by the Spirit (Rom 8:13), and where he fails, it is Christ’s perfect obedience, not his own, that stands for him before God.
7.examples:
Israel, the fewest of all peoples, was made God’s treasured possession by sheer love, called to make no alliance with Canaan’s gods and to trust the God who broke Egypt to clear the land before her little by little.

Every believer is loved in the same way: not because we were lovely, but because God set his love on us. So we rest our assurance on his faithfulness, meet fear by remembering what he has done, accept slow growth in holiness as a mercy, and give no room to the idols of the heart.

keyVerse.quote: but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
keyVerse.note: Here is the reason for Israel’s whole existence, and it is no reason in Israel: God loves because he loves, and he keeps his word. Election rests on nothing but his free love, which is why nothing in his people can undo it. The same love sent Christ to die for us “while we were still sinners” (Romans 5:8).

7.reflection:
God chose Israel not for size or goodness but “because the LORD loves you” (v. 8). How does it change the way you see yourself, on good days and bad, to know that God’s love for you in Christ has no cause in you?

The ban on intermarriage was about faith, not race: “they would turn away your sons from following me” (v. 4). Which relationships and influences most shape your faith, and your children’s, and what does this passage say to Christians thinking about marriage?

Israel’s fear of the nations was realistic, yet God told them to “remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh” (v. 18). What has God done, in Scripture and in your own life, that you can rehearse when you are afraid?

God clears the land “little by little” (v. 22) and warns that keeping the idols’ gold will be a snare (v. 25). Where are you impatient with slow growth, and is there anything that came with an old sin that you are still holding on to?

8.title: Remember the LORD Your God: Man Does Not Live by Bread Alone
8.text: <sup>1</sup>"The whole commandment that I command you today you shall be careful to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and possess the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers.<sup>2</sup>And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.<sup>3</sup>And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years.<sup>5</sup>Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.<sup>6</sup>So you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God by walking in his ways and by fearing him.<sup>7</sup>For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs, flowing out in the valleys and hills,<sup>8</sup>a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey,<sup>9</sup>a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, in which you will lack nothing, a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper.<sup>10</sup>And you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.<sup>11</sup>"Take care lest you forget the LORD your God by not keeping his commandments and his rules and his statutes, which I command you today,<sup>12</sup>lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them,<sup>13</sup>and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied,<sup>14</sup>then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery,<sup>15</sup>who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness, with its fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water, who brought you water out of the flinty rock,<sup>16</sup>who fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers did not know, that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end.<sup>17</sup>Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.'<sup>18</sup>You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.<sup>19</sup>And if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish.<sup>20</sup>Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.
8.overview:
Where we are. Moses has told Israel that God chose them in love and will drive out the nations before them (chapter 7). Before he turns to Israel’s own stubbornness (chapter 9), he looks back over the forty years in the wilderness and forward to the plenty of the land, and sets the two side by side.

The message. The wilderness was God’s fatherly school: he let his people hunger and then fed them, to teach them that life comes not from bread but from his word. The land will be the harder test, because plenty tempts the heart to grow proud and forget the Giver. So remember: every good thing, even the strength to earn it, comes from him, and to forget him is to perish.

Why it was said. A generation raised on manna was about to eat from fields and live in houses it had not built (see the introduction). Moses knew that comfort, not hardship, would be their undoing, as it later was.

How the chapter makes its case. Remember the whole forty-year road, by which God humbled and tested you (vv. 1–2): he let you hunger and fed you with manna to teach you to live by his word (v. 3), kept your clothes and feet, and disciplined you as a father his son (vv. 4–5). Now he brings you into a good land; eat, be full, and bless him (vv. 6–10). But beware: when you have eaten and built and multiplied, your heart may be lifted up and forget the God who led you through the terrible wilderness to do you good in the end (vv. 11–16). Do not say your own power got you this wealth, for he gives the power (vv. 17–18). If you forget him and serve other gods, you will perish like the nations (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. To Christ in his own life and by pattern. Israel hungered forty years and grumbled; Jesus hungered forty days in the wilderness and, when the tempter told him to turn stones into bread, answered with verse 3: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). He trusted his Father where Israel failed, in her place and ours. And he is himself the bread the manna pictured: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

For us. Hardship is not proof that God has left you; it is the training of a Father. Plenty is not proof that you have done well; it is a gift to be received with thanks. Thank him when you are full, give first, and feed daily on Christ and his word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wilderness years were not wasted: they were God’s fatherly school. Israel must keep the whole commandment and remember the whole road of forty years, by which God humbled them and tested them to reveal what was in their hearts (vv. 1–2). He let them hunger and then fed them with manna, so that they would learn that life depends not on bread but on every word from his mouth (v. 3). He kept their clothes from wearing out and their feet from swelling, and in all of it he was disciplining them as a father trains his son (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: Hardship in God’s hands is a father’s training, meant to humble and to teach dependence. Trials are a school of faith, not a sign that he has left.
verseByVerse.examples: God still uses hard seasons to wean his children from relying on themselves and to teach them to live by his Word.

verseByVerse.quote: "The whole commandment that I command you today you shall be careful to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and possess the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers. And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must remember the whole forty-year road, because God led them through it on purpose, to humble them and test what was in their hearts.

The LORD your God has led you. Moses says God led them, not that he allowed them to wander. To those living through it, the wilderness looked like the punishment for refusing at Kadesh to enter the land, which it was. Moses now says it was also a route, chosen by God, who walked at the head of the column. Both are true: the years were a judgment and a planned journey.

The whole way. Not just the highlights: the water from the rock and the graves at Kibroth-hattaavah (where those who craved meat were buried, Numbers 11:34), the manna and the serpents, the days when God was unmistakable and the far greater number of days when nothing happened at all. A memory that keeps only the rescues will not help much when the next stretch is dull.

To know what was in your heart. Testing is not God gathering information he lacks; the test was so that they would know. Nobody discovers what he actually believes while things are comfortable. Pressure does not create character; it reveals it, and then, in God’s hands, changes it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God let Israel go hungry and then fed them with manna, to teach them that life comes not from bread itself but from the word of the God who gives it.

He humbled you and let you hunger. The order of the verbs holds the lesson: he humbled, he let you hunger, then he fed. God arranged the hunger. He brought a vast company into a place with no food, let them get genuinely hungry, and only then sent bread, so that they would learn what they could not have learned in a fertile country.

Fed you with manna. The manna itself taught it: bread that appeared overnight, could not be stored, had to be gathered fresh each morning, and stopped the day after they ate the produce of the land (Joshua 5:12). Israel was fed for forty years because God spoke, not because a harvest grew.

Man does not live by bread alone. This is not a verse about preferring spiritual things to physical ones; the manna filled real stomachs. The point is the source. Bread keeps a man alive because God says so; take away the word and the bread does nothing.

The true Son in the wilderness. Centuries later the tempter said to a man forty days without food, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread”, and he answered from this verse (Matthew 4:3–4). Israel hungered forty years and grumbled; the true Son hungered forty days and trusted his Father where Israel had failed, in her place and ours. Then he said what no Israelite could have expected: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35).

How many were fed? The census figures of Numbers imply some two million people, though some scholars think the Hebrew word for “thousand” there can mean a smaller military unit, which would make the number much smaller. Either way, it was far more than the desert could feed.

verseByVerse.quote: Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years. Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s care reached down to clothes and feet through forty years, and all of it, the hunger included, was the training a father gives his son.

Your clothing did not wear out. Clothing that did not wear out and feet that did not swell are not the miracles anybody would have chosen to record. Not the sea or the fire: just forty years of walking in a desert, and the cloak lasted and the feet held up. Anyone who has walked any distance knows how much that matters, and how little anybody thanks God for it. God’s care runs down into things nobody notices. Most Christians could list God’s dramatic answers; very few keep any account of forty years of feet that did not give out.

As a man disciplines his son. The word means to train or bring up, the word for raising a child rather than punishing a criminal. Israel’s forty years were not a father losing his temper but a father raising a child, and the hunger was part of the upbringing.

For suffering Christians. Hebrews presses this on suffering Christians: “It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons” (Hebrews 12:7). Hardship is not evidence that God has withdrawn; it is evidence that we are his children. That does not mean each sorrow is punishment for a particular sin (John 9:3); it means no sorrow lies outside a Father’s hands, and none is wasted. And the Father did not spare his own Son this road: “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), so he walks it with us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Good Land: Bless the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Moses describes the land, with open delight. Israel is to keep God’s commands, walking in his ways and fearing him, because he is bringing them into a good land (v. 6): water springing up from the ground, wheat and barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olives and honey, bread without scarcity, and hills full of iron and copper (vv. 7–9). There they will eat and be full, and then they must bless the LORD for the good land he has given them (v. 10). Gratitude at the full table is the hinge of the chapter, the defence against the danger that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: God is a generous giver, and the right response to plenty is to bless him for it.
verseByVerse.examples: Every good gift, from a meal to a harvest, is an occasion for thanks to the Father who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: So you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God by walking in his ways and by fearing him. For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs, flowing out in the valleys and hills, a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey, a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, in which you will lack nothing, a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper. And you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is bringing his people into a land of rich and good gifts, and when they have eaten and are full, they must bless him for it.

A good land. Moses describes the land with open delight. Every item on the list is chosen for people who have eaten the same thing every morning for forty years: water that comes up out of the ground by itself, bread from a field instead of off the sand, vines, figs, pomegranates and olives, named so they can taste them in advance, and then iron and copper. God is not embarrassed to describe the goodness of the material world to his people. He made it, and he is about to give them a great deal of it, and the passage has no trace of the suspicion of physical pleasure that has clung to religion since.

Eat, be full, and bless. Verse 10 is the turning point of the chapter, and the defence against the disaster the next ten verses describe. Prosperity does not have to ruin anyone; it ruins when it arrives without gratitude, because a full stomach and a short memory are exactly the conditions in which people stop needing God. The Jewish practice of saying grace after the meal, when you are full and least inclined to, comes from this verse, and it is wiser than our habit of thanking God only while still hungry. “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4).

A better land. Canaan was a gift and a picture. Its plenty pointed beyond itself to the inheritance Christ secures for his people, “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Peril of Plenty: Do Not Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Plenty is more dangerous than the desert. When Israel has eaten, built good houses and multiplied its herds and silver, its heart may be lifted up and forget the LORD who brought it out of Egypt, led it through a terrifying wilderness, and gave it water from the rock and manna from heaven, all to do it good in the end (vv. 11–16). The proud heart will say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth”, but it is the LORD who gives power to get wealth, keeping his covenant (vv. 17–18). To forget him and follow other gods is to perish like the nations (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Plenty tempts the heart to pride and to forget God; remembering where everything came from keeps it humble.
verseByVerse.examples: The more comfortable a Christian’s life, the more deliberately he needs to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: "Take care lest you forget the LORD your God by not keeping his commandments and his rules and his statutes, which I command you today, lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied, then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness, with its fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water, who brought you water out of the flinty rock, who fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers did not know, that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessings of the land can become the road to ruin: when Israel is full and rich, its heart may grow proud and forget the God who carried it through the wilderness to do it good.

Then your heart be lifted up. The catalogue of dangers is a catalogue of blessings: full stomachs, good houses, growing herds, more silver. Everything on it is something God gives, and Moses names it all as the road to ruin. It happens in two steps: first a quiet pride that nobody notices in himself, then forgetting, which follows almost automatically. A man who has begun to feel important does not decide to stop depending on God. He simply finds one day that he has, and cannot say when. It is not usually rebellion; it is drift.

Fiery serpents and scorpions. Against that Moses sets a memory, and chooses the details: serpents, scorpions, thirsty ground, flinty rock, manna. That is what he wants remembered in the good houses, not a general sense of having been helped. Comfort blurs the details first, and it is the details that keep the memory true.

To do you good in the end. One of the tenderest phrases in Deuteronomy. He humbled and tested them not to break them, nor finally to punish them. The whole hard road had a kindness at the end that they could not see from inside it, as every believer’s road does: “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

Why do rich societies forget God? It has long been noticed that faith tends to thin out as a country grows richer. The political scientists Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart, in Sacred and Secular (2004), argued that religion declines where life feels secure, and many conclude that faith was only ever a coping strategy for hard times. Moses would accept the observation and reverse the conclusion. Plenty does not disprove God; it makes him easy to stop noticing. Nobody in a comfortable suburb holds a debate and votes God out. The diary fills, needs are met before they are felt, and prayer comes to seem unnecessary, like a torch in a lit room. It even feels like maturity. But Jesus told of a rich farmer whose barns were too small, who told his soul to relax, eat, drink and be merry, and who was called a fool that same night (Luke 12:16–21). The full table is where we most need a Saviour, because it is where we are most sure we do not.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must never credit its wealth to its own strength, because it is the LORD who gives the very power to gain it, in faithfulness to his covenant.

Beware lest you say in your heart. God quotes the sentence back before anybody has said it, as he did with their fear in 7:17, so that they will recognise it when they hear themselves think it. It is said in the heart: not a boast at dinner, but the private assessment a man makes when he looks at what he has built and credits it all to himself. It is the more dangerous because he never questions it.

It is he who gives you power to get wealth. The correction is not that Israel did nothing; they did farm and build. It goes one step further back. The energy, health, intelligence, opportunity and decades of peace were none of them self-generated, and anyone who traces the chain honestly runs out of his own contributions very quickly. Paul asks a self-congratulating church the same question: “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

That he may confirm his covenant. The prosperity is not a reward for performance. It is the keeping of an old promise.

How do I remember the LORD when things go well? The danger is quiet, so the remedy has to be deliberate. Timothy Keller often pointed out that in years of pastoral work almost nobody came to him confessing greed, because it hides so well in the one who has it. Thank him first: when the pay rise, the sale or the good report comes, thank God by name before you tell anyone else. Give first: set aside your giving when the money comes in, not from what is left at the end of the month, saying with David, “For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chronicles 29:14). Tell the true story: when someone asks how you did it, include the health, the teachers, the open doors and the God who gave them. Stay with his people: busy, successful seasons are exactly when Sunday worship quietly gets squeezed out; guard it most then.

The gift no one earns. Above all, remember this: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Someone who knows he has received Christ for nothing finds it easier to hold everything else with an open hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish. Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel forgets the LORD and serves other gods, it will perish just like the nations it is dispossessing: being chosen makes it more answerable, not less.

So shall you perish. The chapter ends without softening. Israel is watching God destroy the Canaanites for idolatry, and Moses says: if you do what they did, you will get what they got. The covenant is not a lucky charm that protects them whatever they do. Centuries later Assyria and Babylon carried both kingdoms, Israel and Judah, off for precisely this sin. Amos put it bluntly: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2).

Because you would not obey. The root is ordinary. The book whose great confession begins “Hear, O Israel” warns here of a people who would not listen.

Written for our instruction. Paul hands the chapter to the church: “Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction … Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:11–12). The warning was never for Israel only, and the danger it names is not persecution. It is a good house and a full table and a heart that has quietly stopped remembering.

Not the last word. The God of this book promised to receive his people when they return to him with all their heart (4:29–31), and the one who has forgotten may still come home. God sent his Son so “that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

8.theology:
Not by bread alone. The manna taught that life depends on God’s word, not on the harvest (8:3). Jesus kept that lesson in the wilderness where Israel failed (Matt 4:4), and he is himself the bread of life.

The danger of plenty. The real threat is a full table and a proud heart (8:14, 17). Self-sufficiency grows out of comfort and ends in forgetting God.

A Father’s discipline. The wilderness was an upbringing, not an abandonment (8:5; cf. Heb 12). God trains only those he has already made his sons, and he aims at their good.
8.examples:
Israel was led through forty years of wilderness to learn dependence on God’s word, and then warned that the good land would tempt her to forget the Giver.

Many of us are among the most prosperous Christians in history, and the same danger stands at our door. We trace every good thing, even the ability to earn, back to a Father’s hand, accept hard seasons as his training, and feed on Christ, helped by the Spirit, whose work is to bring Christ’s words to our remembrance (John 14:26).

keyVerse.quote: And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The wilderness had a lesson, and this verse states it: life depends not on bread but on the God who speaks. Jesus answered the tempter with these words after fasting forty days, trusting his Father where Israel had grumbled, and he is himself the bread of life who satisfies all who come to him (John 6:35).

8.reflection:
Moses tells Israel to “remember the whole way” the LORD has led them (v. 2), not only the highlights. What might you learn by looking back over the whole of your life with God, including the dull and the hard stretches?

God let his people hunger to teach them that “man does not live by bread alone” (v. 3). How have times of need taught you to depend on God’s word, and how does Jesus’ use of this verse in his own temptation help you?

Verse 5 says God disciplines his people “as a man disciplines his son”, and Hebrews 12 applies it to Christians. How does seeing hardship as a Father’s training rather than his absence change the way you face it, and how could you say this gently to someone who is suffering?

Moses warns against saying, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (v. 17). Where are you most tempted to credit yourself, and which habit in this chapter (thanking first, giving first, telling the true story) could you begin this week?

9.title: Not Because of Your Righteousness: Grace Alone for a Stubborn People
9.text: <sup>1</sup>"Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven,<sup>2</sup>a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?'<sup>3</sup>Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God. He will destroy them and subdue them before you. So you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly, as the LORD has promised you.<sup>4</sup>"Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, 'It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land,' whereas it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you.<sup>5</sup>Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you, and that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.<sup>6</sup>"Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.<sup>7</sup>Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD.<sup>8</sup>Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you.<sup>9</sup>When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words that the LORD had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly.<sup>11</sup>And at the end of forty days and forty nights the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them; they have made themselves a metal image.'<sup>13</sup>"Furthermore, the LORD said to me, 'I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stubborn people.<sup>14</sup>Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.'<sup>15</sup>So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands.<sup>16</sup>And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you.<sup>17</sup>So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.<sup>18</sup>Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed, in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger.<sup>19</sup>For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you, so that he was ready to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time also.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time.<sup>21</sup>Then I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook that ran down from the mountain.<sup>22</sup>"At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath.<sup>23</sup>And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, 'Go up and take possession of the land that I have given you,' then you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice.<sup>24</sup>You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.<sup>25</sup>"So I lay prostrate before the LORD for these forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you.<sup>26</sup>And I prayed to the LORD, 'O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand.<sup>27</sup>Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin,<sup>28</sup>lest the land from which you brought us say, "Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness."<sup>29</sup>For they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power and by your outstretched arm.'
9.overview:
Where we are. Moses is still preaching his second sermon on the plains of Moab. Chapter 8 warned that full stomachs would make Israel forget the LORD; chapter 9 turns to the subtler danger of victory. The story it begins, the golden calf, runs on to 10:11.

The message. You are not getting the land because you are good. You are getting it because the nations are wicked and because God swore an oath to your fathers, and you are a stubborn people who have rebelled from the day you left Egypt. Israel is alive at all only because a mediator lay on his face before God and pleaded, not their record, but God’s own name, promise and redemption.

Why it was said. The new generation is about to watch walled cities fall (see the introduction). Success breeds the conviction that we earned it, and a nation that believed it had won Canaan by its own virtue would soon become as proud and corrupt as the nations it replaced.

How the chapter makes its case. The cities are huge and the Anakim legendary, but the LORD goes ahead as a consuming fire (vv. 1–3). Then the warning, three times: not because of your righteousness (vv. 4–6). The proof is Horeb, where the covenant was broken while God was still writing it, and God offered to destroy the people and start again with Moses (vv. 7–14). Moses smashed the tablets before their eyes, fasted forty days for them, prayed even for Aaron, and ground the calf to dust (vv. 15–21). Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah and Kadesh show the calf was no single lapse (vv. 22–24). The chapter ends with Moses’ prayer, which pleads nothing but who God is and what he has done (vv. 25–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Moses stood between a guilty people and the wrath they had earned, and even offered to be blotted out in their place (Exodus 32:32). Jesus, the greater Mediator, was cut off in his people’s place, and now “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). And the verdict “you are a stubborn people” is a need only a new heart can meet, which the law commands but cannot give (10:16; 30:6).

For us. We are tempted to read God’s blessings as proof of our goodness, and his discipline as proof that he has given up on us. Both forget the gospel. We are accepted for Christ’s sake, not ours, so we can be honest about our record, and pray, as Moses did, with nothing to plead but God’s mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Not Because of Your Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not take the land as a reward for her goodness: it is God’s judgment on Canaan and the keeping of his oath to the patriarchs. Moses grants everything the spies once said, great nations, walls up to heaven, the dreaded Anakim, and sets beside it the LORD going ahead as a consuming fire (vv. 1–3). Then, knowing what victory does to people, he warns three times not to say in their hearts that righteousness won it (vv. 4–6). The reasons lie outside Israel: the wickedness of the nations and the word sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The section ends with the bluntest charge in the book: “you are a stubborn people.”
verseByVerse.theology: Inheritance is a gift of grace, never a reward. God blesses the undeserving for his own name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s conquest was grace, not wages, and so is the believer’s salvation: it rests on Christ’s righteousness, not ours.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven, a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?' Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God. He will destroy them and subdue them before you. So you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly, as the LORD has promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The obstacles are as great as the spies said, but the LORD goes ahead of Israel as a consuming fire, so the land will be taken.

Who can stand before the sons of Anak? Moses quotes the spies’ report back at them: “fortified up to heaven” is the phrase from 1:28, and the Anakim were the terror that broke the last generation (Numbers 13:28–33). He does not shrink the obstacle; he sets beside it the LORD, who goes over before them “as a consuming fire.” Compare the Anakim with Israel and the proverb is right; compare them with God and it no longer matters. The last generation gave a true answer to the wrong question.

He will destroy them… So you shall drive them out. God will do it, and Israel will do it, in one sentence and without contradiction, which is how Scripture always speaks of the work of God and the work of his people (Philippians 2:12–13).

The fire that goes before. The same fire will threaten Israel itself at Horeb (v. 15; 4:24). God’s holiness is good news only for those it is not against, and in Christ the fire fell on the one who went before us.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, 'It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land,' whereas it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you. Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you, and that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. "Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God gives victory, do not tell yourself you deserved it: the land is his judgment on Canaan and his faithfulness to his promise, and Israel is a stubborn people.

Do not say in your heart. The point of the chapter, made three times in three verses because Moses knows what victory does to people. Each time Israel’s claim is cut away more sharply, ending in the charge “you are a stubborn people”: literally hard of neck, like an ox that will not turn under the yoke, the word God used at the calf (v. 13; Exodus 32:9).

After the LORD your God has thrust them out. Success produces this temptation, as in chapter 8 a full stomach did. A man who has just watched God do something remarkable through him is in more spiritual danger than one who has just failed, because he is tempted to credit the result to himself.

Because of the wickedness of these nations. Neither real reason lies in Israel: the land is judgment on Canaan, not reward for Israel (see the introduction on the hard commands), and it keeps the oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, men centuries dead.
