That leaves Israel nothing to claim. It is grace stated as plainly as Paul states it: “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:5).

The only righteous one. Only one Israelite could ever have said “because of my righteousness” and told the truth, and Jesus did not keep the inheritance for himself but shares it with stubborn people, who enter on his merit. Every Christian who has begun to feel that his standing with God depends on how the last few months have gone should read these three verses slowly.

Why do we need to be the good guys? Almost every nation tells its history as a story in which it won because it deserved to, and so do movements and individuals; listen to anyone explain a promotion or a divorce. We cannot bear to be merely fortunate, still less forgiven. Deuteronomy, the founding document of a nation, tells its people on the eve of victory that they are not the good guys, because God loves them too much to let victory curdle into pride. The moralist must admit he has no record to stand on; the cynic who says nobody is good must hear that God gives anyway. Christians have stopped needing to win the argument about their own goodness: the verdict went against them and in Christ they are accepted anyway, so they can be honest about their history, their nation and themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — The Golden Calf: Provoking God to Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The proof that Israel has no righteousness to boast of is the golden calf. Moses tells them to remember what they did to God, not only what God did for them, and sums up forty years as rebellion from Egypt to Moab (v. 7). Horeb is the worst of it (vv. 8–10): while Moses fasted forty days and God wrote the covenant with his own finger, the people at the foot of the mountain were making an idol. God tells Moses to go down, calls them “your people”, and says, “Let me alone, that I may destroy them,” offering to make a greater nation from Moses instead (vv. 11–14). The covenant was broken while it was being written.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin runs deep even in God’s redeemed people, which is why their standing has to rest on grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Even in our most privileged moments we are prone to wander, and that keeps us dependent on mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD. Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you. When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water. And the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words that the LORD had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must remember not only what God did for them but what they did to him, above all at Horeb, where they broke the covenant while God was still writing it.

Remember and do not forget. In chapter 8 Moses told them to remember God’s kindness; here, their own rebellion. A memory that keeps only the mercies produces sentimentality, one that keeps only the failures despair; Israel is to hold both. And the failures are not a bad patch but the whole history, from Egypt “until you came to this place”.

Even at Horeb. Moses spent forty days on the mountain without bread or water while God wrote the covenant with his own finger, and during those same days, at the foot of the same mountain, the nation was casting a calf. The covenant was broken while it was being written, by people who weeks earlier had said, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (Exodus 19:8). Nearness to holy things is no protection from idolatry.

Forty days and forty nights. Jesus, the true Israel, also fasted “forty days and forty nights” in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), and where Israel turned to an idol the moment their leader was out of sight, he refused every temptation and worshipped his Father alone, answering the devil from this book.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of forty days and forty nights the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant. Then the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them; they have made themselves a metal image.' "Furthermore, the LORD said to me, 'I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stubborn people. Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told Moses the people had already broken the covenant, and offered to destroy them and start again with him, words meant to draw out the prayer that would save them.

Your people whom you have brought from Egypt. God’s words to Moses are abrupt: not “my people” but “your people”. He hands them back to Moses, the way a father says “your son” to his wife when the boy has disgraced himself.

A metal image. The calf was probably meant as an image of the LORD himself, or a pedestal for him, since Aaron called the feast that followed a feast “to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5). That makes it no better: the God who showed no form at Horeb forbids being worshipped by an image of our own making (4:15–16; 5:8–9).

Let me alone… I will make of you a nation mightier. A genuine offer of a fresh start from Moses’ own line, as tempting as any worn-out leader could imagine. But nothing restrains the Almighty, so why say this to a man? The words forbid, but they really invite: to tell someone not to hold you back is to tell him he can, and Moses at once began to hold God back. God tells his intercessors what he is about to do in terms that all but invite them to plead against it, as Abraham found over Sodom: “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do” (Genesis 18:17).

Does prayer change God’s mind? The threat was real, and God used it to draw out Moses’ intercession (vv. 18–19; 10:10). His eternal purpose included the prayer as the means by which he spared Israel (compare Jeremiah 18:7–10), so prayer is never pointless, and when Scripture speaks of God relenting it speaks in human terms, not of a God surprised or improved by our advice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Moses Breaks the Tablets and Destroys the Calf
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses comes down to find the covenant already broken, deals with the sin openly, and then intercedes for the guilty. With the mountain burning behind him he sees the calf and smashes the tablets before the people’s eyes, a public sign that the covenant lies in pieces (vv. 15–17). Then he falls on his face before the LORD for forty days and nights without food, afraid of God’s anger against them, and the LORD listens to him that time also (vv. 18–19). He prays even for Aaron, the man who made the calf (v. 20). Finally he burns the idol, grinds it to dust and throws it into the stream, so that nothing is left to recover (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The broken tablets act out the broken covenant, and the ground-up calf shows that God tolerates no rivals.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian, forgiven in Christ, destroys a cherished idol in the Spirit’s strength rather than merely setting it aside.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands. And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you. So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses came down, saw the calf, and smashed the tablets in front of the people to show them the covenant was already broken.

You had turned aside quickly. A mountain on fire behind him, and in his arms the only stones God himself had written on. Then the word that stings, “quickly”: not after a generation of drift, but within weeks, while their leader was still up the hill.

Before your eyes. There was anger in it (Exodus 32:19), but this was not a man losing his temper where nobody could see. In the ancient world a broken treaty could be marked by breaking its tablet, and Moses was showing them what they had already done, like tearing up a marriage certificate in front of the bride on the wedding day because she had already been unfaithful.

What only God could mend. Moses could break the tablets but not rewrite them; God wrote them again (10:1–4). In the new covenant he writes his law on the heart itself (Jeremiah 31:33), sealed in Christ’s blood (Hebrews 8:10–12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed, in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger. For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you, so that he was ready to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time also. And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time. Then I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook that ran down from the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses spent another forty days on his face for the people who had betrayed him, prayed even for Aaron who made the calf, and destroyed the idol completely.

I lay prostrate before the LORD. The greatest thing about Moses: forty more days on his face without food, “because of all the sin that you had committed”. He was afraid, not for himself, since God had just offered him a dynasty, but for them. Then the words that carry the chapter: “But the LORD listened to me that time also.”

And I prayed for Aaron also. His own brother, the man who made the calf and then lied about it (Exodus 32:24). Aaron lived to serve as Israel’s first high priest because Moses prayed for him. He prayed hardest for the man who had wronged him most.

A greater Intercessor. Moses offered to be blotted out of God’s book in the people’s place, and God would not take it (Exodus 32:32–33); Moses was a sinner himself. Jesus was cut off for his people, prayed for the men who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and prays for failing disciples as Moses prayed for Aaron: “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

Grinding it very small. Burned, crushed, ground to dust and thrown into running water, so it could never be gathered again. There is a way of dealing with an idol that leaves nothing to come back to, and it is the only way that works (Matthew 5:29–30).

Which forty days? Exodus records a second forty days on the mountain when the tablets were renewed (Exodus 34:28). Most take verses 18 and 25 and 10:10 to describe that period; some see a separate fast. Either way, Moses pleaded and Israel was spared.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — Moses’ Great Intercession: For Your Name’s Sake
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses shows that the calf was no isolated lapse, then gives the prayer that saved Israel, which pleads nothing in them. Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah and Kadesh-barnea each mark a sin committed where God had just provided, and at Kadesh they “did not believe him or obey his voice” (vv. 22–23). His verdict covers all forty years: rebellious “from the day that I knew you” (v. 24). Then the prayer (vv. 25–29): these are your people and your heritage, whom you redeemed; remember Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; do not look at their stubbornness; do not let Egypt say that you could not finish what you began. Every argument rests on God.
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer that prevails appeals not to our merit but to God’s name, promise and saving work.
verseByVerse.examples: We are heard on the same ground: not our worthiness, but the merit and intercession of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath. And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, 'Go up and take possession of the land that I have given you,' then you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice. You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The calf was no single lapse: Israel’s whole journey is marked by places where they rebelled, and the root of it all was unbelief.

At Taberah also. A geography of failure. Taberah, “burning”, where the LORD’s fire fell on the edge of the camp (Numbers 11:1–3). Massah, “testing”, where they quarrelled over water (Exodus 17:1–7). Kibroth-hattaavah, “graves of craving”, where they demanded meat and many died with it still in their mouths (Numbers 11:31–34). Every one was a place where God had already provided.

Did not believe him or obey his voice. Then Kadesh-barnea, in one sentence that reaches the root (1:19–46): believe and obey, in that order, with the failure of the first producing the failure of the second. Disobedience is unbelief acting itself out.

From the day that I knew you. Moses’ verdict on forty years together, and the earlier chapters bear him out. This unflattering account of God’s own people gives the prayer that follows its force: nobody could read Deuteronomy 9 and conclude that Israel deserved to be saved. The Christian reads his own story the same way: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "So I lay prostrate before the LORD for these forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you. And I prayed to the LORD, 'O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin, lest the land from which you brought us say, "Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness." For they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power and by your outstretched arm.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ prayer pleads nothing in the people, only God’s ownership, promise, saving work and name, and on that ground it was heard.

O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people. A masterclass in intercession. Moses does not argue that the people are better than they look, promise they will improve, or mention his own record or the dynasty he was offered. Every argument is about God.

Your people and your heritage. First, they are God’s own, “whom you have redeemed”: God had called them Moses’ people (v. 12), and Moses answers “your people”. Second, the promise to the patriarchs, made before any of these sinners existed. Third, he asks God not to regard their stubbornness: he denies none of it, which is what a man asks when he has no case. Fourth, most boldly, God’s reputation: Egypt will say the LORD could not finish what he started, or that he hated them.

Praying with nothing to plead. Every argument rested on what God had already said and done. That is how we pray with nothing of our own, and it works, because those are the only grounds that ever have. Praying “in Jesus’ name” is this plea, not a formula (John 16:23–24).

A greater Intercessor. Jesus prays on the same ground, and better: not that we deserve to be kept, but that he bought us with his own blood. “Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

9.theology:
Grace, not righteousness. Moses leaves Israel nothing of her own to point to (9:4–6). Already the Old Testament teaches that God accepts his people by grace, which the gospel states outright: “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9).

The depth of sin. Israel’s whole history was rebellion (9:24), and honest remembrance of it guards against pride. We are more sinful than we dare admit, and more loved than we dare hope.

The mediator. Moses pleaded God’s name, promise and redemption (9:18, 25–29), foreshadowing Christ, who intercedes for his people on the ground of his own sacrifice (Heb 7:25).
9.examples:
On the brink of conquest, Israel was warned never to credit her own righteousness, since she had survived only because Moses pleaded for her.

Christians remember their own rebellion honestly, which keeps them humble and grateful; they grind their idols to dust rather than negotiate with them; and they pray with confidence, not because they deserve a hearing but because Christ’s finished work stands for them.

keyVerse.quote: Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter defends this sentence. The land is a gift, and the people who receive it have earned only judgment, as the calf at Horeb proves. It is the Old Testament’s plainest statement that God’s blessings rest on his grace and promise, never on our merit, which is the ground every believer stands on in Christ.

9.reflection:
Moses warns that the danger comes “after the LORD your God has thrust them out” (v. 4), in the moment of success. Why does success tempt us to think we deserved it? Where have you been tempted to read a blessing as proof of your goodness?

Israel broke the covenant at the foot of the mountain, at the height of their privilege (vv. 8–12). What does this teach about the human heart, and why is being close to holy things no guarantee of faithfulness?

Moses prayed for forty days for the people who had betrayed him, even for Aaron (vv. 18–20), and pleaded nothing but God’s name and promise (vv. 26–29). Who is hard for you to pray for, and what would it look like to pray for them on Moses’ ground?

Moses could only plead; Jesus “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). How does knowing that Christ prays for you change the way you face your own failures?

10.title: Circumcise Your Hearts: What Does the LORD Require of You?
10.text: <sup>1</sup>"At that time the LORD said to me, 'Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood.<sup>2</sup>And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.'<sup>3</sup>So I made an ark of acacia wood, and cut two tablets of stone like the first, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hand.<sup>4</sup>And he wrote on the tablets, in the same writing as before, the Ten Commandments that the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly. And the LORD gave them to me.<sup>5</sup>Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark that I had made. And there they are, as the LORD commanded me."<sup>6</sup>(The people of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried. And his son Eleazar ministered as priest in his place.<sup>7</sup>From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with brooks of water.<sup>8</sup>At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name, to this day.<sup>9</sup>Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.)<sup>10</sup>"I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, so that they may go in and possess the land, which I swore to their fathers to give them.'<sup>12</sup>"And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>13</sup>and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which I am commanding you today for your good?<sup>14</sup>Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it.<sup>15</sup>Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples, as you are this day.<sup>16</sup>Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.<sup>17</sup>For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe.<sup>18</sup>He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing.<sup>19</sup>Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>20</sup>You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear.<sup>21</sup>He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen.<sup>22</sup>Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 ended with smashed tablets and Moses on his face for forty days. Chapter 10 finishes that story (vv. 1–11) and then turns from history to appeal, with “And now, Israel” (v. 12), leading towards the closing call of chapter 11 before the detailed laws begin in chapter 12.

The message. The God who owns the highest heaven has rewritten the covenant his people broke and set his love on them for no reason in them. So give him what he asks: fear, love, obedience, a heart that is no longer stubborn, and a love for the outsider like his own. Everything he asks is for your good, and the heart he asks for is the one thing Israel cannot give itself.

Why it was said. A generation that has just been told it is stubborn (9:6) needs to hear that God has not given up on it, and what he now asks. As they enter a land full of gods who could be bribed and courts that favoured the powerful, they must know a God who takes no bribe and defends the widow (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Grace first: God writes the same words on new tablets, kept in the ark (vv. 1–5); the priesthood continues after Aaron, and Levi’s inheritance is the LORD himself (vv. 6–9); God, unwilling to destroy, sends them on (vv. 10–11). Then the great question, what does the LORD require of you, answered in one sentence (vv. 12–13). Its ground is astonishing love: the owner of heaven set his heart on their fathers (vv. 14–15). So circumcise your hearts (v. 16), love the sojourner as the impartial God does (vv. 17–19), and hold fast to the God who made seventy people as many as the stars (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by promise. “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” is a command no stubborn heart can obey, and Deuteronomy itself promises that God will do it (30:6), which he does in Christ by the Spirit (Colossians 2:11). The law on new stones points to the law written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). And the only Israelite who ever gave God everything this chapter requires was Jesus, who loved his Father with all his heart, for us.

For us. What God asks of us is for our good, and he asks it of people he has already forgiven. Look at your heart, not only your outward religion, and ask him to do what you cannot. Then love the outsider, because you were one, and Christ came and got you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — New Tablets: Grace Rewrites the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the smashed covenant by writing it again, the plainest picture of grace in the books of Moses. He tells Moses to cut two new tablets like the first and to make an ark of wood to hold them (vv. 1–2). Moses cuts the stone; God writes on it the same Ten Commandments he had spoken from the fire, not a lower standard for a people who had failed the first (vv. 3–4). The tablets are laid in the ark, “and there they are” (v. 5): the covenant restored and kept at the heart of Israel’s worship, beneath the lid where atoning blood would be sprinkled.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace rewrites what sin destroyed: God restores the covenant his people broke and keeps his word among them.
verseByVerse.examples: In Christ, God restores what our sin breaks and writes his law on hearts of flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time the LORD said to me, 'Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.' So I made an ark of acacia wood, and cut two tablets of stone like the first, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hand. And he wrote on the tablets, in the same writing as before, the Ten Commandments that the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly. And the LORD gave them to me. Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark that I had made. And there they are, as the LORD commanded me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the calf God did not lower his law or abandon his people: he wrote the same words again on new tablets and had them kept in the ark.

Cut for yourself two tablets of stone. God’s answer to the smashed covenant is the plainest picture of grace in the books of Moses. Israel broke the covenant while it was being written; Moses broke the tablets to show what they had done; and God says: cut two more, and I will write the same words again.

The words that were on the first tablets. Not a lower standard for a people who had failed the higher one. God begins again at exactly the point where they failed. And Moses cuts the stone, but God does the writing: man can prepare the tablets, only God can put anything on them worth having. That matters at verse 16, when the subject moves from stone to hearts, and in the new covenant, where God writes his law on the heart itself (Jeremiah 31:33).

Make an ark of wood. The most sacred object in Israel was a plain box to house a covenant broken before the ink was dry, and God chose to meet his people above it, at its lid, the mercy seat (Numbers 7:89). The broken law lay under a lid sprinkled with sacrificial blood on the Day of Atonement: the whole gospel in a piece of furniture. Paul uses the Greek Old Testament’s word for that lid when he says God put Christ forward as a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath, “by his blood” (Romans 3:25; compare Hebrews 9:5).

A question of timing. Moses says he made the ark before going up; Exodus has Bezalel make it later (Exodus 37:1). Moses is summarising, not giving a timetable: he tells what was done under his command.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — The Levites Set Apart; Moses Prevails
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A short travel note and the end of the intercession story show God keeping his people after the calf. Aaron, who made the calf and was spared through Moses’ prayer, dies, and his son Eleazar serves as priest in his place, so the priesthood goes on (vv. 6–7). At that time God sets apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark, stand before him and bless in his name; Levi receives no land, for “the LORD is his inheritance” (vv. 8–9). Then Moses returns to the mountain: the LORD listened “that time also,” was unwilling to destroy Israel, and sends Moses to lead them into the land (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God provides servants to carry his word and bless his people, and their true inheritance is God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who serve the church in the word are not promised much on earth, but they are promised the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: (The people of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried. And his son Eleazar ministered as priest in his place. From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with brooks of water. At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name, to this day. Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A travel note records that the priesthood went on after Aaron’s death, and that Levi was set apart to serve God with no land, because the LORD himself was Levi’s inheritance.

There Aaron died. The sermon pauses for a travel note (the ESV prints vv. 6–9 in brackets), and it is not out of place. Aaron, spared only because Moses prayed (9:20), served as high priest until his death, and his son succeeded him: the mercy of chapter 9 seen in a family line.

To carry the ark of the covenant. Levi has three duties: carry the ark on the road, stand before God when the camp settles, and bless the people in his name. Because Levi’s work is God’s service, “therefore” Levi gets no land. On the day the country was divided, eleven tribes walked away holding a map: this ridge, that valley, the olive terraces, the boundary stone with a grandfather’s name on it. Levi was handed nothing to leave a son, and instead was given God.

The LORD is his inheritance. One of the great sentences of the Old Testament. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted, the health returned, the debts cleared, and God himself were not there: would that be heaven? The hesitation shows where our hearts have drifted. The answer is not to love God’s gifts less but to find that the Giver is the inheritance that includes all the rest. Every acre the other tribes received could be taken, and eventually was, by drought, debt, Assyria and time; Levi held the one inheritance no army could reach.

Offered to every believer. In Christ every believer is a priest (1 Peter 2:9), and Levi’s inheritance is ours, “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4), with God himself at its heart. Asaph found it after nearly losing his faith: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25).

Uncertain wording. None of these places can be located with confidence (Beeroth Bene-jaakan means wells of the sons of Jaakan). Numbers lists similar names in another order (Numbers 33:30–33) and places Aaron’s death on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:28). Probably Moserah was the district around Mount Hor, and Israel passed this way more than once.

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you. And the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, so that they may go in and possess the land, which I swore to their fathers to give them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing about the people had changed, yet the God who had threatened to destroy them was unwilling to, and sent them on to the land, because a mediator had prayed.

The LORD was unwilling. On the mountain God said, “Let me alone, that I may destroy them” (9:14); now he says, go and lead them into the land I promised. The calf is still powder in a stream and the same men are in the camp. What stands between the two sentences is forty days of a man on his face.

Unwilling, not unable. Not “unable”, and not persuaded against his will: “unwilling”. When it came to it, he did not want to. The intercession was real and God answered it, and behind the answer was a mercy in God’s heart all along. That is why Moses dared to pray: nobody lies on the ground for forty days pleading with someone he thinks is looking for an excuse to destroy.

Arise, go on your journey. Forgiveness sends the forgiven on. The Father who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32) is not reluctantly sparing us but gladly bringing us home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–13 — What Does the LORD Require?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses gathers everything God asks into one sentence, and says it is for Israel’s good. After all the history he asks, “what does the LORD your God require of you?” (v. 12). The answer runs from the heart to the hands: fear him, walk in his ways, love him, serve him with all your heart and soul, and keep his commandments (vv. 12–13). Awe, love and obedience belong together. The final phrase changes how the whole list sounds: these commands are given “for your good,” by a God who has just forgiven and restored the people he addresses.
verseByVerse.theology: True religion is wholehearted, reverent love for God, and his commandments are for our good.
verseByVerse.examples: The same call to fear, walk, love, serve and keep describes the Christian life, now lived in love for God in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which I am commanding you today for your good?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God asks of his people comes down to fearing, loving and obeying him with the whole heart, and all of it is for their good.

What does the LORD your God require of you? After all the history and warnings, Moses asks the question directly and answers it in one sentence, one of the great summaries of the Old Testament, to which Micah will write a companion (Micah 6:8).

To fear the LORD your God. The list runs from the attitude of the heart, fear, reverent awe, to actual obedience, keeping the commandments, and in the middle, holding the two together, love and service with all the heart and soul. Deuteronomy will not let them be separated. Awe without love is terror; love without obedience is sentiment; obedience without either is drudgery. Jesus named the love at the centre of this list the great and first commandment (Matthew 22:37–38).

For your good. God gives commandments not to make life narrow but for his people’s flourishing, the very point the serpent contradicted in Eden. Read with verse 13, the question becomes: what does God ask of you, other than the things that are for your good? And he asks it of a people he has just forgiven and restored.

Who has ever done it? Only one person has ever feared, walked, loved, served and kept with all his heart and soul. Of Jesus it is written, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8; compare Hebrews 10:5–7). His obedience is counted to those who trust him, and his Spirit grows the same love in them. This list was never the way to earn God’s favour: Israel was already redeemed and chosen (v. 15), and obedience is love’s answer to grace, never its price.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — Heaven Belongs to God, Yet He Set His Love on You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who owns everything set his love on Israel for no reason in Israel. Verse 14 lifts our eyes to the scale of God: heaven, the heaven of heavens, the earth and all in it belong to him, so he needs nothing and no one. Verse 15 turns on one word, “yet”: this God set his heart in love on the patriarchs and chose their descendants above all peoples. Election is not explained by anything in the chosen, as chapter 9 has shown, but it is not arbitrary either. It is love, freely given by the God who did not need them.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who owns all things freely chose to love a particular people, and the wonder of election is how low he stooped.
verseByVerse.examples: The God who needs nothing has set his love on us in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it. Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples, as you are this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who owns all heaven and earth, and needs nothing, freely set his love on Israel’s fathers and chose their descendants.

The heaven of heavens. The Hebrew way of saying the highest heaven, everything above and beyond what anyone can see. All of it is his, with the earth and all that is in it (Psalm 24:1). He lacks nothing and needs nobody.

Yet the LORD set his heart in love. And yet the owner of the heaven of heavens set his heart on a family of nomads and their descendants: not because he needed them, which verse 14 rules out, and not because they were impressive, which chapter 9 rules out. “Set his heart” is a word of attachment, of desire, of being drawn (7:7–8).

Chose their offspring after them. God did not choose arbitrarily, like a man picking a number; he chose in love, which is not explained by anything in the chosen. Nobody asks a man why he loves his own child and expects a list of the child’s qualifications. The New Testament says God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), and shares the same astonishment: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Circumcise Your Hearts; Love as God Loves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The love God has shown must reach Israel’s heart and then the outsider. Israel is to cut away the hardness of heart that the outward sign of circumcision could not touch (v. 16). The reason is God himself: the God of gods and Lord of lords takes no bribe and shows no favouritism, and so he defends the fatherless and widow and gives the sojourner food and clothing (vv. 17–18). Israel, once sojourners in Egypt, must love the sojourner too (v. 19). The section ends where Israel’s worship should: fear him, hold fast to him, praise him, for he made seventy people as many as the stars (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Outward religion is not enough; the heart itself must be cut and changed. God’s own justice and compassion are the pattern for his people’s love.
verseByVerse.examples: The new covenant gives the changed heart, and Christians welcome the outsider because God first welcomed them.

verseByVerse.quote: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must deal with the hardness of the heart itself, which the outward sign of circumcision could not touch, a command that only God can fulfil.

Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart. Circumcision was the physical mark of the covenant, cut into every Israelite boy on the eighth day, the sign that he belonged to God’s people. Moses turns it inward: there is something in the human heart like an uncircumcised foreskin, a covering and hardness that must be cut away before there can be real belonging. Israel had the outward mark and was still “stubborn”. A person may bear every external sign of belonging and be untouched underneath.

The prophets and Paul. That is the burden of the prophets afterwards: “all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart” (Jeremiah 9:26). Paul says it to people trusting their pedigree: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29).

An impossible command. No one can cut away his hardness with the very heart that is hard. Deuteronomy knows it. Twenty chapters later the same verb returns, and now God does it: “And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart” (30:6). Here it is commanded; there it is promised. Ezekiel’s great sentence sounds like the answer to this verse, because it is: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The circumcision of Christ. Believers are “circumcised with a circumcision made without hands… by the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11): what the command demanded and the promise held out, the Spirit does when he joins us to Christ. We obey the command by bringing our hard hearts to the only one who can soften them.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe. He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest God of all cannot be bribed or impressed, and so he takes up the cause of those nobody else defends; Israel, once a stranger itself, must love the stranger too.

Not partial and takes no bribe. Five titles, then two negatives that do the work. He is “not partial”, literally he does not lift up faces, favouring the great; and he “takes no bribe”, unlike the gods of the nations, who were thought to be won over by gifts. The New Testament gives the title “Lord of lords” to Jesus (Revelation 19:16).

The fatherless and the widow. He spends his attention on the orphan, the widow and the foreigner, the three groups with no legal standing and no one to speak for them, and his impartiality is not cool neutrality: it puts him on the side of the people nobody else is on the side of. And it is practical: “food and clothing”, not sympathy only but dinner and a coat (James 1:27).

Love the sojourner. The inference is not “therefore admire him” but “Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.” You were one, and somebody came and got you. God’s people treat the outsider as God treated them when they were outside, the logic of Christian mercy in one line (Matthew 18:32–35). Christ himself was carried into Egypt as a refugee child (Matthew 2:14), and he has made outsiders like us family: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

What this looks like. The New Testament carries it over: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers” (Hebrews 13:2). The sojourner today is the refugee family on the next street, the overseas student alone at Christmas, the person sitting alone at the back of church. Learn a name, and use it next week. Open your table: a meal at home says more than a welcome desk. Help with the practical things: a lift, a form, a call to the landlord, a warm coat. Speak up when they are mocked, cheated or talked about as a problem. The motive is the one Moses gives: you were one.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear. He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen. Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to cling to God alone and boast in him alone, the God who turned seventy people into a nation as many as the stars.

Hold fast. Dabaq, the word of 4:4 again: cling, stick, be glued to. It is not a word about opinions but about grip. Jesus answered the devil from this very charge, “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10, quoting 6:13).

He is your praise. Not only the one who deserves praise: he himself is Israel’s boast. A small nation with no army and no land had one glory, and it was God (Jeremiah 9:23–24).

Seventy persons. A village: one extended family going down to Egypt in a famine (Genesis 46). (Stephen’s seventy-five in Acts 7:14 follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 46:27, which counts some further descendants of Joseph.) Four centuries later, a nation nobody can count, on the border of the land promised to Abraham, a childless man once told to try counting the stars (Genesis 15:5). Seventy people and a promise: that is all God started with, and he has never needed more. The church began the same way, about a hundred and twenty in an upstairs room (Acts 1:15), and will end as “a great multitude that no one could number” (Revelation 7:9), Abraham’s offspring in Christ.

10.theology:
A circumcised heart. The stubborn heart itself must be cut and changed (10:16). The command exposes a need it cannot meet, but what is commanded here is promised in 30:6 and given in the new covenant, where God himself changes the heart by the Spirit (Jer 31:33; Rom 2:29).

What the LORD requires. Life with God comes down to fearing, loving and serving him, walking in his ways and keeping his commands, all for your good (10:12–13). Christ met this demand perfectly, and the Spirit works it in us.

The God who loves the lowly. The Lord of heaven, who needs nothing, set his love on a small, undeserving people (10:14–15) and defends the fatherless, the widow and the sojourner (10:17–19). His people love the outsider because they were once outsiders loved by grace.
10.examples:
God rewrote the covenant Israel had broken, gave the Levites himself as their inheritance, and called his people to circumcise their hearts and love the sojourner as he had loved them.

In Christ, God restores what our sin breaks and by his Spirit does the heart-work we could never do. We hold fast to him as our portion and our praise, and we love the outsider and the vulnerable because we were strangers brought near by grace.

keyVerse.quote: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.
keyVerse.note: Everything the chapter asks, fear, love, obedience, love for the stranger, depends on a changed heart, and this verse names the need. It is a command no stubborn heart can obey by itself, which is why Deuteronomy later promises that God will do it (30:6), and the New Testament announces that he does, in the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11).

10.reflection:
God wrote the same words again on new tablets after Israel broke the covenant (vv. 1–4). What does this show about how God deals with failure, and how is it different from simply lowering the standard?

“The LORD is his inheritance” (v. 9). If you had every good gift but not God himself, would it be enough? What helps you treasure the Giver above his gifts?

Moses says God’s commands are “for your good” (v. 13), and calls Israel to circumcise their hearts (v. 16). Why can no one do this for himself, and how does the promise of 30:6 and Colossians 2:11 give hope?

God “loves the sojourner” and Israel must too, “for you were sojourners” (vv. 18–19). Who are the outsiders around you, and what is one practical step you could take this month to welcome them as Christ welcomed you?

11.title: Love and Obey: The Blessing and the Curse Set Before You
11.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always.<sup>2</sup>And consider today (since I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it), consider the discipline of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm,<sup>3</sup>his signs and his deeds that he did in Egypt to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land,<sup>4</sup>and what he did to the army of Egypt, to their horses and to their chariots, how he made the water of the Red Sea flow over them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD has destroyed them to this day,<sup>5</sup>and what he did to you in the wilderness, until you came to this place,<sup>6</sup>and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel.<sup>7</sup>For your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did.<sup>8</sup>"You shall therefore keep the whole commandment that I command you today, that you may be strong, and go in and take possession of the land that you are going over to possess,<sup>9</sup>and that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give to them and to their offspring, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>10</sup>For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables.<sup>11</sup>But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven,<sup>12</sup>a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.<sup>13</sup>"And if you will indeed obey my commandments that I command you today, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>14</sup>he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain, that you may gather in your grain and your wine and your oil.<sup>15</sup>And he will give grass in your fields for your livestock, and you shall eat and be full.<sup>16</sup>Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them;<sup>17</sup>then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit, and you will perish quickly off the good land that the LORD is giving you.<sup>18</sup>"You shall therefore lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.<sup>19</sup>You shall teach them to your children, talking of them when you are sitting in your house, and when you are walking by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.<sup>20</sup>You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates,<sup>21</sup>that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.<sup>22</sup>For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him,<sup>23</sup>then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and mightier than you.<sup>24</sup>Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your territory shall be from the wilderness to the Lebanon, and from the River, the river Euphrates, to the western sea.<sup>25</sup>No one shall be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread, as he promised you.<sup>26</sup>"See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse:<sup>27</sup>the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today,<sup>28</sup>and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known.<sup>29</sup>And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.<sup>30</sup>Are they not beyond the Jordan, west of the road, toward the going down of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, opposite Gilgal, beside the oak of Moreh?<sup>31</sup>For you are to cross over the Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. And when you possess it and live in it,<sup>32</sup>you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today.
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 closes the long opening of Moses’ second address (chapters 5–11), which has laid the foundation of love, memory and grace. It is the last appeal before the detailed laws of chapters 12–26.

The message. Love the LORD and keep his commands, because you have seen with your own eyes what he has done. The land you are entering will keep you looking up to him for every drop of rain, and he calls that care. Lay his words up in your heart and your home, for two ways now lie before you: blessing if you obey, curse if you go after other gods.

Why it was said. The adults Moses addresses had seen the exodus and the wilderness as children; their own children had not (see the introduction). In Canaan they would meet Baal, the storm god who promised rain, and the pull to add him to the LORD as insurance would be strong.

How the chapter makes its case. Remember what your eyes have seen: Egypt judged, the sea, the wilderness, Dathan and Abiram swallowed (vv. 1–7). The land is not like Egypt, watered by human effort, but a land of hills that drinks the rain and that the LORD watches all year (vv. 8–12). Obey, and he will give the early and later rain; turn to other gods, and he will shut the heavens (vv. 13–17). So lay up these words and teach them to your children (vv. 18–21), and the LORD will drive out nations greater than you (vv. 22–25). Finally the choice: blessing and curse, to be proclaimed from Gerizim and Ebal (vv. 26–32).

Where it leads. To Christ, by covenant and by the need it exposes. The chapter sets blessing and curse before a people who will in the end choose the curse, as Moses foresees (31:29). Christ, the only one who loved God and kept his charge always, took the curse on himself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations (Galatians 3:14). And the God whose eyes are on the land all year shows the same care in Christ, who told anxious disciples to “consider the ravens” (Luke 12:24).

For us. We live in an Egypt of irrigation, managing our own supply, and God often moves us into the hills where we cannot. That is his care, not his neglect. Lay his word up in your heart, speak it at your kitchen table, and refuse the quiet idolatry of adding other insurance to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Your Eyes Have Seen: Obey Because You Remember
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to love and obey because they have seen with their own eyes what the LORD has done. Moses binds love and keeping into one command, “always” (v. 1). Then he speaks to the adults who remember, not to the children who have not seen (v. 2), and lists what they witnessed: the signs in Egypt, the Egyptian army drowned in the Red Sea, the long care in the wilderness, and the earth swallowing Dathan and Abiram (vv. 3–6). Mercies and judgments stand side by side, and both show his greatness. “For your eyes have seen” (v. 7): their memories are now their obligation.
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience grows out of remembering what God has done; those who have seen his power have no excuse for unbelief.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians obey in the light of what they have seen of God’s grace in Christ and in their own lives.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always. And consider today (since I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it), consider the discipline of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm, his signs and his deeds that he did in Egypt to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land, and what he did to the army of Egypt, to their horses and to their chariots, how he made the water of the Red Sea flow over them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD has destroyed them to this day, and what he did to you in the wilderness, until you came to this place, and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel. For your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to love God and keep his commands because they have seen with their own eyes his saving acts and his judgments.

Love the LORD your God and keep his charge. Love and obedience in one sentence, as everywhere in Deuteronomy. Love that does not obey is sentiment; obedience that does not love is drudgery. Jesus says the same: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15), and he alone kept the Father’s charge “always”.

Consider today. Moses speaks to those old enough to remember, not their children “who have not known or seen it”: their memories are an obligation. They saw the plagues on Pharaoh, the sea closing over his army, the wilderness, the ground opening under Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:25–33); nobody in the coming generations will. What they do with that decides whether the next generation knows God or has merely heard about him (compare Judges 2:10).

The discipline of the LORD. The list is not all mercies. Pharaoh’s army and Dathan are acts of judgment, set beside the deliverance, and both are grounds for love. A God who never acted against evil would not be worth loving. The wilderness itself was a Father’s training (8:5), as God still trains his children (Hebrews 12:5–11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — The Land God Cares For
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land is a gift that will keep Israel dependent on God, and that dependence is his care. Keeping the commandment brings strength and long life in the land of milk and honey (vv. 8–9). Then the contrast: Egypt was watered by human effort, like a vegetable garden (v. 10); Canaan is hills and valleys that drink the rain from heaven, a land the LORD cares for, his eyes on it from the beginning of the year to the end (vv. 11–12). If they love and serve him, he will send the early and later rain (vv. 13–15). If their hearts are deceived and they serve other gods, he will shut the heavens and they will perish from the land (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: God watches over his people’s land without a break, and daily dependence on him is the rhythm of covenant life.
verseByVerse.examples: The believer looks to heaven for every good gift, including the ones that seem to come by our own effort.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore keep the whole commandment that I command you today, that you may be strong, and go in and take possession of the land that you are going over to possess, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give to them and to their offspring, a land flowing with milk and honey. For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables. But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven, a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God was moving Israel from a land where they could manage their own water to one where they would depend on his rain, and he calls that dependence his care.

Not like the land of Egypt. Egypt was watered by the Nile, which floods on schedule, and by channels opened and closed by hand and foot. An Egyptian farmer did not pray for rain; he dug, and the river came. Water was a matter of engineering.

A land of hills and valleys. Canaan is hills. The rain falls or it does not, and no digging will produce a drop. A farmer there looked up, not across to a river, and could do nothing about it.

A land that the LORD your God cares for. God deliberately moves his people from a country where they could manage their own supply to one where they could not, and he calls it care: “The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.” Anyone whose circumstances have become less controllable than they used to be should hold on to that. The Nile is easier. The hills are where you learn to look up.

The idol of control. Modern life is very like Egypt. We live by irrigation: salaries, insurance, pensions, apps that report everything. These are good gifts, but they breed a quiet conviction that a well-run life ought to be entirely under management, and when something will not be managed, a diagnosis, a child’s choices, we feel cheated. That is how an idol works: it promises control and leaves panic behind. Israel’s move into the hills was a move from engineering to trust.

The Son who trusted. The Son of God entered the least controllable life imaginable, homeless, misunderstood and finally nailed down so that he could not move his hands, and he went through it trusting his Father. Because he did, a believer can lose control of nearly everything and still not lose the One whose eyes are on his life from the beginning of the year to the end (Luke 12:24–32).

Uncertain wording. “Irrigated it” is literally “watered it with your foot”. What the phrase described is not certain: it may mean opening and closing the mud banks of irrigation channels with the foot, or working a foot-powered water wheel or pump. Either way the point is clear: in Egypt water came by human labour, in Canaan by God’s rain.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew says Israel watered Egypt “with your foot” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "And if you will indeed obey my commandments that I command you today, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul, he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain, that you may gather in your grain and your wine and your oil. And he will give grass in your fields for your livestock, and you shall eat and be full. Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them; then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit, and you will perish quickly off the good land that the LORD is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will give the rain if Israel loves and serves him, and will withhold it if they turn to the storm gods of Canaan: the rain is his.

The early rain and the later rain. The autumn rain that softened the ground for ploughing and the spring rain that filled the grain. Miss either and the year fails. James borrows the picture for Christians waiting for Christ’s return: “See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains” (James 5:7).

He will shut up the heavens. The gods of Canaan were fertility gods, and Baal was the storm god, lord of the rain; in a dry spring you went to Baal. So God says: the rain is mine, and if you go to Baal for it I will stop it. He meets them on the exact ground of the temptation. Centuries later Elijah told Ahab, “there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word” (1 Kings 17:1), and on Carmel Baal’s prophets spent a whole day failing to get their storm god to send fire. This verse is the text Elijah stood on.

Lest your heart be deceived. Not “lest you rebel”. Nobody meant to abandon God for Baal; they meant to keep both, with a little insurance for the harvest. Idolatry usually arrives as something added to God, not as a replacement for him.

What it does not mean. This is a covenant promise to Israel in its land, not a rule that every drought today judges a particular sin. God “sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45), and hard providences are never by themselves a verdict on the sufferer.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 5:24 and Joel 2:23 also name these two rains, autumn and spring, as God’s gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Lay Up These Words; Teach Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s words are to fill heart, home and household, and to be handed on, because the future of his people depends on it. Moses repeats the Shema’s instructions: lay up these words, bind them on hand and forehead, teach them to the children at home and on the road, from waking to sleeping, write them on doorposts and gates (vv. 18–20), so that their days may be as long as the heavens are above the earth (v. 21). If they love, walk and hold fast, the LORD will drive out greater nations (vv. 22–23). Wherever they tread will be theirs, from wilderness to Lebanon and Euphrates to the sea, and no one will stand against them (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s word is meant to fill heart and home across the generations.
verseByVerse.examples: Faith is still handed on chiefly at home, in ordinary conversation.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall teach them to your children, talking of them when you are sitting in your house, and when you are walking by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates, that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s words are to fill the heart, shape the home and be passed to the children, and through this ordinary means he keeps his people for generations.

Lay up these words of mine. Moses repeats the Shema’s instructions almost word for word, five chapters on (6:6–9). He is not running out of material; he is sharpening the same edge again.

As long as the heavens are above the earth. One addition comes at the end. The promise is measured against the permanence of the sky, and the means by which it reaches that far is not a monument or an institution but parents talking to children in the kitchen and on the road. It looks fragile, and it is not: institutions preserve documents, families hand on faith.

The word dwelling in us. For the church this verse becomes “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Colossians 3:16): in the heart, at home, in the songs we teach our children.

Are these signs literal? The language is figurative, as in Proverbs 7:3: God’s words are to govern what we do and how we see. Jewish practice took it literally with tefillin (small Scripture boxes worn at prayer) and the mezuzah (on the doorpost); Christians are free but not bound to do the same.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him, then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and mightier than you. Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your territory shall be from the wilderness to the Lebanon, and from the River, the river Euphrates, to the western sea. No one shall be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread, as he promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel loves, walks with and clings to the LORD, he will give them the whole land and no enemy will stand against them.

Holding fast to him. Three verbs recur through this book like a refrain: loving, walking, holding fast. Affection, direction and grip. Take away any one and the others fail.

Every place on which the sole of your foot treads. The promise is extravagant: territory measured by where their feet tread. God gives it, and they must still put their feet on it (Joshua 1:3–5); Israel’s rule reached these borders under Solomon (1 Kings 4:21). And the war would be won in the Canaanites’ minds before Israel arrived, as Rahab of Jericho confirms: “the fear of you has fallen upon us… our hearts melted” (Joshua 2:9, 11).

A national promise. A promise to a nation under a specific covenant, not a formula for a Christian’s circumstances: many who wrote the New Testament were put to death. What carries across is that the outcome does not depend on the size of what is in front of you, for Christ has “all authority in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18).

Where Christians differ: does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists hold that the promise to Abraham’s physical descendants, with its borders, awaits literal fulfilment, and many Christian Zionists see the modern state as its beginning. Many who do not expect a return to the land still expect a great turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–29). This commentary’s view: the land promise was fulfilled in Joshua’s day, “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed” (Joshua 21:45), and it points beyond itself. Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), the patriarchs looked for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), and the meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The land is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit. Christians should still love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation, and hold this difference charitably.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–32 — The Blessing and the Curse Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets before Israel the choice that runs through the whole book: blessing or curse. The blessing comes if they obey the LORD’s commandments; the curse if they turn aside to go after gods they have not known (vv. 26–28). There is no third way. When they enter the land they are to proclaim the blessing from Mount Gerizim and the curse from Mount Ebal, two mountains facing each other near the oak of Moreh, where God first promised the land to Abram (vv. 29–30). They will surely cross and possess it, and then they must be careful to do all the statutes that now follow (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: Every generation faces the choice between blessing and curse, and the curse for disobedience is finally borne by Christ (Gal 3:13).
verseByVerse.examples: The gospel sets life before us in Christ, who bore the curse so that we might receive the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse: the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today, and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses sets before Israel two ways only, blessing for obedience and curse for turning to other gods, the choice that runs through the whole book.

See, I am setting before you. Moses holds two things up before a crowd, the choice he will press for the last time in chapter 30: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life” (30:19). There is no comfortable middle. “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12:30) is the same sentence in a later century.

Other gods that you have not known. A man who turns aside from the way does not stand still in an empty field; he goes after something, gods that have never done anything for him, chosen precisely because they are new.

Who bore the curse? Israel would choose the curse (31:29), as every human heart has. The good news is not that the curse was cancelled but that it was carried: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Christ walked the way of blessing all his life and then stood under the curse at the cross, so that those who trust him receive the blessing he earned.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. Are they not beyond the Jordan, west of the road, toward the going down of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, opposite Gilgal, beside the oak of Moreh? For you are to cross over the Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. And when you possess it and live in it, you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel enters the land, the blessing and the curse are to be proclaimed aloud from two mountains at Shechem, where God first promised the land to Abram.

The blessing on Mount Gerizim. Gerizim and Ebal face each other with Shechem in the valley between, and travellers have long reported that a voice carries across it. The ceremony is laid down in chapter 27 and carried out in Joshua 8:33–35, with half the tribes on each slope and the ark between. Shechem, by the oak of Moreh, is where the LORD first appeared to Abram in Canaan and said, “To your offspring I will give this land” (Genesis 12:6–7). The covenant is proclaimed where the promise was first spoken.

A covenant made visible. God gives his people not only statements but things to stand in and taste: a Passover meal, a rainbow, water, bread and wine. This was a covenant you had to climb a hill to hear.

Worship on this mountain. Gerizim later became the Samaritans’ holy mountain, and a Samaritan woman raised it with Jesus: “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” (John 4:20). His answer moved worship from both mountains to himself: “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23).

Be careful to do all the statutes. Not admire them, not agree with them: do them, which is where chapter 12 and the laws proper begin.

Uncertain wording. Verse 30 is hard to map. Gerizim and Ebal are some thirty miles from the Gilgal by Jericho, so “opposite Gilgal” may mean another Gilgal, or give a general direction from the Jordan valley. The oak of Moreh (the Hebrew may be plural, and the tree may be a terebinth) was a landmark near Shechem. Either way the mountains lie in the heart of the land, at the place of Abram’s first altar.
verseByVerse.note: Shechem, in the valley between them, is where God first promised the land to Abraham (Gen 12:6–7).

11.theology:
Love shown in obedience. Love and obedience are inseparable (11:1; John 14:15). Such love is not the price of God’s favour but the answer to it. Only Christ has loved and obeyed wholly, and he did it in our place; the Spirit who pours God’s love into our hearts (Rom 5:5) makes it possible in us.

The land God cares for. God designed a life of daily, upward dependence in a land on which his eyes never close (11:11–12; cf. Ps 121).

Blessing and curse. Every generation faces this choice, and there is no neutral ground (11:26). The curse fell in the exile, but the gospel’s glory is that Christ redeemed us by “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that all who trust him receive the blessing.
11.examples:
Israel, having seen God’s mighty acts, was called to love and obey him, to depend on the rain of a land he watched over, to fill home and heart with his word, and to choose between blessing and curse.

We obey in the light of God’s grace in Christ, live in daily dependence on the Father who watches over us, hand the gospel to our children, and rejoice that the curse we earned has been borne on the tree, so that we stand on the mountain of blessing.

keyVerse.quote: a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s call to love and obey rests on this picture of God’s constant care. Israel was moved from a land they could water themselves to one where they depended on his rain, and God calls that dependence care. In Christ the same Father’s eyes are on his children every day of the year.

11.reflection:
Moses tells the adults that what their eyes have seen is now an obligation to their children (vv. 2–7). What has God done in your life that the next generation has not seen? How are you passing it on?

Egypt was watered by human effort, Canaan by God’s rain (vv. 10–12). Where do you rely on “irrigation”, systems you control, and how do you respond when life will not be managed? What would it mean to receive that as God’s care?

Israel’s temptation was not to abandon God but to add Baal as insurance (vv. 16–17). What are the “something extra” idols you are tempted to add to God?

Blessing and curse are set before Israel (vv. 26–28), and Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). How does knowing that he bore the curse change the way you hear God’s commands?

12.title: The Central Sanctuary: Worship God His Way, Not Ours
12.text: <sup>1</sup>"These are the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live on the earth.<sup>2</sup>You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>3</sup>You shall tear down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and burn their Asherim with fire. You shall chop down the carved images of their gods and destroy their name out of that place.<sup>4</sup>You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.<sup>5</sup>But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there.
