There you shall go,<sup>6</sup>and there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock.<sup>7</sup>And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.<sup>8</sup>"You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes,<sup>9</sup>for you have not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>10</sup>But when you go over the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to inherit, and when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety,<sup>11</sup>then to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there, there you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, and all your finest vow offerings that you vow to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you.<sup>13</sup>Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see,<sup>14</sup>but at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I am commanding you.<sup>15</sup>"However, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you. The unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the gazelle and as of the deer.<sup>16</sup>Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.<sup>17</sup>You may not eat within your towns the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil, or the firstborn of your herd or of your flock, or any of your vow offerings that you vow, or your freewill offerings or the contribution that you present,<sup>18</sup>but you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all that you undertake.<sup>19</sup>Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.<sup>20</sup>"When the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has promised you, and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire.<sup>21</sup>If the place that the LORD your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock, which the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire.<sup>22</sup>Just as the gazelle or the deer is eaten, so you may eat of it. The unclean and the clean alike may eat of it.<sup>23</sup>Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh.<sup>24</sup>You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.<sup>25</sup>You shall not eat it, that all may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>26</sup>But the holy things that are due from you, and your vow offerings, you shall take, and you shall go to the place that the LORD will choose,<sup>27</sup>and offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but the flesh you may eat.<sup>28</sup>Be careful to obey all these words that I command you, that it may go well with you and with your children after you forever, when you do what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.<sup>29</sup>"When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess, and you dispossess them and dwell in their land,<sup>30</sup>take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.'<sup>31</sup>You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way, for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods.<sup>32</sup>"Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 5–11 laid the foundation: grace, love and the call to remember. Now Moses begins the detailed laws of the covenant (chapters 12–26), and the very first subject is worship. Before Israel is told how to run its courts, its farms or its families, it is told how to approach God.

The message. God decides how he is to be worshipped. Israel must tear down the shrines of Canaan and not borrow their ways, even to worship the LORD; they are to come to the one place he chooses, bring what he asks, and rejoice there as a family before him. Ordinary life is set free, but the approach to God is his to define, and nothing may be added to his word or taken from it.

Why it was said. Canaan was full of hilltop shrines in beautiful places, and a settled people would be tempted to set up their own altars wherever they liked and to copy what seemed to work for their neighbours (see the introduction). That road ended in the fire where Canaanites burned their children (v. 31).

How the chapter makes its case. First demolition: destroy every place of false worship, and do not worship the LORD in that way (vv. 1–4). Then the one place he will choose for his name, where Israel will eat and rejoice before him (vv. 5–7), unlike the wilderness, where each did what was right in his own eyes (vv. 8–14). Ordinary meat may be eaten anywhere, but the blood must be poured out, the holy gifts brought to God’s place, and the Levite never neglected (vv. 15–28). Finally, do not ask how the nations served their gods: add nothing and take nothing away (vv. 29–32).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and promise. The place God chose for his name became Jerusalem and its temple, and the temple pointed to Jesus, in whom God’s name and presence dwell: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21). Now the Father is worshipped “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23) through the Son, who is the one way of approach; the blood poured out at the altar points to his blood; and the joyful meal before the LORD points to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

For us. Worship is not ours to design. The question in every generation is not whether a practice is beautiful or effective but whether God asked for it. Yet the God who narrows the way fills it with joy: come to him through Christ, with your family and the forgotten, and rejoice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Destroy the Places of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The laws begin with worship, and worship begins with demolition. Israel is to be careful to keep these statutes all their days in the land (v. 1). Every place where the nations served their gods, on mountains, hills and under green trees, must be destroyed: altars torn down, pillars smashed, Asherah poles burned, images cut down and their very names wiped out (vv. 2–3). Then the sentence on which the chapter turns: “You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way” (v. 4). The danger is not only false gods but the true God worshipped by borrowed methods.
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be worshipped in the manner of false gods, so their shrines had to go.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers, bought by Christ, refuse to worship God by borrowed methods, however attractive the setting.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live on the earth. You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree. You shall tear down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and burn their Asherim with fire. You shall chop down the carved images of their gods and destroy their name out of that place. You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Israel is taught how to worship, it must destroy every place of false worship, and must not worship even the true God in the nations’ way.

You shall surely destroy. The law proper begins with worship, and worship begins with demolition: altars torn down, pillars broken, Asherim burnt, images cut to pieces, the very names of the places wiped out. Before Israel is told how to worship, she is told what to knock down. This was a command for Israel in its land (see the introduction), never a licence for Christians to attack others’ places of worship (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Under every green tree. The shrines stood on hilltops and under great trees. Canaanite worship was set in beautiful places, and that was part of its power. False religion has often understood atmosphere better than true religion, and a beautiful place can make a false god seem real.

Not in that way. Verse 4 is the turning point. The danger is not only that Israel will worship Baal but that she will worship the LORD in Baal’s manner: the right God, by a borrowed method. That is a subtler failure than idolatry and a commoner one, and the rest of the chapter is built on it (see the note on vv. 29–32).

Cleansing the temple. Jesus overturned the traders’ tables in his Father’s house, zealous that God be worshipped as God wished (John 2:13–17).

Uncertain wording. The Asherim were objects sacred to the goddess Asherah, but exactly what they were is uncertain; the verbs used of them (burn, cut down, plant) suggest wooden poles or living trees beside an altar.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — The Place the LORD Will Choose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Over against the many shrines, God will choose one place for his name, and Israel is to go there and rejoice. They are to seek that place and bring all their offerings and tithes there, eating before the LORD with their households in gladness (vv. 5–7). The wilderness, where each did what was right in his own eyes, will no longer be the pattern once God gives them rest in the land (vv. 8–10). Then all the offerings go to the chosen place, and sons, daughters, servants and the landless Levite rejoice together (vv. 11–12). Burnt offerings may not be made at any place a person happens to like, only where God chooses (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: God decides where and how he is to be met. One chosen place guarded the purity and unity of Israel’s worship, and it points to Christ, the true meeting place with God.
verseByVerse.examples: We come to God through Christ, the true temple and only mediator, not by paths of our own devising.

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go, and there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock. And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of shrines on every hill, God will choose one place for his name, and there his people are to bring their offerings and eat with joy before him.

The place that the LORD your God will choose. God appoints one address, and does not name it. Deuteronomy says “the place that the LORD your God will choose”, or something like it, some twenty times and never says where. The choosing is God’s, and withholding the name keeps it his.

To put his name. His name means his ownership and presence. It was first Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12) and later Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:29). Its fulfilment is Christ, in whom God’s name and presence came to dwell among us: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). God’s people meet him now not at an address but in his Son (John 4:21–24).

You shall rejoice. Then a surprise in a chapter about demolition: “there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice”. The centre of Israel’s worship is a family meal eaten in God’s presence with gladness. God narrows the location of worship and then fills it with roast meat, wine, family and joy, which is how the story finishes: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

The question of date. Many critical scholars date this law to King Josiah’s centralising of worship in Jerusalem (2 Kings 23; see the introduction). But a law written to promote Jerusalem would hardly leave it unnamed, and Shiloh fits a command given before the place was known.
verseByVerse.note: God’s name dwelt first at Shiloh and finally at Jerusalem, where Solomon’s prayer at the temple’s dedication recalls this promise (1 Kgs 8:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes, for you have not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you. But when you go over the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to inherit, and when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety, then to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there, there you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, and all your finest vow offerings that you vow to the LORD. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you. Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see, but at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I am commanding you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the land, worship is no longer to follow each person’s own judgment but God’s choice, because God will give his people rest and a place for his name.

Whatever is right in his own eyes. This is the phrase Judges uses to explain its own horrors: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25; 17:6), the refrain that frames the worst chapters in the Old Testament.

All that we are doing here today. In the land, the wilderness habit would become anarchy, each family with a hilltop and a preference. The problem is not that people did what was wrong in their own eyes but that their own eyes had become the standard. Sincerity is not the issue; the question is who decides. Earnest self-rule, three generations on, is Judges.

To the rest and to the inheritance. The corrective is God’s rest and God’s choice. Judges blames the lack of a king; the answer is the King who gives rest, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). So the New Testament, free about location, still insists that worship is not ours to design: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). The place has changed; the principle has not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — Eating Meat, Blood, and Bringing Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God frees ordinary eating while guarding the holy things, the blood and the Levite. Meat may now be slaughtered and eaten in any town, as freely as gazelle or deer, by clean and unclean alike (vv. 15, 20–22). But the blood must be poured on the ground, for “the blood is the life” (vv. 16, 23–25). Tithes, firstborn animals, vows and freewill offerings must still be eaten before the LORD at the chosen place, with the whole household and the Levite, whom Israel must never neglect (vv. 17–19). Holy offerings go to God’s altar, where their blood is poured out; doing this brings good to Israel and their children for ever (vv. 26–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Life belongs to God, as the poured-out blood showed, while his ordinary gifts are to be enjoyed with thanks.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians honour the blood of Christ, by which life is given, and eat their daily bread with gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: "However, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you. The unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the gazelle and as of the deer. Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water. You may not eat within your towns the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil, or the firstborn of your herd or of your flock, or any of your vow offerings that you vow, or your freewill offerings or the contribution that you present, but you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all that you undertake. Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ordinary meat may now be eaten anywhere, freely and gladly, but the holy offerings belong at God’s place and the Levite must never be forgotten.

You may slaughter and eat meat. A generous concession. In the wilderness, killing a domestic animal for food was tied to the sanctuary (Leviticus 17:3–6); spread over settled country, that would be impossible. So God releases it: meat in any town, “as much as you desire”, like the gazelle and deer that were never offered on the altar. The chapter that restricts sacrifice frees ordinary eating, in warm language. God is not grudging about his people’s dinner tables (1 Timothy 4:4).

Only you shall not eat the blood. Two things stay fixed: the blood poured out, and the holy gifts eaten at the chosen place with the whole household and the Levite.

Take care that you do not neglect the Levite. The Levite had no field and would prosper only if people remembered him. God does not leave the support of his servants to spontaneous goodwill; he commands it, by name, in a paragraph about meat, because the people most likely to be forgotten are the ones with no way of pressing their case. The New Testament carries the principle over: “the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has promised you, and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire. If the place that the LORD your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock, which the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire. Just as the gazelle or the deer is eaten, so you may eat of it. The unclean and the clean alike may eat of it. Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh. You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out on the earth like water. You shall not eat it, that all may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD. But the holy things that are due from you, and your vow offerings, you shall take, and you shall go to the place that the LORD will choose, and offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but the flesh you may eat. Be careful to obey all these words that I command you, that it may go well with you and with your children after you forever, when you do what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meat may be eaten anywhere, but its blood must be poured out, because life belongs to God; and holy offerings must still go to his altar.

The blood is the life. The one restriction comes with a reason. Blood carries life, and life belongs to God; pouring it out handed back what was his. Israel’s cooks were made to think, every time, about the cost of the meal. At the altar the blood was poured out for another reason: God had given it “to make atonement for your souls” (Leviticus 17:11).

Christ offers his own life. Against this rule one saying of Jesus stands out: “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54). It shocked its hearers because of this law: Israel might never consume the life, but Christ gives his own, poured out at the cross, to be received by faith. The blood poured on Israel’s altars pointed to his, for “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Hebrews 9:22).

With your children after you. Even a rule about draining a carcass looks to the next generation: “that all may go well with you and with your children after you.”

Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Genesis 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). But the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:4), and most Christians have concluded that the principle, reverence for the life God gives, remains, while eating meat that is not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine: a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–32 — Do Not Inquire How the Nations Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not copy how the nations worshipped, because their worship ended in the worst evil of all. When the nations are gone, Israel must not be snared into asking how they served their gods so as to do the same (vv. 29–30). “You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way”: the LORD hates everything they did, and they even burned their children in the fire (v. 31). The chapter closes with the rule for all that follows: do everything God commands, adding nothing to it and taking nothing from it (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: Worship is governed by what God has said, and the curiosity that copies pagan worship ends in horror.
verseByVerse.examples: The church worships by God’s word, neither borrowing the world’s methods nor inventing its own.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess, and you dispossess them and dwell in their land, take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.' You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way, for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods. "Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must not borrow the nations’ ways of worship, because that road ended in burning children, and must add nothing to God’s commands and take nothing from them.

How did these nations serve their gods? The man in verse 30 has not stopped believing in the LORD; he means to worship him. He is curious about method, what the neighbours did and what worked, and he wants to borrow it. God calls that a snare.

They even burn their sons and their daughters. That is where borrowed method ends. Nobody arrives at child sacrifice in one step; it is reached by a long series of small adoptions, each of which seemed a matter of form rather than substance, and Israel did arrive there, in the valley of Hinnom, centuries later (Jeremiah 7:31).

You shall not add to it or take from it. As at 4:2, and here specifically about worship. He has said how he will be approached, and the question in every generation is not whether a form is beautiful, effective or moving, but whether he asked for it. Jesus applied the same test: “in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Matthew 15:9). Yet God asks it of a people he has already brought in to eat and rejoice before him: careful worship is the answer of the welcomed, not the fee for entry, and we come only “by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us” (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Where Christians differ: does verse 32 (with v. 4) mean the church may do in worship only what Scripture commands? The Reformed tradition holds the regulative principle: God is to be worshipped only in the ways he has appointed in his word. Lutherans and Anglicans hold the normative principle: what Scripture does not forbid is allowed if it edifies. Both want to honour Scripture; they differ over how far its silence binds, and even Reformed churches apply the principle differently, for example on hymns and instruments. This commentary’s view: the regulative principle, applied with wisdom, is the better reading of passages like this and Leviticus 10. The elements of worship are the reading and preaching of the word, prayer, singing, and the two ordinances, while circumstances such as time, place and order are left to wisdom; additions such as drama, liturgical dance and religious images go beyond what God has asked.

12.theology:
Worship on God’s terms. God will not be approached by the methods of the nations (12:31) or by whatever seems right to us (12:8), and nothing may be added to his commands or taken from them (12:32). None of us worships as purely as this; our acceptance rests on Christ, who gave the Father perfect worship in our place, and by his Spirit we now draw near.

The one chosen place. The single sanctuary points to Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), in whom we worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

The blood is the life. The ban on eating blood (12:23) teaches reverence for life as God’s gift and points towards atonement, fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, by which alone we have life.
12.examples:
Entering the land, Israel was to tear down every shrine, feast at the one place God chose, treat the blood as belonging to God, and refuse to worship the LORD by the methods of the nations.

We come to God not at a building but through Christ. We honour the blood by which we have life, enjoy God’s gifts with thanksgiving, and guard our worship by his Word, refusing both to borrow the world’s methods and to invent our own.

keyVerse.quote: Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s whole concern is that God, not his people, decides how he is to be approached, and this verse states the rule. It guards against borrowing the nations’ ways (vv. 30–31) and against each doing what is right in his own eyes (v. 8). For Christians it means coming to God through Christ alone, in the ways he has given.

12.reflection:
God told Israel, “You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way” (v. 4). Why is worshipping the true God in a borrowed way so dangerous? What modern pressures shape how churches worship?

The centre of Israel’s worship was a joyful family meal before the LORD, shared with servants and the landless Levite (vv. 7, 12, 18). How can our worship and our tables reflect that kind of gladness and welcome?

“Everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes” (v. 8). Where do you see that principle at work in your own approach to God, and how does Christ, the King who gives rest, answer it?

The place God chose for his name is fulfilled in Jesus (John 2:19–21; 4:21–24). What difference does it make that we meet God not at a place but in his Son?

13.title: Warning Against False Prophets: Guard the Heart's Allegiance
13.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder,<sup>2</sup>and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, 'Let us go after other gods,' which you have not known, 'and let us serve them,'<sup>3</sup>you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams. For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>4</sup>You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him.<sup>5</sup>But that prophet or that dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery, to make you leave the way in which the LORD your God commanded you to walk. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>6</sup>"If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which neither you nor your fathers have known,<sup>7</sup>some of the gods of the peoples who are around you, whether near you or far off from you, from the one end of the earth to the other,<sup>8</sup>you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.<sup>9</sup>But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people.<sup>10</sup>You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>11</sup>And all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you.<sup>12</sup>"If you hear in one of your cities, which the LORD your God is giving you to dwell there,<sup>13</sup>that certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which you have not known,<sup>14</sup>then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you,<sup>15</sup>you shall surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword, devoting it to destruction, all who are in it and its cattle, with the edge of the sword.<sup>16</sup>You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again.<sup>17</sup>None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers,<sup>18</sup>if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments that I am commanding you today, and doing what is right in the sight of the LORD your God.
13.overview:
Where we are. The detailed laws began in chapter 12 by guarding the place and manner of Israel’s worship (12:29–32). Chapter 13 guards its object, against the voices that would draw Israel to other gods.

The message. God’s people must love him more than any voice that would lead them away, however impressive, dear or popular. A real miracle does not make a false message true, family ties do not outrank loyalty to the God who redeemed you, and a majority does not make rebellion right. God allows such voices as a test of love, and treats leading his people away from him as the gravest crime in the covenant.

Why it was said. Israel was about to settle among nations full of gods and shrines (see the introduction). The greatest danger would be persuasion from inside, through Israel’s own prophets, homes and towns, and so it proved (1 Kings 12:28).

How the chapter makes its case. Three cases, each closer to home. A prophet whose sign comes true must not be heeded if he calls Israel to other gods, for God is testing their love (vv. 1–5). A brother, child, wife or dearest friend who whispers the same in secret must not be followed, pitied or hidden (vv. 6–11). A town drawn away by worthless men must be investigated with great care and, if the charge is certain, devoted to destruction, so that the LORD may show mercy to the nation (vv. 12–18).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the character of God revealed in him. The jealous love that will not share his people with idols is the love that sent his Son to win them back. There is also a sharp irony in the pattern: Jesus worked signs and was accused under the spirit of this very law, charged with “leading the people astray” (John 7:12) and called an “impostor” (Matthew 27:63). Yet he was the one prophet who never led anyone from the God of the exodus but always to him, the Son who loved the LORD with all his heart and soul, and who says, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

For us. Every voice that speaks about God, however impressive or however loved, must be tested by what it says about him and about Christ. The safeguard is not suspicion of everyone but clinging to the Lord who bought us, and the church’s weapons against false teaching are the word, warning and discipline, never the sword.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The False Prophet Who Works Wonders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he calls Israel to other gods. The case is deliberately the hardest one: the wonder is real, and the man is still false, because what he preaches is rebellion against the LORD who redeemed Israel. God explains why he allows it: he is testing whether his people love him with all their heart and soul (vv. 1–3). The answer to seduction is a chain of six verbs ending in “hold fast to him” (v. 4), and the prophet who has taught rebellion must be put to death, so that the evil is purged from Israel (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A message is tested by whether it is faithful to God’s word, not by signs and wonders, and the test shows whether we truly love him.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians test every teaching by Scripture, however impressive the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, 'Let us go after other gods,' which you have not known, 'and let us serve them,' you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams. For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A message that calls you away from the LORD is false even if a real miracle comes with it; God allows such tests to show whether his people love him with all their heart.

A prophet or a dreamer of dreams. The two recognised ways God spoke to prophets (Numbers 12:6): the man has every outward credential.

The sign comes true. The prediction lands, and the man is still to be rejected, because of what he calls them to. Power does not prove that a message is from God. Pharaoh’s magicians copied the first plagues; the Lord Jesus warned that “false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Matthew 24:24); and Paul says the lawless one comes “with all power and false signs and wonders” (2 Thessalonians 2:9). The test of a message has never been whether something remarkable came with it. It is what the message says about God.

Two tests, not one. Chapter 18 gives the other half: a prophet whose prediction fails has not spoken from the LORD (18:21–22). Failure can prove a man false; fulfilment alone cannot prove him true.

The LORD is testing you. The false prophet is not an accident but an examination God sets, and what is examined is not knowledge but love: the words of the Shema (6:5) are quoted directly. A man who loves God with all his heart is not moved by a wonder-worker, because he is not looking for another god.

What it does not mean. This is no reason to treat every answered prayer as suspect. The warning is aimed at the message, not the miracle: whatever draws us from the God of the Bible is false, however it is accompanied (1 John 4:1).

verseByVerse.quote: You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him. But that prophet or that dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery, to make you leave the way in which the LORD your God commanded you to walk. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to seduction is to cling to the LORD who redeemed you; the prophet who preaches rebellion against him must die, because he is trying to lead a redeemed people back towards slavery.

Walk after the LORD your God. Against the seducer stands a chain of six verbs: walk, fear, keep, obey, serve, hold fast. Life with God is not reduced to any one of them, and the last is the strongest: to be glued to him.

Hold fast to him. The remedy for seduction is not suspicion but attachment. A man is not protected from a false teacher by being sceptical of everybody; he is protected by being fastened to somebody. So the New Testament answers false teaching with “abide” more than “argue”: “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).

How do I hold fast to him? A grip is kept by contact. Stay near his voice. Read his word daily, even briefly; a counterfeit is spotted by those who handle the real thing. Belong to a faithful church. Be known by people who would notice if you drifted. Test what attracts you. When a new teacher excites you, do what the Bereans did, “examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11), and ask what it says about Christ and his cross. Talk to someone before you decide. Enticement works “secretly” (v. 6); bring it into the light with a pastor or a trusted friend. Rest in his grip on you. Your hold is weak and his is not: he “is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24). We cling because we are already held.

Who brought you out of the land of Egypt. The size of the crime is measured by the size of the rescue. The prophet has taught rebellion against the God who “redeemed you out of the house of slavery”. To turn a redeemed people away is not a difference of opinion; it marches them back into the slavery they were bought out of.

So you shall purge the evil from your midst. Paul quotes this refrain to the church: “Purge the evil person from among you” (1 Corinthians 5:13). The seriousness carries over, but the church’s penalty is removal from fellowship, not death (see the note on vv. 9–11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — When the Tempter Is a Loved One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second case is the hardest to bear: the tempter is a brother, a son or daughter, “the wife you embrace” or a friend “who is as your own soul”, and the suggestion comes in secret (vv. 6–7). Five refusals follow: do not yield, listen, pity, spare or conceal (v. 8). The penalty is death after trial, and the one who was enticed must strike first, so that no one can make such a charge and keep his own hands clean (vv. 9–10). The purpose is that all Israel will hear and fear (v. 11). No human love may outrank the love owed to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Allegiance to God comes before the closest human ties.
verseByVerse.examples: We love our families rightly only when we love God first.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which neither you nor your fathers have known, some of the gods of the peoples who are around you, whether near you or far off from you, from the one end of the earth to the other, you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No love, not even for the closest family or dearest friend, may be allowed to lead you away from God: you must not follow, pity, spare or hide the one who tempts you.

Your friend who is as your own soul. The second case is the one that hurts. Not a stranger or a public figure, but a brother, “the son of your mother”, the closest tie; your own child; “the wife you embrace”; “your friend who is as your own soul”, the phrase used of Jonathan’s love for David (1 Samuel 18:1). These are the voices we cannot say no to, and God lists them by relationship because he knows it.

Entices you secretly. Not a public challenge but a quiet conversation nobody else hears.

Nor shall you conceal him. Then five refusals, because one would not be enough: do not yield, listen, pity, spare, or “conceal him”, which is what love usually wants to do. The Lord Jesus said the same about the same relationships, in one of the hardest sentences he ever spoke: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). He was not devaluing families but putting them second to God. For a Christian, whose answer to false teaching is warning and not the sword, this means refusing to follow a loved one away from God, not ceasing to love him; many have gone on praying for a wandering son or husband, and seen him come home.

When family becomes a god. For many modern readers family is the last sacred thing left. It is a lovely instinct, and it can become a crushing one. Parents who need their children to succeed so that their own lives will count, a husband or wife expected to give what only God can give: each loads the people we love with a weight they were never made to carry, and love turns anxious and controlling. Deuteronomy does not love families less than we do. It refuses to let them be God, and so protects them from our worship. Christ makes the same move. He put his mother and brothers second to his Father’s will (Mark 3:31–35), and from the cross he provided for his mother with great tenderness (John 19:26–27). Those who love him first find that they love their families better, and need them less.

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. And all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Israel, where God himself was King, enticing others to idolatry was treason, punished by death after trial; the accuser had to strike first, and the aim was that all Israel would hear and fear.

Your hand shall be first against him. The one who was enticed must strike first: nobody may lay a charge and then step back. Three things need saying, and the third matters most.

What this is not. First, it is not a private killing. The next case requires investigation (“you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently”, v. 14), and Deuteronomy elsewhere demands two or three witnesses (17:6; 19:15). It is a court’s sentence, in a nation whose head of state was God.

A restraint, not a cruelty. Second, the requirement that the accuser strike first makes it impossible to denounce a family member and keep your hands clean. It is a strong check on false or careless accusation.

Not for church or state. Third, and without hedging: no Christian, church or state holds this commission. Israel was a nation ruled directly by God, for a period that has ended. Facing teachers who draw people away, the remedy Paul commands is warning and then exclusion from the fellowship, not execution (Titus 3:10; 2 John 10). “The weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Christians, including some of the Reformers, once used chapters like this to execute heretics, and that was a grievous error. Anyone who uses this chapter to justify violence reads it against Christ.

Why this matters. What does carry across is the seriousness. God treats drawing his people away from him as worse than any other crime in the code, and a church that finds false teaching a matter of taste has lost something this chapter had.

Where Christians differ. A few Christians, called theonomists, hold that Israel’s civil laws, penalties included, should in principle be adopted by nations today. Most, with the Reformed confessions, hold that those laws expired with Israel as a nation, though the justice they express still teaches us (Westminster Confession 19.4).

This commentary’s view. Israel’s civil laws are fulfilled and ended in Christ; no state may punish false worship, and the church’s only sword is the word of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third case is a whole town drawn away by “worthless fellows” (vv. 12–13). Before anything is done, the charge must be investigated three times over and found “true and certain” (v. 14). Then the town is to be treated exactly as the Canaanite cities were, devoted to destruction with everything in it, burnt as a whole burnt offering and never rebuilt (vv. 15–16). Nothing may be kept back, so that the LORD may turn from his anger and show mercy to the nation, as he swore to the fathers (vv. 17–18). The harshest chapter in the book ends with mercy as its goal.
verseByVerse.theology: Corruption of a whole community is to be taken with the utmost seriousness, yet justice still requires careful inquiry into the facts.
verseByVerse.examples: The church guards its purity by dealing patiently and seriously with sin that spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you hear in one of your cities, which the LORD your God is giving you to dwell there, that certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which you have not known, then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you, you shall surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword, devoting it to destruction, all who are in it and its cattle, with the edge of the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a whole town is reported to have gone after other gods, the charge must be searched out with great care; only if it is proved certain is the town to be devoted to destruction, exactly as a Canaanite city would be.

Inquire and make search and ask diligently. Three verbs of investigation, then “true and certain”, before a single step. The greater the outrage, the greater the pressure to act before the facts are in, and the law puts its heaviest demand for evidence where feelings run hottest.

Certain worthless fellows. Literally “sons of belial”, men of no worth; Paul later uses Belial as a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). A whole town does not go over at once. It is talked over by a few persuasive people with nothing to lose, and the rest follow because everybody else is.

Devoting it to destruction. The word used of the Canaanite cities (7:2): an Israelite town that turns to other gods is treated exactly as Canaan was. God has no favourites in judgment (8:20).

Were children killed too? The plain answer is yes: the law as written included the whole city (v. 15), as the flood and Sodom did. The law belonged to Israel as a nation under God and was never a pattern for the church, which bears no sword (John 18:36); no state today has the right to punish anyone for false worship. The law also demanded patient inquiry first, and Scripture records no clear case of it being carried out against an Israelite town for idolatry. And the God who gave it is the same God who pitied the children of Nineveh (Jonah 4:11) and sent his Son to bear judgment for sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again. None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers, if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments that I am commanding you today, and doing what is right in the sight of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guilty town and all its goods are to be burnt as wholly given to God, with nothing kept back, so that God may turn from his anger and show mercy to the nation.

As a whole burnt offering. The city’s plunder is burnt rather than kept, “as a whole burnt offering”, the same safeguard as in 7:25–26: the danger is usually not the idol but some small thing that seemed harmless to keep.

None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand. At Jericho Achan kept some of the devoted things for himself, and “the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel” (Joshua 7:1).

Show you mercy. Verse 17 changes the tone of everything before it. Mercy, compassion, multiplication: three words of tenderness at the end of the harshest chapter in the book, and they are its purpose, so that a nation is still standing to receive what he swore to Abraham.

One God, not two. The God of chapter 13 is not two Gods, one fierce and one kind, taking turns. He is one God, whose fierceness against what destroys his people comes from his love for them. A surgeon who will not cut is not gentle; he is negligent. At the cross the fierceness of his anger against sin and the depth of his mercy to sinners met in one place.

If you obey the voice of the LORD your God. The whole chapter is about listening to the right voice. Three seducers speak, a prophet with a wonder, a loved one in the dark, a townful of neighbours, and against all three stands one sentence: “you shall walk after the LORD your God… and hold fast to him” (v. 4). And he holds fast to his own: the Lord Jesus promised that his sheep, who hear his voice, will never be snatched out of his hand (John 10:27–28).

13.theology:
Truth tested by God’s word. A wonder never proves true a message that contradicts what God has said (13:1–3), for Satan can counterfeit signs (2 Thess 2:9). The lasting test of every teacher is faithfulness to Scripture.

God first. No bond, not spouse, child or friend, may rival our loyalty to God (13:6–8; Matt 10:37). Rightly ordered love holds even our dearest under the love of God, a love the Spirit pours into our hearts.

The seriousness of defection. The penalties belonged to Israel’s unique place as a nation under God and do not pass to the church, but the truth they guard remains: idolatry endangers the whole community, and God purges it in order to show mercy (13:17).
13.examples:
Israel was to refuse even a sign-working prophet, a beloved relative or a whole city that enticed her to idolatry, while inquiring carefully into the facts, so that God might show mercy to a faithful people.

We test every teaching by Scripture, let no relationship rival our allegiance to Christ, and deal seriously with sin in the church. And we rest in the gospel: the wrath against idolatry fell on Christ, who bore God’s fierce anger so that mercy and compassion might flow freely to all who hold fast to him with all their heart.

keyVerse.quote: For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul. You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him.
keyVerse.note: These verses explain why God allows false voices at all, and what protects his people from them. The test is love, in the very words of the Shema, and the defence is not suspicion but clinging to the God who redeemed them. Everything else in the chapter guards that bond.

13.reflection:
A false prophet’s sign comes true, and he is still to be rejected (vv. 1–3). Why are impressive results, numbers or experiences not enough to show that a message is from God? How would you test a teacher who excites you?

The second case names a brother, a child, a spouse and a dearest friend (v. 6). Why are those we love most the voices most able to lead us astray? How can we refuse to follow someone without ceasing to love them?

Verse 4 answers seduction with “hold fast to him”. What practical habits keep you close to the Lord’s voice, and which of them have slipped?

Israel’s penalties belonged to a nation ruled by God, and the church’s weapons are “not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). What does it look like for a church to take false teaching seriously without coercion or cruelty?

14.title: A Holy People: Clean Foods, the Tithe, and the Joy of Worship
14.text: <sup>1</sup>"You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead.<sup>2</sup>For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.<sup>3</sup>"You shall not eat any abomination.<sup>4</sup>These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat,<sup>5</sup>the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep.<sup>6</sup>Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.<sup>7</sup>Yet of those that chew the cud or have the hoof cloven you shall not eat these: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger, because they chew the cud but do not part the hoof, are unclean for you.<sup>8</sup>And the pig, because it parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch.<sup>9</sup>"Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat.<sup>10</sup>And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat; it is unclean for you.<sup>11</sup>"You may eat all clean birds.<sup>12</sup>But these are the ones that you shall not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,<sup>13</sup>the kite, the falcon of any kind;<sup>14</sup>every raven of any kind;<sup>15</sup>the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind;<sup>16</sup>the little owl and the short-eared owl, the barn owl<sup>17</sup>and the tawny owl, the carrion vulture and the cormorant,<sup>18</sup>the stork, the heron of any kind; the hoopoe and the bat.<sup>19</sup>And all winged insects are unclean for you; they shall not be eaten.<sup>20</sup>All clean winged things you may eat.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not eat anything that has died naturally. You may give it to the sojourner who is within your towns, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.<sup>22</sup>"You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year.<sup>23</sup>And before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and flock, that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always.<sup>24</sup>And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry the tithe, when the LORD your God blesses you, because the place is too far from you, which the LORD your God chooses, to set his name there,<sup>25</sup>then you shall turn it into money and bind up the money in your hand and go to the place that the LORD your God chooses<sup>26</sup>and spend the money for whatever you desire—oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household.<sup>27</sup>And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you.<sup>28</sup>"At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns.<sup>29</sup>And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do.
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 guarded Israel’s loyalty against every voice that would lead them to other gods. Chapter 14 turns from the great crisis of apostasy to ordinary life: the graveside, the dinner table and the harvest. A people who belong to the LORD are to be marked out in the everyday.

The message. You belong to God: you are his sons, his holy people, his treasured possession, so let it show in how you grieve, what you eat and what you do with your harvest. Holiness is not only for the sanctuary. It means grief that does not despair, meals that remember whose you are, and a tithe that becomes a joyful feast before God and food for those who have nothing.

Why it was said. Israel would live among Canaanites whose mourning rites, diet and harvest festivals were bound up with their gods (see the introduction). A distinct way of life, down to the kitchen, would keep Israel from being quietly absorbed into the nations around them.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with identity: “You are the sons of the LORD your God”, and so Israel must not gash themselves or shave their heads for the dead (vv. 1–2). Then the table: which land animals, water creatures, birds and insects may be eaten, closing with the rule about carcasses and the young goat in its mother’s milk, all because “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (vv. 3–21). Then the harvest: a tenth is brought each year to the place God chooses and eaten there with rejoicing, the Levite included (vv. 22–27), and every third year it is stored in the towns for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow (vv. 28–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and covenant. The food laws were a fence around one nation until the promised offspring of Abraham came; Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19) and broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14). Now the holy people, God’s “own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), is drawn from every nation and marked out by belonging to Christ, through whom we are sons of God (Galatians 4:4–6). And the feast before the LORD, with the poor at the table, looks ahead to the feast God will spread for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6).

For us. Christians are no longer marked out by menus, but holiness still reaches the ordinary: we grieve with hope because Jesus rose, we enjoy God’s gifts with thanks in his presence, and we make sure those with nothing have a seat at the table.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — A Holy People, Distinct in Grief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s identity comes before Israel’s conduct. Because they are “the sons of the LORD your God” (v. 1) and “a people holy to the LORD” chosen as his treasured possession (v. 2), they must not mourn the dead as the Canaanites did, by gashing their bodies or shaving their foreheads. God does not forbid grief; Israel wept thirty days for Moses. He forbids grief without hope, which turns its pain on the body. The New Testament draws the same line, not forbidding sorrow but sorrow “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness shapes the whole of life, grief included. God’s people mourn differently because they belong to him and have hope.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers weep at gravesides like anyone else, but with hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel belongs to God as his sons and his treasured possession, they must not mourn the dead with the self-harming rites of the pagans.

You are the sons of the LORD your God. First who they are, then how they must live: the Bible never reverses that order. Israel is not told to behave well in order to become God’s sons, but to stop doing something because they already are his sons.

You shall not cut yourselves. The forbidden practice is Canaanite mourning: gashing the skin and shaving the front of the head (literally “between your eyes”) for the dead. The prophets of Baal cut themselves on Carmel to get their god’s attention (1 Kings 18:28), in a world where grief was expressed by damaging yourself.

Grief with hope. God does not forbid grief. Israel mourned Aaron thirty days (Numbers 20:29) and will mourn Moses thirty more (34:8). What is forbidden is grief with no hope in it, which does violence to the body because there is nothing else to do with the pain. Paul draws the same line: “that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Not “do not grieve”, but not as others do. A believer may weep as hard as anybody, yet differently, “since we believe that Jesus died and rose again” (1 Thessalonians 4:14). The Christian’s hope at a grave rests on another grave, found empty.

If you are harming yourself. This law shows a Father who does not want his children hurt, not a rebuke to those who struggle. If you are hurting yourself, tell a pastor or biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too. If you are in danger, get help the same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–21 — Clean and Unclean: Holiness at the Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The longest section of the chapter teaches holiness at the table. Israel may eat land animals that both part the hoof and chew the cud (vv. 4–8), water creatures with fins and scales (vv. 9–10), and clean birds, but not the listed birds of prey and carrion birds, nor winged insects (vv. 11–20). Nothing that has died naturally may be eaten, and a young goat may not be boiled in its mother’s milk (v. 21). The reason given, at beginning and end, is “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (vv. 2, 21): every meal marked Israel out as his, until Christ declared all foods clean.
verseByVerse.theology: The food laws set Israel apart and trained her to live by God’s distinctions; in Christ they have done their work.
verseByVerse.examples: Holiness still reaches the ordinary parts of life, though Christians are no longer bound by the food laws.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not eat any abomination. These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep. Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat. Yet of those that chew the cud or have the hoof cloven you shall not eat these: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger, because they chew the cud but do not part the hoof, are unclean for you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch. "Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat. And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat; it is unclean for you. "You may eat all clean birds. But these are the ones that you shall not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the kite, the falcon of any kind; every raven of any kind; the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind; the little owl and the short-eared owl, the barn owl and the tawny owl, the carrion vulture and the cormorant, the stork, the heron of any kind; the hoopoe and the bat. And all winged insects are unclean for you; they shall not be eaten. All clean winged things you may eat. "You shall not eat anything that has died naturally. You may give it to the sojourner who is within your towns, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to eat only the animals God calls clean, so that every meal marks them out as a people holy to the LORD; these rules served Israel until Christ, who declared all foods clean.

These are the animals you may eat. Land animals must part the hoof and chew the cud; water creatures need fins and scales; the forbidden birds are mostly birds of prey and carrion eaters; and “all clean winged things” includes locusts (Leviticus 11:21–22). Modern readers find it the least promising material in the books of Moses, and ask why.

Why these rules? Scripture does not give a full answer, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. Hygiene is the popular explanation and almost certainly not the point: the text never mentions health. Other suggestions (links with Canaanite ritual, or animals that do not fit neatly into the order of Genesis 1) may be partly right, but the text states none of them.

For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. What the text does say, twice (vv. 2, 21), is that Israel was to be kept distinct: you could not eat dinner in Israel without remembering whose you were. The table became a boundary. A man who could not eat what his neighbour ate could not easily dine in his house, and much of the mingling that led to idolatry was headed off at the kitchen. Verse 21 confirms that the issue is holiness, not health: the animal that died naturally may be given or sold to a foreigner.

The laws lifted. So their lifting was an earthquake. Peter, shown a sheet of unclean animals in Joppa, found himself in a Gentile’s house saying, “God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean” (Acts 10:28), and Mark states it flatly: “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). The wall came down at a dinner table, because that is where it had been built. The food laws were not a mistake later corrected but a fence for a season, until Christ broke down “the dividing wall of hostility” between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14).

Why not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk? Probably because it was a pagan rite, or because it turned what nourished life into the means of death. The Jewish separation of meat and dairy grew from this verse later.

Where Christians differ. Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jewish believers keep the food laws; most Christians hold them fulfilled in Christ.

This commentary’s view. All foods are clean (Acts 10:15); Jewish believers are free to keep their customs as devotion, never as the way of salvation, and no one may bind another’s conscience over food (Colossians 2:16–17).

Uncertain wording. Many of the creatures cannot be identified with certainty, and translations vary. The “rock badger” is probably the hyrax; several birds are educated guesses. The hare and hyrax do not chew the cud as cattle do, but their constant chewing motion looks like it: the law describes animals as an ordinary observer sees them. The bat is among the “birds” because the Hebrew word covers all flying creatures.
verseByVerse.note: The identity of many birds is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Tithe and the Joy of Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The yearly tithe is not a grim tax but a feast. A tenth of the grain, wine and oil, with the firstborn of the flocks, is brought to the place God chooses and eaten there by the family who brought it, “that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always” (v. 23). If the journey is too long, the produce may be sold and the money spent on “whatever your appetite craves”, wine and strong drink included, and the household is to rejoice before the LORD (vv. 24–26). One guard is set on the joy: the landless Levite must not be forgotten (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The tithe is joyful worship that teaches the fear of the Lord: giving and feasting before God train the heart to revere and trust him.
verseByVerse.examples: Giving is meant to be glad worship, not a grim duty.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year. And before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and flock, that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always. And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry the tithe, when the LORD your God blesses you, because the place is too far from you, which the LORD your God chooses, to set his name there, then you shall turn it into money and bind up the money in your hand and go to the place that the LORD your God chooses and spend the money for whatever you desire—oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household. And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each year Israel is to bring a tenth of its harvest to the place God chooses and eat it there with rejoicing, remembering the Levite, so that they learn to fear the LORD.

You shall eat the tithe. This surprises everybody who has heard tithing preached: they eat it, as a family feast at the sanctuary, with the firstborn of the flocks (15:19–23). The stated purpose is “that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always”, and the method of learning it is a good dinner.

Whatever your appetite craves. If the journey is too far, sell the produce, take the money, and buy “whatever your appetite craves”, strong drink named among it, and rejoice before the LORD with your household. God is not merely permitting the feast; he commands it, names the drink, and calls it worship.

Why does religion look so joyless? H. L. Mencken defined Puritanism as the haunting fear that someone, somewhere, may be happy, and the jibe stuck because many have met that kind of religion. The moralist obeys that grim God and is proud of how little he enjoys; the pleasure-seeker runs from the same God to find pleasure elsewhere. Verse 26 overturns them both. Pleasure is not God’s rival but his invention, and it is safest in his presence, where it is shared and received as a gift instead of seized as a right. That is why the first sign Jesus gave was not at a funeral but at a wedding where the wine had run out, and he made more, and better (John 2:1–11). The joyless religion and the godless party both turn out to be too small.

You shall not neglect the Levite. Then the guard against self-indulgence: bring the Levite, the man with no land, to the party. Joy in God’s presence that leaves out the one who cannot pay is not what is commanded.

Where Christians differ: the tithe. Some hold that Christians still owe exactly a tenth to the church; others that the tithe belonged to Israel’s law, supporting the Levites and the worship of a nation under God.

This commentary’s view. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and for churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). A tenth is a helpful benchmark and many should give more; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

Where Christians differ: alcohol. Some argue that biblical wine was unfermented and require abstinence; verse 26, naming “strong drink”, is hard to fit with that view.

This commentary’s view. Wine is God’s gift to be enjoyed with thanks before him, as here (Psalm 104:15). Drunkenness is forbidden (Proverbs 23:29–35; Ephesians 5:18), and love gladly abstains for the sake of a weaker brother or for conscience (Romans 14:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — The Third-Year Tithe for the Vulnerable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every third year the tithe stays at home. It is stored in the towns, and the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, the four who owned no land, “shall come and eat and be filled” (vv. 28–29). Care for the vulnerable is built into the nation’s calendar rather than left to occasional charity, and it happens face to face in the local town. God attaches a promise: he will bless the work of the hands that share what he has given.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s people are marked by generous care for those with no inheritance or protection.
verseByVerse.examples: The church is still called to care for the poor deliberately and regularly, not only when moved.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns. And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every third year the whole tithe is stored in the local towns to feed the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, and God promises to bless those who share what he has given.

At the end of every three years. Every third year the tithe stays home as a local store for the four Deuteronomy always names: the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. None owned land, the only security in a farming economy. So God builds provision for them into the system: every third year, whether anybody feels generous or not.

Within your towns. It happens in the towns, not at the sanctuary, where everybody knew which widow and which foreigner was coming to collect. Israel’s care for the poor was designed to be face to face. James calls it pure religion “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27).

That the LORD your God may bless you. The promise is not a transaction, for God is not for sale; it is a Father’s delight in children who share what he gave them, and the New Testament repeats it without embarrassment: “whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6).

Were there three tithes? Some count three: the Levites’ tithe (Numbers 18), the festival tithe (vv. 22–27) and this one. More likely, in the third year the festival tithe went to the poor instead.

14.theology:
A people holy to the LORD. The refrain of 14:2 and 21 binds the chapter together: holiness shapes how Israel grieves, eats, worships and gives. The food laws are fulfilled in Christ, but the call to holiness in every part of life remains: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).

The joy of worship. The tithe is a feast before the LORD (14:23), and the regular act of giving and rejoicing trains the heart to revere and trust him.

Care for the vulnerable. The third-year tithe built care for the landless into Israel’s life (14:28–29), reflecting the heart of God, who draws near to the lowly.
14.examples:
As God’s holy people, Israel let her identity shape how she grieved and what she ate, feasted on the tithe before the LORD, and made regular provision for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.

We grieve with hope, let holiness reach ordinary life without the food laws, give gladly, and care for the poor deliberately, reflecting the God who became poor for our sake.

keyVerse.quote: For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
keyVerse.note: Every command in the chapter, at the graveside, the table and the harvest, rests on this sentence. Israel is not told to be holy in order to be chosen, but to live as holy because God has already chosen and treasured them. Peter applies the same words to the church of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:9).

14.reflection:
Israel is told who they are before being told how to live (vv. 1–2). Why does that order matter? What difference does it make to obey God as his child rather than to earn his favour?

Christians grieve, but not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). What does grief with hope look like in practice, and how can we support someone who is grieving?

God commands a feast, names the wine, and calls it worship (v. 26). Do you tend to see God as the rival of your joys or their giver? How can enjoyment become an act of worship?

The third-year tithe fed the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow in their own town (vv. 28–29). Who are the vulnerable people within reach of your home and church, and what would face-to-face care for them look like?

15.title: The Year of Release: Open Wide Your Hand
15.text: <sup>1</sup>"At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release.<sup>2</sup>And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor.
