He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed.<sup>3</sup>Of a foreigner you may exact it, but whatever of yours is with your brother your hand shall release.<sup>4</sup>But there will be no poor among you; for the LORD will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess—<sup>5</sup>if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all this commandment that I command you today.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD your God will bless you, as he promised you, and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.<sup>7</sup>"If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, in any of your towns within your land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother,<sup>8</sup>but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.<sup>9</sup>Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, 'The seventh year, the year of release is near,' and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin.<sup>10</sup>You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake.<sup>11</sup>For there will never cease to be poor in the land. 15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 ended with the third-year tithe for those who owned no land. Chapter 15 keeps the same rhythm of sacred time and moves to the seventh year, when debts are released and Hebrew servants go free, closing with the firstborn of the flocks that belong to God.

The message. The God who released Israel from slavery wants a people whose whole economy releases others. Debts are cancelled, the poor are helped with an open hand and an ungrudging heart, and the servant leaves loaded with gifts, because every Israelite master was once a slave whom God set free: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (v. 15). Generosity here is not a mood but the behaviour of people who remember their redemption.

Why it was said. In a farming economy one failed harvest could push a family into debt, and debt into servitude. Left alone, the gap between lenders and borrowers would harden into permanent classes, and Israel would rebuild Egypt inside its own borders (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Every seventh year creditors release their brothers’ debts, because it is “the LORD’s release” (vv. 1–3); in an obedient land there would be no poor at all (vv. 4–6). Since there always will be, Israel must open wide its hand, and God exposes the calculating heart that refuses a loan because the year of release is near (vv. 7–11). The Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year, furnished liberally as Israel was at the exodus, unless he chooses for love to stay for life (vv. 12–18). The firstborn of herd and flock are given back to God and eaten before him (vv. 19–23).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and pattern. Jesus announced his ministry as the great release, “to proclaim liberty to the captives… to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor” (Luke 4:18–19). He taught us to pray “forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12) and cancelled the record of debt against us by nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). He is the Servant who could have gone free and chose to stay out of love, and the God who commands open hands “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

For us. Christians have been released from a debt they could never pay. Hands that have received that much should not stay shut: give freely, lend without calculating, and give without grudging, because the measure of our giving is what we were given in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Year of Release: Canceling Debts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every seventh year, at the end of the seven, creditors must release what they have lent to a fellow Israelite, because “the LORD’s release has been proclaimed” (vv. 1–2). A loan to a foreigner may still be collected (v. 3). God’s design was that “there will be no poor among you” (v. 4), for he would bless an obedient people so richly that they would lend to nations and never borrow (vv. 5–6). The release is God’s, not the creditor’s generosity: it puts the sabbath principle of rest and freedom into the nation’s finances.
verseByVerse.theology: God builds release into the rhythm of his people’s life, and he blesses a people who share his open hand.
verseByVerse.examples: Debts are not cancelled by calendar now, but the generosity behind the law still marks those who have received grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release. And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed. Of a foreigner you may exact it, but whatever of yours is with your brother your hand shall release. But there will be no poor among you; for the LORD will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess— if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all this commandment that I command you today. For the LORD your God will bless you, as he promised you, and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every seventh year Israelite creditors must release their brothers’ debts, because the release is the LORD’s; in an obedient land God’s blessing would have left no one poor.

You shall grant a release. Debts between Israelites are released by law, on a fixed date everybody knew was coming, in the sabbath year when the land itself rested (Leviticus 25:1–7). The ancient world has no clear parallel: kings occasionally cancelled debts on coming to the throne, but Israel had release written into the calendar. And the reason lies in God: “because the LORD’s release has been proclaimed”. It is his release, not the creditor’s generosity.

Of a foreigner you may exact it. The foreigner is not the sojourner, protected throughout Deuteronomy, but a visitor, usually a trader, whose loans were commercial, not relief for poverty.

No poor, yet always poor. Verses 4 and 11 seem to contradict each other until the conditions are read. Verse 4 is what would happen “if only you will strictly obey”; verse 11 is what will happen, because they will not. One is the design, the other the forecast. And it is verse 11 that the Lord Jesus echoes when the disciples object to the ointment poured on him: “For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them” (Mark 14:7). He is not shrugging off poverty; he is quoting the verse that commands open-handedness, and the second half of his sentence is the command.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for release (shemittah) means letting go, and the usual reading is that the debts were cancelled outright. A few scholars think repayment was only suspended for the fallow year. Either way, the generosity demanded in verses 7–11 is the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the poor will never vanish, Israel must never harden its heart or shut its hand, but lend “sufficient for his need, whatever it may be” (vv. 7–8). God foresees the shrewd man who refuses a loan in year six because the release is near; he calls the thought worthless and warns that the poor man’s cry will reach him (v. 9). The giving must be free and the heart ungrudging, and God promises to bless it (v. 10). “There will never cease to be poor in the land” is not a shrug but the reason for the command: open wide your hand (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Generosity begins in the heart: God asks for ungrudging care for the poor, not just the outward act.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers watch for the calculating thought that keeps a hand closed when giving would cost.

verseByVerse.quote: "If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, in any of your towns within your land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a fellow Israelite falls into poverty, do not harden your heart or close your hand: open it and lend him enough for whatever he needs.

You shall not harden your heart. God names the heart before the hand, because the hand does not close on its own. The measure of giving is “sufficient for his need”: not a token or a fixed percentage but the other man’s need, so each case has to be weighed. And “open your hand” pictures a hand spread flat, so that nothing is kept back in the palm.

Heart and hand in John. John turns heart and hand into a test of whether a man is a Christian at all: “But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?” (1 John 3:17). What opens a closed heart is that love of God, “poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5), not a resolve we summon.

How do I open my hand? Start with the heart. When a need comes into view, notice the first excuse that rises (“they will only waste it”, “things are tight this year”) and ask whether it is a reason or a shut hand. Decide first, not last. Put giving at the top of the budget, as Paul told the Corinthians: “On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper” (1 Corinthians 16:2). Look for the brother in front of you. The law speaks of a poor man “in any of your towns”: the family in your church after a redundancy, the neighbour whose car has died. Ask what would be “sufficient for his need”, and meet it quietly where you can. Give in deed, not only in sympathy. “Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18). And give as one who has been given to. Christ held nothing back for us, not even his life, and “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, 'The seventh year, the year of release is near,' and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin. You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake. For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, 'You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sees the calculating heart that refuses a loan because the year of release is near; he commands giving that is free and ungrudging, and since the poor will always be there, the hand must always be open.

The year of release is near. God knows how a shrewd man will handle this law. It is year six; a neighbour needs a loan; in twelve months the debt will be void, so the loan is effectively a gift, and a man who does not want to give finds he is suddenly unable to help. He has broken no law. He has become prudent at the exact moment generosity would cost him.

An unworthy thought. Literally a word of belial, of worthlessness (the phrase used of the “worthless fellows” in 13:13), and God names it though it will never be spoken aloud. The poor man, who does not know why he was refused, cries to the LORD, and God hears him, and the prudent man is guilty of a sin nobody witnessed and he could deny with a straight face.

Your heart shall not be grudging. The antidote is not about the amount. The manner is commanded as well as the act, as in Paul centuries later: “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

What it does not mean. Open-handedness is not enabling: love will not fund harm, and Scripture expects those who can work to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But here the burden of proof lies on the closed hand.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The release reaches people as well as debts. A Hebrew man or woman sold into service goes free in the seventh year (v. 12), and not empty-handed: the master must furnish him liberally from flock, threshing floor and winepress, as God blessed him (vv. 13–14). The reason is the exodus: you were slaves, and God redeemed you (v. 15). If the servant loves his master’s household and chooses to stay, his ear is pierced at the door and he serves for life (vv. 16–17). Release should not feel hard, for he has given good value, and God will bless the master (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who remember their own release set others free generously.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians, redeemed at great cost, give in the manner they were given to.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you. And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress. As the LORD your God has blessed you, you shall give to him. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Hebrew servant must go free in the seventh year and be sent away loaded with gifts, because God set Israel free from Egypt and did not send them away empty.

You shall let him go free. A Hebrew who sold himself into service, the ancient world’s answer to unpayable debt, goes free in the seventh year, and the next provision lifts this above every comparable law in the ancient world: he is not to go “empty-handed”. He leaves with animals, grain and wine, enough to start again. Otherwise freedom would be a formality; a man released with nothing is back in servitude within a year, and God closes that door.

Remember that you were a slave. Israel did not leave Egypt empty-handed either: “Thus they plundered the Egyptians” (Exodus 12:36). Every master must do for his servant what God did for him: the standard is set by the exodus, not the market. Paul reasons the same way about a collection for famine relief: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

What it means to be redeemed. In Deuteronomy the word (padah) means to buy someone out of bondage by paying for him, and Moses uses it of the exodus again and again (7:8; 13:5; 24:18). Israel did not merely escape from Egypt; she was bought out of it, and from then on she belonged to the one who paid. Most of us would rather be self-made than bought. But the gospel names the price: “you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). That is why the law ties redemption to an open hand. A man who knows what he cost cannot send his servant away empty. See Redemption in the Theological Dictionary.

Does the Bible approve slavery? This was debt service: limited to six years, with release, provision and, as verse 16 shows, the right to choose to stay. It is very different from the man-stealing slave trade, which the law punished with death (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). God regulated a practice that existed everywhere (see slavery in the ancient world), and planted the truths that would end it: every person made in God’s image, and in Christ “neither slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28). Honesty requires adding that the law treated foreign slaves less generously (Leviticus 25:44–46); yet even they were protected from brutality (Exodus 21:20, 26–27), and a runaway slave was not to be handed back (23:15–16), a rule unusual in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: But if he says to you, 'I will not go out from you,' because he loves you and your household, since he is well-off with you, then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever. And to your female slave you shall do the same. It shall not seem hard to you when you let him go free from you, for at half the cost of a hired worker he has served you six years. So the LORD your God will bless you in all that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant who loves his master’s household may choose to stay for life, marked by an awl through his ear at the door; but release should never feel hard to the master, who has been well served.

Because he loves you and your household. A servant, offered freedom and a generous start, declines it “because he loves you and your household”. It can only mean the house was good and the master kind. The law that requires generous release has also produced households servants do not want to leave.

Put it through his ear into the door. The ceremony is public and permanent: an awl through the ear at the door, a mark carried for life, saying this man belongs here by choice. “Forever” here means for the rest of his life. The ear is the organ of hearing and obedience, pinned to the door of the house he has chosen. Many Christians have heard an echo of it in a psalm of David: “In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear… I delight to do your will, O my God” (Psalm 40:6–8), a passage Hebrews applies directly to Christ (Hebrews 10:5–7).

I lay it down of my own accord. The link is an echo, not the meaning of the law, but the pattern is real. One servant in history was under no obligation at all, could have walked away at any point, and chose to stay and serve out of love, though it led him to a cross. “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). He delighted to do the Father’s will perfectly, and he did it in our place.

It shall not seem hard to you. God answers the master’s reluctance to lose a good worker: he has had full value, and God will bless him.

Uncertain wording. Verse 18 says literally that the servant has served for “double” a hired worker’s wage. The ESV reads “at half the cost of a hired worker”; others take it as worth twice a hired worker, or the equivalent of one. On every reading the master has had good value.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — The Firstborn Devoted to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with the firstborn males of herd and flock, which are set apart to the LORD (v. 19). They may not be worked or shorn, but are eaten by the household before God, year by year, at the place he chooses (v. 20). A blemished firstborn may not be sacrificed, since God is not to be given the second-rate, but it is not wasted: it is eaten at home like any game, clean and unclean alike sharing it, provided the blood is poured out (vv. 21–23). The best belongs to God, and even what he declines is still his gift.
verseByVerse.theology: The firstborn belongs to God, who claims the best; giving it back is an act of worship and trust.
verseByVerse.examples: We give God the first and best, not what is left over.

verseByVerse.quote: "All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the LORD your God. You shall do no work with the firstborn of your herd, nor shear the firstborn of your flock. You shall eat it, you and your household, before the LORD your God year by year at the place that the LORD will choose. But if it has any blemish, if it is lame or blind or has any serious blemish whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God. You shall eat it within your towns. The unclean and the clean alike may eat it, as though it were a gazelle or a deer. Only you shall not eat its blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The firstborn males of the herds and flocks belong to the LORD and are eaten before him each year; a blemished one may not be offered, but may be eaten at home like any game, so long as the blood is poured out.

All the firstborn males. The claim goes back to the night of the exodus, when the LORD struck down the firstborn of Egypt and spared Israel’s, so that every firstborn in Israel was his from then on (Exodus 13:2, 14–15). That is why the animal may not be worked or shorn for the owner’s profit: it is not his to use, and the yearly meal before God recalls the night Israel’s own firstborn were spared.

Any blemish. God will not be given the second-rate, and Malachi will fiercely rebuke the priests for exactly this: “When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil?… Present that to your governor; will he accept you” (Malachi 1:8). Yet the imperfect animal is not wasted but eaten at home: the law distinguishes what may be offered from what may be enjoyed, and does not despise the second. The blood is poured out, as with all meat eaten at home (12:16, 23–24), because life belongs to God.

The unblemished Firstborn. Every unblemished firstborn given to God points to Christ, offered “like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

Open hands. The whole chapter has been about open hands: debts released, the poor supplied, the servant sent away loaded, the best of the flock given back to God. Every command rests on one sentence in the middle: “you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (v. 15). Generosity in Deuteronomy is the behaviour of people who remember what was done for them, and when they forget and close their hands, the way back is to remember it again.

15.theology:
The economics of grace. The God who released Israel from Egypt builds release into the calendar (15:1–2, 12). The hope that there would be no poor (15:4) is the fruit of a community shaped by gratitude, and it foreshadows the gospel, in which those forgiven an unpayable debt are freed to release others.

Open heart, open hand. Generosity is a matter of the heart, ungrudging and cheerful (15:7–11; cf. 2 Cor 9:7). Because poverty persists in a fallen world, the call is lasting, and Jesus’ words about the poor (Mark 14:7) command compassion rather than excuse its absence.

Redemption remembered. Gratitude for our own redemption (15:15) is what drives Christian giving: the more we grasp how freely Christ saved us, the more freely we give.
15.examples:
Israel was to cancel debts and free servants every seventh year, send the freed servant away well supplied, keep her hand open to the poor, and give the firstborn to the LORD, all because she remembered that she too had been redeemed from slavery.

We who have had the infinite debt of sin cancelled live with open hands, giving cheerfully and enough, and rejoice in Jesus, who proclaimed the true release from sin and death (Luke 4) and whose pierced hands were opened on the cross for our freedom.

keyVerse.quote: You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.
keyVerse.note: This sentence is the root of every command in the chapter. Israel releases debts, opens its hand and sends servants away loaded because God first did all that for them. Christians give for the same reason: we were bought “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).

15.reflection:
God warns against the man who refuses a loan because “the year of release is near” (v. 9). In what ways can we be careful and sensible exactly when generosity would cost us? How do you tell wise caution from a shut hand?

The freed servant was not to go “empty-handed”, because Israel left Egypt loaded with gifts (vv. 13–15). How does remembering what God has given you in Christ change the way you give?

Verse 4 says “there will be no poor among you”; verse 11 says “there will never cease to be poor in the land”. How do these two statements together shape the way Christians think about poverty?

Jesus announced “the year of the Lord’s favor” (Luke 4:19) and cancelled our debt at the cross. What debts, of money or of offence, might God be calling you to release?

16.title: The Three Pilgrimage Feasts: Rejoice Before the LORD
16.text: <sup>1</sup>"Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night.<sup>2</sup>And you shall offer the Passover sacrifice to the LORD your God, from the flock or the herd, at the place that the LORD will choose, to make his name dwell there.<sup>3</sup>You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction—for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste—that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt.<sup>4</sup>No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, nor shall any of the flesh that you sacrifice on the evening of the first day remain all night until morning.<sup>5</sup>You may not offer the Passover sacrifice within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you,<sup>6</sup>but at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell in it, there you shall offer the Passover sacrifice, in the evening at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>And you shall cook it and eat it at the place that the LORD your God will choose. And in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents.<sup>8</sup>For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the LORD your God. You shall do no work on it.<sup>9</sup>"You shall count seven weeks. Begin to count the seven weeks from the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain.<sup>10</sup>Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the LORD your God blesses you.<sup>11</sup>And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there.<sup>12</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.<sup>13</sup>"You shall keep the Feast of Booths seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and your winepress.<sup>14</sup>You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are within your towns.<sup>15</sup>For seven days you shall keep the feast to the LORD your God at the place that the LORD will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful.<sup>16</sup>"Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed.<sup>17</sup>Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.<sup>18</sup>"You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.<sup>19</sup>You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous.<sup>20</sup>Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make.<sup>22</sup>And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 set the seven-year rhythm of release. Chapter 16 sets Israel’s yearly calendar: the three pilgrim feasts kept at the place the LORD will choose. Then, at verse 18, a new part of the law begins, on the people who will lead Israel, judges first, then king, priests and prophets (16:18–18:22).

The message. Israel’s year is to be shaped by remembering and rejoicing: remembering the night God brought them out of Egypt, and rejoicing before him in his harvest gifts with everyone at the table, from sons and daughters to servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows. A people who feast before a just and jealous God must also run just courts and keep his worship free of other gods.

Why it was said. Israel was about to become a nation of farmers in a land where the harvest year belonged to Baal and Asherah, the gods of fertility (see the introduction). Israel’s feasts tied the same seasons, barley, wheat and grape, to the LORD who had redeemed them and who gave the rain and the crops.

How the chapter makes its case. Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are kept in the month of Abib at the chosen place, with “the bread of affliction”, so that Israel remembers the exodus all their days (vv. 1–8). Seven weeks after the grain harvest begins comes the Feast of Weeks, with freewill offerings and a table that includes the poor (vv. 9–12). After the final ingathering comes the Feast of Booths, seven days of being “altogether joyful” (vv. 13–15). Three times a year every man appears before the LORD, never empty-handed, giving as he has been blessed (vv. 16–17). Then judges must give righteous judgment without partiality or bribes (vv. 18–20), and no Asherah or sacred pillar may stand beside the LORD’s altar (vv. 21–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and promise, more clearly than almost anywhere in the law. Jesus died at Passover as “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Spirit was poured out on the day of Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks, when the first great harvest of believers was gathered (Acts 2:1, 41). At the Feast of Booths Jesus offered living water to anyone who was thirsty (John 7:37–38). And he is the righteous Judge the prophets promised, who will not judge by appearances (Isaiah 11:3–4).

For us. The Christian year is shaped by the same gospel. We remember the Lamb at the Lord’s Table, rejoice together with every kind of person Christ has gathered, give as we have been blessed, pursue justice, and refuse to set anything up beside Christ in our worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Passover: Remember the Night of Redemption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The year opens in the month of Abib, the month of the exodus, with Passover. The sacrifice is offered not at home but at the place the LORD will choose (vv. 1–2, 5–6). For seven days Israel eats unleavened bread, “the bread of affliction”, the flat bread of people leaving in haste, so that “all the days of your life” they will remember the day they came out of Egypt (v. 3). No leaven may be seen and no meat left till morning (v. 4). The lamb is eaten at the chosen place, the people return to their tents, and the week ends with a solemn assembly and a day without work (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Passover remembers redemption from slavery and points to Christ, by whose blood his people are delivered from death and bondage.
verseByVerse.examples: At the Lord’s Table the church remembers a greater exodus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night. And you shall offer the Passover sacrifice to the LORD your God, from the flock or the herd, at the place that the LORD will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction—for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste—that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt. No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, nor shall any of the flesh that you sacrifice on the evening of the first day remain all night until morning. You may not offer the Passover sacrifice within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, but at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell in it, there you shall offer the Passover sacrifice, in the evening at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt. And you shall cook it and eat it at the place that the LORD your God will choose. And in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents. For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the LORD your God. You shall do no work on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Passover is kept each year at the place God chooses, with the bread of affliction, so that Israel never forgets the exodus.

The bread of affliction. The year opens with Passover, in Abib, the spring month of the exodus (later called Nisan), and Deuteronomy adds a phrase not in Exodus: unleavened bread is “the bread of affliction”. Flat bread is what you make when there is no time to let dough rise, and it tastes of the night they went. For seven days every year Israel ate poor food on purpose, so that the memory would go in through the mouth as well as the ear, “all the days of your life”.

At the place that the LORD your God will choose. Passover began as a household meal behind a bloodstained door in Egypt; here it becomes a national gathering at the one sanctuary (12:5). That is why Jesus went up to Jerusalem at Passover (Luke 2:41), and died there at it.

Christ, our Passover lamb. Paul applies leaven and lamb to a church in one sentence: “Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The order is fixed: the lamb is sacrificed first, then the leaven (a picture of sin) is swept out. Nobody removes the leaven in order to qualify for the lamb.

Must Christians keep these feasts? They were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and the Lord’s Supper has taken the Passover’s place. Keeping them is a matter of freedom, not obligation (Romans 14:5–6), and never a condition of standing with God (Galatians 4:10–11).

Uncertain wording. Verse 7 says to “cook” the Passover, where Exodus 12:9 forbids boiling it. The Hebrew word usually means boil but can mean cook in general, and 2 Chronicles 35:13 uses it of roasting the Passover, so there is probably no contradiction. “From the flock or the herd” (v. 2) probably includes the other sacrifices of the festival week (2 Chronicles 35:7–9), since Exodus specifies a lamb or goat.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — The Feast of Weeks: Rejoice and Remember
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven weeks are counted from the first cutting of the grain, and then comes the Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival later called Pentecost (v. 9). Each man brings a freewill offering in proportion to what God has given (v. 10). The heart of the paragraph is the guest list: sons and daughters, servants, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow all rejoice together before the LORD at the chosen place (v. 11). The reason is the exodus: “You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt” (v. 12). Those who were once powerless are to make room for the powerless.
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest feast is grateful joy for God’s provision, and its table includes the whole community, especially the vulnerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out, began the gospel harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven weeks. Begin to count the seven weeks from the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain. Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the LORD your God blesses you. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the Feast of Weeks Israel gives as God has blessed them and rejoices with those who own nothing, because they were once slaves themselves.

You shall count seven weeks. Seven weeks after the sickle is first put to the grain comes the Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost from the Greek for “fiftieth”, kept with a freewill offering “as the LORD your God blesses you”. No fixed amount; each man brings in proportion to what the harvest gave him.

The sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. The guest list is the heart of the paragraph. After the family, everyone on it has no claim on the food: servants, the landless Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, the widow. God commands the harvest celebration and then fills the table with people who did not own a field.

You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt. The reason for Israel’s generosity is never that the poor deserve it or that giving is admirable. It is that these people were slaves and somebody came and got them, and they are to treat the powerless as God treated them when they were powerless. A festival where the landless eat with the landowners is not an extra to the worship. It is the worship.

The harvest of Pentecost. At this feast, fifty days after the Passover at which Jesus died, the Spirit was poured out and about three thousand were added to the church (Acts 2:1, 41): the firstfruits of a harvest from every nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Feast of Booths: Joy in God's Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Feast of Booths comes after the last of the harvest, when the threshing floor and the winepress are full (v. 13). It lasts seven days, with the same guest list, and its one great command is joy: Israel is to rejoice, so that they “will be altogether joyful” (vv. 14–15). The section closes by summing up all three feasts: three times a year every man appears before the LORD at the chosen place, and none may come empty-handed (v. 16). The measure of each gift is not a fixed sum but “the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you” (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Abundant joy in God’s provision marks true worship, and each gives in proportion to what he has received.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians worship with full and grateful joy, remembering the Son who came to dwell among us.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep the Feast of Booths seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and your winepress. You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are within your towns. For seven days you shall keep the feast to the LORD your God at the place that the LORD will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful. "Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed. Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Booths is a week of wholehearted joy after harvest; at all three feasts every man comes before the LORD with a gift in proportion to God’s blessing.

You shall rejoice in your feast. The Feast of Booths comes after everything is in. Leviticus adds that Israel lived in booths that week to remember the wilderness journey (Leviticus 23:42–43). Its one instruction above all is “rejoice”, with the same guest list, and then “so that you will be altogether joyful”. God appointed a week of feasting at the most prosperous moment of the year, told them to enjoy it thoroughly, and made sure the widow was there.

Three times a year. Three journeys a year cost every man time and left farms unguarded, and God thought it worth it (see pilgrim feasts).

Not empty-handed. Nobody is told how much. The measure is what God has given him, so the poor man who brings little has met the standard as fully as the rich man who brings much, and the rich man who brings little has not. It is the principle the Lord Jesus applied while watching a widow drop in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44).

The living water was his to give. It was at this feast, on its last and greatest day, that Jesus stood up in the temple and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). A festival that remembered God’s care in the wilderness, water from the rock included, found its meaning in him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight from the feasts the law turns to the courts. Judges and officers are to be appointed in every town, tribe by tribe, and they must judge with righteous judgment (v. 18). Three things are forbidden: perverting justice, showing partiality and taking bribes, because a bribe blinds even the wise and twists the case of the innocent (v. 19). The command is repeated for emphasis, “Justice, and only justice, you shall follow”, and Israel’s life in the land depends on it (v. 20). The people who worship a just God must reflect his justice.
verseByVerse.theology: God demands impartial, incorruptible justice; the God of the feasts is the God of the courts.
verseByVerse.examples: Those justified by the righteous Judge uphold honesty and fairness in their own dealings.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous. Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must have judges in every town who judge righteously, without partiality or bribes: justice must be pursued.

You shall appoint judges and officers. Straight out of the feasting, without a pause, come judges and officers “in all your towns”. Worship and justice are not separate departments; the prophets will spend centuries insisting that a nation cannot have the first while neglecting the second (Amos 5:21–24; Isaiah 1:11–17).

You shall not show partiality. The judges are to be like the God they serve, who “is not partial and takes no bribe” (10:17).

A bribe blinds the eyes of the wise. Not fools: the wise. Money disables good judgment in able men, and invisibly. Nobody who takes a bribe believes his verdict has been affected.

Justice, and only justice. The Hebrew simply repeats the word, tsedeq, tsedeq (justice, justice), and the verb means to pursue. Justice is not something a society drifts into; it has to be run after, by a people whom God had already rescued from Pharaoh’s injustice. Israel’s judges often failed, and the prophets looked for a King who would judge the poor “with righteousness” (Isaiah 11:4). Jesus is that Judge, and he calls his people to “judge with right judgment” (John 7:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–22 — No Idolatrous Symbols Beside the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two short prohibitions close the chapter. No tree may be planted as an Asherah, the symbol of the Canaanite mother-goddess, beside the LORD’s altar (v. 21), and no sacred stone pillar may be set up, “which the LORD your God hates” (v. 22). The danger is not replacing the worship of God but adding to it, decorating his altar with the symbols the neighbours found moving. Israel’s later history shows how real it was: an Asherah would one day stand in the temple itself.
verseByVerse.theology: The worship of God must be kept unmixed with idolatry.
verseByVerse.examples: We refuse to blend the worship of God with the idols of the age, however harmless they look.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make. And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing belonging to other gods, no Asherah and no sacred pillar, may be set up beside the LORD’s altar, because he hates it.

You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah. An Asherah represented the Canaanite mother-goddess; a pillar was a sacred standing stone. Both were attractive: a tree is beautiful, and a standing stone looks ancient and serious.

Beside the altar. Not instead of it. Nobody proposes to replace the worship of God, only to improve the setting with something the neighbours find moving (12:30). Israel’s great failure was rarely a straight swap of gods but addition, on the grounds that it could do no harm. It happened: Josiah had to bring an Asherah out of the house of the LORD itself and burn it (2 Kings 23:6).

Which the LORD your God hates. The reason is startlingly personal: he hates it, as a husband would hate to find another man’s photograph on his wife’s bedside table. She has not committed adultery, but she has wronged him. It is the jealousy of a husband who has given himself wholly, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and who will not share her with anyone.

Uncertain wording. Whether an Asherah was a carved wooden pole or a living tree is not certain; “plant any tree” suggests a tree here, while other passages speak of Asherahs being made and cut down (1 Kings 16:33; Judges 6:25–26).

16.theology:
The calendar of redemption. Passover, Weeks and Booths rehearsed God’s mighty acts each year. They find their fulfilment in Christ, the Passover Lamb, the giver of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2), and the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), literally pitched his tent. The believer keeps a feast of remembrance in the Lord’s Supper, recalling our greater exodus from sin and death.

Commanded joy. Worship is to be glad, abundant and inclusive, drawing in servants, sojourners, orphans and widows (16:11, 15). A joyless religion misrepresents the God of all delight.

Worship and justice together. Honest courts belong with joyful feasts, and the altar must be kept free of every idol God hates (16:18–22). The Spirit given at Pentecost forms such a people, and where we fail, Christ, the one man who always judged rightly, is our righteousness.
16.examples:
Israel’s year was a rhythm of remembering and rejoicing, with every household and every stranger at the table, while she pursued justice in the courts and kept God’s altar clear of idols.

We keep the feast of remembrance at Christ’s table. Our worship is to be joyful and to welcome the vulnerable, our public life marked by the pursuit of justice, and our devotion undivided.

keyVerse.quote: And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.
keyVerse.note: These verses gather the chapter’s two great words, rejoice and remember. Israel’s worship is joyful, it makes room at the table for those who own nothing, and it rests on the memory of redemption. The same shape marks the church’s worship, which remembers Christ’s death and welcomes all whom he has gathered.

16.reflection:
Israel ate “the bread of affliction” every year so that they would remember the exodus “all the days of your life” (v. 3). Why do we need regular reminders of what God has done? How does the Lord’s Supper serve that purpose for you?

God commands joy three times in this chapter (vv. 11, 14, 15). Is joy part of how you think of obedience? What keeps Christian worship from becoming either grim or merely entertaining?

The feasts included servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows (vv. 11, 14). Who is missing from your church’s table, and how could you make room for them?

The danger in verses 21–22 was not replacing God but adding something beside him. What might we be tempted to set up beside Christ in our worship or our lives, on the grounds that it can do no harm?

17.title: Kings and Justice: The King Who Reads the Law
17.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>2</sup>"If there is found among you, within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, a man or woman who does what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, in transgressing his covenant,<sup>3</sup>and has gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which I have forbidden,<sup>4</sup>and it is told you and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and if it is true and certain that such an abomination has been done in Israel,<sup>5</sup>then you shall bring out to your gates that man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you shall stone that man or woman to death with stones.<sup>6</sup>On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness.<sup>7</sup>The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>8</sup>"If any case arises requiring decision between one kind of homicide and another, one kind of legal right and another, or one kind of assault and another, any case within your towns that is too difficult for you, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose.<sup>9</sup>And you shall come to the Levitical priests and to the judge who is in office in those days, and you shall consult them, and they shall declare to you the decision.<sup>10</sup>Then you shall do according to what they declare to you from that place that the LORD will choose. And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you.<sup>11</sup>According to the instructions that they give you, and according to the decision which they pronounce to you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left.<sup>12</sup>The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest who stands to minister there before the LORD your God, or the judge, that man shall die. So you shall purge the evil from Israel.<sup>13</sup>And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again.<sup>14</sup>"When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you possess it and dwell in it and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,'<sup>15</sup>you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers you shall set as king over you. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.<sup>16</sup>Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, 'You shall never return that way again.'<sup>17</sup>And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away, nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold.<sup>18</sup>"And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests.<sup>19</sup>And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them,<sup>20</sup>that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left, so that he may continue long in his kingdom, he and his children, in Israel.
17.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 16 ended by appointing judges in every town:, “Justice, and only justice, you shall follow” (16:20). Chapter 17 carries on with the offices that will govern Israel in the land: the local courts, a central court for hard cases, and the king. Chapter 18 will add the priests and the prophet.

The message. Everyone who holds authority in Israel, from the witness at the town gate to the king on his throne, stands under God and his word. Judgment must be careful and true, hard cases must have a place to be settled, and the king above all must be a brother who reads God’s law every day, so that power never makes him forget whose servant he is.

Why it was said. Israel was about to become a settled nation, and settled nations have courts and kings (see the introduction). God foresaw that Israel would want a king “like all the nations” and wrote the terms in advance.

How the chapter makes its case. First, integrity before God and in court: no blemished sacrifice, and no execution for idolatry without diligent inquiry and two or three witnesses, the witnesses themselves throwing the first stone (vv. 1–7). Next, a court of appeal at the place God will choose, whose verdict must be obeyed (vv. 8–13). Then the king: God may give one, chosen by him and from among their brothers (vv. 14–15), but he must not multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold (vv. 16–17). Instead he must copy out the law, keep it beside him and read it all his life, so that his heart is not lifted up above his brothers (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Israel’s kings broke this law, Solomon most famously, clause by clause. Only one King has kept it: Jesus, who lived by every word of God, rode a donkey instead of a war horse, and was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Ironically, he was condemned by a court that broke this chapter’s rule of witnesses: “their testimony did not agree” (Mark 14:56). And the unblemished offering of verse 1 is finally Christ himself, “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

For us. Whatever authority God gives you, as a parent, a manager, an elder or a citizen, it is held under his word and among brothers and sisters, not above them. The cure for power’s pride is the king’s prescription: a daily life with Scripture open, and a heart that rests on the King who kept the law in our place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Justice in Worship and the Courts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Integrity is required both at God’s altar and in God’s courts. No damaged animal may be offered to the LORD, for giving God what is worth least shows what we think he is worth (v. 1). And even the gravest charge, serving other gods, must be handled with care: diligent inquiry, certainty, and the testimony of two or three witnesses, never one (vv. 2–6). The witnesses must throw the first stone, so that no one gives testimony lightly, and the whole people then joins in purging the evil from Israel (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God demands integrity in worship and rigorous justice in judgment; truth must be established by sufficient witnesses, guarding against false condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: The church today should be just as slow to condemn: no one is disciplined on a single, unsupported accusation.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God. "If there is found among you, within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, a man or woman who does what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, in transgressing his covenant, and has gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which I have forbidden, and it is told you and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and if it is true and certain that such an abomination has been done in Israel, then you shall bring out to your gates that man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you shall stone that man or woman to death with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God must not be given the damaged animal, and no one may be put to death for idolatry until the charge has been diligently investigated and found true and certain.

No blemish. The temptation is obvious and permanent. A farmer has good animals and damaged ones, and the damaged one is worth less at market, so offering it costs him almost nothing. God calls that “an abomination”, a word Deuteronomy uses of idolatry and the occult, because giving God what you could not sell shows what you think he is worth. Malachi makes the charge unanswerable with one question: “Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor?” (Malachi 1:8).

If it is true and certain. Then a case of serving other gods, even the sun, moon and stars. Yet even for the charge most likely to inflame a crowd, the first requirement is not action but investigation, and the standard is not suspicion or rumour but certainty. Israel’s law puts its heaviest demands for evidence exactly where feeling runs hottest, the opposite of what mobs do.

The Lamb without blemish. The law found its goal in the one perfect offering: we were ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Because God gave us his best, we bring him more than our leftovers.

Should the state execute idolaters today? No. The penalty belonged to Israel as a nation under God, and it does not pass to the church or to any state; Jesus forbade uprooting the weeds before the harvest (Matthew 13:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness. The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one may be put to death on one witness’s word, and the witnesses who condemn must be the first to carry out the sentence.

Two or three witnesses. No conviction on a single testimony, however respectable the witness. One person can be mistaken, and one person can lie, and from inside the courtroom there is no telling the difference. Requiring two independent witnesses does not make error impossible; it makes malice costly, because a false charge now needs two people to agree on the same lie.

The hand of the witnesses shall be first. Nobody testifies and walks away. A man who has sworn away another’s life must be first to take it, with his own hands: the strongest deterrent against careless testimony. It is the provision Jesus turned on the men who dragged a woman before him: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7). The earliest manuscripts of John do not contain that story, though many believe it records a true event.

The trial of Jesus. At Jesus’ trial the court sought witnesses, “For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree” (Mark 14:56). By this chapter’s rule the case should have collapsed. The one truly innocent man was condemned by breaking the law, and bore it willingly for the guilty.

In the New Testament. The principle carries over to church discipline, “that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18:16), to Paul’s dealings (2 Corinthians 13:1) and to charges against a minister: “Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). God guards the accused as carefully as he pursues the guilty.

What it does not mean. Not that one person’s report of abuse may be dismissed. The rule governs conviction, not whether a report is taken seriously, passed to the police and investigated, or whether the vulnerable are protected meanwhile. Many wrongs have only one witness; careful inquiry is how other evidence comes to light.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Central Court for Hard Cases
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hard cases are to have a place where they can be settled. When a local court meets a case beyond it, whether of bloodshed, legal right or assault, the parties go up to the place the LORD will choose, to the Levitical priests and the judge in office (vv. 8–9). Their verdict must be followed exactly, without turning to the right or the left (vv. 10–11). Contempt of that court is treated as rebellion against God and punished with death, so that all Israel will hear and fear (vv. 12–13). Ordered authority guards God’s people from everyone becoming his own final court.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides ordered authority and final courts to maintain justice; submission to legitimate authority guards the community from anarchy.
verseByVerse.examples: God still gives ordered authority in church and society, so that hard disputes have somewhere to be settled.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any case arises requiring decision between one kind of homicide and another, one kind of legal right and another, or one kind of assault and another, any case within your towns that is too difficult for you, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose. And you shall come to the Levitical priests and to the judge who is in office in those days, and you shall consult them, and they shall declare to you the decision. Then you shall do according to what they declare to you from that place that the LORD will choose. And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you. According to the instructions that they give you, and according to the decision which they pronounce to you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left. The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest who stands to minister there before the LORD your God, or the judge, that man shall die. So you shall purge the evil from Israel. And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cases too hard for the local courts must go up to the priests and the judge at the place God chooses, and their verdict must be obeyed exactly.

Too difficult for you. God sets up a court of appeal. Cases “too difficult for you” (literally “too wonderful”, beyond your reach) go up from the town gate to the sanctuary. God provides in advance, without shame, for judges who meet cases they cannot settle.

The Levitical priests and the judge. Priest and judge sit together, so the hardest questions are decided where worship and law meet, not in a court that leaves God out. Its verdict is binding, because a legal system with no final court is not a legal system.

Either to the right hand or to the left. A man may not evade a judgment by brushing it aside or by inventing scruples against it. The penalty falls on the man who “acts presumptuously”, refusing the court out of pride, not on the honest man who disagrees.

Why this matters. Without it, every man becomes his own final court, “everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes” (12:8). God’s remedy is a settled place where hard questions are answered. He provides authority so that his people need not carry everything alone.

The final court. Israel’s highest court one day condemned its own Messiah. Behind every human court stands one that cannot err: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). For those who trust that Judge, the verdict has already been given: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Uncertain wording. The three kinds of case are literally “between blood and blood, between plea and plea, between stroke and stroke”. The third word (nega‘) usually means a blow, but it is also the word for a skin disease (Leviticus 13), so some think cases of uncleanness are meant. The ESV’s “assault” is the more likely reading.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The King Like the Nations: God's Restrictions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God permits Israel a king, but on his own terms. Moses foresees the request for a king “like all the nations” (v. 14), and allows it: the king must be one the LORD chooses and one of their own brothers, not a foreigner (v. 15). Then come three prohibitions aimed at the classic temptations of power. He must not multiply horses, the chariot force that would take Israel back to Egypt; wives, the marriage alliances that would turn his heart; or silver and gold, the wealth that would make him feel independent of God (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the king is subject to God's law; the restrictions guard against military self-reliance, divided allegiance, and greed — the besetting sins of power.
verseByVerse.examples: Every kind of authority is still accountable to God, and every leader needs guarding against the same three temptations.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you possess it and dwell in it and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,' you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers you shall set as king over you. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God foresees Israel asking for a king for the wrong reason, permits one, and requires that he be God’s choice and one of their own brothers.

Like all the nations. Centuries before Israel has a king, God permits one, and quotes in advance the poor motive that will produce one. When the day came, Israel used almost these words: “Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations”, and God told Samuel, “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them” (1 Samuel 8:5, 7).

Provision for failure. God does not only plan for his people’s obedience. He makes laws in advance for their failures, so that what they insist on wrongly is less ruinous than it might have been.

One from among your brothers. The terms begin at once: “whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers.” A king given rather than seized, one of them rather than over them. The gospel opens with exactly such a king, chosen by God and born a son of David and of Abraham (Matthew 1:1), our brother by taking our flesh.

The question of date. Many critical scholars date this law after Solomon, because it fits his failures so closely. But horses, foreign wives and treasure were the standing temptations of every ancient king and easily foreseen, and Samuel “told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and he wrote them in a book” at the very start of the monarchy (1 Samuel 10:25), which shows such terms were known early (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.quote: Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, 'You shall never return that way again.' And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away, nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king must not build his security on horses, alliances by marriage or hoarded wealth, the three things most likely to turn a ruler’s heart from God.

Horses. Horses meant chariots, and chariots meant military power. Egypt was the region’s horse market, so a chariot army meant trading with the house of slavery, and God adds: “You shall never return that way again.”

Wives. Royal marriages sealed treaties. The danger named is not political but personal: “lest his heart turn away”.

Silver and gold. Great wealth buys a king independence from his people and, he may come to feel, from God.

Set beside Solomon. Set the list beside the reign of Solomon: “Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen… And Solomon’s import of horses was from Egypt” (1 Kings 10:26, 28); “He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart” (1 Kings 11:3); and “the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone” (1 Kings 10:27). Israel’s wisest king broke all three clauses, and the historian uses Deuteronomy’s own phrase to explain the ruin.

Money, sex and power. The list is startlingly modern: force, sex and money still promise to make us safe, desired and secure. Timothy Keller subtitled his book Counterfeit Gods with the empty promises of money, sex and power. None is evil in itself: horses pulled ploughs, marriage was God’s idea, and the land of Eden had gold (Genesis 2:11–12). The danger is what they become to someone who thinks he needs them in order to be someone.

The King who needed none of them. Watch what the true King did with the same three. He rode into his capital on a borrowed donkey (Matthew 21:5). He took no wife, but gave himself up for a bride (Ephesians 5:25). He owned so little that he was laid in another man’s tomb. He did not need any of them to be who he was, because he lived for his Father and for us. Those who are his can learn to hold all three with an open hand.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain what “cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses” describes. Most take it as trade, as in Solomon’s day. Others think it means paying for horses with people, sending Israelites to Egypt as soldiers or labourers. Either way, the king would be undoing the exodus.
verseByVerse.note: For the whole record, read 1 Kings 10:14–11:8.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–20 — The King Who Reads the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s king must live under God’s word. On taking the throne he must write out a copy of the law himself, checked by the Levitical priests, keep it with him and read it all his life (vv. 18–19). The purposes are spelt out: that he learn to fear the LORD and obey, that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he not turn aside to right or left, so that his dynasty may last (vv. 19–20). The most powerful man in Israel is to be its most diligent student of Scripture.
verseByVerse.theology: The true king is a humble student of God's word, subject to the law, a brother among brothers; this points to Christ, the King who perfectly embodies the law.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone given authority, at home, at work or in the church, needs the same daily correction from Scripture that the king did.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests. And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left, so that he may continue long in his kingdom, he and his children, in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king must write out God’s law for himself and read it every day of his life, so that he learns to fear the LORD and never thinks himself above his brothers.

A copy of this law. Not commission a scribe, but “write for himself”, with the copy checked by the priests, then keep it with him and read it daily. (The Greek translation of “a copy of this law” is where the name Deuteronomy, “second law”, comes from; see the introduction.)

The king under the law. In Egypt the king was a god. In Mesopotamia he was the one who issued the law. In Israel he is the one man required to write the law out longhand and read it daily, because he is under it. The most powerful person in the country is the most thoroughly governed.

That he may learn to fear the LORD his God. The king is a learner, and reading is meant to lead to doing: “by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them”.

Above his brothers. The people he rules are his own family. Power’s characteristic sin is not cruelty but the slow, unnoticed conviction that you are a different kind of person from those you govern. Daily reading of Scripture is God’s prescription against it, and it is the same prescription for every parent, manager, pastor and politician.

One King kept this law. Israel’s kings broke this chapter; when Josiah finally heard the book read, he tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). One King fulfilled it. He was born under the law, answered the devil out of Deuteronomy three times (Matthew 4:1–10), could say “I have kept my Father’s commandments” (John 15:10), and never lifted his heart above his brothers: “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). He kept the law, and then took the curse its breakers had earned.

17.theology:
The king under the Word. In a world of god-kings, Israel's king must write and read Scripture “all the days of his life” and never let his heart be “lifted up above his brothers” (17:18–20). The law stands above the throne.

The temptations of power restrained. Horses, wives, and silver and gold (17:16–17) stand for trust in military strength, a divided heart and greed. Solomon broke every clause, which shows the need for a King whose heart would never turn away.

Rigorous, ordered justice. Unblemished worship (17:1), testimony confirmed by a second witness (17:6), and courts whose verdicts are obeyed (17:8–13): God's justice is careful and protective of truth, and his gift of authority guards the community from anarchy.
17.examples: We give God our best, for we have been given Christ the unblemished Lamb; we require evidence confirmed by more than one witness and honor legitimate authority. And we look to the King who kept the law of the king in our place, our brother whose heart was never lifted up, who trusted God rather than horses, whose love was undivided, who became poor for our sake, and whose Spirit forms in his people the same humble love of God's word. Israel's kings failed; Christ alone is the righteous King we long for.

keyVerse.quote: And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them
keyVerse.note: In a world of god-kings, Israel’s king was to be a lifelong student of God’s word, the most governed man in the nation. The verse shows that all authority among God’s people stands under Scripture, and it finds its fulfilment in the King who kept every word his Father spoke.

17.reflection:
Verse 1 forbids offering God the damaged animal. Where are you tempted to give God your leftovers of time, money or attention, and how does Christ, the Lamb without blemish, change that?

The law demanded careful inquiry and two or three witnesses before anyone was condemned (vv. 4–6). How can we practise the same care when we hear accusations or gossip, while still taking reports of real harm seriously?

The king was forbidden to multiply horses, wives, and silver and gold (vv. 16–17). What are the modern equivalents of these, and which most tempts you to feel secure or important apart from God?

The king was to read God’s law every day so that his heart would not be lifted up above his brothers (vv. 18–20). What authority has God given you, and what would it look like to exercise it as one who sits under his word?

18.title: Prophets, Priests, and the Prophet to Come
18.text: <sup>1</sup>"The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance.<sup>2</sup>They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.<sup>3</sup>And this shall be the priests' due from the people, from those offering a sacrifice, whether an ox or a sheep: they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach.<sup>4</sup>The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep, you shall give him.<sup>5</sup>For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for all time.<sup>6</sup>"And if a Levite comes from any of your towns out of all Israel, where he lives—and he may come when he desires — to the place that the LORD will choose,<sup>7</sup>and ministers in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand to minister there before the LORD,<sup>8</sup>then he may have equal portions to eat, besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony.<sup>9</sup>"When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations.<sup>10</sup>There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer<sup>11</sup>or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead,<sup>12</sup>for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. And because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.<sup>13</sup>You shall be blameless before the LORD your God,<sup>14</sup>for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.<sup>15</sup>"The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen—<sup>16</sup>just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.'<sup>17</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken.<sup>18</sup>I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers.
