And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.<sup>19</sup>And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.<sup>20</sup>But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.'<sup>21</sup>And if you say in your heart, 'How may we know the word that the LORD has not spoken?'—<sup>22</sup>when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You need not be afraid of him.
18.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 16 and 17 set out Israel’s judges and its king. Chapter 18 completes the offices that will lead God’s people in the land: the priests who serve at his altar, and the prophet who will bring his word.

The message. God will provide for his people everything they need to know him, so they must never reach for the dark arts of the nations. He gives the Levites himself as their inheritance, he forbids every attempt to pry into the future or contact the dead, and in their place he promises a voice: a prophet like Moses, one of their own brothers, with God’s own words in his mouth, to whom they must listen.

Why it was said. Moses was about to die, and Israel was entering a land whose people burned their children and consulted diviners and the dead (see the introduction). Who would speak for God when Moses was gone? This chapter is God’s answer.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the priests: the tribe of Levi has no land, for “the LORD is their inheritance”, and lives on fixed portions of Israel’s offerings, every Levite serving on equal terms (vv. 1–8). Next, the forbidden path: child sacrifice and nine ways of seeking hidden knowledge, the very abominations for which the Canaanites are losing their land (vv. 9–14). Then the true path: God will raise up a prophet like Moses, the answer to Israel’s own plea at Horeb never to hear God’s voice directly again (vv. 15–19). Last, a test for those who claim to speak in his name (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. Directly to Christ, by promise. This is one of the great messianic promises of the Old Testament, and the book itself admits it was not fulfilled in Moses’ lifetime or for long after (34:10). Peter and Stephen both name Jesus as the prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22–26; 7:37), and on the mountain the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). He is the mediator Israel asked for at Horeb, one of the brothers who could stand in the fire and speak God’s words in a human voice.

For us. We do not need horoscopes, mediums or a second channel in case God is silent, because God “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2). Our part is the one this chapter gives: to listen to him, to test every voice by his word, and to find, like the Levites, that the Lord himself is enough.
18.theology:
The Prophet like Moses. The promise of 18:15 is fulfilled in Jesus, the mediator in whose mouth God put his words and to whom all must listen.

The God who speaks. Israel must shun all occult practices (18:9–14), humanity's attempt to gain hidden knowledge apart from God. We need not peer into forbidden darkness, for in Christ God has spoken his final word.

The LORD is the minister's inheritance. The Levites have no land and are supported by the people (18:2), the principle Paul applies to gospel ministers (1 Cor 9:14). God's servants find their true portion in God himself.
18.examples: We support those who labor in the Word, refuse every quest for forbidden knowledge, and listen to Jesus, the Prophet greater than Moses. To refuse him is to incur judgment; to listen to him is life. Our calling is the glad obedience of listening to the beloved Son in whom the Father is well pleased.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Priests and Their Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites have no land because the LORD himself is their inheritance, as he promised. Instead of fields they receive God’s food offerings (vv. 1–2): fixed portions of every ox or sheep sacrificed, and the first of the grain, wine, oil and fleece, because God chose them to minister in his name (vv. 3–5). And any Levite from any town who comes to serve at the chosen place is to eat equal portions with those already there (vv. 6–8). God’s servants live on his promise, and among them there is to be no inner circle.
verseByVerse.theology: The provision rests on a promise (v. 2). Levi has no acres because Levi has God, and the arrangement is a pledge God made and keeps. Paul reasons from this statute to the support of gospel ministers (1 Cor. 9:13–14).
verseByVerse.examples: A whole tribe lived without land on what the nation carried to God, so that Israel’s worship never depended on somebody having a free week. A congregation that supports those who labour in the Word is therefore not so much being generous as keeping an arrangement God made, and it frees them to give themselves to the work.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance. They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribe of Levi will own no land, because the LORD himself is their inheritance, exactly as he promised.

As he promised them. Levi’s landlessness is not an oversight or a penalty. It is God keeping a promise (Numbers 18:20), and Moses reminds a tribe with nothing that God said he would do this.

The LORD is their inheritance. Consider what it meant week to week. Every other Israelite could walk to the edge of his ground and see where it stopped. He could farm it badly or well, and either way it was his and his son’s after him. The Levite had no such line to walk. What he had instead was a spoken promise, and a promise is worth only as much as the person who made it.

Living on a promise. God asked a tribe to live its entire history on his word, in public, in front of eleven brothers who could point at their fields. Every generation of Levites was living proof that the word of God will actually feed a family. Paul argues from this arrangement that those who preach the gospel should be supported by it (1 Corinthians 9:13–14).

Our inheritance too. It is the same arrangement every Christian lives on, whether he notices or not: “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). In Christ all believers are “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), and the Levite’s portion becomes ours: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5). Whatever we own or lack, we have him.

verseByVerse.quote: And this shall be the priests' due from the people, from those offering a sacrifice, whether an ox or a sheep: they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach. The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep, you shall give him. For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for all time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests receive fixed portions of every sacrifice and the first of every harvest, because God himself chose them to serve in his name.

Shoulder, cheeks and stomach. The specifics are startlingly domestic: named cuts from every ox or sheep sacrificed, and the first of the grain, wine, oil and fleece.

Fixed portions. The priest received specified parts, not whatever was left. A worshipper could not decide on the day what he felt like handing over; the shoulder was the priest’s before the animal was killed. There was no room for a man to be generous or grudging, and so none for the priest to be flattered or slighted.

The firstfruits of your grain. Not the tenth after the household had taken what it needed, but the first, before anybody knew whether the rest of the harvest would come in. Israel gave away the earliest evidence that the year would be all right while it was still the only evidence.

Chosen to minister. The support is not a wage for services rendered. It follows from a choice God made (v. 5), and the nation’s part was simply to honour what he had decided.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if a Levite comes from any of your towns out of all Israel, where he lives—and he may come when he desires — to the place that the LORD will choose, and ministers in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand to minister there before the LORD, then he may have equal portions to eat, besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Any Levite who comes from his town to serve at the sanctuary must share equally with those already there.

Equal portions. A Levite from the country may come and serve when he desires, and eat the same as everyone else: no reduced allowance for the newcomer, no better share for the men who had been there longest.

No inner circle. Anyone in a church will recognise what this guards against. Wherever people serve together, an inner circle forms: the ones who have been there longest, who know how things are done, who are consulted. It happens without anyone deciding it should, and the man who arrives from outside can serve for years without ever quite getting in.

In the church. God legislated against it in a chapter about priests’ dinners. The New Testament raises the same guard over a matter as small as where a visitor sits: “if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, ‘You sit here in a good place,’… have you not then made distinctions among yourselves” (James 2:3–4)? In Christ’s household the newcomer eats at the same table, from the same dish.

Uncertain wording. The last phrase, “besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony”, is obscure in Hebrew (literally something like “apart from his sales by the fathers”). Levites had no tribal land, though they owned houses and pasture in their towns, so it probably means the newcomer keeps whatever he has from selling family property and still receives his full share. Some think it refers instead to family gifts or inherited dues. The main point, equal portions, is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — No Traffic with the Occult
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not learn the abominations of the nations. The list opens with burning children as offerings, then names every route by which the ancient world tried to reach the future or the dead: divination, fortune-telling, omens, sorcery, spells, mediums and necromancy (vv. 9–11). These practices are why the LORD is driving the Canaanites out (v. 12). Israel instead must be wholehearted before the LORD, not hedging its bets, because God has not allowed his people this way (vv. 13–14). The next verses show why they do not need it.
verseByVerse.theology: The ban does not leave Israel to manage without guidance. It is the first half of an argument that v. 15 completes: the occult is forbidden and a Prophet is promised, in one breath. God does not shut a door without opening a better one.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was surrounded by nations who read the future in animal livers and consulted the dead, and was told to want none of it. The appetite has not changed, and neither has the answer. Horoscopes, mediums and the hunt for hidden knowledge all assume God is silent. He is not, and the reason we may leave the future alone is that it is held by a Father who has already told us what we need. Anyone who has dabbled is not shut out: the Prophet speaks pardon to all who come back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. And because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must not copy the nations’ religion, which burned children and sought hidden knowledge from spirits and the dead, for these abominations are why God is driving the nations out.

Anyone who burns his son or his daughter. The list opens with the darkest practice of all. Parents put children in a fire to secure a harvest or a victory, and every line that follows should be read in the shadow of that one.

Anyone who practices divination. Then eight more, which English blurs, so take them one at a time. To practise divination is to seek a decision by casting lots or reading signs. To tell fortunes is to forecast a person’s future. To interpret omens is to read meaning in ordinary events: a bird, a spill, a shape in the fire. A sorcerer works with potions and spells. A charmer casts spells with chanted words. A medium, a necromancer and one who inquires of the dead all try to contact the dead. Together they cover every route by which the ancient world tried to reach what it could not otherwise know or control.

Because of these abominations. Verse 12 gives the reason the Canaanites are losing their land: “because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.” That answers the question every honest reader of the conquest asks. God is not clearing a country for a favourite. He is judging a civilisation that had been burning its children, after four hundred years of waiting (Genesis 15:16). And the same book warns that Israel will perish in the same way if it does the same (8:20); it did, for these very sins (2 Kings 17:17; 21:6).

Uncertain wording. The exact meaning of several of these terms is not known; the list is meant to be complete rather than technical, and translations vary. “Burns his son or his daughter as an offering” is literally “makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire” (ESV footnote). A few scholars have thought this a dedication rite rather than a killing, but Deuteronomy 12:31 and Jeremiah 7:31 speak plainly of children burned in the fire.
verseByVerse.note: “Burns his son or his daughter” is literally “makes them pass through the fire” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: You shall be blameless before the LORD your God, for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must belong to God wholeheartedly, with no second channel to the spirit world, because he has forbidden it to them.

You shall be blameless before the LORD your God. The word (tamim) means whole, entire, all of a piece, the word used of a sacrificial animal without blemish. It does not chiefly mean sinless. It means undivided: not consulting God on Sunday and a horoscope on Thursday, keeping a second channel open in case the first goes quiet.

Why people seek the occult. The appetite behind the occult is often less wickedness than fear. People consult mediums because someone has died and they cannot bear the silence; they read horoscopes because next year is dark and they want a handhold. Saul went to the medium at Endor the night before he died, and the text says why: “when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him” (1 Samuel 28:6). He wanted a word from God and would not wait for one. What God offers instead is not grim endurance of the silence. It is a voice, promised in the next verse.

What this looks like. Being undivided before God means closing the second channel, and that is usually concrete. Name it. The horoscope you glance at “just for fun”, the tarot app, the lucky ritual before an interview, the medium a grieving friend suggests. Get rid of it. When the gospel reached Ephesus, “a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all” (Acts 19:19); deleting an app is a small modern version. Take the fear to the right place. When the future is dark or the silence after a death is unbearable, ask Isaiah’s question: “should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19). Pray, open the Scriptures, talk it over with a wise believer. Trust the voice you have. God “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), the Prophet promised next, who has gone through death and come back. You need no second channel when the one who holds tomorrow has already spoken, and his word is “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In place of the diviners God promises a voice: a prophet like Moses, from among Israel’s brothers, to whom they must listen (v. 15). The promise grew out of the day at Horeb when the people begged never to hear God’s voice directly again, and God said they were right (vv. 16–17). So he will put his words in a prophet’s mouth, and whoever will not listen to that prophet will answer to God himself (vv. 18–19). The New Testament names this prophet: Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology: Outside Genesis, this is the clearest promise of the coming Messiah in the five books of Moses. A Prophet like Moses means a mediator of a covenant (one who stands between God and the people), an intercessor, and one rejected by his own brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: A people who could not bear to hear God directly were given a man to stand between them and the fire. Now the Mediator has come, and the God whose voice would have killed us has spoken to us in a human voice, at a carpenter’s bench and on a hillside and from a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen— just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.' And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will raise up a prophet like Moses from among Israel’s brothers, and they must listen to him; the promise answers Israel’s own plea at Horeb, which God said was right.

At Horeb. The promise grew out of the day the people begged never to hear God’s voice again, lest they die. The mountain was burning to the heart of heaven, the trumpet sounding, God speaking the Ten Commandments aloud, and the whole nation backed away and begged Moses to make it stop (5:23–27). On the face of it, that is a low point: a people offered the direct voice of God, asking to be spared it.

They are right. God agrees with them. He does not tell them to be braver or rebuke their cowardice. He says they are correct: direct contact between the holy God and sinners, with no one in between, would kill them. And out of that agreement comes the promise of a Prophet. The greatest promise of the Messiah in Deuteronomy grew out of a frightened crowd telling God they could not survive him. He took their terror seriously, called it accurate, and answered it, not by turning down the fire but by providing someone to stand in it on their behalf.

If God would only speak. A common, honest objection asks why God does not simply speak out loud to everyone. Bertrand Russell, asked what he would say if he found himself before God after death, is reported to have answered that he would complain there had not been enough evidence. Horeb is the Bible’s answer, and not the one the sceptic expects. A whole nation once heard the voice, and the result was not settled faith but terror. The problem was never that God was too quiet, but that sinners cannot bear him at full volume; what was in short supply was not evidence but mercy. Then he did something better than shouting from the sky. He sent a Prophet from among the brothers, with a human face and a voice that could be heard across a dinner table, so that people could come near to God without being consumed. He has spoken in his Son (Hebrews 1:2), and what the Son said was “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28).

Is the “prophet like me” one person or the line of prophets? Many Jewish readers took it as the whole line of prophets. But by Jesus’ day many were waiting for one particular Prophet (John 1:21; 6:14), Deuteronomy itself says no prophet like Moses had yet arisen (34:10), and Peter names him: Jesus (Acts 3:22–23). The prophets who followed were partial fulfilments; Christ is the Prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will put his own words in the mouth of this prophet, one of Israel’s brothers, and will himself call to account anyone who refuses to listen.

A prophet like you. Israel had many prophets afterwards and none of them was like Moses. Moses did not merely deliver messages. He mediated a covenant, interceded for a nation under sentence and offered to be blotted out in its place (Exodus 32:32), spoke with God face to face, and was rejected by the brothers he came to rescue (Acts 7:35). A prophet like Moses is a very particular thing, and the description fits Jesus with striking exactness.

From among their brothers. Not an angel, not a voice out of the fire: one of them. The mediator has to be one of the people he stands for, which is exactly the argument Hebrews makes about the incarnation: “he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17).

I will put my words in his mouth. Jesus claimed exactly this: “I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment” about what to say (John 12:49).

I myself will require it. Not the prophet, but God. To ignore this Prophet is to be dealt with by God personally.

Then Peter said who it was. Peter stood in Solomon’s Portico with a healed lame man beside him, quoted this passage, and said who it was about: “God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness” (Acts 3:22–26). Stephen quoted it too, minutes before he was killed (Acts 7:37). And on a high mountain the cloud came down and the Father repeated the command this promise had carried for centuries: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Test of a True Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not everyone who claims to speak for God does so. A prophet who presumes to speak in the LORD’s name what God has not commanded, or who speaks in the name of other gods, must die (v. 20). Israel is given a plain test: if the word does not come to pass, the LORD did not speak it, and the prophet need not be feared (vv. 21–22). Read with chapter 13, which rejects even a prophet whose sign comes true if he leads away from God, it guards God’s people from anyone bold enough to say “thus says the LORD”.
verseByVerse.theology: God does not leave his people at the mercy of a confident speaker: his word can be checked. The final answer, though, is not a better test but a better Prophet.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians must still test the spirits (1 John 4:1), weighing every claim to speak for God against what he has already said.

verseByVerse.quote: But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.' And if you say in your heart, 'How may we know the word that the LORD has not spoken?'— when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You need not be afraid of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet who speaks in God’s name what God has not said, or speaks for other gods, is guilty of a capital crime; a word that does not come true shows that God did not speak it.

A word that does not come true. Israel will hear men claiming to speak for God, so the chapter names two capital offences, speaking presumptuously in the LORD’s name and speaking in the name of other gods, and gives a way to tell.

Is that workable, when some prophecies take centuries? It is, because of how false prophets operate. The man inventing a message in God’s name is nearly always predicting something near: peace this year, victory in this battle, Babylon will not come. Jeremiah faced exactly that, and Hananiah was dead within two months (Jeremiah 28). The test works where the lying is done, in short-term predictions. Some prophecies were conditional, such as Jonah’s against Nineveh (Jonah 3:4, 10; Jeremiah 18:7–10); that is not the same as a prediction that simply fails.

Two tests. Chapter 13 supplies the other half: a prophet whose sign does come true but who says “Let us go after other gods” is to be rejected anyway (13:2–3). So Israel had two criteria, does it come true and does it agree with what God has already said, and a claimant had to pass both. God does not leave his people at the mercy of anyone confident enough to say “thus says the LORD”.

The voice had a face. The chapter’s last word is not a test but a Person. Every prophet died, had to be replaced and could be misunderstood. Then the succession stopped, because the promise was kept in full: “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). The nations strained after the dead for a whisper. Israel was told to wait for a voice. And the voice, when it came, had a face, ate with sinners, wept at a grave, and said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).

A word to preachers. Verse 20 should make anyone who stands up to preach go quiet for a moment. It is a matter of life and death to say God has spoken when he has not. A preacher’s safety lies in staying inside what is written, and the man who wanders outside it is not being bold.

Where Christians differ. Does this condemn modern “prophets” whose predictions fail? Many continuationists hold that a gift of prophecy continues today, fallible and always subordinate to Scripture, to be tested and weighed (1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). Others hold that prophecy as new revelation ended with the apostles.

This commentary’s view. New words from God belonged to the foundation laid by the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2), so no one today speaks with that authority, and one who claims to and is wrong has spoken presumptuously. But all should agree that a failed prediction announced as God’s word is a serious matter, and that every claim must be tested by the completed Scriptures.

keyVerse.quote: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s great promise: instead of diviners and mediums, God will give his people a voice, one of their own brothers speaking God’s own words. Peter and Stephen identify this prophet as Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37), the Son to whom the Father commands us to listen.

18.reflection:
The Levites had no land because “the LORD is their inheritance” (v. 2). What would it look like for you to live as if God himself is enough, whatever you own or lack?

Verses 10–11 forbid every way of seeking hidden knowledge, from fortune-telling to contacting the dead. What modern forms of this are common around you, and what fears or needs drive people to them?

Israel begged never to hear God’s voice directly again, and God said, “They are right” (v. 17). Why could sinners not bear God’s voice, and how does Jesus, the prophet like Moses, answer that problem?

Verses 20–22 warn against speaking in God’s name what he has not said. How should we test claims that “God told me”, and how can we make sure we are listening to the voice God has actually given?

19.title: Cities of Refuge and the Law of Witnesses
19.text: <sup>1</sup>"When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, and you dispossess them and dwell in their cities and in their houses,<sup>2</sup>you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.<sup>3</sup>You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land that the LORD your God gives you as a possession, so that any manslayer can flee to them.<sup>4</sup>"This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life. If anyone kills his neighbor unintentionally without having hated him in the past—<sup>5</sup>as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies—he may flee to one of these cities and live,<sup>6</sup>lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past.<sup>7</sup>Therefore I command you, You shall set apart three cities.<sup>8</sup>And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised to give to your fathers—<sup>9</sup>provided you are careful to keep all this commandment, which I command you today, by loving the LORD your God and by walking ever in his ways— then you shall add three other cities to these three,<sup>10</sup>lest innocent blood be shed in your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, and so the guilt of bloodshed be upon you.<sup>11</sup>"But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities,<sup>12</sup>then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die.<sup>13</sup>Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may be well with you.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.<sup>15</sup>"A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established.<sup>16</sup>If a malicious witness arises to accuse a person of wrongdoing,<sup>17</sup>then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days.<sup>18</sup>The judges shall inquire diligently, and if the witness is a false witness and has accused his brother falsely,<sup>19</sup>then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>20</sup>And the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit any such evil among you.<sup>21</sup>Your eye shall not pity. It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
19.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 16 to 18 set up Israel’s judges, king, priests and prophets. Chapter 19 returns to the courts and the life they protect, beginning a run of laws about killing, war and bloodshed that continues through chapter 21.

The message. God values every human life too highly to let it be taken carelessly, whether by a murderer, by a grieving relative in hot anger, or by a liar in court. So he builds refuge into the map of the land for the man who killed by accident, refuses refuge to the murderer, guards a family’s inheritance from quiet theft, and turns the false witness’s lie back on his own head. Justice in Israel must be both merciful and exact.

Why it was said. Israel had no police force; when someone was killed, the nearest relative, the avenger of blood, pursued the killer (see the introduction on the settled life ahead). Without safeguards, grief would kill the innocent along with the guilty, and courts would be at the mercy of whoever lied most boldly.

How the chapter makes its case. First, three cities of refuge, evenly spread and easy to reach, where the man who killed without hatred may flee and live (vv. 1–7), with three more if the land grows (vv. 8–10), but no shelter for the deliberate murderer, whom the elders hand over (vv. 11–13). Then a single command not to move a neighbour’s boundary stone (v. 14). Last, the law of witnesses: never one alone, and the false witness suffers exactly what he meant to bring on his brother, life for life, eye for eye (vv. 15–21).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The New Testament takes up the language of refuge: believers are those “who have fled for refuge” to “the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18). Yet the manslayer was innocent of murder, while we come guilty, and find shelter because Christ took our penalty. The chapter’s false witnesses meet their match at his trial, where “many false witnesses came forward” (Matthew 26:60) and he stayed silent, and its “eye for eye” he took further, calling his people to give up revenge altogether (Matthew 5:38–39).

For us. Be slow to judge and quick to seek the facts, especially when anger is hot and the crowd is loud. Guard your neighbour’s rights when no one would notice, and never let your words become a weapon. And run where the guilty may run: to Christ, the refuge that no avenger can enter.
19.theology:
Christ our refuge. The refuge does not deny guilt but shelters from judgment; Christ bears the wrath, so that within him we are safe. As the roads were kept clear, the gospel makes him near to all who flee to him.

Justice balanced with mercy. The law shelters the one who killed without intent and refuses refuge to the murderer, to “purge the guilt of innocent blood” (19:13). God's law is neither careless nor cruel.

The integrity of testimony. No one may be condemned on a single witness (19:15), and the false accuser bears what he intended (19:19). The God of refuge is the God of truth, who will not have his courts corrupted by lies.
19.examples: We flee to Christ, our refuge from the wrath we deserve, secure in him though guilty; we uphold careful justice and abhor false witness, marvelling that the innocent One condemned by false witnesses has become the only refuge for sinners.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God builds mercy into the map of the land. Once Israel is settled, three cities must be set apart, the land divided so that one is always within reach (vv. 1–3), where a man who killed his neighbour by accident, like the woodcutter whose axe head flies off, may flee from the avenger of blood (vv. 4–7). If God enlarges the land, three more are to be added, so that no innocent blood is shed (vv. 8–10). But the refuge is no loophole: a man who killed out of hatred and ambush is fetched out by his own town’s elders and handed over, so that the guilt of innocent blood is purged from Israel (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge does not pretend the manslayer is innocent of the death; it shelters him from a vengeance that cannot tell accident from murder until the facts are heard.
verseByVerse.examples: The cities were placed, and the roads kept clear, so that a frightened man could reach one in time. The refuge now is a Person, and preaching the gospel is the road-clearing: our business is to make him reachable, not to make him respectable.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, and you dispossess them and dwell in their cities and in their houses, you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess. You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land that the LORD your God gives you as a possession, so that any manslayer can flee to them. "This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life. If anyone kills his neighbor unintentionally without having hated him in the past— as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies—he may flee to one of these cities and live, lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past. Therefore I command you, You shall set apart three cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must set apart three cities, spread so that anyone can reach one, where a person who has killed someone by accident can escape the avenger of blood and live.

Measure the distances. The country is to be surveyed and the cities placed so that nobody is ever too far from one. Jewish tradition adds that the roads were kept clear and signposted, which fits the Hebrew of verse 3 (see the box below).

The axe head. Two men working side by side on an ordinary afternoon. A loose axe head. One is dead and the other is a killer, and neither of them did anything wrong. Scripture gives a specific accident, not a category, because the man this law exists for is not a criminal and needs to be seen clearly.

The avenger of blood. Without police, the dead man’s nearest relative had the duty of pursuit. He was not taking the law into his own hands; he was the only enforcement there was. But he would set out on the day of the funeral, “in hot anger”, and grief in a hurry cannot tell an accident from a murder. So the whole institution puts distance and time between a death and the killing that would avenge it, long enough for the facts to be heard (Numbers 35:12, 24–25). That is God’s justice written into a map: not indifference to blood, but an absolute refusal to let a man die before anyone has found out what he did.

Outrage at the speed of grief. We have not outgrown the avenger of blood; we have given him a phone. A clip appears, and within hours thousands of strangers have pronounced a verdict on someone whose name they learned that morning, with real passion and almost no facts. Fury in a hurry still cannot tell an accident from a murder, and the crowd never builds a city of refuge. God’s law does not tell the avenger that his anger is unreal; it puts a road, a gate and a hearing between his anger and the man he is chasing. A God who will judge perfectly frees us from having to judge instantly. And the gospel cuts deeper than the mob: every one of us has a case against him that would not survive a fair hearing. People who have had to flee to Christ themselves should be the slowest to pick up a stone.

Is the city of refuge a picture of Christ? Hebrews calls believers those “who have fled for refuge” and now “hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18). The difference is telling: the manslayer was innocent of murder, while we come guilty, and find refuge because Christ bore the penalty. Numbers adds that the manslayer went free when the high priest died (Numbers 35:25, 28), and many Christians have seen there a hint of the great High Priest whose death sets the guilty free (Hebrews 9:15).

Uncertain wording. “You shall measure the distances” in verse 3 is literally “you shall prepare the way for yourself”, and the ESV footnote reads “Hebrew road”. It may mean surveying the land so that the cities are evenly spaced, or building and maintaining the roads to them; both serve the same purpose, that no fleeing man is overtaken “because the way is long” (v. 6).

verseByVerse.quote: And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised to give to your fathers— provided you are careful to keep all this commandment, which I command you today, by loving the LORD your God and by walking ever in his ways— then you shall add three other cities to these three, lest innocent blood be shed in your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, and so the guilt of bloodshed be upon you. "But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities, then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die. Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may be well with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More cities must be added if the land grows, so that no innocent man dies; but a deliberate murderer who flees to a refuge city must be handed over to die.

You shall add three other cities. The three here are west of the Jordan, besides the three Moses had already set apart east of it (4:41–43), six in all (Joshua 20:7–8). The further three were apparently never needed, because Israel never held the full borders promised on condition of its love and obedience (v. 9).

Hates his neighbor and lies in wait. The refuge is not a loophole. A murderer who runs there is fetched out, by the elders of his own town. The three marks of murder are named: he “hates”, he “lies in wait”, he “attacks”: motive, planning and act. The law asks what was in the man, not merely what happened.

No pity. That hard sentence is aimed at the judges. A community that will not carry out a just sentence because it finds it distasteful has stopped protecting the next victim. Paul still calls the governing authority “an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4).

Innocent blood. Murder left unpunished defiles the land, and a nation that shrugs at it shares its guilt.

The same justice. Hold the two halves together, because they are the same justice. The man who killed by accident is sheltered even from a grieving family; the man who killed on purpose is taken out of sanctuary. Mercy that cannot tell the two men apart is not mercy, and severity that cannot tell them apart is not justice. Only at the cross do perfect mercy and perfect justice meet for the truly guilty, so that God is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A single verse forbids moving a neighbour’s landmark, the boundary stone set long ago to mark the inheritance God had given each family. It sits among laws about killing because it is another way of taking what God has given a neighbour, done quietly, without violence and without witnesses. The people it harms are usually those least able to defend themselves, and elsewhere in Scripture God names himself their advocate.
verseByVerse.theology: Because God allotted the land, a moved boundary stone was theft from God as well as from the neighbour. Proverbs returns to it more than once, and ties it to the widow and the fatherless (Prov. 15:25; 22:28; 23:10-11).
verseByVerse.examples: Whoever has quietly lost out to someone stronger may take comfort here: God still takes the side of those who cannot fight back.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not move your neighbour’s boundary stone, because it marks the inheritance God himself gave his family.

The landmark. In a chapter about killing it looks like a change of subject, and it is not. Israel’s land was allotted by God, tribe by tribe and family by family, and the boundary stones marked what he had given. To shift one was to steal from a neighbour and to redraw God’s map.

The quietest crime. No violence, no confrontation. A man goes out at dusk and moves a stone eighteen inches, and does it again a few years later, and there are no witnesses and nothing to report. Meanwhile a family who cannot afford a surveyor is a little poorer every harvest and cannot say why.

Scripture returns to it. And notice who is named alongside it: “Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you” (Proverbs 23:10–11). The people this is done to are those who cannot fight back, and God appoints himself their advocate.

In everyday life. The modern version needs no stone. It is done in contracts, in invoices, in a fee structure a client cannot follow, in a margin quietly taken from someone who will never check. Nobody calls it theft, and no one is charged. The verse is in the Bible for exactly that reason.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Two Witnesses, and the False One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No charge may stand on one witness’s word, in any case at all (v. 15). When a malicious witness accuses someone, both parties come before the LORD, the priests and the judges, who must investigate thoroughly (vv. 16–18). If the witness has lied, he receives exactly what he meant to bring on his brother, so that the evil is purged and others fear to do the same (vv. 19–20). The principle of “life for life, eye for eye” sets a just measure for punishment and a ceiling on revenge (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: God guards the accused as carefully as he pursues the guilty, and turns the false accuser’s own weapon back on him.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone tempted to use the courts, or gossip, to ruin a neighbour should reckon with receiving the same sentence. And it is worth remembering that Christ himself was condemned by false witnesses (Matt. 26:59-60).

verseByVerse.quote: "A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established. If a malicious witness arises to accuse a person of wrongdoing, then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days. The judges shall inquire diligently, and if the witness is a false witness and has accused his brother falsely, then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. And the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit any such evil among you. Your eye shall not pity. It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No charge may stand on one witness alone, and a witness who lies receives the very punishment he tried to bring on his brother.

A single witness. One person cannot be checked. The rule given at 17:6 for capital cases is widened here to “any crime or for any wrong”, so that no dispute in Israel turns on a single voice.

A malicious witness. The procedure is careful: both parties present, before God and the court, with diligent investigation, and the burden on the accuser to make his charge stand.

As he had meant. The penalty is the most exact in the law. The false witness receives precisely the sentence he was trying to obtain. A man who swore away his neighbour’s life loses his own; a man who tried to have him fined pays the fine. The lie comes back down the same road it went out on.

Eye for eye. Verse 21 is one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. It is not permission for revenge but a ceiling on it, and it is addressed to judges, not to the injured man. Where a slight could start a feud that killed a family, the law says: one eye, no more. Jewish interpreters came to apply it as fixing compensation of equal value rather than literal maiming (compare Exodus 21:26–27).

Christ takes it further. Because it was written to restrain vengeance, the Lord Jesus could take it further in the same direction without contradicting it: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil” (Matthew 5:38–39). Moses capped retaliation at one eye; Christ asks his people to give up personal revenge altogether. Then he stood before a council who “were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death” (Matthew 26:59), heard the false witnesses, and “remained silent” (Matthew 26:63). The lie that should have come back on the liars fell on him, and he bore it for them.

What it does not mean. Jesus forbids private revenge, not justice. Courts must still weigh evidence and punish false accusers, and a Christian who has been wronged may rightly go to the police; what he lays down is the desire to pay back for himself (Romans 12:19).

keyVerse.quote: This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life.
keyVerse.note: The verse sums up the chapter’s mercy: God makes a way of escape for the one who would otherwise die before the truth is known. Hebrews takes up this picture for every believer, who has “fled for refuge” to Christ (Hebrews 6:18), the refuge open even to the guilty.

19.reflection:
The avenger of blood set out “in hot anger” (v. 6), and God made sure there was time for the facts to be heard. Where are you tempted to judge people quickly, in person or online, and what would it look like to slow down?

The city of refuge sheltered the innocent man, while Christ shelters the guilty who flee to him (Hebrews 6:18). How does that difference change the way you think about your own sin and about others?

Moving a boundary stone was a quiet theft no one could prove (v. 14). What are the modern equivalents in work, business or family life, and who usually pays for them?

A false witness received what he meant for his brother (v. 19), yet Jesus, falsely accused, stayed silent and bore it for us. How should that shape the way we speak about others and respond when we are wronged?

20.title: Laws of War: The LORD Goes With You to Fight
20.text: <sup>1</sup>"When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people<sup>3</sup>and shall say to them, 'Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them,<sup>4</sup>for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.'<sup>5</sup>Then the officers shall speak to the people, saying, 'Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it.<sup>6</sup>And is there any man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man enjoy its fruit.<sup>7</sup>And is there any man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.'<sup>8</sup>And the officers shall speak further to the people, and say, 'Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own.'<sup>9</sup>And when the officers have finished speaking to the people, then commanders shall be appointed at the head of the people.<sup>10</sup>"When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it.<sup>11</sup>And if it responds to you peaceably and it opens to you, then all the people who are found in it shall do forced labor for you and shall serve you.<sup>12</sup>But if it makes no peace with you, but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it.<sup>13</sup>And when the LORD your God gives it into your hand, you shall put all its males to the sword,<sup>14</sup>but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city, all its spoil, you shall take as plunder for yourselves. And you shall enjoy the spoil of your enemies, which the LORD your God has given you.<sup>15</sup>Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of the nations here.<sup>16</sup>But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes,<sup>17</sup>but you shall devote them to complete destruction, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, as the LORD your God has commanded,<sup>18</sup>that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.<sup>19</sup>"When you besiege a city for a long time, making war against it in order to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?<sup>20</sup>Only the trees that you know are not trees for food you may destroy and cut down, that you may build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls.
20.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 19 guarded innocent life in Israel’s towns and courts. Chapter 20 turns to the hardest setting for that concern, war, and gives Israel the rules for its battles as it prepares to enter the land.

The message. When Israel goes to war, the LORD goes with them and fights for them, so their confidence must rest on him, not on numbers or chariots. Because the victory is his, the army can send home the newly married and the frightened, offer peace before striking a blow, and spare the fruit trees. The one exception, the Canaanite cities, is God’s unique judgment on a corrupt religion, given so that Israel will not learn its abominations.

Why it was said. Israel was about to fight nations with chariots and walled cities (see the introduction). Ancient warfare was brutal, and kings boasted of massacres and scorched earth. Israel needed to know who would win its battles, and how a people who belonged to God must fight.

How the chapter makes its case. First, faith before the battle: the priest, not the general, speaks first, “Hear, O Israel… Do not fear” (vv. 1–4). Then generous exemptions, the new house, the young vineyard, the betrothed and the fainthearted, so that only believing men remain (vv. 5–9). Next, peace before war: distant cities must be offered terms first, and the women and children of a city that resists are spared (vv. 10–15). The cities of Canaan are the exception, devoted to destruction lest they teach Israel their practices (vv. 16–18). Last, restraint even in a siege: the fruit trees must not be cut down (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The God who “goes with you to fight for you” (v. 4) won the decisive battle in his Son, who “disarmed the rulers and authorities” on the cross (Colossians 2:15). The offer of peace before judgment is the shape of the gospel: “We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). And the judgment that fell on Canaan finally fell, for all who trust him, on Christ himself.

For us. Christ’s kingdom is never advanced by the sword, but every believer still faces battles, against sin, fear and the devil, that are bigger than he is. The word before each one is the priest’s: do not fear, for the Lord is with you. Fight trusting him, offer peace before anything else, and leave standing what is good.
20.theology:
The LORD fights for his people. Before battle the priest preaches faith, not strategy (20:4). Holy war rests on God's presence, not human strength, and so does the believer's warfare (Rom. 8:31).

God saves by a believing few. The exemptions reduce the army (20:5–8), for God is not impressed by numbers or resources; he delights to save by the few who trust him, that the glory may be his alone.

Justice tempered by restraint. Terms of peace precede the siege (20:10), and even the fruit trees are spared (20:19). The judgment of the Canaanites was God's unique act on a people whose wickedness was complete, pointing to the cross, where judgment fell on Christ, and to the gospel's offer of peace.
20.examples: We face our battles knowing the Lord goes with us; we rejoice that the God of holy war offers peace to the world in the gospel, having borne his own judgment against sin at the cross; and in Christ, who has triumphed over sin, death and the devil, we are more than conquerors.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Before the Battle: the Priest and the Exemptions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s confidence in battle must rest on God, not on numbers. Facing a larger army with horses and chariots, Israel must not fear, because the God who brought them out of Egypt is with them (v. 1). The priest, not the general, speaks first, calling “Hear, O Israel” and promising that the LORD goes with them to give them the victory (vv. 2–4). Then the officers send home every man with a new house, an unharvested vineyard or a bride not yet married, and anyone who is afraid, before commanders are appointed (vv. 5–9). God wants a believing army, not the largest one.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel goes to war on the ground of who is with her: the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you (v.4). And the army is deliberately reduced rather than maximised, so that the victory can belong to nobody else.
verseByVerse.examples: God is not served by people pushed to do more than he has asked, and the church’s strength has never lain in its numbers. A believer who has had to step back from some work for a season has not left the Lord’s army.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. And when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people and shall say to them, 'Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel faces a stronger army, it must not be afraid, because the LORD who rescued them from Egypt goes with them to fight for them and give them the victory.

Horses and chariots and an army larger than your own. God admits the facts first. The enemy does have horses and chariots, and the army is larger. Israel had no chariots, and on open ground infantry against chariots was badly outmatched. Faith does not pretend the danger is small; it remembers who brought them “up out of the land of Egypt”, where they had faced the greatest chariot army of all.

The priest shall speak. Not the general. The priest delivers not a strategy but a sermon, and it opens like the Shema: “Hear, O Israel” (6:4).

Do not fear. The priest piles up four words for fear, faint, fear, panic and dread, because fear comes in more than one form. Against them he sets no argument about Israel’s strength, only one fact: God is with them. That is what Paul asks after eight chapters of Romans: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

The battle that decided everything. It was fought by one man with no army at all, when Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). “We do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12), but our battles are fought under the same word: the Lord goes with you.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers shall speak to the people, saying, 'Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it. And is there any man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man enjoy its fruit. And is there any man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.' And the officers shall speak further to the people, and say, 'Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own.' And when the officers have finished speaking to the people, then commanders shall be appointed at the head of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the battle, men with a new house, an unharvested vineyard or a bride waiting, and anyone afraid, are sent home, because God wants a believing army, not the biggest one.

Let him go back to his house. God releases men so that they will not die before enjoying the good things he has given them. A vineyard took years before its fruit could be eaten (Leviticus 19:23–25), and the man who had planted one and not yet tasted it is sent home. That is not military logic. It is a Father protecting his children’s joy in a war he intends to win himself.

The fearful. Few armies would grant this: anyone frightened may leave, without penalty. The reason is practical, “lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own”, because fear is contagious and travels faster than courage. But the effect is that the army is reduced to men who believe God will do what he said.

A believing army. God strips the numbers down so that nobody can give the credit to anyone but him, as he told Gideon: “The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me’” (Judges 7:2).

Excuses at the banquet. In Jesus’ parable the guests refuse the great banquet with almost these reasons: a field, oxen, a new wife (Luke 14:18–20). What exempted a man from war cannot exempt him from the gospel’s feast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — Terms of Peace, and the Cities of Canaan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must offer peace before it wages war. A distant city that accepts the terms becomes a subject people; one that refuses may be besieged, but its women, children and livestock are spared (vv. 10–15). The cities of the six named nations within the land are a different case: they are to be devoted to destruction, as God’s judgment on their abominations and so that they cannot teach Israel to sin against the LORD (vv. 16–18). The text marks this command as the exception, limited to one land and one moment.
verseByVerse.theology: Two sets of rules are set side by side deliberately. War outside Canaan begins with an offer of peace and spares women and children — a striking restraint by ancient standards. The herem (the ban, devoting a people wholly to God for destruction) inside Canaan is an act of God’s judgment, limited to a named list of nations, and its stated purpose in v.18 is to protect Israel. It is a model for nobody; the New Testament rules it out (John 18:36; 2 Cor. 10:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples: Judgment fell only where peace had been refused, and that is still the order of God’s dealings: the gospel’s terms come first, and they are far better than any city in Canaan was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it. And if it responds to you peaceably and it opens to you, then all the people who are found in it shall do forced labor for you and shall serve you. But if it makes no peace with you, but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it. And when the LORD your God gives it into your hand, you shall put all its males to the sword, but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city, all its spoil, you shall take as plunder for yourselves. And you shall enjoy the spoil of your enemies, which the LORD your God has given you. Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of the nations here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before attacking a distant city, Israel must offer peace; if the city fights, its men may be killed, but its women and children must be spared.

Terms of peace. Israel’s wars are to begin with an offer, before a blow is struck. If the city accepts, its people become subject labourers; if it refuses and fights, the siege follows and the men are killed, but “the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city” are spared.

Measured against its world. By our standards this is harsh. Against the actual practice of the ancient Near East it is a remarkable restraint. Assyrian kings recorded with pride the flaying of prisoners and pillars of severed heads; annihilating a resisting city was common and boasted about. Israel must offer peace first, and may not kill the women and children even of a city that chose war. These are rules for that time, limiting war in a brutal world, not a model for warfare today.

Peace before judgment. The offer of peace before judgment is how God himself acts throughout Scripture. Nineveh got forty days and a preacher. Judah got centuries of prophets. And the gospel has the same shape: “We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20), terms offered freely before anything falls.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes, but you shall devote them to complete destruction, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, as the LORD your God has commanded, that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cities of Canaan are the exception: they are to be devoted to destruction as God’s judgment, so that their religion does not teach Israel to sin.

A different case. Verses 10–15 apply to “all the cities that are very far from you”. This is the marked exception: not Israel’s foreign policy but a limited act of judgment, inside one territory, against six named nations, at one moment in history. To “devote them to complete destruction” (herem) means handing something over wholly to God, beyond human use (see 7:2).

Lest they teach you. The stated purpose (v. 18) is protective. Not land-hunger or racial superiority, but containment of a religion that burned children (12:31), so that it would not be taught to Israel. The tragic footnote is that Israel did not carry it out, the religion was taught to her, and within a few centuries Israelites were burning their own children in the Valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 7:31).

Three things to hold together. This is judgment, executed after four centuries of divine patience (Genesis 15:16). It is unrepeatable: no nation, church or person has held this commission since, and Christ’s kingdom does not fight with swords (John 18:36). And it remains hard, and Scripture does not remove the difficulty; what it does is set beside it a God who, when judgment finally fell on sin in earnest, arranged for it to fall on himself.

But women and children? This is the hardest question in the chapter, and it should be felt. Scripture answers it from God’s side: the whole people fell under judgment, as the world did in the flood and Sodom in the fire, and the Judge of all the earth, who gives every life, has the right to take any life (Genesis 18:25). It shows mercy at the edges: Rahab and her household turned to the LORD and were spared (Joshua 6:25). And it fences the command off as unique to that moment: in Israel’s own courts children must not be put to death for their fathers’ crimes (24:16). What happens to little children before God is in hands kinder and wiser than ours; the God who commanded this is the God who pitied the children of a pagan city (Jonah 4:11).

Was it carried out literally? The language of total destruction is partly the idiom of ancient war: Joshua says “he left none remaining” (Joshua 10:40), yet Canaanites remained (Joshua 15:63; Judges 1). The command was real, and so was Israel’s partial obedience.

Textual note. Chapter 7 names seven nations; the Hebrew list here names six, leaving out the Girgashites, whom the Greek Old Testament includes. Both lists stand for the whole.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–20 — Do Not Destroy the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even in a long siege, Israel must not destroy the fruit trees. They may eat from them, but may not cut them down, for the trees are not the enemy: “Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?” (v. 19). Only trees that do not bear food may be felled for siegeworks (v. 20). In the middle of a war manual, God draws a line between the combatant and the field he stands in, and protects the life that will feed people long after the battle is over.
verseByVerse.theology: Even a war God has authorised is fenced. What sustains life is not to be destroyed to win a battle, and the reason given is what a fruit tree is (it feeds people and is nobody’s enemy), not what Israel stands to gain.
verseByVerse.examples: An army under orders left the olive groves standing, and the same God still asks whether the thing we are about to destroy in order to win was ever the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you besiege a city for a long time, making war against it in order to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you? Only the trees that you know are not trees for food you may destroy and cut down, that you may build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in a long siege, Israel must not cut down the fruit trees, which are not the enemy and will feed people long after the battle.

Scorched earth. A besieging army normally cut down the orchards, for timber, for siege ramps, and to ruin the district so it could not recover. An olive tree can take many years to bear well; destroying the groves meant a generation of poverty for whoever was left. God forbids it, even while Israel besieges the city the trees belong to.

Not everything is a target. The tree has done nothing, it cannot fight, and it will be feeding people long after the quarrel is settled. War does not license the destruction of everything within reach; there is a line between the combatant and the field he stands in, and God draws it in the middle of a manual on siegecraft. The verse stands near the root of later principles of restraint in war, and it comes from a God whose care runs down into things nobody thought to protect. Not a sparrow falls “apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29), and he notices the olive grove too.

Where Christians differ. May Christians fight in war at all? Pacifists, such as Anabaptists and Quakers, hold that Jesus’ call to love enemies rules out all killing, and their witness deserves respect. Most Christians have held that a state may use force to defend the innocent, with restraints like these: a just cause, peace offered first, and protection for those not fighting.

This commentary’s view. Jesus forbids personal revenge, not the state’s lawful use of force, service as a soldier or police officer, or the defence of the vulnerable. But Christ’s kingdom itself is never advanced by the sword or by coercion.

Uncertain wording. “Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?” is a compressed Hebrew phrase. The ESV and most modern versions read it as a question; the King James Version reads it as a statement, “for the tree of the field is man’s life”. Either way the point is the same: the trees feed people and are not the enemy.

keyVerse.quote: for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter follows from this sentence. Because the battle is the LORD’s, Israel can send home the fearful, offer peace first and spare the trees. Christians hear it fulfilled in Christ, who won the decisive victory on the cross and goes with his people in every fight against sin and fear.

20.reflection:
The priest admitted the enemy had chariots and a larger army, then said, “Do not fear” (vv. 1–4). What battles are you facing that look bigger than you, and what difference does it make that the Lord goes with you?

God sent home the newly married, the man with a new house and the fearful (vv. 5–8). What does this show about God’s care for ordinary joys, and about where real strength comes from?

Israel had to offer peace before attacking a city (v. 10), and the gospel offers peace before judgment (2 Corinthians 5:20). How should that shape the way we share the gospel and deal with those who oppose us?

The command to destroy the cities of Canaan (vv. 16–18) is one of the hardest in Scripture. How do the reasons the Bible gives, and the cross where judgment fell on Christ, help you hold on to God’s goodness while still feeling its weight?

21.title: Various Laws: A Hanged Man Is Cursed by God
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"If in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess someone is found slain, lying in the open country, and it is not known who killed him,<sup>2</sup>then your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities.<sup>3</sup>And the elders of the city that is nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke.<sup>4</sup>And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley.<sup>5</sup>Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled.<sup>6</sup>And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley,<sup>7</sup>and they shall testify, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed.<sup>8</sup>Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel, so that their blood guilt be atoned for.'<sup>9</sup>So you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God gives them into your hand and you take them captive,<sup>11</sup>and you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife,<sup>12</sup>and you bring her home to your house, she shall shave her head and pare her nails.<sup>13</sup>And she shall take off the clothes in which she was captured and shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife.<sup>14</sup>But if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.<sup>15</sup>"If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved, and both the loved and the unloved have borne him children, and if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved,<sup>16</sup>then on the day when he assigns his possessions as an inheritance to his sons, he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn,<sup>17</sup>but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.<sup>18</sup>"If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen to them,<sup>19</sup>then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city at the gate of the place where he lives,<sup>20</sup>and they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.'<sup>21</sup>Then all the men of the city shall stone him to death with stones. So you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.<sup>22</sup>"And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree,<sup>23</sup>his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
21.overview:
Where we are. We are in the middle of Moses’ long second sermon, in the detailed laws for life in the land (chapters 12–26). Chapter 20 dealt with war; chapter 21 turns to hard cases at home and in the town, where human life, guilt and family loyalty meet.

The message. Every human life matters to God, and guilt does not go away because nobody can be charged. So God makes his people deal with blood they cannot trace, protects people who have no one to speak for them, takes rebellion against his order seriously, and sets a limit even on the shame of the condemned. Behind it all stands a God who will not overlook sin and will not forget the weak.

Why it was said. Israel was about to become a settled nation of towns and farms, with no king yet and justice in the hands of local elders (see the introduction). These laws taught them that their land was the LORD’s, that bloodshed defiled it, and that the powerful, whether soldiers, husbands or fathers, were answerable to him for how they treated the powerless.

How the chapter makes its case. It moves through five cases. An unsolved murder must be atoned for by the nearest town, which washes its hands and prays for God to accept atonement (vv. 1–9). A woman captured in war must be given a month to mourn, taken as a true wife, and never sold as a slave (vv. 10–14). The firstborn son of an unloved wife keeps his double share, whatever his father feels (vv. 15–17). A grown son who is a confirmed rebel, a glutton and a drunkard, is brought by both parents to the elders and put to death (vv. 18–21). And the body of an executed criminal, hung up as a sign that he is under God’s curse, must be buried before nightfall (vv. 22–23).

Where it leads. Here the New Testament itself points the way. Paul takes the last verse, “a hanged man is cursed by God”, and declares that “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).
