The chapter also exposes a need it cannot meet: blood guilt that no one can pay for, and a rebellious son who can only be condemned. The answer is the obedient Son who was taken outside the city and hung on a tree in the rebels’ place, so that God’s acceptance of atonement rests on his blood, not a heifer’s.

For us. Take human life as seriously as God does, especially the lives nobody else notices. And when your own guilt rises up, do not try to pay it off with misery: look to the one who bore the curse, and rest in the atonement God has already accepted.
21.theology:
Christ became a curse for us. On the tree of Calvary the sinless Son bore the curse we deserved (21:23; Gal. 3:13), so that the verse which once made a crucified Messiah unthinkable became the reason for the church's hope.

The preciousness of innocent blood. Even an unsolved murder must be solemnly addressed (21:9); no bloodshed is too obscure to matter to God. Hebrews sets such rites beside the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience as no animal could (Heb. 9:13–14).

Justice for the vulnerable. The law guards the captive woman and the unloved wife's firstborn (21:10–17), and takes rebellion against God-given authority seriously (21:18–21), a rebellion the gospel answers by Christ bearing our judgment, that rebels might become beloved children.
21.examples: We rest in the gospel proclaimed from this chapter: Christ became a curse for us, so that the God who would not overlook a single drop of innocent blood has dealt fully with all our guilt at the cross, where the blessed One was cursed that the cursed might be blessed. So we honor human life and defend the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every life matters to God, and blood that cannot be traced must still be dealt with before him. When a body is found in open country and the killer is unknown, the elders measure which town is nearest (vv. 1–2). Its elders take an unworked heifer to an untilled valley with running water and break its neck there, with the priests present (vv. 3–5). Then they wash their hands over it, swear that they neither shed the blood nor saw it shed, and pray that the LORD will accept atonement for his redeemed people (vv. 6–8). So the guilt of innocent blood is removed from Israel (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Innocent blood pollutes the land, and God will not let an unsolved killing be quietly forgotten. The ritual is a confession by the whole community that a death has occurred which the community cannot account for. Even where no one can be charged, atonement is sought.
verseByVerse.examples: A whole town stopped work over a stranger nobody could name, because his blood mattered to God. A society that can absorb unexplained deaths without flinching has lost something this ritual existed to protect, and the blood that finally answers for all such bloodshed was not a heifer’s but Christ’s.

verseByVerse.quote: "If in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess someone is found slain, lying in the open country, and it is not known who killed him, then your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities. And the elders of the city that is nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke. And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley. Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled. And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley, and they shall testify, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed. Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel, so that their blood guilt be atoned for.' So you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a murder cannot be solved, God still requires it to be dealt with before him: the nearest town must disown the deed and ask him to accept atonement, because no human life is too obscure to matter.

Someone is found slain. A body lies in open country and nobody knows who killed him. In most societies, ancient or modern, that is where the matter ends. In Israel it is where a ceremony begins: grown men with measuring lines walk out into a field to establish which town is nearest to a corpse nobody can name.

The heifer. The heifer has never worked, the valley has never been ploughed or sown, and water runs through it: everything in the scene is untouched. This is no ordinary sacrifice on an altar but a solemn act that answers for the killing away from the town. The priests stand by, because the matter is settled before the LORD.

They shall testify. First comes an oath: the elders wash their hands and swear, “Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed.” If anyone in that town knew anything, the ceremony would give him a very uncomfortable morning.

Accept atonement. Then the prayer, the heart of the passage. They ask for atonement for a crime they did not commit and cannot solve, because blood shed in the land defiles it (Numbers 35:33), and they ask it for “your people Israel, whom you have redeemed” (v. 8).

What atonement means. In ordinary speech, to atone is to make up for something: work harder, pay it back, feel bad enough for long enough. Many of us live like that, and it never feels finished. The Hebrew word here (kipper) points the other way: guilt covered by a payment, a life given in place of the guilty, something God accepts, not something the guilty achieve. The elders do not offer to make amends; they cannot. See Atonement in the Theological Dictionary.

The atonement God has accepted. That is the shape of the gospel. Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience as no animal could (Hebrews 9:13–14), for he “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26), and God has accepted it. So when an old wrong surfaces late at night, do not try to pay it off again with misery. Confess it, and rest on the atonement God has already accepted.

No life too obscure. A stranger killed by someone nobody could find, and the whole leadership of the nearest town stops work and stands before God about it. What a contrast with a world that scrolls past a body on the news.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “a valley with running water” is uncertain. The Hebrew word usually means “enduring” or “ever-flowing”, so most modern versions think of a stream that never dries up; older versions read “a rough valley”. Either way the place is wild and unfarmed, which is the point.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Captive Woman and the Unloved Wife’s Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God protects people whom no one else will defend. A soldier who wants to marry a woman captured in war must first take her into his home and give her a full month to mourn her parents; she becomes a true wife, and if he no longer wants her she goes free and may never be sold or made a slave (vv. 10–14). A man with two wives may not pass over the firstborn son of the wife he does not love: that son keeps his double share of the inheritance, whatever his father’s feelings (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Neither law describes God’s ideal; both restrain a sinful practice and set a minimum of protection for the powerless. The captive is given time, dignity and — if the marriage fails — freedom rather than sale. The unloved wife’s son is protected from a father’s partiality, because justice may not be bent by affection.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s law named the two people least able to defend themselves and gave them rights. The test of any household, church or company is still what happens to the person in it who cannot appeal to anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God gives them into your hand and you take them captive, and you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife, and you bring her home to your house, she shall shave her head and pare her nails. And she shall take off the clothes in which she was captured and shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife. But if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God puts strict limits on what a soldier may do with a woman captured in war: she must be given time to mourn, made a true wife, and never sold or treated as a slave. The law is read rightly for what it restrains, not only for what it permits.

You see among the captives a beautiful woman. This law troubles modern readers, and it should. In other ancient armies a soldier who wanted a captive woman simply took her; captured women were spoil. Here that is stopped.

Bring her home to your house. Home, not the camp. She shaves her head, pares her nails and takes off “the clothes in which she was captured”, signs of mourning and of leaving her old life behind.

Lament her father and her mother a full month. The law does not say that she chose this marriage, and that silence is part of why the passage is hard. What it does is take from the soldier every freedom it can. For a month he may not touch her, while she grieves for parents probably killed in the battle he fought; he must live with her sorrow before anything can happen at all.

She shall be your wife. A wife and not a concubine, with a wife’s standing. Then the provision that closes the last door: if he no longer delights in her, “you shall let her go where she wants.” She cannot be sold or reduced to a slave, and the law says why: “you have humiliated her”. God takes her side, in the written law, against the man who holds all the power.

What this is not. This is not God’s picture of marriage, and nobody should pretend it is. It is God regulating a brutal practice in a brutal world and putting a floor beneath a woman with no advocate, no family and no rights: meeting people where they are, restraining the worst, protecting the person nobody else will protect. The Lord Jesus said as much about divorce: “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8).

A better husband. The law could only limit a soldier’s power over a captive. Christ found his bride captive and won her by giving himself for her (Ephesians 5:25); he did not humiliate her, but bore humiliation for her.

Uncertain wording. “Pare her nails” is literally “do her nails”, and it may mean trimming them or letting them grow. Either way, with the shaved head and new clothes, it marks mourning and the end of her old life.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved, and both the loved and the unloved have borne him children, and if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved, then on the day when he assigns his possessions as an inheritance to his sons, he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn, but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A father may not let his affections rewrite the inheritance: the firstborn son of a wife he does not love keeps his double share. God protects a boy at the very point where he is least likely to be defended, in his own home, from his own father.

Loved and unloved. God does not endorse the situation. Polygamy brings misery wherever it appears in Scripture, and the phrase “the one loved and the other unloved” recalls the household of Jacob, where Leah was the unloved wife and Reuben her firstborn (Genesis 29:30–32). (Reuben later lost his birthright through his own sin, not his father’s preference: Genesis 35:22; 1 Chronicles 5:1.) The law is written about a mess God did not design.

A double portion of all that he has. The firstborn received twice the share of each of his brothers (see inheritance and the firstborn), along with the duty of heading the family. He gets it not because he is preferred or even liked, but because he is “the firstfruits of his strength”.

Justice in the home. There is no court a boy can appeal to against being loved less, so God writes his protection into the law. When favouritism becomes injustice, God sees it.

God and the unloved. See what God repeatedly does with the unloved. In Jacob’s house Leah was the unloved wife, and it was through her son Judah that the Messiah came. God’s habit of lifting the overlooked runs through the genealogies. And in Christ, the true firstborn (Colossians 1:18), the unloved are brought into the family and made heirs with him (Romans 8:17).
verseByVerse.note: Joseph’s two sons, each counted as a tribe, show the double portion at work (Gen. 48:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — The Stubborn and Rebellious Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rebellion against the authority God has set in the home is a serious evil. The son in view is no small child but a confirmed rebel, a glutton and a drunkard, who has refused repeated discipline (v. 18). Both his parents must bring him to the elders at the town gate and lay the charge in public (vv. 19–20). The men of the city then put him to death, so that evil is removed and all Israel hears and fears (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Rebellion against authority in the home is serious because the home is where every person first meets authority. The civil penalty belonged to Israel as a nation under God and is not carried into the church age; the seriousness of the sin is.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents grieving over a grown child who has rejected everything they taught may notice that the law brought in the elders and the whole town. Parents are not asked to carry such grief by themselves, and no child is beyond the reach of the Son who bore the rebel’s sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen to them, then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city at the gate of the place where he lives, and they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.' Then all the men of the city shall stone him to death with stones. So you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A grown son who has become a confirmed rebel against his parents, and so against the order God set in the home, is to be judged publicly by the elders and put to death. The law should be read carefully, neither dismissed nor used as a threat.

A stubborn and rebellious son. Not a small child: he is “a glutton and a drunkard”, an adult with an established way of life, and repeated discipline has failed.

His father and his mother. The safeguards are formidable. Both parents must bring the charge, the two people least likely to want their son executed, which rules out an abusive father using the law as a weapon in a temper.

The elders of his city at the gate. The case then goes to the elders at the gate, in public, and the community judges. It is not a family matter settled at home, and the parents do not carry out the sentence.

All Israel shall hear, and fear. Some later rabbis held that this law was never actually applied. Whether or not that is so, its stated purpose is to warn others off.

The fifth commandment. Underneath it lies the fifth commandment (5:16): the home is where a person first meets authority at all. A society in which that collapses has nothing to govern the next generation with. The son’s rebellion against his parents is, at bottom, rebellion against the God who gave them to him.

The rebel and the Son. Do not miss where the chapter is going. Israel is told to bring the rebellious son out to be stoned, and two verses later we are told what happens to a man hung on a tree. There is a rebellious son in this story, and it is every one of us (Isaiah 1:2). And there was a Son who was not rebellious at all, who was falsely called “a glutton and a drunkard” (Matthew 11:19), and he is the one who was taken outside the city and executed, bearing the judgment so that rebels might become beloved children (Galatians 4:4–5).

What it does not mean. The civil penalty belonged to Israel as a theocracy, a nation ruled directly under God, which has ended; no church or parent holds it now, though the moral principle, honour for parents, remains. Nor does it warrant harshness: discipline must be loving and never given in anger. Parents grieving over a grown child in rebellion may still pray, wait and keep the door open, as the father of the prodigal did (Luke 15:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — A Hanged Man Is Cursed by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the death of the condemned has a limit set by God. When an executed criminal’s body is hung on a tree as a public sign, it must be taken down and buried the same day, because a hanged man is under God’s curse, and the land the LORD gives must not be defiled (vv. 22–23). The New Testament hears in these verses the shape of the cross, where Christ became a curse for us.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul uses this verse to explain what happened on the cross. The law’s severest sentence becomes the gospel’s deepest comfort.
verseByVerse.examples: A body on a tree was the visible sign of God’s curse. Christians look at a man on a tree and see the curse they had earned, borne by someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The body of an executed criminal, hung up as a sign that he lies under God’s curse, must be buried the same day; and this is the verse Paul used to explain the cross, where Christ became a curse for us.

Hanged on a tree. This is not execution by hanging; Israel usually executed by stoning. The body was hung up afterwards, on a pole or a tree, as a public sign that this man was under the curse of God.

You shall bury him the same day. Even that had a limit. The body must come down before nightfall, because a corpse left hanging defiles the land where God lives.

A hanged man is cursed by God. Now hold that verse in one hand and a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem in the other. Every Jew watching a crucifixion knew this text, which made a crucified Messiah not merely implausible but blasphemous: the one place a man could hang and prove he was under God’s curse was the last place the Christ could ever be. Paul had thought exactly that, and had persecuted the church over it (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Christ became a curse. Then, converted, he took the verse that had made Christianity impossible and made it the centre of the gospel: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us … ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13). He quotes it in a shortened form close to the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint.

The exchange. The law pronounces a curse on everyone who does not keep it (27:26), which is everybody. On a hill outside the city, the one man who had never earned it took the place the law reserved for the cursed, so that the sentence would land on him. He was, in the terms of this statute, “a curse for us”, a phrase Paul chooses as deliberately as he says that God “made him to be sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Taken down before dark. “Since it was the day of Preparation … the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away” (John 19:31): men keeping Deuteronomy 21:23 to the letter while the Son of God hung under its curse for them.

From murder to atonement. The chapter that begins with a murder nobody could atone for ends with the atonement for everything. Israel washed its hands over a heifer and asked God to accept it. He accepted something else instead: the blood of his own Son.

Uncertain wording. “Cursed by God” translates a compressed Hebrew phrase, literally a curse of God. Most take it, as Paul did, to mean that the hanged man is under God’s curse. Some Jewish interpreters read it as an insult to God: a body made in his image left hanging dishonours him. The first is the more natural reading and the one the New Testament follows.

keyVerse.quote: his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God.
keyVerse.note: This is the verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Paul before his conversion, and it became the verse by which he explained the cross: Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The chapter that opens with blood no one could atone for closes with the curse that Christ would bear for everyone who trusts him.

21.reflection:
The elders of the nearest town had to stop everything and stand before God over the death of a stranger (vv. 1–9). What does this show about how God values every human life, and whose lives do we tend to overlook?

The laws about the captive woman and the unloved wife’s son (vv. 10–17) protect people with no one to speak for them. Who are the people with no advocate around you, and how can you speak up for them?

The stubborn and rebellious son (vv. 18–21) is a hard passage. How does it help you to see that every one of us is that son, and that Christ, the obedient Son, was the one taken outside the city to die?

Paul read verse 23 as a description of the cross (Galatians 3:13). What does it mean to you that Christ became “a curse for us”, and how does that change the way you deal with your own guilt?

22.title: Laws on Community Life: Love Your Neighbor in the Details
22.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep going astray and ignore them. You shall take them back to your brother.<sup>2</sup>And if he does not live near you and you do not know who he is, you shall bring it home to your house, and it shall stay with you until your brother seeks it. Then you shall restore it to him.<sup>3</sup>And you shall do the same with his donkey or with his garment, or with any lost thing of your brother's, which he loses and you find; you may not ignore it.<sup>4</sup>You shall not see your brother's donkey or his ox fallen down by the way and ignore them. You shall help him to lift them up again.<sup>5</sup>"A woman shall not wear a man's garment, nor shall a man put on a woman's cloak, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>6</sup>"If you come across a bird's nest in any tree or on the ground, with young ones or eggs and the mother sitting on the young or on the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the young.<sup>7</sup>You shall let the mother go, but the young you may take for yourself, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long.<sup>8</sup>"When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it.<sup>9</sup>"You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed, lest the whole yield be forfeited, the crop that you have sown and the yield of the vineyard.<sup>10</sup>You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.<sup>11</sup>You shall not wear cloth of wool and linen mixed together.<sup>12</sup>"You shall make yourself tassels on the four corners of the garment with which you cover yourself.<sup>13</sup>"If any man takes a wife and goes in to her and then hates her<sup>14</sup>and accuses her of misconduct and brings a bad name upon her, saying, 'I took this woman, and when I came near her, I did not find in her evidence of virginity,'<sup>15</sup>then the father of the young woman and her mother shall take and bring out the evidence of her virginity to the elders of the city in the gate.<sup>16</sup>And the father of the young woman shall say to the elders, 'I gave my daughter to this man to marry, and he hates her;<sup>17</sup>and behold, he has accused her of misconduct, saying, "I did not find in your daughter evidence of virginity." And yet this is the evidence of my daughter's virginity.' And they shall spread the cloak before the elders of the city.<sup>18</sup>Then the elders of that city shall take the man and whip him,<sup>19</sup>and they shall fine him a hundred shekels of silver and give them to the father of the young woman, because he has brought a bad name upon a virgin of Israel. And she shall be his wife. He may not divorce her all his days.<sup>20</sup>But if the thing is true, that evidence of virginity was not found in the young woman,<sup>21</sup>then they shall bring out the young woman to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her to death with stones, because she has done an outrageous thing in Israel by whoring in her father's house. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>22</sup>"If a man is found lying with the wife of another man, both of them shall die, the man who lay with the woman, and the woman. So you shall purge the evil from Israel.<sup>23</sup>"If there is a betrothed virgin, and a man meets her in the city and lies with her,<sup>24</sup>then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones, the young woman because she did not cry for help though she was in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor's wife. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>25</sup>"But if in the open country a man meets a young woman who is betrothed, and the man seizes her and lies with her, then only the man who lay with her shall die.<sup>26</sup>But you shall do nothing to the young woman; she has committed no offense punishable by death. For this case is like that of a man attacking and murdering his neighbor,<sup>27</sup>because he met her in the open country, and though the betrothed young woman cried for help there was no one to rescue her.<sup>28</sup>"If a man meets a virgin who is not betrothed, and seizes her and lies with her, and they are found,<sup>29</sup>then the man who lay with her shall give to the father of the young woman fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her. He may not divorce her all his days.<sup>30</sup>"A man shall not take his father's wife, so that he does not uncover his father's nakedness.
22.overview:
Where we are. Moses is still working through the laws for life in the land (chapters 12–26). Chapter 21 dealt with life, death and the family; chapter 22 carries the same concerns into the farmyard, the roof, the wardrobe and the marriage bed.

The message. Loving your neighbour is not a feeling but a thousand small refusals to look away. God cares about the stray ox, the fallen donkey, the bird on her nest, the unguarded roof, the boundaries he built into creation, and above all the honour and safety of women who could not protect themselves. Love does not hide from its neighbour’s trouble, and God does not hide from the cry of the weak.

Why it was said. Israel was to be a holy people in ordinary life, not only at the sanctuary (see the introduction). In a world where women had little standing and the powerful could easily shame or use the powerless, these laws wrote God’s protection into the daily customs of a farming people.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with your neighbour’s lost or fallen animals: you may not pretend you did not see (vv. 1–4). A cluster of short laws follows: keep the distinction between the sexes, spare the mother bird, build a parapet so no one falls, keep seeds, animals and fabrics unmixed, and wear tassels as a reminder (vv. 5–12). Then come laws on marriage and sexual sin. A husband who slanders his bride is punished and may never divorce her (vv. 13–21). Adultery is a capital crime, but a woman attacked where no one could hear her is treated as a victim, like a person murdered (vv. 22–27). A man who violates an unbetrothed girl must pay and provide for her for life, and a man may not take his father’s wife (vv. 28–30).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God he reveals, and by the need these laws expose. Jesus told the story of the Good Samaritan as Deuteronomy 22:4 with a man in the ditch instead of a donkey, and he himself is the one who did not pass by but “came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). The bridegroom who defends his bride’s honour points to the Christ who gave himself for the church to present her “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). And the God who hears the cry no one else heard is the God who in Christ draws near to the overpowered and the ashamed.

For us. Do not arrange not to see your neighbour’s need. Guard other people’s lives, names and bodies as God does, and if you have been wronged or shamed, know that the God of this chapter is on your side and that Christ bore shame to cover yours.
22.theology:
Love your neighbor in the details. Returning a lost animal, lifting a fallen burden, building a safe roof (22:1–8): love sees, stops and helps.

Honoring God's created order. The laws of distinction (22:5–12) trained Israel to honor the order God has woven into creation, for he is a God of order, not confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33); the ceremonial details are fulfilled in Christ, but his people still reverence the good distinctions he has made.

The sanctity of marriage and sexual integrity. These laws (22:13–30) protect the vulnerable and assess guilt justly, because marriage reflects Christ and his church (Eph. 5:31–32). None of us is clean here, in deed or in thought (Matt. 5:28); but Christ was faithful in our place and his purity is counted ours, so the fallen may confess and be washed (1 Cor. 6:11), and the Spirit who now dwells in us makes holiness possible.
22.examples: We are called to the same seeing love, stooping to serve as Christ our Good Samaritan stooped to bind our wounds, and we treasure sexual holiness not as joyless restriction but as God's wise design, reflecting Christ's covenant love for his bride.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Do Not Ignore Your Brother’s Loss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love does not look away from a neighbour’s trouble. If you see your brother’s ox or sheep straying, you must take it back to him; if he lives far off or you do not know him, keep it at home and care for it until he comes looking (vv. 1–2). The same goes for anything he loses (v. 3). And if his donkey or ox has fallen under its load, you must help him lift it up (v. 4). Four times the law forbids ignoring what you have seen.
verseByVerse.theology: It is not enough to refrain from theft; a man who walks past his neighbour’s loss has broken this command.
verseByVerse.examples: The sin these verses name is still the easiest one to commit and the hardest to notice, because it looks exactly like minding your own business.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep going astray and ignore them. You shall take them back to your brother. And if he does not live near you and you do not know who he is, you shall bring it home to your house, and it shall stay with you until your brother seeks it. Then you shall restore it to him. And you shall do the same with his donkey or with his garment, or with any lost thing of your brother's, which he loses and you find; you may not ignore it. You shall not see your brother's donkey or his ox fallen down by the way and ignore them. You shall help him to lift them up again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you see your neighbour’s animal straying or fallen, you must not look away: you must bring it back or help him lift it, whatever it costs you.

Your brother’s ox or his sheep going astray. “Brother” means a fellow Israelite, and Exodus 23:4–5 extends the duty even to an enemy’s animal. The Hebrew is more pointed than “ignore”: it says, you shall not hide yourself from them. The picture is of a man who sees, and then arranges not to have seen: he looks the other way and is home before he has to think about it.

The most respectable sin. Nothing has been stolen and nobody struck. A man has simply declined to be involved in somebody else’s problem, and most countries have no law against that.

Bring it home. The demands are not small: feeding somebody else’s ox at your own cost until he comes looking, or heaving a loaded animal that has “fallen down by the way” back onto its feet. Nobody repays you, and the law does not make it optional.

Who is my neighbour? Centuries later a lawyer asked, “And who is my neighbor?”, and the Lord Jesus told him of a man lying by a road, and a priest and a Levite who, “when he saw him he passed by on the other side” (Luke 10:29–32). He was not inventing a new ethic. He was telling the story of Deuteronomy 22:4 with a man in the ditch instead of a donkey.

Remember your own rescue. We were never the passers-by in this story but the ones fallen by the way, and the Lord did not hide himself from us: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). People who have been carried home find it hard to walk past someone lying in the road.

How do I stop passing by? The sin begins with the eyes, so obedience does too. Do not arrange not to see. Notice the colleague who has gone quiet, the elderly neighbour whose curtains stay shut, the newcomer standing alone after church. Do the next small thing. Today that may be a phone call, a lift to the hospital, or an hour with a form someone cannot fill in. “Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:4). Accept the cost. It will be inconvenient and probably unthanked, which is exactly what the law expected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–12 — Distinctions, and the Guilt of Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are to honour the order he built into creation and guard the life of others. Men and women must not dress as the other sex (v. 5). Take the eggs or young from a nest but let the mother go (vv. 6–7). Build a parapet on a flat roof, so that no one falls and blood guilt does not come on your house (v. 8). Do not mix seed in a vineyard, yoke an ox with a donkey, or weave wool with linen (vv. 9–11). Wear tassels on your cloak (v. 12), a daily reminder of God’s commands.
verseByVerse.theology: Life is to be safeguarded before an accident happens, and a man who does not build a parapet bears the guilt of blood. And the distinctions God built into creation (male and female, one kind and another) are to be respected rather than blurred.
verseByVerse.examples: Every new roof had a wall round it because somebody’s child might fall. A small precaution taken for other people’s safety is a way of loving them before they know they need it.

verseByVerse.quote: "A woman shall not wear a man's garment, nor shall a man put on a woman's cloak, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD your God. "If you come across a bird's nest in any tree or on the ground, with young ones or eggs and the mother sitting on the young or on the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the young. You shall let the mother go, but the young you may take for yourself, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long. "When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it. "You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed, lest the whole yield be forfeited, the crop that you have sown and the yield of the vineyard. You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together. You shall not wear cloth of wool and linen mixed together. "You shall make yourself tassels on the four corners of the garment with which you cover yourself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the ordinary things of life, clothing, birds’ nests, roofs, fields and cloth, God teaches his people to honour the order he made and to guard other people’s lives.

A man’s garment. The first law forbids deliberately presenting oneself as the other sex, which God calls “an abomination”, because he made us male and female (Genesis 1:27). It concerns what is the distinctive dress of each sex in a given culture, so it does not forbid women wearing trousers, which both sexes wear today. But it bears directly on transgender identity: the body God gave is part of who he made us. The church should say so with compassion for those who struggle, and welcome them to Christ.

Let the mother go. Take the eggs or the young if you are hungry, but let the mother fly. It costs nothing and it preserves the future, and God attaches to this smallest of kindnesses the promise he elsewhere attaches to honouring your parents: “that it may go well with you, and that you may live long” (compare 5:16).

A parapet. Flat roofs were living space (see houses and flat roofs). A man who does not build a low wall round the edge may “bring the guilt of blood upon” his house: he has pushed nobody, but God calls the resulting death his. That is negligence, being answerable for harm you could easily have prevented, and it speaks to anyone who employs, builds, drives or has children in the house. God asks not whether harm was intended, but whether it was foreseeable and cheap to prevent.

Two kinds of seed. Fields not sown with two kinds of seed, ox and donkey not yoked together, wool and linen not woven into one cloth: no reason is given. What can be said is that Israel was taught, in the most ordinary things she touched, that God made a world with real boundaries, and that the urge to blur every line he has drawn is not harmless.

Tassels. Their reason is given in Numbers: “it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them” (Numbers 15:39), a reminder sewn into the clothes a man put on every morning. Jesus wore them; the sick woman who touched “the fringe of his garment” (Matthew 9:20) was reaching for the tassel this law required.

Must Christians avoid blended fabrics? No. Like the food laws, these were signs of Israel’s separateness, fulfilled in Christ, who has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–15; Acts 10:15). The distinction between men and women is different: it rests on creation, not on Israel’s calling, and so it remains.

Uncertain wording. “A man’s garment” is literally “a man’s thing”, a word that can mean clothing, equipment or weapons; some think of a woman taking up a warrior’s gear, but most take it of anything that marks a man as a man. In verse 9, “be forfeited” is literally “become holy”: the mixed crop was taken from the farmer and treated as belonging to the sanctuary.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wife’s good name is a real possession, and God defends it. A husband who comes to hate his bride and falsely accuses her of not being a virgin must face her parents’ evidence before the elders at the gate (vv. 13–17). If he lied, he is whipped, fined a hundred shekels paid to her father, and may never divorce her (vv. 18–19). If the charge is true, she is put to death for sexual sin in her father’s house (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The law puts the burden of proof on the accuser and treats a woman’s reputation as something that can be stolen. Where the charge is true, the penalty is grave; but most of the paragraph deals with the case where the woman is being lied about.
verseByVerse.examples: A man who tried to ruin his wife’s name found the court, the money and the law all on her side. Before passing on a damaging story about anyone, especially someone with less power than you, ask whether it has been proved.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any man takes a wife and goes in to her and then hates her and accuses her of misconduct and brings a bad name upon her, saying, 'I took this woman, and when I came near her, I did not find in her evidence of virginity,' then the father of the young woman and her mother shall take and bring out the evidence of her virginity to the elders of the city in the gate. And the father of the young woman shall say to the elders, 'I gave my daughter to this man to marry, and he hates her; and behold, he has accused her of misconduct, saying, "I did not find in your daughter evidence of virginity." And yet this is the evidence of my daughter's virginity.' And they shall spread the cloak before the elders of the city. Then the elders of that city shall take the man and whip him, and they shall fine him a hundred shekels of silver and give them to the father of the young woman, because he has brought a bad name upon a virgin of Israel. And she shall be his wife. He may not divorce her all his days. But if the thing is true, that evidence of virginity was not found in the young woman, then they shall bring out the young woman to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her to death with stones, because she has done an outrageous thing in Israel by whoring in her father's house. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband who tires of his wife and tries to be rid of her by destroying her good name will be judged, punished and bound to provide for her for life: God defends a woman’s honour.

The elders of the city in the gate. The husband claims his bride was not a virgin, but the law does not simply accept the charge. Her parents bring the evidence to the elders at the gate, and her father speaks for her: “I gave my daughter to this man to marry, and he hates her.” That phrase tells the court what is really going on.

A hundred shekels of silver. If the man is lying, he is whipped and fined “a hundred shekels of silver”, paid to her father: twice the payment of verse 29, an enormous sum (see the shekel), going to her family rather than the state.

He may not divorce her all his days. This is not a punishment of her. He tried to destroy her and failed; now she has a permanent claim on his house and income. In a society where a discarded woman had nothing, the law makes her secure for life, at the expense of the man who wanted her gone.

Brings a bad name upon her. The paragraph assumes that a reputation is a real possession and that stealing one is a matter for the courts. It is the cheapest thing to take and the hardest to restore, and God treats slander against a woman’s honour more seriously than most churches manage.

If the thing is true. Verses 20–21, the death penalty where the charge proved true, are stern. They belonged to Israel’s civil law, which ended when Israel ceased to be a nation ruled directly under God’s law. What remains is the moral principle: sexual faithfulness before and in marriage (Hebrews 13:4). And the gospel offers what the law could not: Christ gave himself for a bride who was not pure, to make her clean and present her to himself “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:25–27).

Uncertain wording. We do not know exactly what “evidence of virginity” was. Most likely it was the bedding or garment of the wedding night, kept by the bride’s family, which is why they “spread the cloak before the elders” (v. 17). A few suggest instead evidence that she had menstruated before the marriage, so that she was not pregnant. The first is the usual view.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — Sexual Sin, and the Cry That Was Not Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sexual sin is grave, but God distinguishes the guilty from the victim. Adultery brings death on both (v. 22). Where a betrothed woman is with another man in a town and does not cry for help, both are guilty (vv. 23–24). But if he seizes her in open country, only he dies: she is like a person murdered, who cried out with no one to rescue her (vv. 25–27). A man who violates an unbetrothed girl must pay her father and provide for her for life (vv. 28–29), and no man may take his father’s wife (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The distinctions are the point. Where consent was given, both are guilty; where a woman is overpowered in open country, only the man dies, and the law compares her to a murder victim. In a world where a violated woman was routinely blamed, God writes her innocence into the statute.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has been assaulted and then blamed, by others or by herself, should hear what this law says: God put the guilt on the attacker, and any church that assumes otherwise is not reading its own Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man is found lying with the wife of another man, both of them shall die, the man who lay with the woman, and the woman. So you shall purge the evil from Israel. "If there is a betrothed virgin, and a man meets her in the city and lies with her, then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones, the young woman because she did not cry for help though she was in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor's wife. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. "But if in the open country a man meets a young woman who is betrothed, and the man seizes her and lies with her, then only the man who lay with her shall die. But you shall do nothing to the young woman; she has committed no offense punishable by death. For this case is like that of a man attacking and murdering his neighbor, because he met her in the open country, and though the betrothed young woman cried for help there was no one to rescue her. "If a man meets a virgin who is not betrothed, and seizes her and lies with her, and they are found, then the man who lay with her shall give to the father of the young woman fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her. He may not divorce her all his days. "A man shall not take his father's wife, so that he does not uncover his father's nakedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adultery is a grave sin for both who commit it, but where a woman was overpowered with no one to rescue her, God treats her as a victim, not a sinner, and puts all the guilt on the man.

Both of them shall die. Adultery is a capital crime for both who freely commit it (v. 22), a sin against God, the betrayed spouse and the whole community. A betrothed woman was legally bound to her husband-to-be (see weddings and betrothal), so lying with her counted as adultery.

She did not cry for help. Where a man and a betrothed woman are found together in a town, both are guilty, “the young woman because she did not cry for help though she was in the city” (v. 24), where a cry would have been heard.

Like murder. In open country only the man shall die, and the law explains why with a comparison nobody expects: “this case is like that of a man attacking and murdering his neighbor” (v. 26). She is not a participant in a shared sin or a woman with questions to answer, but somebody who was attacked. The presumption runs in her favour: “though the betrothed young woman cried for help there was no one to rescue her” (v. 27). In open country it could not be disproved either way, and God gives the benefit of the doubt to the person who was overpowered.

In favour of the woman. Set that against how such women have been treated in most of history, and in some churches within living memory. Where the law of Moses could not establish the facts, it decided in favour of the victim and said so in writing. That is the heart of God, the God who in Christ hears the cry no one else heard (Psalm 34:18).

He may not divorce her all his days. Verse 29 is harder for modern readers: a man who violates an unbetrothed girl must pay her father fifty shekels and marry her, and “He may not divorce her all his days.” That reads as monstrous until the situation is understood. Such a woman had no marriage prospects and no means of support; the law makes the man permanently liable for her, with no way of walking away. It is not a reward for him but a life sentence of provision, in that world the only protection available to her.

His father’s wife. Verse 30 forbids a man to marry his stepmother, even after his father’s death; to “uncover his father’s nakedness” is to dishonour his father’s marriage (Leviticus 18:8). Paul was appalled to find this very sin tolerated in the church at Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:1).

Did she have to marry him? Not necessarily. The parallel law in Exodus 22:16–17 lets her father refuse the marriage outright while the man still pays in full, and most interpreters read the two laws together: the marriage was a protection her family could claim, not a sentence passed on her. Some also note that the Hebrew verb in verse 28 is milder than the one in verse 25, so that the case may include seduction as well as force. Either way the law binds the man, never the woman, and nothing here gives cover to anyone who presses a victim to stay with the one who harmed her. Today she should be brought to safety at once, and the crime reported to the police.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncover his father’s nakedness” is literally “uncover his father’s skirt” (ESV note).

keyVerse.quote: You shall not see your brother’s donkey or his ox fallen down by the way and ignore them. You shall help him to lift them up again.
keyVerse.note: This verse sums up the chapter’s love of neighbour: not a feeling but a refusal to look away from someone else’s trouble. Jesus retold it in the parable of the Good Samaritan, and lived it, when he did not pass us by but stooped to lift us up.

22.reflection:
Verses 1–4 forbid “hiding yourself” from a neighbour’s loss. Where are you most tempted to arrange not to see someone else’s trouble, and what would the next small step of help look like?

The man who fails to build a parapet brings “the guilt of blood” on his house (v. 8). What risks to other people, in your home, work, driving or online life, are you responsible to guard against?

The laws in verses 13–29 consistently protect women who could not protect themselves, and treat a woman overpowered in the field as a victim, not a sinner. What does this show about God’s heart, and how should churches respond when someone discloses abuse?

Christ did not pass by on the other side but came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10). How does being rescued yourself change the way you see people in need?

23.title: The Assembly of the LORD: Holiness and Compassion
23.text: <sup>1</sup>"No one whose testicles are crushed or whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>"No one born of a forbidden union may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of his descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>"No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of them may enter the assembly of the LORD forever,<sup>4</sup>because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you.<sup>5</sup>But the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam; instead the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loved you.<sup>6</sup>You shall not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days forever.<sup>7</sup>"You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother. You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land.<sup>8</sup>Children born to them in the third generation may enter the assembly of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every evil thing.<sup>10</sup>"If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, then he shall go outside the camp. He shall not come inside the camp,<sup>11</sup>but when evening comes, he shall bathe himself in water, and as the sun sets, he may come inside the camp.<sup>12</sup>"You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out to it.<sup>13</sup>And you shall have a trowel with your tools, and when you sit down outside, you shall dig a hole with it and turn back and cover up your excrement.<sup>14</sup>Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.<sup>15</sup>"You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you.<sup>16</sup>He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him.<sup>17</sup>"None of the daughters of Israel shall be a cult prostitute, and none of the sons of Israel shall be a cult prostitute.<sup>18</sup>You shall not bring the fee of a prostitute or the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD your God in payment for any vow, for both of these are an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>19</sup>"You shall not charge interest on loans to your brother, interest on money, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent for interest.<sup>20</sup>You may charge a foreigner interest, but you may not charge your brother interest, that the LORD your God may bless you in all that you undertake in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>21</sup>"If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, for the LORD your God will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin.<sup>22</sup>But if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin.<sup>23</sup>You shall be careful to do what has passed your lips, for you have voluntarily vowed to the LORD your God what you have promised with your mouth.<sup>24</sup>"If you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes, as many as you wish, but you shall not put any in your bag.<sup>25</sup>If you go into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain.
23.overview:
Where we are. Moses continues the laws for life in the land (chapters 12–26). After the family and sexual laws of chapters 21–22, chapter 23 turns to who may join Israel’s worshipping assembly, the holiness of the army’s camp, and a run of neighbourly laws.

The message. “The LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp” (v. 14), and his presence shapes everything: who may gather for worship, how the camp is kept, how the weak are treated and how words are kept. Holiness here is not withdrawal from ordinary life but God’s nearness reaching into all of it, and it walks hand in hand with mercy: the runaway slave finds refuge, the poor brother borrows without interest, and the hungry traveller may eat.

Why it was said. Israel was about to settle among nations whose worship included ritual prostitution and whose laws sent runaway slaves back to their masters (see the introduction). God was forming a people whose worship, camp and economy would show that he lived among them, and the memory of Egypt and the wilderness was to shape how they treated others.

How the chapter makes its case. First comes the assembly: certain people are barred from it, Ammonites and Moabites because of what their nations did, while the Edomite is a brother and the Egyptian’s grandchildren may enter (vv. 1–8). The war camp must be kept clean, down to burying waste with a trowel, because God walks in it (vv. 9–14). An escaped slave must not be handed back, Israel’s sons and daughters must not serve as cult prostitutes, and a brother in need must not be charged interest (vv. 15–20). Vows freely made must be kept (vv. 21–23), and a hungry traveller may eat from a neighbour’s field but not harvest it (vv. 24–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the God he reveals. The prophets promised that the eunuch and the foreigner would be welcomed into God’s house (Isaiah 56:3–7), and Ruth the Moabite became an ancestor of Jesus; in Christ the barred door is opened to all who believe (Acts 8:27–39). The God who walked in Israel’s camp came to dwell among us in Jesus, and now lives in his people by his Spirit. Jesus “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), the place of the unclean, to make an unclean people holy, and he is the refuge of every runaway who flees to him.

For us. God is present in the whole of your life, not only on Sunday, so let holiness reach the ordinary corners. Be a refuge for the vulnerable, lend without exploiting need, keep your word when it costs, and give thanks that in Christ outsiders like us have been brought near.
23.theology:
The holiness of God's dwelling place. “The LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp” (23:14), so no corner of life is too ordinary to be touched by his presence. Now God's people are themselves his temple (1 Cor. 6:19; Eph. 2:21–22).

Barriers broken in Christ. The exclusions taught the gravity of approaching a holy God; in Christ the ones once shut out are brought near (Eph. 2:13–14). Christ has opened a new and living way into God's presence for all who come by faith.

Holiness wedded to compassion. Refuge for the runaway (23:15–16), no interest from the poor brother (23:19), vows kept (23:21–23), the hungry fed (23:24–25): the people among whom God walks reflect his holiness and his mercy alike.
23.examples: We are God's temple, indwelt by the Spirit; we rejoice that in Christ the far-off are brought near; and we join holiness with open-handed compassion, keeping our word and refusing to profit from a brother's poverty, for the God among us is both holy and merciful.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Who May Enter the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Entry into Israel’s worshipping assembly was a holy privilege, guarded by God. Men emasculated and those born of a forbidden union were excluded (vv. 1–2). Ammonites and Moabites were barred for generations, because their nations refused Israel food and water and hired Balaam to curse her, though the LORD turned the curse into blessing out of love (vv. 3–6). Yet the Edomite is a brother and the Egyptian is not to be abhorred, for Israel had lived in Egypt; their grandchildren may enter the assembly (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The exclusions are ceremonial, not a verdict on anyone’s soul, and Scripture itself dissolves them. The door that this chapter narrows, the prophets and then the gospel throw open.
verseByVerse.examples: No one need fear that something in their birth or their body, which they never chose, shuts them out from Christ. The eunuch who asked what prevented his baptism was baptised that same day (Acts 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "No one whose testicles are crushed or whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD. "No one born of a forbidden union may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of his descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD. "No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of them may enter the assembly of the LORD forever, because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you. But the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam; instead the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loved you. You shall not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days forever. "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother. You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land. Children born to them in the third generation may enter the assembly of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God guarded entry to Israel’s worshipping assembly, barring some for their physical state or birth and two nations for their hostility; yet even here he forbids hatred, and the barred door would not stay barred.

The assembly of the LORD. The list makes modern readers uncomfortable, as it should. But these exclusions are from the assembly, the formal gathering of Israel for worship, not from the covenant or from God’s mercy, and they are ceremonial, not verdicts on anyone’s soul. Verse 1 most likely has in view men castrated, as some were in pagan worship and at royal courts; like the rules on blemished sacrifices, it taught that God’s worship called for wholeness.

Bread and water, and Balaam. The Ammonite and Moabite exclusion is national: nobody is turned away for something he himself has done. The grounds are what those two nations did: they refused Israel bread and water on the way out of Egypt and hired Balaam to curse her (v. 4).

Because the LORD your God loved you. Verse 5 is one of the loveliest asides in the book. Israel did not even know at the time that a king was trying to have her cursed. Balak paid a fortune, Balaam climbed three mountains, and out came blessing every time, while the people below slept through it all (Numbers 22–24).

Edomite and Egyptian. Then the surprises. The Edomite descends from Esau and so is “your brother”. Even the Egyptian, whose nation enslaved Israel and drowned their sons, may not be abhorred, “because you were a sojourner in his land”: whatever else Egypt did, it fed them in a famine. God will not let the wrong become hatred; the grandchildren of Egyptians may enter the assembly.

Ruth the Moabite. The barred door does not stay barred. Ruth the Moabite becomes the great-grandmother of David and an ancestor of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). How, if Moabites were barred? Many Jewish and Christian readers have answered that the law shut out Moab the hostile nation, not the Moabite who took Israel’s God as her own (Ruth 1:16) and came to shelter under his wings (Ruth 2:12): faith brought her in.

A name better than sons and daughters. Isaiah promises the faithful eunuch “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters”, and the foreigner a welcome in God’s house (Isaiah 56:3–7). In Acts an Ethiopian eunuch is baptised on the road (Acts 8:27–39). In Christ the ceremonial barriers are gone, and the outsider and the ashamed are brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “born of a forbidden union” (v. 2) is rare, and its exact meaning is uncertain. Most likely it means a child of an incestuous or otherwise forbidden marriage (see 22:30), as Jewish tradition took it, not simply one born outside marriage; some think of children of mixed marriages. “Even to the tenth generation” means permanently, as “forever” in verse 3 shows.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God walks in the midst of his people, the army’s camp must be holy. Soldiers must keep themselves from every evil thing (v. 9). A man made ritually unclean at night must stay outside the camp until he has washed at evening (vv. 10–11). Toilets must be outside the camp, and every soldier must carry a trowel to bury his waste (vv. 12–13). The reason is God’s presence: he walks in the camp to save them, and must see nothing indecent there (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness reaches into the latrine arrangements, not because God is fussy but because he is present (v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: A soldier carried a trowel among his weapons. The God who walks among his people is present in the most ordinary hours of the day, not only in the hour of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every evil thing. "If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, then he shall go outside the camp. He shall not come inside the camp, but when evening comes, he shall bathe himself in water, and as the sun sets, he may come inside the camp. "You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out to it. And you shall have a trowel with your tools, and when you sit down outside, you shall dig a hole with it and turn back and cover up your excrement. Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God himself walks among his people, the camp must be kept holy, down to the most undignified details of daily life.

Every evil thing. An army at war is tempted to think the usual rules are suspended; verse 9 says the opposite. Even ritual uncleanness, which was not moral sin, kept a man outside the camp until he had washed at evening (vv. 10–11).

A trowel with your tools. Every soldier carries a trowel alongside his weapons. It is the most undignified verse in the Pentateuch and one of the most instructive, because of the reason attached.

God walks in the camp. The ground is not hygiene or military discipline but the presence of God. The Hebrew verb is the one used of God “walking in the garden in the cool of the day” (Genesis 3:8): he is not merely overhead but moving among the tents. A camp with God walking through it cannot be arranged like a camp without him.

Holiness in the ordinary. We tend to file holiness under religion: worship, prayer, morality. This chapter files it under the latrine trench. No zone of ordinary life is too undignified to be touched by the fact that God is present, and a man who thinks holiness begins at the sanctuary door has not read verse 13.

Your body is a temple. The God who walked in Israel’s camp came to dwell among us in his Son (John 1:14), and now lives in his people by his Spirit. Paul grounds sexual purity in exactly that fact: “do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you” (1 Corinthians 6:19)? The camp is now the believer’s own body. God still walks in it.

Outside the gate. Outside the camp was the place of the unclean. Hebrews says that “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). He went to the unclean place to make unclean people fit for God’s presence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — The Runaway Slave and the Brother’s Loan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people must protect the vulnerable and refuse to profit from sin or from a neighbour’s need. An escaped slave who flees to Israel must not be handed back but allowed to live wherever he chooses, unharmed (vv. 15–16). No Israelite may serve as a cult prostitute, and money gained that way may not be offered to God (vv. 17–18). No interest may be charged on a loan to a fellow Israelite, though it may be charged to a foreigner, and God will bless such generosity (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: A nation God freed from slavery must be a refuge for the enslaved, and a people God provided for must not profit from a brother’s ruin.
verseByVerse.examples: A runaway arriving in Israel was told to choose a town and live there. The test of a Christian community is still what happens to the person who arrives with nothing and nothing to offer.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him. "None of the daughters of Israel shall be a cult prostitute, and none of the sons of Israel shall be a cult prostitute. You shall not bring the fee of a prostitute or the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD your God in payment for any vow, for both of these are an abomination to the LORD your God. "You shall not charge interest on loans to your brother, interest on money, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent for interest. You may charge a foreigner interest, but you may not charge your brother interest, that the LORD your God may bless you in all that you undertake in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must shelter the runaway slave, refuse money made by ritual prostitution, and never profit from a poor neighbour’s need: holiness shows itself in mercy and in clean money.

An escaped slave. Set this law beside the ancient world and the contrast is total. The legal codes and treaties we know from the period, such as Hammurabi’s laws and Hittite treaties, required the return of fugitive slaves, and Hammurabi prescribed death for harbouring one (see slavery in the ancient world).

You shall not give up to his master a slave. Israel, so far as we know alone, reverses it. (Most think the law has in view a slave fleeing into Israel from a foreign master.) The runaway is not returned. He chooses where he lives, “in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him”, and Israel is forbidden to wrong him.

A nation of escaped slaves. A nation of escaped slaves is told to be, permanently, the country where escaped slaves are safe. And every sinner who runs from a cruel master to Christ finds the same welcome: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

What about Onesimus? Paul sent the runaway Onesimus back, but willingly, as a believer, and “as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), not as this law forbids.

The wages of a dog. Cult prostitutes, male and female, probably served in Canaanite fertility worship. Money gained by sin cannot be offered to God: he does not want worship paid for by what he hates.

Interest from a brother. The distinction is between commerce and need. A foreigner borrowing in Israel was usually a merchant borrowing to trade; a brother borrowing was usually a farmer who had lost a harvest, and to profit from that is to build your income on your neighbour’s disaster. The line he draws is not between kinds of people but between kinds of transaction.

Is charging interest sin? No. The law forbade interest on relief loans to a poor brother, and allowed it in trade (v. 20); Jesus assumes money earning interest with bankers (Matthew 25:27). Ordinary lending is not sin; exploiting the needy is.

Uncertain wording. “Cult prostitute” translates a word meaning “holy one”, used of people attached to pagan shrines; how far sex was part of that worship is debated, though verse 18 suggests it. “The wages of a dog” is most likely a contemptuous term for a male prostitute’s earnings; a few take it literally.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — Vows, and a Neighbour’s Field
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people keep their word and share their fields. Nobody has to make a vow, but a vow once spoken to God must be kept without delay (vv. 21–23). A hungry traveller may eat his fill of grapes or grain from a neighbour’s vineyard or field, but may not fill a bag or put a sickle to the crop: meeting a need is welcome, starting a harvest is theft (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody is required to vow; if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin (v.22). God asks only that the promises we make be kept. And his law makes room for hunger without making room for greed.
verseByVerse.examples: The same line still holds wherever generosity is offered: taking what you need is one thing, and taking advantage is another.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, for the LORD your God will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin. But if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin. You shall be careful to do what has passed your lips, for you have voluntarily vowed to the LORD your God what you have promised with your mouth. "If you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes, as many as you wish, but you shall not put any in your bag. If you go into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A vow is voluntary, but once spoken to God it must be kept; and a hungry traveller may eat from a neighbour’s field, but may not harvest it. God is strict about keeping your word, and generous about meeting real need.

Vows. Nobody has to vow, and there is no spiritual advantage in it. But the moment a man opens his mouth, it binds him, and God will require it.

What has passed your lips. What God is strict about is not vows as such but keeping your word. Ecclesiastes puts it bluntly: “It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). And the Lord Jesus, rather than tightening the law of vows, went deeper: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37), because a man whose ordinary word is reliable needs no vows and oaths to back it up.

All the promises of God. Behind all this stands a God who has never once gone back on his word. “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20), every one of them kept in Christ at the cost of the cross. People who live on promises like that learn, slowly, to let their own yes mean yes.

How do I keep my word? Promise slowly. Before you say yes, ask whether you can actually do it: “It is a snare to say rashly, ‘It is holy,’ and to reflect only after making vows” (Proverbs 20:25). Write it down. Many broken promises are simply forgotten ones, and “I’ll pray for you” and “I’ll ring you next week” are promises too. Keep it when it costs. God’s guest is one “who swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). When you cannot, say so early. Go to the person, own it without excuses, and ask what would put it right.

No basket, no sickle. A hungry traveller may eat as much as he wants, on the spot, from any field in Israel, but may not take a bag or a sickle. The line between meeting a need and starting a harvest is drawn exactly: the moment you reach for a tool, you are a thief.

The disciples in the grainfields. That is the law the disciples were keeping when they walked through the grainfields on a Sabbath, plucking heads of grain and rubbing them in their hands (Luke 6:1). The Pharisees who objected were not accusing them of theft, which Deuteronomy 23:25 made impossible, but of harvesting on the wrong day.

keyVerse.quote: Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the whole chapter: God’s presence among his people is the reason for every rule, from the assembly to the latrine. It looks forward to the day when God would dwell among us in Christ, and now makes his home in his people by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

23.reflection:
The assembly laws barred certain people, yet Ruth the Moabite and the eunuch of Isaiah 56 were welcomed. How does this help you see what has changed in Christ, and who might feel shut out of your church today?

God’s presence in the camp reached even to burying waste with a trowel (vv. 12–14). Which ordinary, unglamorous parts of your life do you tend to treat as outside God’s concern?

Israel, a nation of escaped slaves, was to be a refuge for runaway slaves (vv. 15–16) and was not to profit from a poor brother’s need (vv. 19–20). What would it look like for you or your church to be a refuge for the vulnerable, and to handle money without exploiting anyone?

Verses 21–23 say a promise freely made must be kept. Where do you find it hardest to let your yes mean yes, and how does God’s faithfulness to his promises in Christ encourage you?

24.title: Laws Protecting the Vulnerable: Remember You Were a Slave
24.text: <sup>1</sup>"When a man takes a wife and marries her, if then she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, and she departs out of his house,<sup>2</sup>and if she goes and becomes another man's wife,<sup>3</sup>and the latter man hates her and writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, or if the latter man dies, who took her to be his wife,<sup>4</sup>then her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD. And you shall not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.<sup>5</sup>"When a man is newly married, he shall not go out with the army or be liable for any other public duty. He shall be free at home one year to be happy with his wife whom he has taken.<sup>6</sup>"No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge, for that would be taking a life in pledge.<sup>7</sup>"If a man is found stealing one of his brothers of the people of Israel, and if he treats him as a slave or sells him, then that thief shall die. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>8</sup>"Take care, in a case of leprous disease, to be very careful to do according to all that the Levitical priests shall direct you. As I commanded them, so you shall be careful to do.<sup>9</sup>Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>"When you make your neighbor a loan of any sort, you shall not go into his house to collect his pledge.<sup>11</sup>You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you make the loan shall bring the pledge out to you.<sup>12</sup>And if he is a poor man, you shall not sleep in his pledge.<sup>13</sup>You shall restore to him the pledge as the sun sets, that he may sleep in his cloak and bless you. And it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the sojourners who are in your land within your towns.<sup>15</sup>You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin.<sup>16</sup>"Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not pervert the justice due to the sojourner or to the fatherless, or take a widow's garment in pledge,<sup>18</sup>but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this.<sup>19</sup>"When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in the field, you shall not go back to get it. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands.<sup>20</sup>When you beat your olive trees, you shall not go over them again.
