It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.<sup>21</sup>When you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you shall not strip it afterward. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.<sup>22</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this.
24.overview:
Where we are. Moses is near the end of the detailed laws for life in the land (chapters 12–26). After the laws of the assembly, the camp and the neighbour’s field in chapter 23, chapter 24 gathers laws for the weakest people in Israel: the divorced wife, the poor borrower, the day labourer, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.

The message. Remember that you were a slave, and the LORD redeemed you: so treat the vulnerable as God treated you. Twice the chapter grounds its laws in that memory (vv. 18, 22). Grace received becomes mercy given, and mercy here is very practical: a cloak handed back at sunset, wages paid before dark, a sheaf left in the field.

Why it was said. In the world Israel was entering, the poor were easily stripped of their tools, their dignity and their pay, and a wife could be sent away with nothing (see the introduction). God wrote limits into Israel’s law so that a people redeemed from slavery would not become slave-drivers themselves.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins by regulating divorce: a woman sent away with a certificate, who has married another man, may not be taken back by her first husband (vv. 1–4). A new husband stays home for a year to make his wife happy (v. 5). Then come laws protecting life and dignity: no millstone taken in pledge, no kidnapping, careful obedience in skin disease, no creditor entering a poor man’s house, and a poor man’s cloak returned at sunset (vv. 6–13). Workers must be paid the same day, each person dies only for his own sin, and justice may not be bent for the sojourner, the fatherless or the widow (vv. 14–18). Finally, the edges of the harvest are left for those with nothing (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The chapter’s refrain, redemption from slavery, is the pattern of the greater redemption Christ won, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Boaz, who went beyond the gleaning law for Ruth and then redeemed her, foreshadows the Redeemer born of their line. And though this law forbade a husband to take back a wife who had gone to another, the LORD himself, through Jeremiah, invites his unfaithful people to return to him (Jeremiah 3:1, 12): in Christ the faithful Husband receives a bride the law could not restore.

For us. Remember what you were when Christ found you, and let that memory make you generous. Pay what you owe on time, protect the dignity of those who depend on you, leave margins in your life for others, and if your marriage has been broken, know that Christ does not turn you away.
24.theology:
Compassion grounded in redemption. Every law of mercy here rests on “the LORD your God redeemed you” (24:18). Having been shown mercy in Christ, we leave generous margin for the poor.

God defends the defenseless. The poor man's cloak (24:13), the worker's wages (24:15), the gleaner's portion (24:19–21): God hears their cry (cf. James 5:4), and his people may never use legal rights to crush the weak.

Marriage, and God’s allowance for hard hearts. The divorce law limited the damage of hard hearts; God's design was always the lifelong union of Genesis 2:24, and the year for the newlywed (24:5) shows his delight in the joy of marriage, pointing to Christ, who heals hard hearts and restores marriage as a picture of his unbreakable covenant love.
24.examples: Redeemed from a slavery deeper than Egypt's, we deal justly and generously with the poor and the worker, looking to Christ, who became poor that we might become rich. Where we have been hard-hearted, he who kept these laws perfectly in our place forgives, and his Spirit makes us open-handed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God regulates a practice he never designed, to limit its harm. Moses does not command divorce but describes it: a husband finds “some indecency” in his wife, writes her a certificate, puts it in her hand and sends her away; she marries another man, who also divorces her or dies (vv. 1–3). Only then comes the single command: her first husband may not take her back, for that would be an abomination that brings sin on the land (v. 4). Marriage is not a revolving door, and a woman is not property to be passed on and reclaimed.
verseByVerse.theology: The law regulates a practice already happening rather than approving it, and puts two limits round it.
verseByVerse.examples: A husband or wife in a hard marriage should not read this passage as an exit sign: Jesus read it as evidence of hard hearts, and sent his hearers back to what God made marriage to be.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man takes a wife and marries her, if then she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, and she departs out of his house, and if she goes and becomes another man's wife, and the latter man hates her and writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, or if the latter man dies, who took her to be his wife, then her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD. And you shall not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses does not command or approve divorce; he regulates a practice already going on, protecting the woman with a written certificate and forbidding her first husband ever to take her back once she has married another.

When a man takes a wife. This is the passage the Pharisees brought to Jesus. Verses 1–3 only describe a situation: when a man does this, and if she does that. The command does not arrive until verse 4, and it is a single prohibition: “her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife.”

May not take her again to be his wife. So the law does not institute, command or approve divorce. It legislates one thing about a practice already going on: a woman may not be handed on and taken back like property, as if marriage were a revolving door.

Puts it in her hand. Here is an easily missed protection. A man could otherwise send his wife away with a word at the door and later deny it, leaving her unable to remarry or return. A document in her hand made her status clear and her freedom provable. It is not much. It was more than anyone else gave her.

Jesus and this text. The Pharisees framed it as a command: “Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?” Jesus corrected the verb: “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:7–8). Not commanded; allowed. And he sent them back past Deuteronomy to Genesis 2, to what marriage was before anything went wrong.

Would you return to me? Jeremiah takes up this very law: “If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man’s wife, will he return to her?” By this law unfaithful Israel could never come back. Yet the LORD says, “Return, faithless Israel” (Jeremiah 3:1, 12). God does what the law forbade a husband to do. In Christ the faithful Husband gives himself for an unfaithful bride and takes her back for ever (Hosea 3:1; Ephesians 5:25).

If your marriage has ended. If you are reading this from inside a marriage that has ended, this chapter is not a loophole and it is not a verdict on you. It is God putting a fence round a wound he never wanted, to keep the damage from spreading further. Divorce on wrong grounds is sin, but it is not beyond forgiveness, and those who have sinned here find mercy in Christ.

Where Christians differ. May a divorced person remarry? Some Christians hold that remarriage is never allowed while the first spouse lives. Others allow divorce for adultery only, and some for many reasons. The Reformed confessions, such as the Westminster Confession (24.5–6), hold that adultery (Matthew 19:9) and desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15) free the innocent party to remarry.

This commentary’s view. The Westminster position is the better reading, held while honouring brothers who take the stricter view out of reverence for Christ’s words. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: the abuser has abandoned the marriage in all but name. Anyone in danger should seek safety at once, without waiting for any ruling, and the abuse should be reported; the elders of the church help judge each case.

Uncertain wording. “Some indecency” is literally the nakedness of a thing, a phrase found elsewhere only in 23:14 (“anything indecent”), and its exact meaning is uncertain. In Jesus’ day Hillel’s school read it as anything displeasing, Shammai’s as a sexual or shameful fault. It is probably not adultery itself, which carried the death penalty (22:22), but some serious shameful conduct; Jesus reads it on the narrow side. Why the woman is “defiled” (v. 4) is also uncertain: probably that, having been another man’s wife, she was now forbidden to the first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — A Year at Home, and the Cloak Returned at Sunset
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God protects young marriages and the dignity of the poor. A newly married man is free from war and public duty for a year, to make his wife happy (v. 5). No one may take a family’s millstone in pledge, for that takes their life (v. 6). Kidnapping a fellow Israelite to enslave or sell him is a capital crime (v. 7). Israel must follow the priests’ instructions in skin disease, remembering Miriam (vv. 8–9). A creditor must wait outside for a pledge and return a poor man’s cloak by sunset, which God calls righteousness (vv. 10–13).
verseByVerse.theology: God cares for the joy of a young marriage and for the dignity of a debtor, and writes both into the nation’s law. A millstone may not be taken at all, for that would be taking a life in pledge.
verseByVerse.examples: A debtor kept his dignity at his own door and slept warm. The way a strong party collects from a weak one is still, in God’s reckoning, a spiritual matter.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man is newly married, he shall not go out with the army or be liable for any other public duty. He shall be free at home one year to be happy with his wife whom he has taken. "No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge, for that would be taking a life in pledge. "If a man is found stealing one of his brothers of the people of Israel, and if he treats him as a slave or sells him, then that thief shall die. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. "Take care, in a case of leprous disease, to be very careful to do according to all that the Levitical priests shall direct you. As I commanded them, so you shall be careful to do. Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt. "When you make your neighbor a loan of any sort, you shall not go into his house to collect his pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you make the loan shall bring the pledge out to you. And if he is a poor man, you shall not sleep in his pledge. You shall restore to him the pledge as the sun sets, that he may sleep in his cloak and bless you. And it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God guards a young marriage’s first year, and he guards the poor man’s livelihood, freedom, privacy and sleep: mercy towards the weak is what he calls righteousness.

A year at home. No war, no civic office, no committee. God writes into Israel’s national law that a young husband is to stay home for twelve months, and the stated purpose is not household management or children but that he should “be happy with his wife”. It rebukes every culture that fits a young marriage around a career.

The millstone. The handmill was how a family made its daily bread (see millstone). Taking it as security is not debt collection; it is starvation with paperwork, and God calls it “taking a life in pledge”.

Stealing one of his brothers. Kidnapping a person to enslave or sell him is a capital crime (v. 7; Exodus 21:16). Paul lists “enslavers” among those the law condemns (1 Timothy 1:10), and the modern trade in human beings stands under the same judgment.

Remember what the LORD did to Miriam. In a case of skin disease, Israel must follow the priests’ instructions carefully (Leviticus 13–14). The reminder of Miriam, struck with the disease for speaking against Moses and shut outside the camp for seven days (Numbers 12), warns that no one is above God’s rules. Jesus touched such sufferers and made them clean (Mark 1:40–42).

Stand outside. Then three laws about lending, each guarding a poor man’s dignity as carefully as his property. The creditor waits at the door. He does not walk through a poor man’s home choosing what to take, and the debtor brings out what he can spare. A man who owes money has not forfeited the privacy of his house.

The cloak at sunset. The outer cloak was a labourer’s blanket (see clothing). So the pledge is handed over each morning and given back each evening for as long as the debt runs, which makes it almost useless as security and entirely effective as a daily reminder to the lender that this man is poor and needs his cloak.

Righteousness for you. Handing a coat back at sunset is called righteousness; God does not reserve that word for the sanctuary. Timothy Keller often pointed out that in the Old Testament tsedaqah is warmer and more ordinary: a life of right relationships, dealing with family, neighbours and the poor with fairness and generosity, day after day. Most of us want to be in the right far more than we want to do right by those who depend on us, and none of us has been right with God and neighbour for one whole day.

The LORD is our righteousness. That is why the prophets longed for a King whose name would be “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6), and why Paul says God made Christ to be sin “so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Being counted righteous in him does not make the cloak unimportant; it frees us to hand it back gladly. This week, think of someone waiting on your payment, your reply or your fairness, and do the right thing before the sun goes down.

Uncertain wording. “Leprous disease” translates a Hebrew word for a range of skin conditions, and even mould in cloth and walls (Leviticus 13–14). It probably did not usually mean leprosy in the modern sense (Hansen’s disease), and exactly which diseases it covered is unknown.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprous disease” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Justice for the weak must be prompt, personal and remembered. A poor hired worker, Israelite or foreigner, must be paid before sunset, for he depends on it and his cry reaches God (vv. 14–15). No one may be put to death for another’s sin: each dies for his own (v. 16). The sojourner and the fatherless must not be denied justice, nor a widow’s garment taken in pledge (v. 17), because Israel was once a slave in Egypt and the LORD redeemed her (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: God makes the worker’s need, not the employer’s convenience, the measure of when wages are due.
verseByVerse.examples: The delayed invoice, the withheld payment and the squeezed subcontractor are all in this verse, and God hears the same cry.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the sojourners who are in your land within your towns. You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin. "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin. "You shall not pervert the justice due to the sojourner or to the fatherless, or take a widow's garment in pledge, but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay the poor worker before sunset, punish no one for another’s sin, and never bend justice for the stranger, the orphan or the widow: Israel must treat the weak as God treated her when she was a slave.

He counts on it. The reason God gives is a picture of a day labourer’s life: no savings, no reserve; he was paid at sunset, and his family ate that night. A day’s delay is a hungry evening, and the employer may not even notice he has caused one. The foreign labourer gets identical protection, though he is usually the worker whose pay is most easily cut.

Lest he cry against you. The worker cannot sue or afford to lose the work, so he prays, and that prayer reaches God. James takes this verse and makes it terrifying: “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you” (James 5:4). Now it is not merely the man crying; the wages cry.

Each one … for his own sin. Human courts may punish only the guilty; family members may not be executed in the criminal’s place. King Amaziah obeyed this law (2 Kings 14:6), and Ezekiel builds on it (Ezekiel 18:20).

The sojourner, the fatherless and the widow. These three had no family to defend them in court, so God names them as his own concern (10:18). Even a widow’s garment may not be taken as a pledge.

Remember you were a slave. Verse 18 gives the ground of the whole paragraph, as throughout this book. Israel is to treat her workers and her weak as God treated her when she was the slave labour of Egypt.

What this looks like. Most of us employ someone, if only the plumber or the babysitter. Pay on time. “The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning” (Leviticus 19:13). If you run a business, pay small suppliers first, not last; thirty days’ delay is nothing to you and a month’s rent to them. Pay what was agreed. Do not haggle down a job after it is done, or invent faults to trim the bill. Pay fairly, not merely legally. “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1). Ask who is waiting on you. If someone is chasing money you owe, that is the cry of verse 15; make the call today.

How your Master pays. What we earned was death, yet he gives what we never earned: “For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23). People paid so generously should be the last to keep a worker waiting.

Does verse 16 contradict “visiting the iniquity of the fathers” (Exodus 20:5) or Achan’s family (Joshua 7)? No. Verse 16 binds human courts. Exodus speaks of God’s providence, as children suffer the consequences of their parents’ sin and repeat it, and Achan’s case was God’s own judgment, not a court’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people must leave a margin of their harvest for those with nothing. The forgotten sheaf stays in the field, the olive trees are beaten only once, and the vineyard is not stripped bare; what is left belongs to the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow (vv. 19–21). The reason is the memory of slavery in Egypt (v. 22), and God promises to bless the work of their hands (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: What is left at the edges of the harvest is not charity administered by the owner but a standing right of the poor, gathered by their own work with their own hands, and its ground is Israel's own slavery (v. 22).
verseByVerse.examples: The question these verses put to any Christian is whether he uses up all his money and time himself, or deliberately leaves some over for people in need.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in the field, you shall not go back to get it. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you beat your olive trees, you shall not go over them again. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. When you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you shall not strip it afterward. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands his people to leave part of every harvest for the poor, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, because they themselves were once the ones with nothing.

Forget a sheaf in the field. Three provisions work the same way. The forgotten sheaf stays where it fell. The olive trees are beaten once and not gone over again. The vineyard is picked and not stripped.

You shall not go over them again. Israel is commanded to farm inefficiently. Every instinct of a working farmer is overruled. What is left is not the owner’s to give; it already belongs to somebody else.

The genius of it. A widow did not queue at a landowner’s door or explain her situation. She walked into the field, worked with her own hands, and took home what she gathered, owing nobody anything. The system provided food without requiring humiliation, which is more than most welfare has ever managed.

Ruth in the field. It is the law under which the loveliest book in the Old Testament happens. A Moabite widow with nothing goes out to glean in a field that turns out to belong to Boaz, and he tells his young men to pull out extra stalks and leave them for her (Ruth 2:16): a man going beyond the margin the law required, which is exactly what the law was training him to want to do.

Therefore I command you. The reason is the one already given in verse 18. Not because the poor deserve it, and not because generosity is admirable, but because these people were once the ones with nothing, and somebody came and got them.

For your sake he became poor. A Christian reads that sentence with a larger Exodus behind it. We were the ones with nothing, and the Lord Jesus, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Many Christians have also seen in Boaz, who went beyond the margin and then redeemed the widow gleaning in his field, a picture of the greater Redeemer from his own line.

keyVerse.quote: but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the reason behind every law of mercy in the chapter: Israel is to treat the weak as God treated her when she was weak. For Christians the memory is of a greater redemption, and grace received in Christ becomes the motive for grace shown to others.

24.reflection:
Jesus said Moses allowed divorce “because of your hardness of heart” (Matthew 19:8). How does this chapter help us understand both the seriousness of divorce and God’s care for those whose marriages have broken?

The laws in verses 6–15 protect the poor borrower’s livelihood, privacy and sleep, and the worker’s daily pay. Who depends on you for payment, fairness or a reply, and what would it look like to do right by them before the sun goes down?

Twice the chapter says, “You shall remember that you were a slave” (vv. 18, 22). How does remembering what Christ has redeemed you from shape the way you treat people with less than you?

The gleaning law built margins into Israel’s farming for the poor, and Boaz went beyond it for Ruth. Where could you leave “margins” of time, money or attention in your life for others?

25.title: Levirate Marriage and Honest Weights: Justice in the Details
25.text: <sup>1</sup>"If there is a dispute between men and they come into court and the judges decide between them, acquitting the innocent and condemning the guilty,<sup>2</sup>then if the guilty man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall cause him to lie down and be beaten in his presence with a number of stripes in proportion to his offense.<sup>3</sup>Forty stripes may be given him, but not more, lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, your brother be degraded in your sight.<sup>4</sup>"You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.<sup>5</sup>"If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no son, the wife of the dead man shall not be married outside the family to a stranger. Her husband's brother shall go in to her and take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother to her.<sup>6</sup>And the first son whom she bears shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then his brother's wife shall go up to the gate to the elders and say, 'My husband's brother refuses to perpetuate his brother's name in Israel; he will not perform the duty of a husband's brother to me.'<sup>8</sup>Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and if he persists, saying, 'I do not wish to take her,'<sup>9</sup>then his brother's wife shall go up to him in the presence of the elders and pull his sandal off his foot and spit in his face. And she shall answer and say, 'So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house.'<sup>10</sup>And the name of his house shall be called in Israel, 'The house of him who had his sandal pulled off.'<sup>11</sup>"When men fight with one another and the wife of the one draws near to rescue her husband from the hand of him who is beating him and puts out her hand and seizes him by the private parts,<sup>12</sup>then you shall cut off her hand. Your eye shall have no pity.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small.<sup>14</sup>You shall not have in your house two kinds of measures, a large and a small.<sup>15</sup>A full and fair weight you shall have, a full and fair measure you shall have, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>16</sup>For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>17</sup>"Remember what Amalek did to you on the way as you came out of Egypt,<sup>18</sup>how he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God.<sup>19</sup>Therefore when the LORD your God has given you rest from all your enemies around you, in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess, you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget.
25.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 25 is the last chapter of the detailed laws for life in the land (chapters 12–26) before Moses turns to worship and covenant renewal in chapter 26. Like chapters 21–24, it gathers laws for ordinary situations.

The message. God watches the places nobody else watches, and he guards the people who cannot guard themselves. The guilty man under the lash, the ox at work, the childless dead man and his widow, the customer who cannot check the scales, the stragglers at the back of the column: each is protected here. To fear God is to treat them as he sees them, and the one who preys on them “did not fear God” (v. 18).

Why it was said. As a settled nation with courts, farms and markets, Israel would give the strong many quiet ways to take advantage of the weak (see the introduction). These laws build God’s care into the details of public life, so that a redeemed people would not reproduce the cruelty they had known.

How the chapter makes its case. Even a guilty man may be beaten only in proportion and never more than forty strokes, because he remains “your brother”, and the ox that works may eat (vv. 1–4). A widow left without a son is to be married by her husband’s brother, so that the dead man’s name survives and she is not cast out; a brother who refuses is publicly shamed (vv. 5–10). After a startling law on a fight comes the ethical centre: no false weights or measures, for dishonesty is an abomination to the LORD (vv. 11–16). Finally Israel must remember Amalek, who attacked the faint and weary at the rear, and one day blot out his memory (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The brother who builds up his dead brother’s house is the pattern behind Boaz, and Boaz points to Christ, the Kinsman-Redeemer who did not count the cost, took our nature to become our near relative, and gives us his name and an inheritance that cannot be lost. He also took the stripes the law limited, for others (Isaiah 53:5). And the God who would not forget the stragglers at the back of the column is the Good Shepherd who goes after the one that is lost.

For us. Fear God where no one is checking: in your pricing, your timesheets, the way you speak of someone who has failed, and the way you treat the slow and the weak. And take comfort that the God who saw the back of the column sees you when you are faint and weary, and his Son will not leave you behind.
25.theology:
Integrity in the marketplace. “All who act dishonestly are an abomination to the LORD” (25:16); the rigged scale stands in the same category as idolatry (cf. Prov 11:1). Redeemed by a Kinsman who paid in full, the believer is called to scrupulous honesty in every transaction.

The dignity of persons and the worker. Even the guilty are not to be degraded (25:3), and the working ox eats (25:4), which Paul applies to gospel laborers (1 Cor. 9:9).

The kinsman-redeemer. A kinsman-redeemer was a near relative who stepped in at his own cost to rescue a family member’s land, freedom or name. Levirate marriage (marrying a dead brother’s childless widow) preserved a dead brother's name and protected his widow (25:5–10), and something like it is at work in Ruth and Boaz. It points to Jesus, our great Redeemer, who gives us his name and secures our inheritance forever.
25.examples: We pursue honesty in all our dealings, support those who labor for the gospel, rejoice in Christ our kinsman-Redeemer, and trust the God who remembers every wrong done to the weak.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Forty Stripes, and the Ox That Treads
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Justice must never forget the humanity of the person it punishes, or the needs of the one who works. When a court finds a man guilty and he deserves a beating, the judge must watch it carried out, measure it to the offence and stop at forty strokes (vv. 1–3), because the man under the lash is still “your brother”. The same mercy reaches the animal on the threshing floor: the ox that treads out the grain may eat as it works (v. 4). Paul takes this small law as a principle for paying those who labour in the gospel.
verseByVerse.theology: Both laws protect the party who cannot protect himself: the cap on strokes keeps a criminal under sentence your brother, and the muzzle law lets even a working animal eat from what it is producing.
verseByVerse.examples: The sentence stopped short of stripping a man of his humanity, and the ox ate as it worked. It is still fair to ask whether the people who do the work in our churches and businesses are allowed to eat from what they produce.

verseByVerse.quote: "If there is a dispute between men and they come into court and the judges decide between them, acquitting the innocent and condemning the guilty, then if the guilty man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall cause him to lie down and be beaten in his presence with a number of stripes in proportion to his offense. Forty stripes may be given him, but not more, lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, your brother be degraded in your sight. "You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even a guilty man under punishment remains a brother, so the penalty must be measured, supervised and limited; and the ox that works must be allowed to eat.

Forty stripes, but not more. The judge must see the beating done “in his presence”, so it cannot become private cruelty, and the number of strokes must match the offence, never more than forty.

Your brother be degraded in your sight. The man is guilty, sentenced and being punished, and God still calls him “your brother”. The limit keeps a legal penalty from becoming the destruction of a human being, and keeps the watching community from seeing him as less than one of them. Discipline corrects; it must never degrade, even in how we speak of the fallen.

Forty lashes less one. Later Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine, in case of a miscount, which is why Paul writes, “Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one” (2 Corinthians 11:24). He knew this law from the wrong end of it.

The ox that treads. On the threshing floor the ox walked in circles all day with the grain under its feet. The animal that does the work may eat from the work.

For our sake. Paul quotes this verse twice, both times about paying people. For the support of preachers he asks, “Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake?” (1 Corinthians 9:9–10). For elders he sets it beside Jesus’ saying that the labourer deserves his wages, and calls both Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18).

The stripes he took. The law limited the stripes a guilty brother could receive. The innocent Son was flogged (John 19:1) and took stripes he did not deserve, for “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish law had the man assessed first, so that he received only as many strokes as he could bear (Mishnah, Makkot 3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — Levirate Marriage, and the Sandal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God protects the widow and the name of the dead through the costly duty of a brother. If a married man dies without a son, his brother is to marry the widow, and their first son will carry the dead man’s name and inheritance (vv. 5–6). The brother may refuse, but not quietly: the widow brings him before the elders at the gate, pulls off his sandal, spits in his face and declares his shame, and his family carries the nickname (vv. 7–10). This is the background to Boaz and Ruth.
verseByVerse.theology: The provision keeps a widow inside a family rather than destitute outside it, and keeps a dead man’s name in Israel. The refusal is not criminal, only shameful; the law will not compel a marriage, and so it shames instead.
verseByVerse.examples: Taking up a duty that costs us and earns no credit is rare. Christ is the Kinsman who did not decline: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. 2:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no son, the wife of the dead man shall not be married outside the family to a stranger. Her husband's brother shall go in to her and take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother to her. And the first son whom she bears shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel. And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then his brother's wife shall go up to the gate to the elders and say, 'My husband's brother refuses to perpetuate his brother's name in Israel; he will not perform the duty of a husband's brother to me.' Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and if he persists, saying, 'I do not wish to take her,' then his brother's wife shall go up to him in the presence of the elders and pull his sandal off his foot and spit in his face. And she shall answer and say, 'So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house.' And the name of his house shall be called in Israel, 'The house of him who had his sandal pulled off.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow and raise a son in the dead man’s name, so that neither she nor his name would be lost; refusing this costly duty brought public shame.

The duty of a husband’s brother. This is levirate marriage, from the Latin levir, brother-in-law. The first son “shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel” (v. 6), and inherit his land. Two people are protected: the widow, who had no income, inheritance or standing without a husband or son and would otherwise leave the family with nothing; and the dead man, whose name and portion in Israel would disappear.

What it cost him. The brother takes on a wife and raises a son who will not count as his own and will inherit the dead man’s land rather than his. Judah’s son Onan took the privilege and refused the duty, and the LORD was displeased (Genesis 38:8–10).

I do not wish to take her. The law does not compel him; it shames him. The widow brings him to the elders at the gate; if he persists she pulls his sandal off his foot and spits in his face, and his household is known ever afterwards as “The house of him who had his sandal pulled off” (v. 10). The one he wronged is given the public voice. To set foot on land was to claim it, so removing his sandal declared that he had walked away from a claim he should have taken up.

The background to Ruth. In Ruth 4 a nearer kinsman will take Naomi’s field until he hears that Ruth comes with it: “I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance” (Ruth 4:6), and he draws off his sandal. Boaz was not her brother-in-law, and there the sandal seals a transaction rather than shames, but the story runs in the spirit of this law, and Boaz, with more to lose and less to gain, steps forward.

The Kinsman who did not hold back. Behind Boaz stands Christ. He became our near kinsman, sharing our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14–17), and did not count the cost to himself. Where the reluctant brother would not build up another’s house, Christ gives his name to those who had none and brings them into an inheritance “that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4).

For us. Levirate marriage belonged to Israel’s civil law, but its heart still binds us: love that spends itself on those who cannot repay, especially the widow (James 1:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honesty in hidden places matters to God as much as worship. A brief and startling law about a fight punishes a woman who seizes a man’s genitals to rescue her husband (vv. 11–12), guarding a man’s ability to father children, which the preceding law also protects. Then comes the chapter’s ethical centre: no heavy and light weights in the same bag, no large and small measures in the same house (vv. 13–14), but full and fair ones, with the promise of long life in the land (v. 15). Dishonesty is an abomination to the LORD (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God cares about the scales on a market stall as much as about the altar in the sanctuary: fraud is theft dressed as trade.
verseByVerse.examples: Whoever handles other people’s money, in a shop, an office or a church treasury, is handling something God watches closely.

verseByVerse.quote: "When men fight with one another and the wife of the one draws near to rescue her husband from the hand of him who is beating him and puts out her hand and seizes him by the private parts, then you shall cut off her hand. Your eye shall have no pity. "You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small. You shall not have in your house two kinds of measures, a large and a small. A full and fair weight you shall have, a full and fair measure you shall have, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God requires honesty in the hidden details of trade, and calls false weights an abomination, as he does idolatry. Before that, a brief law punishes a woman who seizes a man’s genitals in a fight.

When men fight with one another. The injury threatened a man’s ability to father children, which the law guarded carefully (compare vv. 5–10), and “your eye shall have no pity” forbids the court to set the penalty aside out of sympathy for her motive. It is the only mutilation in the law, it belonged to Israel’s civil law, and it does not apply today.

Two kinds of weights. Trade ran on stone weights carried in a pouch and measures kept at home. A dishonest trader had two sets: the heavy stone for buying and the light one for selling. The theft was invisible, small each time, and fell hardest on the poor, who could not check and would not be believed if they complained. The law forbids even owning the second set, “in your bag” or “in your house”, and promises long life in the land to honesty (v. 15).

An abomination to the LORD your God. Deuteronomy uses this word for idolatry, the occult and child sacrifice. A rigged scale stands in the same category, because cheating those who trust you is no smaller sin for being quiet: “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1).

Two weights today. The fee that is not explained, the estimate written to be exceeded, the clause the other party will not understand, the padded timesheet. Where we have used them, the way back is the one Zacchaeus took: owning up and paying back. And Christ came to Zacchaeus’s house before he had repaid a penny (Luke 19:5–9).

Uncertain wording. “Cut off her hand” uses a verb that normally means to cut off and the ordinary word for the palm of the hand. A few scholars suggest a shaming shaving instead, since a related form of the verb is used of clipped hair (Jeremiah 9:26), or take “palm” to mean her own groin, so that the penalty mirrors the offence. These readings are possible but unproven; amputation of the hand remains the most likely sense.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God does not forget cruelty done to the weak. Israel must remember how Amalek attacked them on the road out of Egypt, not at the front but at the rear, where the faint and weary straggled, because he did not fear God (vv. 17–18). When the LORD has given Israel rest in the land, they are to blot out Amalek’s memory, and they must not forget (v. 19). The sentence waits for God’s time, and it stands as a warning that no cruelty to the defenceless goes unseen.
verseByVerse.theology: Amalek attacked the people least able to defend themselves, and he did not fear God. This is judgment on a particular nation for a particular cruelty, delayed until Israel has rest: God settling an account the victims could not.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who was hurt when they were weakest, and has never seen justice done, may take this passage to heart: God keeps such accounts open, and he does not forget.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember what Amalek did to you on the way as you came out of Egypt, how he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God. Therefore when the LORD your God has given you rest from all your enemies around you, in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess, you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God never forgets cruelty against the defenceless: Amalek preyed on Israel’s weakest stragglers, so Israel must remember and, in God’s time, blot out his memory.

Faint and weary. Picture the column: former slaves, women, children, old people and animals strung out over miles, and at the back the sick, the elderly and mothers with small children, who could not keep up. That is where Amalek attacked (Exodus 17:8–16): not the front, where the fighting men were, but “your tail, those who were lagging behind you”.

He did not fear God. They picked off the weakest people in a refugee column because it was easy, and the text gives the diagnosis in five words. Cruelty towards the defenceless is, in Scripture, the surest sign that a man believes nobody is watching.

Blot out the memory. The sentence is deferred until Israel has rest. Centuries pass before Saul is sent to carry it out (1 Samuel 15).

God saw it. The people at the back of that column had nobody. Most died without anyone learning their names. God saw it, wrote it into the nation’s law and kept the account open for generations. The God who notices the ox on the threshing floor and the widow at the gate has never looked away from the back of the column. In Christ he came to it himself, the Shepherd who “will gather the lambs in his arms” (Isaiah 40:11) and came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

Did God really command the destruction of a whole people? When the sentence came, it included everyone (1 Samuel 15:3), and that is among the hardest things in the Old Testament. It was the judgment of the Judge of all the earth on a people who kept up this cruelty for generations (1 Samuel 15:33), not a licence for ethnic hatred: the same law forbids Israel to abhor the Egyptian (23:7). It was a single command for one moment in Israel’s history, never a pattern since; no nation or Christian may take it up, and Christ commands his people to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44). And it looks ahead to the last judgment, when God will deal with every unrepented cruelty, and the Judge will be the one who bore judgment for his enemies (Acts 17:31). Questions remain, especially about the children, and we leave them with the God who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25).

keyVerse.quote: For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s laws are about hidden places: a pouch of weights, a closed court, a family matter, the rear of a column. This verse says that God sees them all, and that quiet dishonesty is no small thing to him. It calls for honesty that is rooted in the fear of God rather than the fear of being found out.

25.reflection:
The law limits even a just punishment so that the guilty man is not “degraded in your sight” (v. 3). How do we talk about people who have fallen or been punished, and what would it look like to keep seeing them as brothers and sisters?

Paul uses the unmuzzled ox to argue that those who teach the word should be supported (1 Corinthians 9:9–10). How well does your church care for those who labour among you, and what could you do about it?

The brother-in-law who refused the widow wanted to keep what was his. How does Boaz, and behind him Christ, show a different way of using what we have? Who has God placed near you who needs a kinsman’s help?

Where in your work or money are the “two kinds of weights” most tempting today, the small hidden advantage nobody will check? How does knowing that God sees, and that Christ welcomes the dishonest who turn, change the way you deal with it?

26.title: Firstfruits and Covenant Affirmation: You Are His Treasured Possession
26.text: <sup>1</sup>"When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance and have taken possession of it and live in it,<sup>2</sup>you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you harvest from your land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you shall put it in a basket, and you shall go to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name to dwell there.<sup>3</sup>And you shall go to the priest who is in office at that time and say to him, 'I declare today to the LORD your God that I have come into the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us.'<sup>4</sup>Then the priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the LORD your God.<sup>5</sup>"And you shall make response before the LORD your God, 'A wandering Aramean was my father. And he went down into Egypt and sojourned there, few in number, and there he became a nation, great, mighty, and populous.<sup>6</sup>And the Egyptians treated us harshly and humiliated us and laid on us hard labor.<sup>7</sup>Then we cried to the LORD, the God of our fathers, and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great deeds of terror, with signs and wonders.<sup>9</sup>And he brought us into this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>10</sup>And behold, now I bring the first of the fruit of the ground, which you, O LORD, have given me.' And you shall set it down before the LORD your God and worship before the LORD your God.<sup>11</sup>And you shall rejoice in all the good that the LORD your God has given to you and to your house, you, and the Levite, and the sojourner who is among you.<sup>12</sup>"When you have finished paying all the tithe of your produce in the third year, which is the year of tithing, giving it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat within your towns and be filled,<sup>13</sup>then you shall say before the LORD your God, 'I have removed the sacred portion out of my house, and moreover, I have given it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all your commandment that you have commanded me. I have not transgressed any of your commandments, nor have I forgotten them.<sup>14</sup>I have not eaten of the tithe while I was mourning, or removed any of it while I was unclean, or offered any of it to the dead. I have obeyed the voice of the LORD my God. I have done according to all that you have commanded me.<sup>15</sup>Look down from your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless your people Israel and the ground that you have given us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.'<sup>16</sup>"This day the LORD your God commands you to do these statutes and rules. You shall therefore be careful to do them with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>17</sup>You have declared today that the LORD is your God, and that you will walk in his ways, and keep his statutes and his commandments and his rules, and will obey his voice.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you, and that you are to keep all his commandments,<sup>19</sup>and that he will set you in praise and in fame and in honor high above all nations that he has made, and that you shall be a people holy to the LORD your God, as he promised."
26.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 26 closes the long body of laws that began in chapter 12. Before Moses turns to the blessings and curses (chapters 27–28), he gives Israel two short liturgies, set words to say in worship, and then a solemn exchange of vows between the LORD and his people.

The message. Everything you have is a promise kept, so bring the first of it to God with thanks, tell the story of how he rescued you, share it with those who have nothing, and know whose you are. The law ends not with a rule but with a relationship: the LORD is Israel’s God, and Israel is his treasured possession.

Why it was said. A people about to receive farms, vineyards and harvests would be tempted to forget that they had been slaves and wanderers, and to treat the land as their own achievement (see 8:11–18 and the introduction). These liturgies put the memory of grace into their mouths every year, and the care of the poor into their hands.

How the chapter makes its case. The worshipper brings the first of his harvest in a basket and declares that God has kept his promise (vv. 1–4). He then tells Israel’s story as his own, from a wandering ancestor through slavery and rescue to the land, sets down the basket and rejoices with the Levite and the sojourner (vv. 5–11). Every third year he gives the tithe to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, declares before God that he has done so, and prays for blessing on the whole nation (vv. 12–15). Finally the two parties to the covenant declare what they are to each other (vv. 16–19).

Where it leads. By covenant, promise and pattern. “I will be their God, and they shall be my people” is the heart of every covenant, and Israel’s half failed within a generation; it is renewed in the new covenant and secured by Christ, who gave himself “to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14). Christ is also the firstfruits of the great harvest, the first of the dead to be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20), the proof in God’s hands that the rest will follow. And the confession that turns “he” into “we” is the way every believer says of the cross, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

For us. Give to God first and gladly, not from what is left over. Tell your own story as part of his, beginning with what you were and what he did. Let your giving reach real people in need. And rest in the declaration you could never earn: in Christ you are his treasured possession.
26.theology:
Worship rooted in redemption. As the offering is presented, the worshiper recites the story of grace (26:5–9). True worship rehearses God's saving acts and makes them personal; the gift in the hand and the gospel on the lips belong together.

Worship inseparable from compassion. The worshiper declares before God that he has cared for the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow (26:12–13); worship is hollow without it (James 1:27).

Mutual belonging. Israel declares the LORD her God, and the LORD declares her his “treasured possession” (26:17–18). The covenant is a bond of love, and in Christ every believer belongs to “a people for his own possession” (1 Pet. 2:9).
26.examples: We give God our first and best in gratitude, rehearsing our own redemption: enslaved, we cried out, and Christ delivered us. Our worship overflows in care for the poor, and we rest in the deepest joy of the redeemed: in Christ, God says over us, “You are mine.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Basket at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every harvest in the land is a promise God has kept, and the first of it belongs to him. When Israel has settled in the land, each farmer is to take some of the first of his harvest in a basket to the place God chooses (vv. 1–2). There he tells the priest that he has come into the land the LORD swore to give (v. 3), and the priest sets the basket before the altar (v. 4). The gift is not payment but testimony: the proof in his hands that God has done what he said.
verseByVerse.theology: The offering is small and the words are everything. A man standing in a field promised to his ancestors says out loud that God has kept his word, and the fruit in the basket is the evidence.
verseByVerse.examples: The first of the harvest went to God before any of it was eaten. Christian giving keeps the same shape: the first and best, brought before the rest is enjoyed, with words attached that say why.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance and have taken possession of it and live in it, you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you harvest from your land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you shall put it in a basket, and you shall go to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name to dwell there. And you shall go to the priest who is in office at that time and say to him, 'I declare today to the LORD your God that I have come into the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us.' Then the priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of every harvest was brought to God as testimony that he had kept his promise to give the land.

The man this law is for. He is the first in his family for centuries to harvest a crop from ground that belongs to him. His father may have been born in a tent in the wilderness; his grandfather was a slave.

Some of the first. Not the tithe, which comes later in the chapter, but simply some of the firstfruits of the harvest, in a basket, carried by hand, before anything is eaten, stored or sold.

I declare today. His one sentence to the priest declares that God has kept his promise. Not “I have worked hard”, not even “thank you”, but: you said you would do this, and here is the fruit of it in my hands. Centuries behind him stands Abraham, a childless old man told to count the stars (Genesis 15:5), and this basket of figs is the proof.

Set it down before the altar. The basket is set down before the altar, not burned on it. This is not payment; it is testimony with something in a basket to prove it.

Christ the firstfruits. Firstfruits were the pledge that the rest of the harvest would follow. So Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). His resurrection is God’s promise already in hand: the whole harvest of his people will be raised.

Do firstfruits apply to Christians? The law ended with the sanctuary and the land, but the principle remains: give to God first and gratefully, not from what is left over (Proverbs 3:9; 1 Corinthians 16:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — A Wandering Aramean Was My Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship begins by telling the story of what God has done, and owning it as your own. Standing at the altar, the worshipper recites Israel’s history: a wandering Aramean ancestor, a descent into Egypt, harsh slavery, a cry to the LORD, a mighty rescue, and the gift of a good land (vv. 5–9). Halfway through, “he” becomes “us” and “we”. Only then does he set down his basket as a gift from the God who gave the harvest, worship, and rejoice with the Levite and the sojourner (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel’s confession of faith is a story of rescue, and it ends in joy shared with the Levite and the sojourner, who have no harvest of their own.
verseByVerse.examples: Asked why he had come with a basket, a farmer told the story of the exodus. A Christian has the same kind of answer and no other: not our standards or our tradition, but that we were slaves to sin and Christ came for us.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you shall make response before the LORD your God, 'A wandering Aramean was my father. And he went down into Egypt and sojourned there, few in number, and there he became a nation, great, mighty, and populous. And the Egyptians treated us harshly and humiliated us and laid on us hard labor. Then we cried to the LORD, the God of our fathers, and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great deeds of terror, with signs and wonders. And he brought us into this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey. And behold, now I bring the first of the fruit of the ground, which you, O LORD, have given me.' And you shall set it down before the LORD your God and worship before the LORD your God. And you shall rejoice in all the good that the LORD your God has given to you and to your house, you, and the Levite, and the sojourner who is among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worshipper tells the story of Israel’s rescue as his own story, beginning with nothing to boast of and ending with a gift from God, and then worships and shares the feast.

A wandering Aramean. This confession, often counted among the oldest creeds in the Bible, begins at the bottom. Not “my father was a patriarch”, but a landless nomad with no country and no standing. The father is most likely Jacob, whose mother came from Aram, who spent twenty years there working for “Laban the Aramean” (Genesis 31:20, 41), and who went down into Egypt with seventy persons (10:22).

From “he” to “us”. Watch the pronouns move. It starts with “my father” and “he went down”: history, somebody else. Then, without warning: “the Egyptians treated us harshly … we cried to the LORD … the LORD brought us out of Egypt” (vv. 6–8). The man saying this was not in Egypt, nor was his father, yet every Israelite was taught to place himself inside a rescue that happened before he existed.

At the Lord’s Table. That is what a Christian does at the Lord’s Table. Not “he died for people”, but “who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). The events are historical and the pronoun is personal, and a faith that cannot say “for me” has not yet become a person’s own.

A story, not a proposition. A wanderer, a descent into slavery, a cry, a hearing, a rescue, a land: no doctrine is stated and no proposition defended. It is a story in six verses, and it was the answer every Israelite child was given when he asked why his family lived as it did (compare 6:20–23).

Who writes your story? The modern self is supposed to be its own author: find your own truth, choose your identity, treat every inherited story, family, faith or nation, as a draft to edit or discard. That brings freedom, and exhaustion. A self that must author itself must also justify itself, and every chapter becomes a performance review. The man with the basket has been spared that. He did not invent his story; he was written into it, and it begins not with his achievements but with a wanderer, a slave camp and a God who heard a cry. Strangely, that is what makes it his, not a cage but a home. The gospel offers every reader the same exchange. You can stop drafting a self that will win approval, and be written into a better story, whose decisive chapter happened outside a city wall long before you were born, and whose last chapter is not a verdict on your performance but a homecoming (Revelation 21:3).

Which you have given me. Then, at last, the basket. Even the harvest he grew himself is called a gift. And the scene ends where Deuteronomy always ends, in rejoicing shared with the Levite and the sojourner. The man with no land is at the table.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “wandering” (’obed) usually means perishing or lost, so older versions read “a Syrian ready to perish” (KJV). It can also describe a straying animal or a man without a home. Either way the point is the same: Israel’s ancestor was a needy, rootless man, and everything that followed was God’s doing.
verseByVerse.note: The “wandering Aramean” is most likely Jacob, whose mother and wives came from Aram.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Generosity to the needy is part of worship, and God expects it to be real and specific. Every third year the tithe is given in the local towns to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, so that they may eat and be filled (v. 12). The worshipper then declares before God that he has given it all, kept none back and defiled none of it with mourning, uncleanness or offerings to the dead (vv. 13–14). He ends not by asking a reward for himself but by praying that God will bless all his people and the land (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Giving to the poor is a sacred trust, not an optional kindness. The declaration is not a claim to sinlessness but a redeemed man's honest account, and it ends not in self-congratulation but in a request for blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: God still asks what we have actually given to those in need, and vague good intentions are no answer. Where honesty shows a shortfall, Christ's faithfulness covers it and the way back is open.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you have finished paying all the tithe of your produce in the third year, which is the year of tithing, giving it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat within your towns and be filled, then you shall say before the LORD your God, 'I have removed the sacred portion out of my house, and moreover, I have given it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all your commandment that you have commanded me. I have not transgressed any of your commandments, nor have I forgotten them. I have not eaten of the tithe while I was mourning, or removed any of it while I was unclean, or offered any of it to the dead. I have obeyed the voice of the LORD my God. I have done according to all that you have commanded me. Look down from your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless your people Israel and the ground that you have given us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every third year the worshipper had to declare before God that he had truly given the tithe to the needy and kept it holy, and then pray for blessing on the whole nation.

The year of tithing. The third-year tithe stayed in the local towns for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow (14:28–29), “so that they may eat within your towns and be filled” (v. 12). Now the worshipper must stand before God and say whether he has actually given it.

I have obeyed the voice of the LORD my God. The declaration assumes that God will ask, that the food reaching the widow in your town is a matter he takes account of, and that a man ought to be able to say plainly whether it happened, rather than offer a general impression of himself as generous. Most of us keep a comfortable vagueness about what we give and to whom; this liturgy names the four kinds of people, so the man knows exactly which faces he is being asked about.

Look down from heaven. The man who has just given away a tenth of his harvest to people who cannot repay him does not ask for a reward. He asks God to bless the whole nation and the land, “as you swore to our fathers” (v. 15).

What it does not mean. “I have not transgressed any of your commandments” is not a claim to be sinless. He is speaking of the commands about the tithe. Only one man could say the larger thing truly: “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Our generosity is accepted in him, not offered as a record to stand on.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes belonged to the order of Levites and sanctuary. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and for churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Some Christians hold that a tenth is still required. This commentary’s view is that a tenth is a good benchmark and a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and many should give more.

Uncertain wording. The practices behind verse 14 are not known exactly. “Offered any of it to the dead” most likely means food left for the dead in pagan custom, though some think of food given to a house in mourning. Either way, what was holy to the LORD was kept from death and its rites.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law ends in an exchange of vows between God and his people. The LORD commands Israel to keep his statutes with all her heart and soul (v. 16). Israel has declared that the LORD is her God and that she will walk in his ways (v. 17), and the LORD has declared that Israel is his treasured possession, whom he will set high above the nations as a people holy to him (vv. 18–19). Israel’s half will fail; God’s half will stand, and is fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The declaring in vv. 17–18 is mutual and formal, as at a wedding, and God’s half is the larger one.
verseByVerse.examples: The same exchange stands at the centre of the Christian faith: I will be their God, and they shall be my people (Heb. 8:10).

verseByVerse.quote: "This day the LORD your God commands you to do these statutes and rules. You shall therefore be careful to do them with all your heart and with all your soul. You have declared today that the LORD is your God, and that you will walk in his ways, and keep his statutes and his commandments and his rules, and will obey his voice. And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you, and that you are to keep all his commandments, and that he will set you in praise and in fame and in honor high above all nations that he has made, and that you shall be a people holy to the LORD your God, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law ends with an exchange of vows: Israel declares that the LORD is her God, and the LORD declares that Israel is his treasured possession, a promise only he could keep.

You have declared today. The law ends as a wedding does: a formal, public, mutual declaring, with both parties on the record. Everything since chapter 12 turns out to be the terms of a relationship, now said aloud by both sides. “With all your heart and with all your soul” (v. 16) echoes the great command (6:5): the terms are meant to be kept in love.

Treasured possession. Israel’s half is to walk in his ways. God’s half is larger: he calls Israel his segullah, the word for a king’s personal treasure, kept apart from the state treasury (Exodus 19:5). He will set her “in praise and in fame and in honor high above all nations” (v. 19), “a people holy to the LORD your God”.

Only one side kept it. Israel’s half was obedience, which she failed within a generation. God’s half did not depend on her. The prophets give the same promise again after Israel’s failure, “And I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33), Hebrews quotes it of the new covenant (Hebrews 8:10), and the last chapters of the Bible say it once more with nothing left to go wrong: “they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

Bought for his own possession. Paul says how the treasured possession was secured: Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14). It was bought. Peter applies Israel’s titles to the church, “a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). The law of Moses ends with two parties declaring what they are to each other, and one of them kept his word.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you
keyVerse.note: The whole body of law ends in this exchange of vows, and God’s half is larger than Israel’s. Israel promised obedience and failed; the LORD promised to make them his own, and kept his word. In Christ the same promise reaches every believer: a people bought to be his treasured possession (Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 2:9).

26.reflection:
The man with the basket declares that God has kept his promise (v. 3). What has God given you that you have come to treat as your own achievement, and how could you thank him for it specifically?

The confession moves from “my father … went down” to “we cried” and “he brought us out” (vv. 5–8). How would you tell your story as part of God’s story? Why does it matter to say of Christ, “who loved me and gave himself for me”?

The tithe liturgy names the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, and asks the worshipper to say plainly what he has given (vv. 12–14). Who are the people your giving should reach, and how specific are you about what actually reaches them?

Verses 17–19 are like a wedding: two parties declaring what they are to each other. How does knowing that God calls you his treasured possession change the way you obey him?

27.title: The Covenant at Shechem and the Curses
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying, "Keep the whole commandment that I command you today.<sup>2</sup>And on the day you cross over the Jordan to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall set up large stones and plaster them with plaster.<sup>3</sup>And you shall write on them all the words of this law, when you cross over to enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, a land flowing with milk and honey, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you.<sup>4</sup>And when you have crossed over the Jordan, you shall set up these stones, concerning which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall plaster them with plaster.<sup>5</sup>And there you shall build an altar to the LORD your God, an altar of stones. You shall wield no iron tool on them;<sup>6</sup>you shall build an altar to the LORD your God of uncut stones. And you shall offer burnt offerings on it to the LORD your God,<sup>7</sup>and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and shall eat there, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God.<sup>8</sup>And you shall write on the stones all the words of this law very plainly."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses and the Levitical priests said to all Israel, "Keep silence and hear, O Israel: this day you have become the people of the LORD your God.<sup>10</sup>You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments and his statutes, which I command you today."<sup>11</sup>That day Moses charged the people, saying,<sup>12</sup>"When you have crossed over the Jordan, these shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.<sup>13</sup>And these shall stand on Mount Ebal for the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.<sup>14</sup>And the Levites shall declare to all the men of Israel in a loud voice:<sup>15</sup>"'Cursed be the man who makes a carved or cast metal image, an abomination to the LORD, a thing made by the hands of a craftsman, and sets it up in secret.' And all the people shall answer and say, 'Amen.'<sup>16</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who dishonors his father or his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>17</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who moves his neighbor's landmark.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>18</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who misleads a blind man on the road.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>19</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who perverts the justice due to the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>20</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with his father's wife, because he has uncovered his father's nakedness.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>21</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with any kind of animal.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>22</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with his sister, whether the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>23</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with his mother-in-law.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>24</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who strikes down his neighbor in secret.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>25</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who takes a bribe to shed innocent blood.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>26</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'
27.overview:
Where we are. With the laws complete (chapters 12–26) and the vows exchanged (26:16–19), Moses now tells Israel how to seal the covenant once they have crossed the Jordan. Chapter 27 is a ceremony to be held in the land, at the twin mountains of Ebal and Gerizim; chapter 28 will set out the blessings and curses in full.

The message. You are God’s people today, so obey him, and know that his law reaches into the places no one else can see. Israel was to write the law plainly in public, build an altar for sacrifice and joy, and then say “Amen” to God’s curse on secret sin, ending with a curse on anyone who does not keep the whole law. The ceremony puts in the open what God requires, and the sacrifice he provides.

Why it was said. A new generation, most of them born in the wilderness, had to take the covenant as their own rather than inherit it as a family tradition (see the introduction). And a nation settling into towns and farms would find many ways to sin where no court could reach.

How the chapter makes its case. On entering the land Israel must set up large plastered stones on Mount Ebal and write the law on them very plainly, and build an altar of uncut stones for burnt offerings, peace offerings and rejoicing (vv. 1–8). Moses and the priests declare that “this day” Israel has become the LORD’s people, and must therefore obey (vv. 9–10). Six tribes are to stand on Gerizim for blessing and six on Ebal for the curse, while the Levites proclaim curses on sins mostly done in secret, and the people answer “Amen” to each (vv. 11–25). The last curse covers the whole law (v. 26).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by covenant. No one can say “Amen” to verse 26 and survive it, and Paul quotes it to show that all who rely on the law are under a curse (Galatians 3:10). But on the mountain of cursing stood an altar of uncut stone, where sacrifice was made before a single curse was read. That pointed to Calvary, where “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that our Amen is now said to God’s promises (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. Ask what you do when you believe no one is watching, for God is. Do not try to stand before him on your own record; flee to the one who bore the curse. And then live as someone already fully known and loved, the same in the dark as in the light.
27.theology:
The curse of the law drives us to Christ. The law demands a whole obedience no sinner can render (27:26), and so it cannot make anyone right with God; Christ redeemed us from its curse by becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:10, 13).

The altar at the mountain of cursing. The altar of uncut stones stands on Ebal, the mountain of curse (27:5–7). Where the curse falls, there the sacrifice stands, because at the cross the curse and the sacrifice met in the body of Christ.

Who we are comes before what we do. “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey” (27:9–10). Israel obeys because she is God's people, not to become them, and the believer's obedience is the joyful working out of an identity freely given by grace.
27.examples: The curse of verse 26 drives us out of self-righteousness into the arms of Christ, who bore in our place the curse we earned by failing to keep the whole law, so that the blessing of Abraham flows to all who believe. We obey not to become God's people, but because, in Christ, we already are, and his Spirit now works that obedience in us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Law on Stones, and an Altar of Uncut Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law is to be published for all to read, and beside it stands an altar for sacrifice and joy. On the day Israel crosses the Jordan, they must set up large stones, coat them with plaster and write all the words of the law on them (vv. 1–3), on Mount Ebal (v. 4). There they are to build an altar of uncut stones, untouched by iron, offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, eat and rejoice before the LORD (vv. 5–7). The law must be written “very plainly” (v. 8). What God requires and the sacrifice he provides stand together on one hill.
verseByVerse.theology: Beside the written law God sets an altar, and beside the altar a meal and rejoicing.
verseByVerse.examples: The same two things still stand together, in the same order: the law that shows us what we are, and beside it a sacrifice we contributed nothing to.
