verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying, "Keep the whole commandment that I command you today. And on the day you cross over the Jordan to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall set up large stones and plaster them with plaster. And you shall write on them all the words of this law, when you cross over to enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, a land flowing with milk and honey, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you. And when you have crossed over the Jordan, you shall set up these stones, concerning which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall plaster them with plaster. And there you shall build an altar to the LORD your God, an altar of stones. You shall wield no iron tool on them; you shall build an altar to the LORD your God of uncut stones. And you shall offer burnt offerings on it to the LORD your God, and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and shall eat there, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God. And you shall write on the stones all the words of this law very plainly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On Mount Ebal Israel was to set up the law in writing for everyone to read and, beside it, an altar of uncut stones for sacrifice and rejoicing: what God requires, and the sacrifice he provides.

Large plastered stones. Plastered stone takes writing well and can be read at a distance. The law is to be published, set up in the open, where anyone walking past can read the terms of the covenant for himself, written “very plainly” (v. 8). Joshua did exactly this (Joshua 8:30–35).

No iron tool. Field stones, taken as they were found, with no chisel work. Exodus gives the reason: “if you wield your tool on it you profane it” (Exodus 20:25). A shaped stone is one a man has contributed to; the altar where atonement is made must contain nothing of human workmanship.

Law and altar. So on one hill stand two things: a written law, produced with great care, so that everyone knows exactly what is required, and an altar no human hand has improved, where the blood goes. That is the whole Bible on a single hillside. The law shows us what God requires; the altar points to the sacrifice he provides in Christ, to which we add nothing.

You shall rejoice. At that altar Israel is to sacrifice, eat and rejoice, on Mount Ebal, the mountain of the curse. Before a word of the curses has been read, there is an altar on that hill, and a meal, and gladness.

Textual note. The Hebrew text names Mount Ebal here (v. 4); the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Samaritans’ own copy of the five books of Moses, reads Mount Gerizim, their holy mountain, and many scholars think it was changed to suit them. A large ancient structure on Mount Ebal has been identified by some archaeologists as an early altar, though that remains debated.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–10 — This Day You Have Become the People of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people obey because they belong to him, not in order to belong. Moses and the Levitical priests call the whole nation to silence and declare that “this day” Israel has become the people of the LORD her God (v. 9). The new generation, most of them born in the wilderness, take the covenant as their own. Only then comes the command: “You shall therefore obey” (v. 10). The order of grace first and obedience second runs through the whole book.
verseByVerse.theology: Each generation must take the covenant as its own: nobody inherits it like an heirloom.
verseByVerse.examples: Every command in the New Testament stands on the same footing — you are a chosen race… therefore (1 Pet. 2:9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and the Levitical priests said to all Israel, "Keep silence and hear, O Israel: this day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments and his statutes, which I command you today."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new generation becomes God’s people for themselves today, and because they are his, they must obey.

This day. An odd thing to say. Israel had been the people of the LORD since the Passover forty years earlier, and since Abraham in a sense. Moses means what he meant in 5:3: the covenant is not an heirloom. Most of those before him were born in the wilderness. Today, as they hear these words, they become the people of God for themselves, not merely the children of people who were. Every generation, and every child raised in a believing home, must one day own the faith in the same way.

Therefore. This is the pulse of the whole book. Not “obey, and you will become his people”, but “you have become his people; now obey”. Peter writes to scattered Christians in the same order: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9), and only then, “Beloved, I urge you” (1 Peter 2:11). Reverse the two and you have a different religion. It is the commonest mistake made about the Bible, and it is made most often by the people trying hardest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — The Twelve Curses from Mount Ebal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees what is done in secret, and his people must agree with his verdict on it. Six tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim for the blessing and six on Mount Ebal for the curse (vv. 11–13), while the Levites proclaim curses aloud (v. 14). The curses fall on idolatry set up in secret, contempt for parents, moving a boundary stone, misleading the blind, perverting justice for the weak, sexual sins inside the family, murder in secret and bribery to kill the innocent (vv. 15–25). After each the whole nation answers, “Amen.”
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law reaches the places no one else can see.
verseByVerse.examples: God is the only witness who has never missed anything. That is why the altar was built on Ebal before the first curse was read: the sins nobody saw have a sacrifice provided for them too.

verseByVerse.quote: That day Moses charged the people, saying, "When you have crossed over the Jordan, these shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. And these shall stand on Mount Ebal for the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali. And the Levites shall declare to all the men of Israel in a loud voice: "'Cursed be the man who makes a carved or cast metal image, an abomination to the LORD, a thing made by the hands of a craftsman, and sets it up in secret.' And all the people shall answer and say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who dishonors his father or his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who moves his neighbor's landmark.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who misleads a blind man on the road.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who perverts the justice due to the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with his father's wife, because he has uncovered his father's nakedness.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with any kind of animal.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with his sister, whether the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with his mother-in-law.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who strikes down his neighbor in secret.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who takes a bribe to shed innocent blood.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel was to say “Amen” to God’s curse on sins mostly done in secret, because God sees where no one else does.

Gerizim and Ebal. Two hillsides face each other across a valley near Shechem, with acoustics that carry a voice across, and the tribes are arranged on the slopes. (The blessings from Gerizim are not recited here; chapter 28 supplies them.) A sentence goes up from the valley floor, and a nation answers with one word: “Amen”, so be it, we agree.

Sets it up in secret. The curses have something in common that is easy to miss: almost every one is a sin nobody would see. The idol is hidden. The boundary stone is moved at dusk. The blind man never knows who turned him the wrong way. The widow cannot prove the verdict was bought. The incest happens inside a house. Twice the text says “in secret” outright (vv. 15, 24).

No witness but God. This is deliberate. Chapter 28 will deal with the nation’s public life; chapter 27 deals with what a man does when there is no witness, and makes a whole nation say “Amen” to a curse on exactly those things. Anyone can keep the law where he can be seen. This list marks the places where a person’s real character is found, and where God is the only one watching.

The ring that makes you invisible. In Plato’s Republic Glaucon tells of a shepherd who finds a ring that makes him invisible, and asks whether anyone who owned it would stay just. His suspicion is that most of our goodness is reputation management: we are honest because we are watched. The internet has handed many of us the ring: an anonymous account, a private browser, a transaction nobody will audit. These curses read like a list of what people do when they think the ring is on. Scripture is more sobering than Glaucon: Jesus said that what has been “whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops” (Luke 12:3).

Fully known, and still loved. Yet the gospel does not answer by making us more afraid of being seen. It tells us that we have already been seen completely, every secret on this list included, by the one who then went to the place of the curse in our stead. A person who knows he is fully known and still loved no longer needs the ring. He can be the same in the dark as in the light, because the dark holds nothing he is hiding from the only Judge who matters.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 26 — Cursed Be Everyone Who Does Not Keep the Whole Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last curse covers the whole law, and Israel agrees to it. Where the earlier curses named particular sins, this one falls on anyone who does not confirm the words of the law by doing them (v. 26). All the people say “Amen.” Paul quotes this verse to show that everyone who relies on the law for acceptance with God is under a curse, and that Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:10–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The law’s last word over the whole nation is a curse, but it is not the Bible’s last word.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel pronounced a curse on herself and said Amen to it. That curse was carried off by a man on a tree, and the believer now says Amen to God’s promises instead (2 Cor. 1:20).

verseByVerse.quote: "'Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final curse falls on anyone who does not keep the whole law, and Israel said “Amen” to it; Paul shows that this curse condemns all who rely on the law, and that Christ bore it for us.

The whole law. The first eleven curses name particular sins. The twelfth names the whole law and requires all of it. A nation stood on a mountainside and said “Amen” to that, putting themselves under it out loud, with their own voices, as the last word of the ceremony.

In Galatia. Centuries later Paul writes to churches persuaded that keeping the law is how a person gets right with God. He says that “all who rely on works of the law are under a curse”, and reaches for this verse: “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them” (Galatians 3:10). He quotes the wording of the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, which spells out “all”; the Hebrew already means the whole law.

The logic of the curse. If the law blesses the man who keeps it, it must curse the man who does not, and the standard is “all things”. So whoever puts himself under the law as a way of being accepted has put himself under a sentence that will certainly fall, because nobody has kept all of it, and the law has no provision for partial obedience.

By becoming a curse for us. That is why Mount Ebal is not the end of the story, and why three verses later Paul writes one of the sweetest sentences in the New Testament: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

A true Amen. Israel said “Amen” to her own curse on a hillside in Canaan. It was a true and honest Amen, and the curse did fall, but on someone else, on a hill outside a city, centuries after the last Israelite who shouted it was dust. The Amen we now say is to God’s promises, not to a curse: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

keyVerse.quote: Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.
keyVerse.note: The last curse gathers up all the others and requires the whole law. Israel said “Amen” to it, and Paul quotes it to show that no one can be right with God by the law (Galatians 3:10). It shuts every mouth, and so it sends us to the Christ who became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

27.reflection:
On Mount Ebal the written law and the altar of uncut stones stood side by side (vv. 1–8). Why do we need both? What happens to people who have only one of them?

Moses says, “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey” (vv. 9–10). Why does the order matter so much, and where are you tempted to reverse it?

Most of the curses fall on sins done in secret (vv. 15–25). What would you do if you were sure no one would ever know, and how does the gospel free you to be the same person in the dark as in the light?

Israel said “Amen” to a curse that would one day fall on Christ (v. 26; Galatians 3:13). How does that change the way you face your failures, and what promises of God can you say “Amen” to today?

28.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 28 is the longest in Deuteronomy and closes Moses’ second address. Chapter 27 told Israel to say “Amen” to the curses on Mount Ebal; now Moses sets out in full the blessings that will follow obedience (vv. 1–14) and the far longer curses that will follow disobedience (vv. 15–68), as the sanctions of the covenant.

The message. The covenant has two faces, and the same God stands behind both. If Israel listens to him, his blessing will chase her down in every corner of ordinary life; if she turns away, his curse will pursue her just as surely, to siege, exile and slavery. And the root of the ruin is named with startling precision: not only rebellion, but serving God without joy when he had given them everything (v. 47).

Why it was said. Ancient treaties ended with blessings and long lists of curses, and Israel’s covenant with her King takes the same shape (see the introduction). A people about to enjoy plenty needed to know that the land was held under covenant, and that the God who gives can also take away.

How the chapter makes its case. Blessings overtake the obedient in city and field, womb and herd, basket and bowl, coming in and going out, with victory, rain and honour among the nations (vv. 1–14). Then the same blessings are turned over one by one into curses: disease, drought, defeat, madness, loss of home, family and harvest, the stranger rising above his hosts (vv. 15–46). The cause is named, joyless service amid abundance, and the punishment fits it: service to enemies in hunger, and a siege so terrible that parents turn on their children (vv. 47–57). The chapter ends in scattering, dread by day and night, and a return to Egypt where no one will even buy them as slaves (vv. 58–68).

Where it leads. By covenant and by the need it exposes. Israel’s history followed this chapter to the letter, through Assyrian and Babylonian exile, and Jesus wept over Jerusalem before its fall to Rome (Luke 19:41–44). But only one Israelite ever obeyed every word, and in him the blessings reach those who failed (Romans 5:19), while “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). This chapter shows the size of what he bore.

For us. These are not promises of wealth for obedient Christians, nor threats of curse on those in Christ, for he has borne the curse. But they show God’s generous heart and his holy seriousness. Ask whether your service has gone dull in a season of plenty, and come back to the cross, where gladness begins again.
28.theology:
Christ bore the covenant curse. The catalogue of curse reveals what sin deserves. On the cross Christ absorbed the full weight of the broken covenant, even God-forsakenness (Matt. 27:46), so that all who trust him might receive the covenant blessing instead (Gal. 3:13–14).

The holiness and justice of God. God will not be mocked (Gal. 6:7). The severity of the curses, and their fulfillment in Israel's exile, prove that his word is true.

The peril of joyless prosperity. The root of the curse was failing to serve God “with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things” (28:47). Ingratitude amid blessing is the seedbed of ruin.
28.examples: We read this chapter as a measure of what our sin deserves, a backdrop against which the cross blazes all the brighter: here is what Christ bore, so that we might never be forsaken and might receive every spiritual blessing in him. Let us serve our God with gladness of heart, the joy his Spirit gives, never taking his grace for granted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Blessings That Overtake You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s blessing pursues the obedient into every corner of life. If Israel listens to the LORD, his blessings will come upon her and overtake her (vv. 1–2): in city and field, in children, crops and herds, in basket and kneading bowl, in coming in and going out (vv. 3–6). Enemies will come one way and flee seven (v. 7); barns, land and rain will be blessed, and Israel will be established as God’s holy people, so that the nations fear her (vv. 8–10). She will lend and not borrow, be the head and not the tail, if she does not turn aside to other gods (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s blessing reaches the most ordinary parts of life, and it is the gift of a Father to children already his, not wages earned.
verseByVerse.examples: God’s people may look for his kindness in the kitchen and on the doorstep, not only in church, though the note below warns against turning these national promises into a private formula.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if you faithfully obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all his commandments that I command you today, the LORD your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth. And all these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you, if you obey the voice of the LORD your God. Blessed shall you be in the city, and blessed shall you be in the field. Blessed shall be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground and the fruit of your cattle, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock. Blessed shall be your basket and your kneading bowl. Blessed shall you be when you come in, and blessed shall you be when you go out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel obeys, God’s blessing will chase her down and catch her in every ordinary part of life, at home and away, in family, field and kitchen.

Overtake. The word is used of an army running down a fleeing enemy. God describes his own goodness as something that chases his people and catches them. We picture blessing as something to be sought or deserved; here it is behind Israel on the road, gaining on her.

Basket and bowl. Look at what the blessings are: a basket, a kneading bowl, the doorway of a house. There is not one religious item in the list. God’s blessing is promised over the bowl a woman makes bread in and the threshold a man crosses twice a day, which is where almost the whole of any life is lived.

Blessed shall you be when you come in. The pairs cover everything: city and field, coming in and going out, the beginning and end of every journey. The same picture turns up in the best-loved line of the Psalter, “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 23:6), where the Hebrew behind “follow” is the word for pursue. The pursuit has not slackened: God “has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3).

Does this national covenant apply to modern nations? It was made with Israel as God’s covenant nation; no other nation stands in that relation to him. God does judge nations for injustice (Proverbs 14:34), but no country can claim these promises as its own. And verse 12 is a picture of national blessing, not a ban on borrowing; Scripture warns against debt (Proverbs 22:7) but does not forbid it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD will cause your enemies who rise against you to be defeated before you. They shall come out against you one way and flee before you seven ways. The LORD will command the blessing on you in your barns and in all that you undertake. And he will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. The LORD will establish you as a people holy to himself, as he has sworn to you, if you keep the commandments of the LORD your God and walk in his ways. And all the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD, and they shall be afraid of you. And the LORD will make you abound in prosperity, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your livestock and in the fruit of your ground, within the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give you. The LORD will open to you his good treasury, the heavens, to give the rain to your land in its season and to bless all the work of your hands. And you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow. And the LORD will make you the head and not the tail, and you shall only go up and not down, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today, being careful to do them, and if you do not turn aside from any of the words that I command you today, to the right hand or to the left, to go after other gods to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing widens from the household to the nation, with victory, plenty and honour, but it rests on a condition that only Christ has met.

Flee before you seven ways. One road in and seven roads out: a rout, an army that arrived in formation and left in every direction at once.

Not a formula for finances. These verses are the raw material of a great deal of bad preaching. They are national promises under a particular covenant, attached to a land, not a formula a Christian can apply to his own finances. The New Testament nowhere transfers them in that form; several of its own writers were poor, and several were martyred. Job’s friends reasoned that prosperity follows righteousness and suffering follows sin, and God said at the end that they had “not spoken of me what is right” (Job 42:7). God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them rich or always healthy.

What carries over. What does carry over is the heart of God they show. He is not stingy; the language here is extravagant, and it is his own. Whatever a believer’s circumstances, he deals with a God whose instinct towards his people is to give: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

If you obey. The blessing has a condition, and verse 15 turns on it. Only one Israelite ever kept every word without turning aside “to the right hand or to the left” (v. 14), and in him, whose obedience is counted as ours, the blessing reaches those who fail (Romans 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–46 — The Curses That Overtake You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The curse pursues the disobedient as surely as the blessing pursues the obedient. If Israel will not listen, every blessing of verses 3–6 is reversed in the same words (vv. 15–19). Disease, drought and a sky of bronze follow (vv. 20–24); then defeat and unburied dead (vv. 25–26), the boils of Egypt and madness (vv. 27–29), the loss of bride, house, vineyard, herds and children before their eyes (vv. 30–35), exile with their king (vv. 36–37), failed harvests and the stranger rising above them (vv. 38–44). These curses will be a sign and a wonder against them for ever (vv. 45–46).
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue is deliberately relentless: the covenant that promises blessing for obedience also carries consequences for breaking it.
verseByVerse.examples: A nation heard its own blessings read back to it as threats. The New Testament does not repeal these curses; it shows where they finally fell.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD your God or be careful to do all his commandments and his statutes that I command you today, then all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you. Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field. Cursed shall be your basket and your kneading bowl. Cursed shall be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock. Cursed shall you be when you come in, and cursed shall you be when you go out. "The LORD will send on you curses, confusion, and frustration in all that you undertake to do, until you are destroyed and perish quickly on account of the evil of your deeds, because you have forsaken me. The LORD will make the pestilence stick to you until he has consumed you off the land that you are entering to take possession of it. The LORD will strike you with wasting disease and with fever, inflammation and fiery heat, and with drought and with blight and with mildew. They shall pursue you until you perish. And the heavens over your head shall be bronze, and the earth under you shall be iron. The LORD will make the rain of your land powder. From heaven dust shall come down on you until you are destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel disobeys, the same blessings are turned over one by one into curses, and disease, drought and a sky like bronze pursue her as surely as the blessing would have.

Overtake you. The same verb returns, because the curses pursue too. Verses 16–19 are verses 3–6 turned over, in nearly the same order and words: the basket, the bowl, the doorway, now pursued by curse.

One covenant, two faces. That structure is the message of the chapter. These are not two unrelated lists but one covenant with two faces, and the same God stands behind both. What he gives for obedience he may withhold for disobedience. Verse 20 names the root: “because you have forsaken me”.

The LORD will make the pestilence stick to you. Then the catalogue: pestilence, wasting disease, fever, drought, blight, mildew, a sky like bronze and earth like iron, and dust for rain. The blessings took fourteen verses; the curses take fifty-four, and the disproportion is deliberate. Ancient treaties between a great king and his vassals closed with blessings and a much longer list of curses, and one Assyrian treaty of the seventh century BC even threatens a sky of bronze and ground of iron, as verse 23 does.

Do these curses fall on Christians? “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Believers still suffer, and the Father disciplines them (Hebrews 12:6), but that is not the covenant curse; there are no “generational curses” on those in Christ.

Uncertain wording. In verse 22 the Hebrew consonants for “drought” are the same as those for “sword”, which is how the KJV reads it. The ESV takes “drought”, which suits a list of fevers and crop diseases; either way the point stands.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD will cause you to be defeated before your enemies. You shall go out one way against them and flee seven ways before them. And you shall be a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. And your dead body shall be food for all birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth, and there shall be no one to frighten them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory promised in verse 7 is reversed: Israel will flee seven ways, become a horror to the nations, and lie unburied.

Flee seven ways before them. The army that marched out in good order scatters in every direction, the exact reverse of verse 7.

Your dead body shall be food for all birds. To lie unburied was the last disgrace in the ancient world, a sign that no one was left to care for the dead. The prophets saw this curse come true (Jeremiah 7:33; 16:4), and Psalm 79:2–3 mourns it after Jerusalem fell.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will strike you with the boils of Egypt, and with tumors and scabs and itch, of which you cannot be healed. The LORD will strike you with madness and blindness and confusion of mind, and you shall grope at noonday, as the blind grope in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. And you shall be only oppressed and robbed continually, and there shall be no one to help you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The diseases God once sent on Egypt will fall on Israel, and with them a blindness of mind in full daylight and a helplessness with no one to save.

The boils of Egypt. The people he promised to spare from “the diseases of Egypt” (7:15; Exodus 15:26) will suffer them (Exodus 9:9–11) if they become like Egypt. Then comes a sickness of the mind: madness, blindness, confusion. To grope at noonday, in full light, is the picture of a people who have the light of God’s word and cannot see by it (compare Isaiah 59:10).

No one to help. The phrase recurs (vv. 29, 31), and verse 32 adds “you shall be helpless”. Not merely loss, but loss while watching and being unable to act.

Uncertain wording. The diseases named in verse 27 cannot all be identified. “Tumors” translates a word that may mean swellings of various kinds (the KJV has “emerods”, that is, haemorrhoids), and “scabs and itch” may describe skin diseases we can no longer name exactly. The point is clear: sickness without cure.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall betroth a wife, but another man shall ravish her. You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not enjoy its fruit. Your ox shall be slaughtered before your eyes, but you shall not eat any of it. Your donkey shall be seized before your face, but shall not be restored to you. Your sheep shall be given to your enemies, but there shall be no one to help you. Your sons and your daughters shall be given to another people, while your eyes look on and fail with longing for them all day long, but you shall be helpless. A nation that you have not known shall eat up the fruit of your ground and of all your labors, and you shall be only oppressed and crushed continually, so that you are driven mad by the sights that your eyes see. The LORD will strike you on the knees and on the legs with grievous boils of which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every hope is cut off just before it is fulfilled, and Israel must watch others enjoy her bride, house, vineyard, herds and children.

You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. A bride, a house, a vineyard, the herds, and at last the children. These are the very things the law protected: a man who had built a house, planted a vineyard or betrothed a wife was sent home from the battle line to enjoy them (20:5–7). Under the curse someone else enjoys them all. The prophets turn this curse round in their promises: “They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 65:21).

Driven mad by the sights that your eyes see. The repeated phrases, “before your eyes”, “before your face”, “your eyes look on”, make Israel a helpless spectator of her own loss, the particular cruelty of every disaster that happens to one’s children. The paragraph closes as it began, with boils that cannot be healed, now “from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head” (v. 35; compare v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD will bring you and your king whom you set over you to a nation that neither you nor your fathers have known. And there you shall serve other gods of wood and stone. And you shall become a horror, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples where the LORD will lead you away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curse will end in exile: king and people carried to a foreign land, serving the lifeless gods they chased, and mocked by the nations they were meant to draw to God.

Other gods of wood and stone. The punishment matches the sin. A people that wanted other gods will be taken where nothing else is on offer, serving idols far from home (4:27–28). In exile they would find out what the gods they had chased were worth.

A byword. The nation chosen to display God’s goodness would end as a cautionary tale told by the nations she was meant to attract.

Where Christians differ: how verse 36 came to name a king. On the book’s own account it was spoken centuries before Israel had a king, and those who hold to Moses’ authorship see here God’s foreknowledge. Many scholars date the book’s final form to the time of the kings and read these verses as written with exile in view. This commentary’s view: as in the introduction, the substance is Moses’ own, and the God who knows the end from the beginning warned Israel long before.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather in little, for the locust shall consume it. You shall plant vineyards and dress them, but you shall neither drink of the wine nor gather the grapes, for the worm shall eat them. You shall have olive trees throughout all your territory, but you shall not anoint yourself with the oil, for your olives shall drop off. You shall father sons and daughters, but they shall not be yours, for they shall go into captivity. The cricket shall possess all your trees and the fruit of your ground. The sojourner who is among you shall rise higher and higher above you, and you shall come down lower and lower. He shall lend to you, and you shall not lend to him. He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every labour of the farming year will come to nothing, and the stranger Israel was told to protect will rise above her.

You shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather in little. Locust, worm, falling olives, cricket: every labour is undone. Even the children “shall not be yours” (v. 41). Haggai told the returned exiles the same, “You have sown much, and harvested little” (Haggai 1:6), and gave the same reason: they had put God’s claims last.

He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail. The sojourner, the landless outsider Israel was told to protect (10:18–19; 24:17), rises above his hosts. These verses deliberately reverse verses 12–13, where Israel lends to many nations and is “the head and not the tail”.

Uncertain wording. “Cricket” (v. 42) translates a rare word that seems to mean a whirring or buzzing insect; it may be a kind of locust (so the KJV). The exact creature is unknown, but the picture of crops stripped is plain.

verseByVerse.quote: "All these curses shall come upon you and pursue you and overtake you till you are destroyed, because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God, to keep his commandments and his statutes that he commanded you. They shall be a sign and a wonder against you and your offspring forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curses will pursue Israel until she is destroyed, because she would not listen, and she will become a sign of judgment as Egypt once was.

Pursue and overtake. Verse 45 stacks three verbs of pursuit in one sentence (come, pursue, overtake), and gives the reason: “because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God”.

A sign and a wonder. Everywhere else in Deuteronomy “signs and wonders” are what God did in Egypt to save his people (4:34; 6:22; 26:8). Now Israel herself would become the sign, a marvel of judgment, as Egypt once was. Yet the curse is not the last word: chapter 30 promises that when the scattered people return to the LORD, he will gather them again (30:1–6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 47–57 — Because You Did Not Serve Him with Gladness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter names the root of the ruin, and the punishment fits it. Israel did not serve the LORD “with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things” (v. 47), so she will serve her enemies in hunger and nakedness under a yoke of iron (v. 48). A distant, ruthless nation will swoop like an eagle, devour the land and besiege every town (vv. 49–52). In the siege the most refined men and women will eat their own children and hide the food from their families (vv. 53–57).
verseByVerse.theology: God cares not only whether he is served but how.
verseByVerse.examples: The same warning stands over any comfortable church: God notices the difference between service that is merely dutiful and service that is glad. The way back is not forced feeling but return to the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things, therefore you shall serve your enemies whom the LORD will send against you, in hunger and thirst, in nakedness, and lacking everything. And he will put a yoke of iron on your neck until he has destroyed you. The LORD will bring a nation against you from far away, from the end of the earth, swooping down like the eagle, a nation whose language you do not understand, a hard-faced nation who shall not respect the old or show mercy to the young. It shall eat the offspring of your cattle and the fruit of your ground, until you are destroyed; it also shall not leave you grain, wine, or oil, the increase of your herds or the young of your flock, until they have caused you to perish. "They shall besiege you in all your towns, until your high and fortified walls, in which you trusted, come down throughout all your land. And they shall besiege you in all your towns throughout all your land, which the LORD your God has given you. And you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters, whom the LORD your God has given you, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemies shall distress you. The man who is the most tender and refined among you will begrudge food to his brother, to the wife he embraces, and to the last of the children whom he has left, so that he will not give to any of them any of the flesh of his children whom he is eating, because he has nothing else left, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in all your towns. The most tender and refined woman among you, who would not venture to set the sole of her foot on the ground because she is so delicate and tender, will begrudge to the husband she embraces, to her son and to her daughter, her afterbirth that comes out from between her feet and her children whom she bears, because lacking everything she will eat them secretly, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in your towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruin comes because Israel served God without gladness amid plenty, so she will serve her enemies in hunger, and suffer a siege so terrible that parents eat their children.

Without joyfulness. Alongside forsaking him (v. 20) and not obeying (v. 45), the chapter names a cause nobody expects. They were, on the face of it, still serving: the sacrifices offered, the feasts kept. What had gone was gladness, and God treats that absence as grounds for the ruin of a nation.

Because of the abundance of all things. The joylessness grew in the good years. Prosperity did not make them rebellious; it made them dull. They had so much that God became one item among many, and the thanking stopped, then the gladness, and the serving went on with nothing inside it.

A religion of duty. That should stop anybody who has settled into a religion of duty. God is not indifferent to the difference between obedience and delight. A man can attend, give, serve and behave, and be under this verse the whole time without suspecting it, because nothing measurable is missing. Yet the way back is open: gladness is not manufactured but given, as the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22), to those who return and remember what they have received.

How does gladness come back? Not by trying to feel happy in church. Joy is a response, so it returns when we look again at what we are responding to. Count the abundance. The dullness grew in the good years, so begin there: at the end of each day name three specific gifts, not “everything” but this meal, this friend, this answered prayer. “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). Go back to the cross. The deepest gift is not the house or the job but forgiveness; read one of the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion slowly and ask what it cost him. Sing with others. “Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!” (Psalm 100:2). Gladness is caught as well as made. Share the feast. Deuteronomy’s joy always had the widow at the table (16:14), and generosity thaws a dull heart. Ask for it. “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12) is a prayer God delights to answer, for Christ endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2), and that joy is what he shares with his people.

You shall serve your enemies. The sentence fits the crime. They would not serve God with gladness while they had everything; they will serve enemies in hunger while they have nothing (v. 48). Then comes the siege, in the most harrowing verses in the Pentateuch: the refined and gentle turning on their own children for food (vv. 53–57), a horror Scripture records as fulfilled in Samaria and in Jerusalem (2 Kings 6:28–29; Lamentations 4:10).
verseByVerse.note: Josephus records the same horror in the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 (Jewish War 6.3.4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 58–68 — Scattered, and No Resting Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Disobedience ends in being undone and scattered. If Israel will not fear the glorious and awesome name of the LORD, the plagues of Egypt will cling to her and her numbers will dwindle (vv. 58–62). As the LORD delighted to do her good, he will delight to bring her to ruin; she will be plucked off the land and scattered to the ends of the earth (vv. 63–64). There she will find no rest, but a trembling heart and dread by night and day (vv. 65–67), and at last be shipped back to Egypt, offering herself as a slave with no buyer (v. 68).
verseByVerse.theology: The specificity is extraordinary — a nation from far away with an unknown language, siege, cannibalism, dispersion, and a return to Egypt in ships. Israel’s later history reads like a commentary on these verses. And yet Deuteronomy has already said what lies past them: from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him (4:29).
verseByVerse.examples: The last word of the covenant curse was a slave nobody would buy. But there is a rest for the people of God that no exile can reach (Heb. 4:9), and it was bought by Christ, who himself had nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8:20).

verseByVerse.quote: "If you are not careful to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that you may fear this glorious and awesome name, the LORD your God, then the LORD will bring on you and your offspring extraordinary afflictions, afflictions severe and lasting, and sicknesses grievous and lasting. And he will bring upon you again all the diseases of Egypt, of which you were afraid, and they shall cling to you. Every sickness also and every affliction that is not recorded in the book of this law, the LORD will bring upon you, until you are destroyed. Whereas you were as numerous as the stars of heaven, you shall be left few in number, because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God. And as the LORD took delight in doing you good and multiplying you, so the LORD will take delight in bringing ruin upon you and destroying you. And you shall be plucked off the land that you are entering to take possession of it. "And the LORD will scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth to the other, and there you shall serve other gods of wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known. And among these nations you shall find no respite, and there shall be no resting place for the sole of your foot, but the LORD will give you there a trembling heart and failing eyes and a languishing soul. Your life shall hang in doubt before you. Night and day you shall be in dread and have no assurance of your life. In the morning you shall say, 'If only it were evening!' and at evening you shall say, 'If only it were morning!' because of the dread that your heart shall feel, and the sights that your eyes shall see. And the LORD will bring you back in ships to Egypt, a journey that I promised that you should never make again; and there you shall offer yourselves for sale to your enemies as male and female slaves, but there will be no buyer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends in exile: Israel plucked off the land, scattered among the nations, living in dread by night and day, and sold back to Egypt with no buyer; this is the curse Christ bore.

Like the eagle. A hard-faced nation from far away (vv. 49–50), and then dispersion from one end of the earth to the other (v. 64). Israel’s history followed these words: the northern kingdom fell to Assyria and Judah to Babylon (2 Kings 17; 25), and Jesus foretold Jerusalem’s fall to Rome in the same terms (Luke 21:24).

The LORD will take delight in bringing ruin. Verse 63 is the hardest sentence in the book, and it should not be softened. God is not indifferent when he judges, nor an official unwillingly applying rules; what he delights in is his own holiness upheld. Yet through Ezekiel he says, “For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone” (Ezekiel 18:32). Both stand, and a reader who finds them hard to hold together is reading correctly. And when the Son of God came near Jerusalem before its fall, he wept over it (Luke 19:41–44).

A trembling heart. Life in exile is described with psychological exactness. Anyone who has lived through a season of dread knows verse 67 from the inside: “In the morning you shall say, ‘If only it were evening!’ and at evening you shall say, ‘If only it were morning!’” Each is longed for while the other is endured, and neither brings relief. Written more than two and a half thousand years ago, on any dating, not a word of it is out of date.

If this describes your nights. It is not proof that you are under this curse. God’s own children have known dread like it (Psalm 88; 2 Corinthians 1:8–9), and the curse has already fallen on Christ in their place. The one who said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28) meets the anxious there. There is no shame in seeking help from your pastor, friends and a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up, as well as in prayer; if medicine is needed, taking it is no failure of faith. If dread ever turns into thoughts of ending your life, tell someone and get help the same day.

No buyer. The last line is the bitterest. Back to the house of slavery, by sea this time, by “a journey that I promised that you should never make again” (v. 68), and so worthless that nobody will buy them even as slaves. The exodus is run backwards.

The size of what he bore. That is where the covenant curse ends. The only reason a Christian can read this chapter without despair is that Paul told us where its whole weight went, onto someone who had never earned a line of it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Deuteronomy 28 shows the size of what he bore. Read it to the end, then read that sentence again, and you will not think the cross was a small thing.

keyVerse.quote: Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things,
keyVerse.note: Among the causes of Israel’s ruin, this is the one nobody expects: not open rebellion, but service without joy in a time of plenty. It shows that God cares about the heart of our obedience, not only its outward form. And it points us to Christ, whose gift of himself is the deepest reason for gladness.

28.reflection:
The blessings of verses 3–6 rest on baskets, bowls and doorways rather than religious things. What would it look like to see God’s goodness in the most ordinary parts of your week?

Many preachers have used this chapter to promise health and wealth to those who obey. Why is that a misuse of it, and what does carry over from these promises to Christians today?

Verse 47 says Israel “did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things.” Where has plenty made your faith dull, and which of the ways back to gladness could you take this week?

Paul says Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). After reading this chapter, what does that tell you about the size of what he bore, and how should it shape the way you face your own fears and failures?

29.title: The Covenant Renewed in Moab: The Secret Things Belong to God
29.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the words of the covenant that the LORD commanded Moses to make with the people of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he had made with them at Horeb.<sup>2</sup>And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land,<sup>3</sup>the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders.<sup>4</sup>But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear.<sup>5</sup>I have led you forty years in the wilderness. Your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet.<sup>6</sup>You have not eaten bread, and you have not drunk wine or strong drink, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.<sup>7</sup>And when you came to this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon and Og the king of Bashan came out against us to battle, but we defeated them.<sup>8</sup>We took their land and gave it for an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of the Manassites.<sup>9</sup>Therefore keep the words of this covenant and do them, that you may prosper in all that you do.<sup>10</sup>"You are standing today, all of you, before the LORD your God: the heads of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel,<sup>11</sup>your little ones, your wives, and the sojourner who is in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water,<sup>12</sup>so that you may enter into the sworn covenant of the LORD your God, which the LORD your God is making with you today,<sup>13</sup>that he may establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he promised you, and as he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.<sup>14</sup>It is not with you alone that I am making this sworn covenant,<sup>15</sup>but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today.<sup>16</sup>"You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we came through the midst of the nations through which you passed.<sup>17</sup>And you have seen their detestable things, their idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold, which were among them.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest there be among you a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations. Beware lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit,<sup>19</sup>one who, when he hears the words of this sworn covenant, blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart.' This will lead to the sweeping away of moist and dry alike.<sup>20</sup>The LORD will not be willing to forgive him, but rather the anger of the LORD and his jealousy will smoke against that man, and the curses written in this book will settle upon him, and the LORD will blot out his name from under heaven.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for calamity, in accordance with all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Law.<sup>22</sup>And the next generation, your children who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will say, when they see the afflictions of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick—<sup>23</sup>the whole land burned out with brimstone and salt, nothing sown and nothing growing, where no plant can sprout, an overthrow like that of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath—<sup>24</sup>all the nations will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?'<sup>25</sup>Then people will say, 'It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt,<sup>26</sup>and went and served other gods and worshiped them, gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them.<sup>27</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against this land, bringing upon it all the curses written in this book,<sup>28</sup>and the LORD uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath, and cast them into another land, as they are this day.'<sup>29</sup>"The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
29.overview:
Where we are. The blessings and curses of chapter 28 have just been read. Now Moses begins his final address (chapters 29–30), in which the covenant is renewed on the plains of Moab with the whole nation, from the heads of the tribes down to the woodcutter and the water-carrier, and with generations not yet born.

The message. You have seen everything God can show, and you still cannot see, because a heart to understand is something only God can give. So do not deceive yourself: the person who hears God’s warnings and quietly tells himself “I shall be safe” is in the gravest danger of all. And do not torment yourself over what God has kept hidden; act on what he has made plain.

Why it was said. The generation on the plains of Moab had grown up on manna and miracles, and was about to take a covenant oath of its own (see the introduction). Moses knew that a crowd can swear together while one heart in it is already turning away, and that Israel’s history would prove it.

How the chapter makes its case. Moses rehearses forty years of wonders and care, then says that the LORD has not yet given them a heart to understand; obedience is still their duty (vv. 1–9). The whole people, down to the lowest and to those not yet born, stands before God to enter his sworn covenant (vv. 10–15). Moses warns against the hidden root of idolatry and the man who blesses himself while walking in stubbornness (vv. 16–21), and pictures a ruined land whose meaning even foreigners can read: “because they abandoned the covenant” (vv. 22–28). He ends by drawing the line between the secret things, which belong to God, and the revealed things, which belong to us so that we may do them (v. 29).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes. A heart to understand cannot be produced by evidence, ceremony or oath; it must be given. Chapter 30 promises that God will give it (30:6), and the prophets call that gift the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26). Jesus opened blind eyes as a sign of what he had come to do, and God now shines in our hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The greatest of God’s secret things, his plan to save, has been made known in Christ (Romans 16:25–26).

For us. Pray for open eyes, for yourself and for others, because argument alone has never made anyone see. Beware of the comfortable heart that hears God’s warnings and assumes they are meant for someone else. And leave the hidden things with God, while you get on with the plain things he has told you to do.
29.theology:
The need for a new heart. Evidence cannot cure a heart that cannot perceive (29:4). This cries out for the new covenant promise (ch. 30) that God himself will give the heart we lack (John 3:3; 1 Cor. 2:14).

The danger of presumption. To presume on grace while clinging to sin (29:19) is the most dangerous spiritual condition; the all-seeing God knows every secret turning of the heart and calls us to genuine repentance.

The secret and the revealed. Mature faith trusts God's sovereignty over what we cannot understand and obeys what he has plainly revealed (29:29). Where God has spoken, we obey; where God is silent, we trust.
29.examples: We confess that we were blind until God gave us eyes to see, the gift of the new covenant given in the Spirit. We heed the warning against nursing secret sin, trust God's goodness over all that is hidden, and by that same Spirit devote ourselves to what he has plainly revealed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — You Have Seen, and You Do Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seeing is not the same as understanding, and the heart that understands is God’s gift. Moses rehearses forty years of wonders: the plagues on Egypt, the signs, the clothes and sandals that did not wear out, the food God supplied without bread or wine, the victories over Sihon and Og (vv. 1–3, 5–8). In the middle of it he says something startling: “to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear” (v. 4). Yet he still commands obedience (v. 9), for their inability is no excuse, and it points ahead to the new heart promised in chapter 30.
verseByVerse.theology: The heart to understand is God’s to give, and the answer to its lack is the promise of 30:6.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody argues himself into faith, which is why Christians pray for eyes to be opened as well as offering arguments.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words of the covenant that the LORD commanded Moses to make with the people of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he had made with them at Horeb. And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land, the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders. But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear. I have led you forty years in the wilderness. Your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet. You have not eaten bread, and you have not drunk wine or strong drink, that you may know that I am the LORD your God. And when you came to this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon and Og the king of Bashan came out against us to battle, but we defeated them. We took their land and gave it for an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of the Manassites. Therefore keep the words of this covenant and do them, that you may prosper in all that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel had seen every wonder, yet lacked a heart to understand, which only God can give; and that did not cancel their duty to obey.

Besides the covenant at Horeb. Verse 1 is a heading: the covenant in Moab renews the one made at Horeb (Sinai) with the next generation. (In Hebrew Bibles it is the last verse of chapter 28.)

Not given a heart. Moses sets forty years of wonders beside verse 4. They saw everything, the plagues, the sea, the mountain, the bread on the ground, and Moses says they still cannot see. Not that they refused to look, but that they have not been given the ability. No generation has had more evidence, and it did not produce a heart to understand, because evidence and understanding are different things and the second is a gift.

Your sandals have not worn off. Verse 5, tucked in beside all that, is as tender as anything in the book. They could not see, and he kept their shoes on their feet for forty years anyway. He fed them himself, without bread or wine (v. 6).

Paul’s use of it. Paul takes up this language about the Israel of his own day: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear” (Romans 11:8). And he says of everyone, without exception: “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Blessed are your eyes, for they see. The gift Moses could not hand over arrived in person. The Lord Jesus opened the eyes of the blind as a sign of what he had come to do, and said to his disciples, “blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear” (Matthew 13:16). The God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” now shines in hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The heart to understand is given by the Son, through his Spirit.

Argument and prayer. Nobody has ever been argued into the kingdom. That does not make argument useless (Moses is arguing at this very moment), but it changes what we pray for. We ask God to open eyes, because only he can.

If God had not given them a heart to understand, how can they be blamed? The inability is real, and only God can cure it (30:6); but it is the inability of a will that does not want to obey, not an excuse. So Moses at once commands obedience (v. 9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — All of You Are Standing Here Today
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant embraces everyone, the least as fully as the greatest, and reaches forward to generations unborn. The whole nation stands before the LORD: heads of tribes, elders and officers, men, wives and little ones, and the foreigner who chops the wood and draws the water (vv. 10–11). All of them enter the same sworn covenant, by which God makes them his people and himself their God, as he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (vv. 12–13). And the covenant includes “whoever is not here with us today” (vv. 14–15), the children and grandchildren who must one day make it their own.
verseByVerse.theology: The list goes deliberately to the bottom of society, and the covenant reaches past the people present to generations unborn.
verseByVerse.examples: A slave drawing water stood in the same covenant as the head of a tribe, and the ground at the foot of the cross is no less level: there is neither slave nor free… for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal. 3:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "You are standing today, all of you, before the LORD your God: the heads of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel, your little ones, your wives, and the sojourner who is in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water, so that you may enter into the sworn covenant of the LORD your God, which the LORD your God is making with you today, that he may establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he promised you, and as he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. It is not with you alone that I am making this sworn covenant, but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone, from the leaders to the foreign woodcutter, the little ones and those not yet born, enters the same covenant on the same terms.

Woodcutter and water-carrier. Read the list from the bottom up. The last two named are the woodcutter and the water-carrier, the lowest jobs in the camp, done by resident foreigners, the people nobody would think to mention. They stand in the same covenant as the heads of the tribes, not in an annexe or as observers, and the text names their trades so nobody can miss it.

Your little ones, your wives. The women and the little ones are there too, which ancient treaty ceremonies did not usually trouble to record. This is not a covenant between God and the men of standing, with everybody else covered by association. Everybody is present and everybody is party to it.

That he may be your God. At its heart the covenant is a relationship: God makes them his people and gives himself as their God (v. 13), as he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The same promise runs through the whole Bible to its last pages: “they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

Whoever is not here. Verse 15 stretches it further still: people not yet born are included in a covenant made on one day in Moab. That is why Deuteronomy insists so hard that each generation must make it its own (5:3). The covenant reaches forward; entering it has to be done by every person for himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The deadliest danger is the hidden heart that hears the warnings and decides they do not apply to it. Israel has seen the idols of Egypt and the nations at close quarters (vv. 16–17). Moses warns against anyone whose heart is turning away, a hidden root that bears poisonous fruit (v. 18), and above all against the man who blesses himself, saying “I shall be safe” while walking in stubbornness (v. 19). God will single him out for the curses (vv. 20–21). Such unbelief spreads, until the whole land lies ruined like Sodom and foreigners ask why (vv. 22–24), and the answer is plain: they abandoned the covenant (vv. 25–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief nursed in secret does not stay private; what one person hides can spread to many.
verseByVerse.examples: The person in most danger in any church is rarely the one who is worried about himself, and the one who is worried may take the warning straight to Christ, who casts out no one who comes (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we came through the midst of the nations through which you passed. And you have seen their detestable things, their idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold, which were among them. Beware lest there be among you a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations. Beware lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The danger is not open idolatry but a heart quietly turning away, a hidden root that will bear poison for many.

You know how we lived in the land of Egypt. Israel had lived among idols in Egypt and had just passed through the lands of Edom, Moab and the Amorites. They had seen the “detestable things” at close quarters. The Hebrew word is contemptuous, and the list, “wood and stone, of silver and gold”, says what these gods are made of. Familiarity is the danger: what a person has seen often enough stops looking strange.

Whose heart is turning away today. The danger is located with great precision. It is not an idolater in the open; it is “a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today”: turning, present tense, while the ceremony is going on.

A root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit. Something underground, invisible, and spreading. Hebrews takes the image and hands it to the church unaltered: “See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:15).

verseByVerse.quote: one who, when he hears the words of this sworn covenant, blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart.' This will lead to the sweeping away of moist and dry alike. The LORD will not be willing to forgive him, but rather the anger of the LORD and his jealousy will smoke against that man, and the curses written in this book will settle upon him, and the LORD will blot out his name from under heaven. And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for calamity, in accordance with all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who hears God’s curses and privately tells himself he is safe is in the gravest danger of all, and God will single him out.

I shall be safe. Such a man is present. He hears the curses read out and takes the oath with everybody else, and privately reassures himself that none of it applies to him. This is the most dangerous condition in Deuteronomy precisely because it is comfortable. He is not troubled about his sin; he is settled, and nothing in the service touched him.

It will not stay hidden. His unbelief does not stay hidden from God. His jealousy “will smoke”, like the anger of a wronged husband; the LORD “will single him out from all the tribes of Israel” (v. 21); and the man who said “I shall be safe” finds that the curses he heard read out “settle upon him”.

Where Christians differ. Arminian Christians, many of them godly and earnest, read warnings like this as showing that true believers can fall away and be lost.

This commentary’s view. The man described here blesses himself while walking in stubbornness: a hypocrite who was never truly the LORD’s. The warning is real, aimed at everyone in the covenant community, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own (Hebrews 3:12–14).

Uncertain wording. “This will lead to the sweeping away of moist and dry alike” (v. 19) is a compressed Hebrew phrase whose exact sense is unclear. Most take it as a proverb for total ruin, the watered and the parched together: one man’s secret unbelief spreads, like the root of verse 18, and harms others. The King James Version renders it “to add drunkenness to thirst”, a picture of the sinner feeding his appetites.

verseByVerse.quote: And the next generation, your children who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will say, when they see the afflictions of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick— the whole land burned out with brimstone and salt, nothing sown and nothing growing, where no plant can sprout, an overthrow like that of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath— all the nations will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One person’s secret unbelief, spreading, can end in a land ruined like Sodom.

One person in a crowd. The consequences described are national and terrible: a land like Sodom, burned and salted, so that passing travellers ask, “Why has the LORD done thus to this land?” But the origin of it is one person, in a crowd, quietly deciding that the warnings are for other people.

Admah, and Zeboiim. These were cities of the plain destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 10:19; 14:2; 19:24–25). Hosea later heard God say of his people, “How can I make you like Admah? How can I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart recoils within me” (Hosea 11:8). The judgment threatened here is one God grieves to carry out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then people will say, 'It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt, and went and served other gods and worshiped them, gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against this land, bringing upon it all the curses written in this book, and the LORD uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath, and cast them into another land, as they are this day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruin will explain itself: Israel abandoned the covenant for gods that were never theirs.

Because they abandoned the covenant. The answer is given by the onlookers themselves: even foreigners will be able to read the meaning of the ruin. The charge is unfaithfulness, serving “gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them”, which recalls how the Most High divided the nations and kept Israel for himself (4:19–20; 32:8–9).

Uprooted. The people that let a poisonous root grow among them (v. 18) is at last “uprooted” from its land. “As they are this day” speaks as if the exile had already happened, so certain is it if the covenant is broken. Yet the chapter does not end there (see the note on v. 29), and chapter 30 promises a return.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has kept some things to himself and given us others, and what he has given is for doing. After the warnings of exile, Moses draws a boundary that steadies faith. The secret things, what God has not explained about his purposes and ways, belong to him. The revealed things belong to Israel and their children forever, and they are given for a purpose: “that we may do all the words of this law”. The verse frees us from demanding what God has withheld and calls us to act on what he has made plain.
verseByVerse.theology: There is a line, and God draws it. Some things he has kept; some he has given, and what is given is for obedience, not speculation.
verseByVerse.examples: Keeping to this line saves a great deal of anguish about why God allows what he allows, whom he has chosen, and what the future holds: the hidden part belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God has not told us belongs to him; what he has told us is ours forever, given so that we would do it.

The secret things. The verse draws a line that saves an enormous amount of grief. There are things God has not told us: why this and not that; why now and not then; how his sovereignty and our choices fit together; what he is doing in an event that has broken somebody’s life. Moses says plainly that they “belong to the LORD”. They are not information we are owed. They are his property.

The things that are revealed. There are things he has told us, and they are described in the warmest terms: they “belong to us and to our children forever”. Revelation is not a loan. What God has said is ours, permanently, and our children’s after us.

That we may do. The closing words, which give the purpose, are usually left off when this verse is quoted. The revealed things are not given for speculation but for obedience.

The mystery disclosed. The New Testament adds a glorious turn. It speaks of “the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed” (Romans 16:25–26), and the mystery is Christ, and Christ in his people (Colossians 1:26–27). The greatest of God’s secret things has been carried across the line and given to us.

In everyday life. The two halves are easily confused in the same person. It is remarkably easy to spend years worrying at the hidden things, the questions that have no answer this side of glory, while leaving the plain ones undone. A man can hold strong opinions about God’s eternal plan and not have forgiven his brother.

When you cannot understand. The comfort in it is real. When you cannot understand what God is doing, you are not failing. You are standing at a boundary he drew on purpose, and on this side of it there is quite enough to be getting on with.

keyVerse.quote: But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear.
keyVerse.note: After forty years of wonders, Moses says the real problem is not a lack of evidence but a heart that cannot see, and only God can give a new one. The verse sets up the promise of 30:6 that God will circumcise their hearts, and it explains why Israel’s story ends in exile and longs for the new covenant fulfilled in Christ.

29.reflection:
Israel had seen more miracles than any generation in history, yet Moses says they had not been given a heart to understand (v. 4). Why is evidence not enough, and how should that change the way we pray for people who do not believe?

The woodcutter, the water-carrier, the wives and the little ones stand in the same covenant as the tribal leaders (vv. 10–15). Who in your church is easily overlooked, and what would it mean to treat them as full members of God’s people?

The man in verse 19 hears the warnings and tells himself, “I shall be safe.” What are the signs that someone has grown comfortable in sin, and how can we help one another not to drift into that state?

“The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us” (v. 29). Which unanswered question about God’s ways troubles you most, and what plain thing has he told you to do that you could act on this week?

30.title: The Promise of Restoration: God Will Circumcise Your Heart
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"And when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before you, and you call them to mind among all the nations where the LORD your God has driven you,<sup>2</sup>and return to the LORD your God, you and your children, and obey his voice in all that I command you today, with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>3</sup>then the LORD your God will restore your fortunes and have mercy on you, and he will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God has scattered you.<sup>4</sup>If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you, and from there he will take you.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD your God will bring you into the land that your fathers possessed, that you may possess it. And he will make you more prosperous and numerous than your fathers.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD your God will put all these curses on your foes and enemies who persecuted you.<sup>8</sup>And you shall again obey the voice of the LORD and keep all his commandments that I command you today.<sup>9</sup>The LORD your God will make you abundantly prosperous in all the work of your hand, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your cattle and in the fruit of your ground. For the LORD will again take delight in prospering you, as he took delight in your fathers,<sup>10</sup>when you obey the voice of the LORD your God, to keep his commandments and his statutes that are written in this Book of the Law, when you turn to the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>11</sup>"For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off.<sup>12</sup>It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?'<sup>13</sup>Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, 'Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?'<sup>14</sup>But the word is very near you.
