It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.<sup>15</sup>"See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil.<sup>16</sup>If you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you today, by loving the LORD your God, by walking in his ways, and by keeping his commandments and his statutes and his rules, then you shall live and multiply, and the LORD your God will bless you in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>17</sup>But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them,<sup>18</sup>I declare to you today, that you shall surely perish. You shall not live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to enter and possess.<sup>19</sup>I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live,<sup>20</sup>loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days, that you may dwell in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them."
30.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 29 diagnosed Israel’s deepest problem: after forty years of wonders, the LORD had not yet given them a heart to understand (29:4). Chapter 30 completes Moses’ final address, and it is the turning point of the book: Moses looks past the curses and the coming exile to what God will do on the far side of them.

The message. Israel will fail and be scattered, but that is not the end of the story. When they turn back, God will gather them from the ends of the earth, and he will do for them what they could never do for themselves: he will circumcise their hearts so that they love him (v. 6). His word is not out of reach; it is near. So choose life, for the LORD himself is your life.

Why it was said. Moses has just foretold, in terrible detail, that this people would break the covenant and lose the land (chapters 28–29; see the introduction). A nation told that much about its failure needed to know whether there was any hope beyond it, and whether God’s demands were simply beyond them.

How the chapter makes its case. First the promise of return: when Israel, scattered among the nations, remembers and turns to the LORD, he will have mercy and gather them even from “the uttermost parts of heaven” (vv. 1–5). Then the heart of it: God will circumcise their hearts, turn the curses onto their enemies and delight in them again (vv. 6–10). The command is not too hard or far away, not in heaven or beyond the sea, but in their mouth and heart (vv. 11–14). Finally Moses sets life and death before them, calls heaven and earth to witness, and pleads, “choose life”, for the LORD “is your life and length of days” (vv. 15–20).

Where it leads. By promise. Verse 6 is the seed of the new covenant: what God commanded (10:16) he now promises to do himself, and the prophets take it up (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26). Jesus told Nicodemus he must be born again, and Paul reads verses 11–14 of Christ himself, who came down from heaven and rose from the dead, so that “the word is near you” in the gospel (Romans 10:6–9). Christ gathers the scattered children of God (John 11:52), and he is the life Moses urged Israel to choose (John 11:25).

For us. No one has wandered too far for God to fetch back. What he asks of us, a heart that loves him, he gives in Christ by his Spirit. You do not have to climb to heaven or search the world to find him: believe the word that has been brought near, and hold fast to the one who is your life.
30.theology:
The new covenant: God circumcises the heart. God promises to do what the law commanded but could not produce (30:6), working in us by his Spirit what we could never do (Ezek. 36:26; Rom. 2:29). Salvation is God's sovereign work from first to last.

The word is very near. Paul applies 30:14 to the gospel of faith (Rom. 10:6–8): we need not ascend to heaven or descend to the depths, for Christ has done it all, and in him God has come near to us.

Choose life. God's work in the heart does not cancel human responsibility but enables it; the God who commands the choice gives the new heart that makes it possible (30:19–20). The call still sounds to all: hold fast to the Lord, who is himself our life.
30.examples: The promise is fulfilled in the new covenant: God has given us by his Spirit a new heart that loves him, and where our love still falls short, Christ, who loved the Father with all his heart in our place, is our righteousness. The word of faith is as near as our mouths and hearts, and the call still sounds: choose life; hold fast to him, for he is your life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — From the Uttermost Parts of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: However far God’s people are scattered, he will gather them when they turn back to him. Moses speaks of the curses of chapter 28 not as a possibility but as a certainty: “when all these things come upon you” (v. 1). Then he looks to the far side of them. Israel, driven among the nations, will remember, return to the LORD with all their heart, and obey (vv. 1–2). God will restore their fortunes, have mercy, and gather them, even from “the uttermost parts of heaven” (vv. 3–4), bringing them into the land and making them more numerous than their fathers (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is made before the failure has happened, and its reach is unlimited (v. 4): God undertakes to cross any distance to gather his people.
verseByVerse.examples: No one reading this has wandered beyond God’s reach: there is no far country in Scripture that has ever been out of range.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before you, and you call them to mind among all the nations where the LORD your God has driven you, and return to the LORD your God, you and your children, and obey his voice in all that I command you today, with all your heart and with all your soul, then the LORD your God will restore your fortunes and have mercy on you, and he will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you, and from there he will take you. And the LORD your God will bring you into the land that your fathers possessed, that you may possess it. And he will make you more prosperous and numerous than your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel will be scattered under the curse, but when they turn back, God will have mercy and gather them home from however far they have gone.

When all these things come upon you. Chapter 28 ended with a nation scattered to the ends of the earth, offering itself for sale with no buyer. Chapter 30 begins on the far side of that. Moses is not describing a possibility. He is telling a people on the border of the promised land what will happen after they have lost it, and what God will do next.

The uttermost parts of heaven. Verse 4 sets the reach of it: as far as anything can be. It is put in deliberately as the extreme case. Imagine an Israelite in Babylon reading it and thinking of the ones taken further, the ones nobody has heard of, the ones lost track of. The verse is written for exactly that worry, and it answers it. There is no distance in this sentence that God does not undertake to cross.

No distance too far. The same reach appears in the Lord Jesus’ shepherd going after one sheep out of a hundred, and in the running father of Luke 15 who sees his son “while he was still a long way off”. Nobody in Scripture has ever gone too far to be fetched back.

Where Christians differ. Is this regathering fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists see a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel.

This commentary’s view. The circumcised heart of verse 6 is the work of the new covenant, and Christ died “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52). The fullest fulfilment is Christ gathering his people from every nation, including, as many believe, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26). Faithful Christians differ on these details, and charity becomes them; all agree that no one is gathered home except through Christ.

Uncertain wording. “Restore your fortunes” (v. 3) translates a Hebrew idiom whose exact sense is debated. Older translations render it “turn thy captivity” (King James Version), linking it with the return from exile; many scholars now take it more broadly as “restore your fortunes”, a reversal of everything lost. In this context both meanings are in view, since the restoration described is a return from being scattered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to do himself the very thing he commanded: to change his people’s hearts so that they love him. He wished for such a heart (5:29) and commanded it (10:16); now he promises to circumcise the heart of his people and their offspring, so that they love him with all their heart and live (v. 6). The curses will fall on their enemies instead (v. 7). Israel will obey again (v. 8), and the LORD will delight to prosper them as he delighted in their fathers (vv. 9–10). Obedience is the fruit of the new heart, not the price of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The law commands a love nobody can produce; the covenant exposes the failure; and here God undertakes to work in his people what he demands from them.
verseByVerse.examples: A people who could not change their own hearts were told God would change them, and that same promise is what makes anyone a Christian: born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. And the LORD your God will put all these curses on your foes and enemies who persecuted you. And you shall again obey the voice of the LORD and keep all his commandments that I command you today. The LORD your God will make you abundantly prosperous in all the work of your hand, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your cattle and in the fruit of your ground. For the LORD will again take delight in prospering you, as he took delight in your fathers, when you obey the voice of the LORD your God, to keep his commandments and his statutes that are written in this Book of the Law, when you turn to the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to do for his people what they could never do for themselves: to cut away the stubbornness of their hearts so that they love him and live.

Circumcise your heart. This is the sentence the whole book has been building toward. Three verses side by side give the argument of Deuteronomy in miniature. First, a wish: “Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments” (5:29). Then a command: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn” (10:16), which asks of a man the one operation he cannot perform on himself. Now, at 30:6, a promise: what God wished for, and then commanded, he now undertakes to do himself.

The gospel in Deuteronomy. That is the gospel, in the fifth book of Moses, centuries before Jeremiah and long before Christ. God requires of us what we cannot produce, and then undertakes to produce it in us. The law was never a ladder to climb up to God; it was a mirror that shows us our sin, and this verse is what God does about what the mirror shows.

So that you will love. The command of 6:5, the greatest commandment, which no sinner has ever kept for an hour and only one Man ever kept at all, is here promised as the result of God’s work rather than the condition of it. Then obedience follows (v. 8), and God delights in his people again (v. 9).

The new covenant. The prophets take this verse and make it the definition of the new covenant: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33); “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). And the Lord Jesus told a religious teacher who knew all of this that he must be born again, and was astonished he did not recognise it: “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?” (John 3:10). It was in his Bible. It is here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — The Word Is Very Near You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word is not out of reach; he has brought it near. Moses shuts off an excuse before it is made: the commandment is not too hard or far away (v. 11). No one needs to climb into heaven or cross the sea to fetch it (vv. 12–13). It is already in their mouth and in their heart, so that they can do it (v. 14). Paul reads these verses of Christ, who has come down from heaven and risen from the dead, so that the word of faith is near everyone who hears the gospel (Romans 10:6–9).
verseByVerse.theology: God has already brought his word down and put it within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: The excuse that God’s will is out of reach is closed off for us too, and more firmly: the Word himself came down.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, 'Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has brought his word near, plain and spoken, so no one can say it was out of reach; and Paul hears in these verses the nearness of Christ in the gospel.

Not far off. Moses is closing off an excuse before it is made. Nobody in Israel will be able to say that God’s will was inaccessible, that someone would have had to climb into heaven or cross an ocean to find out what he wanted. God has brought it down and said it out loud. The word is already in their mouths, because they have just heard it and can repeat it.

The word is near you. Paul does something extraordinary with this passage. Writing about the righteousness that comes by faith, he reads these verses of Christ: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down) or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart’ (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim)” (Romans 10:6–8).

Paul’s logic. His logic is exact. Deuteronomy’s point is that nobody has to fetch God’s word from an inaccessible place because God has already delivered it. Paul’s point is that nobody has to fetch Christ from heaven or from the grave, because God has done both: Christ came down from heaven and up from the grave, the work is finished, and the news has been brought to you.

Only receive. So the gospel asks nothing of a man except that he receive what has been brought. Not an ascent, not a voyage, not a search. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9): mouth and heart, the two words Moses used, and nothing else required.

Can anyone keep the law, if it is “not too hard”? The command was near and plain, not hidden in heaven; and God promised the heart to obey it (v. 6). But the law as a way to earn life is beyond sinners (Romans 8:3). Christ has come near, and believing in him is not beyond anyone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets two ways before Israel and pleads with them to choose life, because the LORD himself is their life. Life and good stand on one side, death and evil on the other (v. 15). Loving the LORD, walking in his ways and keeping his commands lead to life and blessing in the land (v. 16); a heart that turns away to other gods leads to certain ruin (vv. 17–18). Heaven and earth are called as witnesses (v. 19). The life to be chosen is defined at the end: loving the LORD, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, “for he is your life and length of days” (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The book’s great either-or reaches its climax, and there is no third option. To choose life is to choose a Person.
verseByVerse.examples: A nation stood on the plain and was told to choose. Anyone still undecided about Christ is being asked the same question, and it is asked in love.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil. If you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you today, by loving the LORD your God, by walking in his ways, and by keeping his commandments and his statutes and his rules, then you shall live and multiply, and the LORD your God will bless you in the land that you are entering to take possession of it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them, I declare to you today, that you shall surely perish. You shall not live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to enter and possess. I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live, loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days, that you may dwell in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are only two ways, life and death, and Moses pleads with Israel to choose life, which is not a set of blessings but the LORD himself.

Choose life. Everything since chapter 11 has been coming to this. Two ways, two outcomes, and no third option, no comfortable middle where a person can live without deciding. Moses summons the sky and the ground as legal witnesses, and puts it to them.

He is your life. Then the definition, the most important thing in the paragraph: the life to be chosen is loving the LORD, obeying his voice and holding fast to him (v. 20). It is not a lifestyle, nor even a set of blessings. The thing being chosen is a Person, and the three verbs are the ones this book has used from the beginning: love, obey, cling.

How completely he was right. The same call is still being made in the same terms. “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). And the one who says it is not offering a way to life; he told Martha, on the way to her brother’s grave, what he actually is: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). Moses said “he is your life” to a crowd on a plain in Moab, and did not know how completely he was right.

After the promise. Two things guard this from misuse. First, the command to choose comes after the promise of verse 6. God does not tell Israel to produce a new heart and then choose. He promises to circumcise their hearts, and then calls them to choose, and the calling is the very means by which he does it. Nobody has ever had to work out how divine sovereignty and human choosing fit together in order to obey a verse like this. Moses did not explain it; he simply said “choose”.

A call to the failing. Second, it is addressed to people who have been hearing for thirty chapters how badly they will fail. This is not a call to the confident. It is made to a nation whose exile has just been predicted in detail, and it is made anyway, and it is meant.

Why does endless choice feel like a trap? Our culture has made choosing itself sacred. We choose careers, cities, beliefs, even identities, and the right to choose feels like the essence of freedom. Yet the psychologist Barry Schwartz, in The Paradox of Choice (2004), argued that beyond a certain point more options leave people less satisfied and more anxious, because every choice made means many others lost, and nothing chosen ever feels quite enough. Moses sets before Israel something very different from a menu: two ways, and a life that is a Person. That sounds narrowing until you notice that the freedom we really want is not the freedom to keep choosing for ever, but the freedom to rest in something worth choosing. A man who never closes a door never comes home. The gospel does not abolish choice; it gives choice a home. And before Israel chose, God had already chosen her, and promised the heart that would choose him back (v. 6). We choose life because Life first chose us.

What it does not mean. The verse is about life with God in the covenant; the sanctity of unborn life, though real, rests on other texts (Psalm 139:13–16).

Where Christians differ. Does “choose life” teach that fallen people can choose God by their own power? Arminian readers, many of them earnest Christians, say the command implies the ability.

This commentary’s view. A command shows what is right, not what we are able to do (Romans 8:7–8). The choice is real and must be made; and God gives the heart that chooses (v. 6; Philippians 2:12–13).

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live.
keyVerse.note: What God wished for (5:29) and commanded (10:16), he here promises to do himself. The greatest commandment becomes the fruit of God’s work rather than the condition of it, and the prophets build the new covenant on this promise, fulfilled when Christ gives his people new hearts by his Spirit.

30.reflection:
Moses speaks of exile with “when”, not “if” (vv. 1–5), yet promises that God will gather his people from the farthest places. Is there anyone you have begun to think has gone too far to be brought back? How does this passage speak to that?

God wished for a new heart (5:29), commanded it (10:16), and here promises to give it (30:6). Why does it matter that the promise comes after the command, and how does this help us understand the gospel?

Paul reads verses 11–14 of Christ, who has come down from heaven and risen from the dead (Romans 10:6–9). What “ascents” or “voyages” do people attempt in order to find God or make themselves acceptable, and what does it mean that the word is near?

Moses says that the life to be chosen is the LORD himself (v. 20). How is choosing a Person different from choosing a lifestyle, and what would “holding fast to him” look like in your week?

31.title: Moses' Farewell and the Law Deposited
31.text: <sup>1</sup>So Moses continued to speak these words to all Israel.<sup>2</sup>And he said to them, "I am 120 years old today. I am no longer able to go out and come in. The LORD has said to me, 'You shall not go over this Jordan.'<sup>3</sup>The LORD your God himself will go over before you. He will destroy these nations before you, so that you shall dispossess them, and Joshua will go over at your head, as the LORD has spoken.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD will do to them as he did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, and to their land, when he destroyed them.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD will give them over to you, and you shall do to them according to the whole commandment that I have commanded you.<sup>6</sup>Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you."<sup>7</sup>Then Moses summoned Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land that the LORD has sworn to their fathers to give them, and you shall put them in possession of it.<sup>8</sup>It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses wrote this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel.<sup>10</sup>And Moses commanded them, "At the end of every seven years, at the set time in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths,<sup>11</sup>when all Israel comes to appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing.<sup>12</sup>Assemble the people, men, women, and little ones, and the sojourner within your towns, that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, and be careful to do all the words of this law,<sup>13</sup>and that their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, as long as you live in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, the days approach when you must die. Call Joshua and present yourselves in the tent of meeting, that I may commission him." And Moses and Joshua went and presented themselves in the tent of meeting.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD appeared in the tent in a pillar of cloud. And the pillar of cloud stood over the entrance of the tent.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, you are about to lie down with your fathers. Then this people will rise and whore after the foreign gods among them in the land that they are entering, and they will forsake me and break my covenant that I have made with them.<sup>17</sup>Then my anger will be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them and hide my face from them, and they will be devoured. And many evils and troubles will come upon them, so that they will say in that day, 'Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?'<sup>18</sup>And I will surely hide my face in that day because of all the evil that they have done, because they have turned to other gods.<sup>19</sup>"Now therefore write this song and teach it to the people of Israel. Put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel.<sup>20</sup>For when I have brought them into the land flowing with milk and honey, which I swore to give to their fathers, and they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods and serve them, and despise me and break my covenant.<sup>21</sup>And when many evils and troubles have come upon them, this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring). For I know what they are inclined to do even today, before I have brought them into the land that I swore to give."<sup>22</sup>So Moses wrote this song the same day and taught it to the people of Israel.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD commissioned Joshua the son of Nun and said, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the people of Israel into the land that I swore to give them. I will be with you."<sup>24</sup>When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book to the very end,<sup>25</sup>Moses commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD,<sup>26</sup>"Take this Book of the Law and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.<sup>27</sup>For I know how rebellious and stubborn you are. Behold, even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious against the LORD. How much more after my death!<sup>28</sup>Assemble to me all the elders of your tribes and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears and call heaven and earth to witness against them.<sup>29</sup>For I know that after my death you will surely act corruptly and turn aside from the way that I have commanded you. And in the days to come evil will befall you, because you will do what is evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger through the work of your hands."<sup>30</sup>Then Moses spoke the words of this song until they were finished, in the ears of all the assembly of Israel:
31.overview:
Where we are. Moses’ great addresses are finished, and the covenant has been renewed on the plains of Moab (chapters 29–30). Chapter 31 begins the closing scenes of his life: at a hundred and twenty he hands over the leadership to Joshua, entrusts the written law to the priests, and receives from God a song for Israel to learn.

The message. Leaders die, and God’s people will prove unfaithful, but God does not leave or forsake them. He goes before them himself, he gives them his written word to keep them, and he provides a witness that will speak for him when they fail. The future of God’s people never rested on Moses, nor on their own steadiness, but on the LORD who goes with them.

Why it was said. Israel was about to lose the only leader most of them had ever known, and to face fortified cities without him (see the introduction). They needed to know who would lead them, how God’s word would be kept among them, and what to make of the troubles God foresaw.

How the chapter makes its case. Moses announces that he will not cross the Jordan; the LORD himself will go before them, and Joshua will lead, and he charges both people and Joshua to be strong and courageous (vv. 1–8). He writes the law and commands that it be read to the whole people every seventh year at the Feast of Booths (vv. 9–13). At the tent of meeting God commissions Joshua, tells Moses plainly that Israel will forsake him after his death, and gives a song to be taught as a witness (vv. 14–23). The finished book is placed beside the ark as a witness, and Moses gathers the elders to hear the song (vv. 24–30).

Where it leads. By pattern and promise. Moses brings the people to the border but cannot take them in; another must do it, and his name, Joshua, is the Hebrew form of “Jesus”. Hebrews notes that even Joshua did not give the final rest (Hebrews 4:8), and points to the greater Joshua who leads his people home. The promise “he will not leave you or forsake you” is handed to Christians in Hebrews 13:5, and the foreseen unfaithfulness of the people points to the need for a new heart that only Christ’s Spirit gives.

For us. Our courage rests not on our strength or on our leaders, but on the one who goes before us and will never leave us. Read and hear God’s word together, children included. Sing what is true, because what we sing in health is what we will have in the dark. And when the word exposes our failure, let it send us to the mercy it promises.
31.theology:
God's faithful presence is the ground of courage. “Be strong and courageous… for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you” (31:6, 8). Biblical courage is God-confidence, not self-confidence. The promise is passed on to every believer (Heb 13:5–6) and is fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel, who pledged, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

The written, preserved, proclaimed Word. Moses writes the law down and has it read to every generation, children and sojourners included (31:11–13). Scripture is God's enduring, authoritative witness, the means by which faith is passed from generation to generation (Rom 10:17; 1 Tim 4:13).

God's foreknowledge and grace. God foretells Israel's apostasy before they enter the land (31:16), yet covenants with them still and provides, in advance, the Song as a witness to call them back. The God who foreknew the full depth of our sin set his love on us anyway and provided in Christ the remedy for the very unfaithfulness he foresaw.
31.examples: Moses faced his own death and Israel's coming failure with the same confidence he gave Joshua. We face every uncertain future on the same ground: Christ is Immanuel, with us always, and his Spirit in us is the strength the command calls for. We treasure the Word read aloud as the means by which faith passes to our children.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people can be strong and courageous because the LORD himself goes before them, whoever their leader. Moses announces that at a hundred and twenty he will not cross the Jordan (vv. 1–2). The LORD will go over ahead of them and give them the land as he gave them Sihon and Og, and Joshua will lead them (vv. 3–5). So Moses tells the nation, “Be strong and courageous”, for the LORD will not leave or forsake them (v. 6). Then, in front of everyone, he gives Joshua the same charge and the same promise (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The command is given twice in eight verses, and its ground is never Israel’s strength: it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you. God repeats the whole charge to Joshua himself after Moses dies (Josh. 1:5-9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dying man told his successor to be brave, in public, and gave him the reason. Now: the same promise is the ground of every Christian’s courage, and we hold it with more light than Joshua had.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses continued to speak these words to all Israel. And he said to them, "I am 120 years old today. I am no longer able to go out and come in. The LORD has said to me, 'You shall not go over this Jordan.' The LORD your God himself will go over before you. He will destroy these nations before you, so that you shall dispossess them, and Joshua will go over at your head, as the LORD has spoken. And the LORD will do to them as he did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, and to their land, when he destroyed them. And the LORD will give them over to you, and you shall do to them according to the whole commandment that I have commanded you. Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you." Then Moses summoned Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land that the LORD has sworn to their fathers to give them, and you shall put them in possession of it. It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses will not cross, but the LORD himself will go before Israel, with Joshua at their head, so they can be strong and unafraid.

I am no longer able to go out and come in. This is the language of leading in war and public life. Moses says he can no longer do it, though at his death his eye was still undimmed (34:7); the real reason is that the LORD has said he will not cross. What follows is the measure of him: no complaint, no going back over the sentence passed at Meribah, straight into encouragement.

Be strong and courageous. The command is to be brave; the reason is that the LORD himself is going with them. Moses then charges Joshua “in the sight of all Israel”, so the whole nation hears what its new leader has been promised. It is the last kindness of a leader who will not see the outcome.

A greater Joshua. Moses, the giver of the law, can bring the people to the border but not across it; another must lead them in. Hebrews observes that even Joshua did not give them the final rest (Hebrews 4:8), and points to the One who does. In Greek the two names are the same: Jesus is the greater Joshua, who brings his people into a rest no river or grave can keep them from.

He will not leave you or forsake you. When Hebrews quotes the promise, it applies it, unexpectedly, to money: “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). The word given to a man about to invade a country is handed to Christians worrying about the bills, because it is the same promise and the same God.

What it does not mean. The conquest was God’s unique judgment through Israel at one moment in history. It gives no warrant for violence in God’s name today (John 18:36).
verseByVerse.note: Moses' 120 years fall into three forties: in Egypt, in Midian, and in the wilderness (Acts 7:23, 30, 36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Read This Law Every Seven Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s written word is to be read aloud to all his people, so that each generation learns to fear him. Moses writes the law and entrusts it to the priests who carry the ark and to the elders (v. 9). Every seventh year, in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths, it must be read to the whole assembly: men, women, little ones, and the sojourner in their towns (vv. 10–12). The purpose is that they may hear, learn to fear the LORD and do his words, and that children who have not yet known it may learn too (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason for gathering everybody is stated twice: that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD, and that their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn. Faith is passed on by hearing long before it is grasped.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation gathered every seven years and simply listened to Scripture read from beginning to end. Now: the public reading of the Word is still commanded (1 Tim. 4:13) and is still the thing most easily crowded out of a service.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses wrote this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel. And Moses commanded them, "At the end of every seven years, at the set time in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths, when all Israel comes to appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing. Assemble the people, men, women, and little ones, and the sojourner within your towns, that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, and be careful to do all the words of this law, and that their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, as long as you live in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every seventh year the law was to be read aloud to everyone, children and foreigners included, so that each generation would learn to fear the LORD.

Men, women, and little ones. The Feast of Booths, when the nation is gathered anyway, becomes a long reading in the open to an enormous crowd. The striking part is who must be there: the little ones, who will fidget and understand almost nothing, are required to come. A child who has sat under Scripture from before he could follow it has something in him that a child who arrived at fifteen does not, and God builds that into the national calendar.

The year of release. The timing is chosen too: “at the set time in the year of release” (v. 10), the year debts were cancelled (15:1–2), so that the law was heard again in the year that showed most plainly what kind of God had given it.

The sojourner within your towns. The foreigner living among them is there too, hearing the law of a God who was not his by birth.

The command kept. Nehemiah 8 is this command being kept, centuries later, after the exile: Ezra standing on a wooden platform from early morning until midday, reading the Book of the Law to “the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard”, and the people weeping as they listened. They simply read the Bible aloud, and it moved them to tears.

Where Christians differ. Did Moses write Deuteronomy? Many scholars hold that it was written in the seventh century BC and “found” in the temple under Josiah (2 Kings 22) to support his reforms. The book itself says “Moses wrote this law” (31:9, 24), and Jesus speaks of it as Moses’ (Mark 10:3–5). Its covenant shape resembles treaties of the second millennium BC, though scholars also point to likenesses with seventh-century Assyrian treaties, so that argument is not decisive either way. The book also has a narrator who speaks of Moses in the third person (1:1–5), and the account of Moses’ death (chapter 34) was added by a later inspired hand, perhaps Joshua; how much editing there was, and when, is still debated among faithful scholars.

This commentary’s view. The substance is Moses’, as the book and our Lord say, and what Josiah found was a neglected copy of an old book, which is why its words terrified him (2 Kings 22:11–13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — A Song for a Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God foresees Israel’s unfaithfulness and provides for it, not by withdrawing his covenant, but by a new leader and a song that will witness for him. At the tent of meeting, in the pillar of cloud, God summons Moses and Joshua (vv. 14–15). He tells Moses that after his death the people will chase other gods and break the covenant, and that he will hide his face (vv. 16–18). So he commands a song to be written and taught, to stand as a witness when the troubles come (vv. 19–22). Then he commissions Joshua himself: “I will be with you” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God plants the testimony before the sin: it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring, so that when they need it they will find they already know it by heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God buried the truth in a tune because he knew where they were going. Now: he still gives his people songs to carry them where sermons cannot reach.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, the days approach when you must die. Call Joshua and present yourselves in the tent of meeting, that I may commission him." And Moses and Joshua went and presented themselves in the tent of meeting. And the LORD appeared in the tent in a pillar of cloud. And the pillar of cloud stood over the entrance of the tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself commissions Joshua at the tent: the change of leader is his doing.

Present yourselves in the tent of meeting. Joshua has already been named before the people (vv. 7–8); now God himself commissions him, at the tent and in the pillar of cloud that had led Israel since the Exodus. The presence that met Moses at the tent, where the young Joshua used to stay (Exodus 33:9–11), now stands at its entrance for Joshua.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, you are about to lie down with your fathers. Then this people will rise and whore after the foreign gods among them in the land that they are entering, and they will forsake me and break my covenant that I have made with them. Then my anger will be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them and hide my face from them, and they will be devoured. And many evils and troubles will come upon them, so that they will say in that day, 'Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?' And I will surely hide my face in that day because of all the evil that they have done, because they have turned to other gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Moses plainly that Israel will forsake him for other gods, and that he will then hide his face from them.

They will forsake me. Not “may” but “will”: on the day he commissions Joshua, God states that this nation will abandon him, and when. The cause is the one diagnosed in chapter 8: not persecution but prosperity, when they “are full and grown fat” (v. 20).

Whore after the foreign gods. The covenant is a marriage, and idolatry is unfaithfulness to a husband (Jeremiah 3:1; Hosea 2:2–13). Notice the echo: they “will forsake me”, and so “I will forsake them” (vv. 16–17).

I will hide my face. This is the reverse of the priestly blessing, “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25). When the troubles come the people will say, “our God is not among us”: true, but only half the truth, for they see the loss without yet confessing the sin. God answers that his face is hidden “because of all the evil that they have done” (v. 18).

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore write this song and teach it to the people of Israel. Put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel. For when I have brought them into the land flowing with milk and honey, which I swore to give to their fathers, and they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods and serve them, and despise me and break my covenant. And when many evils and troubles have come upon them, this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring). For I know what they are inclined to do even today, before I have brought them into the land that I swore to give." So Moses wrote this song the same day and taught it to the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing Israel will turn away, God gives them a song to memorise, so that when disaster comes it will testify that he warned them.

Why a song. Facing certain betrayal, God does not withdraw the covenant or reduce the promises. He commissions a song and has it memorised, because songs last: sermons are forgotten and laws shelved, but a tune learned in childhood comes back by itself.

A witness for me. In a court a witness speaks when the facts are disputed. When disaster comes and Israel asks why, the song still in their mouths will testify that God warned them and was faithful (32:4–6), and that the fault was theirs. “I know what they are inclined to do even today” (v. 21): God makes this covenant with no illusions about his people, and still makes it. Moses obeyed at once, writing the song “the same day” (v. 22).

What we sing in health. Anyone who has sat with a dying believer whose memory has largely gone, and heard them join in a hymn learned as a child, knows that God was right about this. What we sing in health is what we will have in the dark, which is a serious argument for being careful about what the church sings.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD commissioned Joshua the son of Nun and said, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the people of Israel into the land that I swore to give them. I will be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD himself now gives Joshua the charge, grounded in his presence.

I will be with you. Moses had spoken this charge to Joshua before the people (vv. 7–8); now the LORD speaks it himself. The ground of courage is the last clause. Joshua is not told that he is strong enough; he is told who goes with him (see the note on vv. 1–8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Book Beside the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The written law is placed beside the ark as a permanent witness, because Moses knows Israel will turn aside after his death. When the book is finished to the very end, Moses commands the Levites to place it by the ark of the covenant (vv. 24–26). He tells them bluntly that they have been rebellious while he lived and will be worse after he dies (v. 27). He gathers the elders and officers to hear the words, calling heaven and earth to witness (vv. 28–29), and then speaks the whole song in the ears of the assembly (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ farewell assessment is unsparing: even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious… How much more after my death!
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the last act of Israel’s greatest leader was to leave a written record that would outlive and outrank him. Now: the same book is still beside us, and still says what it said whether we like it or not.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book to the very end, Moses commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, "Take this Book of the Law and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against you. For I know how rebellious and stubborn you are. Behold, even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious against the LORD. How much more after my death! Assemble to me all the elders of your tribes and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears and call heaven and earth to witness against them. For I know that after my death you will surely act corruptly and turn aside from the way that I have commanded you. And in the days to come evil will befall you, because you will do what is evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger through the work of your hands." Then Moses spoke the words of this song until they were finished, in the ears of all the assembly of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The finished book is set beside the ark as a lasting witness, because Israel will grow worse after Moses dies.

By the side of the ark. The tablets went inside the ark; the book goes alongside, where it can be taken out, read, and produced in evidence. Israel now has a written record of the terms, kept at the holiest place in the nation, that will outlive every person present. It still does: it has outlived Moses, and Joshua, and the monarchy, and the exile, and every empire that has handled it since.

I know how rebellious and stubborn you are. There is no flattery in his farewell. He tells them it will be worse when he is gone, and he leaves a book so that nobody can say they were not told. There is a hard love in that: what they need is not his good opinion but the truth in writing.

A witness that sends us to mercy. The same verdict stands over us: none of us keeps this book as it deserves (Ecclesiastes 7:20). But the God who foresaw Israel’s rebellion and kept his covenant anyway has given his Son, who kept the law perfectly in our place and whose obedience is counted ours (Romans 5:19). So the witness that accuses us also sends us back by confession to the mercy it promised (30:1–3; 1 John 1:9).

keyVerse.quote: It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed.
keyVerse.note: Moses is about to die and Israel is about to face the nations without him, yet the courage he commands rests on God, not on any leader. Hebrews hands this same promise to Christians (Hebrews 13:5), because it is the same God who goes before his people in Christ.

31.reflection:
Moses accepted without complaint that he would not cross the Jordan, and spent his last days strengthening the man who would (vv. 1–8). What does his example teach about handing on responsibility and about finishing well?

God required that the little ones be present when the law was read (vv. 12–13). What does that say about children in church, and how can we help them sit under God’s word from their earliest years?

God knew Israel would forsake him, yet gave them a song so that the truth would stay in their mouths (vv. 19–22). What songs or hymns have carried you through hard times, and how should that shape what we sing together?

The book beside the ark was a witness against Israel (v. 26). How can the same Scriptures that expose our sin also lead us to God’s mercy in Christ?

32.title: The Song of Moses: The Rock, His Work Is Perfect
32.text: <sup>1</sup>"Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.<sup>2</sup>May my teaching drop as the rain, my speech distill as the dew, like gentle rain upon the tender grass, and like showers upon the herb.<sup>3</sup>For I will proclaim the name of the LORD; ascribe greatness to our God!<sup>4</sup>"The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he.<sup>5</sup>They have dealt corruptly with him; they are no longer his children because they are blemished; they are a crooked and twisted generation.<sup>6</sup>Do you thus repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people? Is not he your father, who created you, who made you and established you?<sup>7</sup>Remember the days of old; consider the years of many generations; ask your father, and he will show you, your elders, and they will tell you.<sup>8</sup>When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he divided mankind, he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God.<sup>9</sup>But the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob his allotted heritage.<sup>10</sup>"He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.<sup>11</sup>Like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings, catching them, bearing them on its pinions,<sup>12</sup>the LORD alone guided him, no foreign god was with him.<sup>13</sup>He made him ride on the high places of the land, and he ate the produce of the field, and he suckled him with honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock.<sup>14</sup>Curds from the herd, and milk from the flock, with fat of lambs, rams of Bashan and goats, with the very finest of the wheat— and you drank foaming wine made from the blood of the grape.<sup>15</sup>"But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him and scoffed at the Rock of his salvation.<sup>16</sup>They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger.<sup>17</sup>They sacrificed to demons that were not God, to gods they had never known, to new gods that had come recently, whom your fathers had never dreaded.<sup>18</sup>You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth.<sup>19</sup>"The LORD saw it and spurned them, because of the provocation of his sons and his daughters.<sup>20</sup>And he said, 'I will hide my face from them; I will see what their end will be, for they are a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.<sup>21</sup>They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.<sup>22</sup>For a fire is kindled by my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol, devours the earth and its increase, and sets on fire the foundations of the mountains.<sup>23</sup>"'And I will heap disasters upon them; I will spend my arrows on them;<sup>24</sup>they shall be wasted with hunger, and devoured by plague and poisonous pestilence; I will send the teeth of beasts against them, with the venom of things that crawl in the dust.<sup>25</sup>Outdoors the sword shall bereave, and indoors terror, for young man and woman alike, the nursing child with the man of gray hairs.<sup>26</sup>I would have said, "I will cut them to pieces; I will wipe them from human memory,"<sup>27</sup>had I not feared provocation by the enemy, lest their adversaries should misunderstand, lest they should say, "Our hand is triumphant, it was not the LORD who did all this."'<sup>28</sup>"For they are a nation void of counsel, and there is no understanding in them.<sup>29</sup>If they were wise, they would understand this; they would discern their latter end!<sup>30</sup>How could one have chased a thousand, and two have put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had given them up?<sup>31</sup>For their rock is not as our Rock; our enemies are by themselves.<sup>32</sup>For their vine comes from the vine of Sodom and from the fields of Gomorrah; their grapes are grapes of poison; their clusters are bitter;<sup>33</sup>their wine is the poison of serpents and the cruel venom of asps.<sup>34</sup>"'Is not this laid up in store with me, sealed up in my treasuries?<sup>35</sup>Vengeance is mine, and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip; for the day of their calamity is at hand, and their doom comes swiftly.'<sup>36</sup>For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their power is gone and there is none remaining, bond or free.<sup>37</sup>Then he will say, 'Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge,<sup>38</sup>who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offering? Let them rise up and help you; let them be your protection!<sup>39</sup>"'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand.<sup>40</sup>For I lift up my hand to heaven and swear, As I live forever,<sup>41</sup>if I sharpen my flashing sword and my hand takes hold on judgment, I will take vengeance on my adversaries and will repay those who hate me.<sup>42</sup>I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh— with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the long-haired heads of the enemy.'<sup>43</sup>"Rejoice with him, O heavens; bow down to him, all gods, for he avenges the blood of his children and takes vengeance on his adversaries. He repays those who hate him and cleanses his people's land."<sup>44</sup>Moses came and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>45</sup>And when Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel,<sup>46</sup>he said to them, "Take to heart all the words by which I am warning you today, that you may command them to your children, that they may be careful to do all the words of this law.<sup>47</sup>For it is no empty word for you, but your very life, and by this word you shall live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."<sup>48</sup>That very day the LORD spoke to Moses,<sup>49</sup>"Go up this mountain of the Abarim, Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel for a possession.<sup>50</sup>And die on the mountain which you go up, and be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother died in Mount Hor and was gathered to his people,<sup>51</sup>because you broke faith with me in the midst of the people of Israel at the waters of Meribah-kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, and because you did not treat me as holy in the midst of the people of Israel.<sup>52</sup>For you shall see the land before you, but you shall not go there, into the land that I am giving to the people of Israel."
32.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 31 God told Moses that Israel would forsake him after his death, and commanded a song to be taught as a witness. Chapter 32 is that song, the Song of Moses, followed by Moses’ last charge to the people and God’s command that he climb Mount Nebo to die.

The message. God is the Rock: faithful, just and unchanging, the Father who found his people in the wilderness and carried them like an eagle. His people repaid him by growing fat and forgetting him, and he will judge them. But he will not destroy them, for his own name’s sake; when their strength is gone he will have compassion, and he alone kills and makes alive. Israel must learn the song by heart, because this word is their very life.

Why it was said. God knew that Israel would turn away in the land (31:16–21; see the introduction). The song was put in their mouths in advance, so that when disaster came they would already know why: not because God had failed, but because they had.

How the chapter makes its case. God is named the Rock whose work is perfect, set against a crooked generation (vv. 1–6). The song remembers how he chose Israel, found him in a howling waste, carried him like an eagle and fed him (vv. 7–14). Then Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, turning to demons and new gods, and God answers with jealousy and judgment (vv. 15–25). He stops short of wiping them out, lest their enemies boast (vv. 26–33), and declares that vengeance is his and that he will vindicate his people when their power is gone (vv. 34–38), ending in the great claim, “I kill and I make alive”, and a call to the heavens to rejoice (vv. 39–43). Moses teaches the song, calls it “your very life”, and is sent up the mountain to die (vv. 44–52).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by promise. Paul says “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). He reads verse 21 as the Old Testament’s prediction that the gospel would go to the nations (Romans 10:19), and verse 43 as proof that the Gentiles would rejoice with God’s people (Romans 15:10), while Hebrews applies verse 43 to the worship of the Son (Hebrews 1:6). The God who kills and makes alive raised Jesus from the dead, and holds his people in a hand from which no one can snatch them (John 10:28–29). In Revelation the redeemed sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).

For us. Beware of prosperity that makes you forget the God who gave it. Leave vengeance to him. When your strength is gone, that is often when he shows his compassion. And treat his word not as a resource but as your very life.
32.theology:
The Rock whose work is perfect. “The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice” (32:4). When we cannot trace his hand in trial or judgment, we trust his character: the Rock does not move (32:39).

The tender love of God and the tragedy of ingratitude. God kept Israel as the apple of his eye (32:10–11), yet Jeshurun (a pet name for Israel) grew fat and kicked (32:15). Prosperity, not affliction, turned them away, and God's lavish love makes ingratitude the basest folly.

Vengeance belongs to God; the song of Moses and the Lamb. “Vengeance is mine, and recompense” (32:35): the righteous Judge will settle every account. Yet the song ends with God atoning for his people (32:43), and the redeemed will sing it with the song of the Lamb (Rev 15:3), celebrating the final rescue won by Christ.
32.examples: Israel was given this song to learn by heart; so, in a sense, are we. We rest on the Rock when we cannot trace his hand, marvel that he found us in our lostness, guard against the prosperity that breeds ingratitude, and leave vengeance to the righteous Judge. One day, in Christ, we will sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Rock, and the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is the Rock, perfect and faithful, who found Israel in the wilderness, carried her like an eagle and filled her with good things. The song calls heaven and earth to listen and prays that its words may fall like rain (vv. 1–3). It names God “the Rock”, whose work is perfect, and sets beside him a crooked generation that repays its Father with corruption (vv. 4–6). Then it remembers: the Most High chose Israel as his own portion (vv. 7–9), found him in a howling waste, guarded him like the apple of his eye, carried him like an eagle (vv. 10–12), and fed him with honey from the rock and the finest of the wheat (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The Rock is the song’s main name for God and appears five times. Against it stands the tenderness of vv. 10-11, the eye guarded and the eagle catching its young: strength and tenderness in one God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation was told where God had found it and who had carried it. Now: the same two things are still true of every believer, and both are needed — a Rock that does not move, and wings underneath when the nest is stirred.

verseByVerse.quote: "Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth. May my teaching drop as the rain, my speech distill as the dew, like gentle rain upon the tender grass, and like showers upon the herb. For I will proclaim the name of the LORD; ascribe greatness to our God! "The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he. They have dealt corruptly with him; they are no longer his children because they are blemished; they are a crooked and twisted generation. Do you thus repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people? Is not he your father, who created you, who made you and established you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is the perfect, faithful Rock, and his people have repaid their Father with corruption.

Give ear, O heavens. The song opens by summoning the universe as an audience, and as witnesses, since Moses has already called heaven and earth to testify against Israel (4:26; 30:19; 31:28).

May my teaching drop as the rain. His image for his preaching is rain, not a hammer: he wants his words to soak in slowly and make something grow.

The Rock, his work is perfect. A rock does not move, does not erode in a season, does not give under pressure; in a desert it is also the only shade there is. The song establishes God’s character before a word of accusation is spoken, so Israel’s corruption is measured against a standard already set. And Paul, recalling the wilderness, says of the rock that followed Israel, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4): the name this song gives God is a name the New Testament gives the Son.

Do you thus repay the LORD? The question of verse 6 is a father’s, not a judge’s: the language of a parent who cannot understand what has happened.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 5 is compressed and hard to construe. The King James Version renders it “their spot is not the spot of his children”. The general sense is clear: the corruption is Israel’s own, not God’s, and it makes them unlike the children he made.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember the days of old; consider the years of many generations; ask your father, and he will show you, your elders, and they will tell you. When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he divided mankind, he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God. But the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob his allotted heritage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is the LORD’s treasured portion, and remembering that is the cure for ingratitude.

Remember the days of old. The song turns from accusation (vv. 5–6) to history. The father and the elders are the nation’s memory, and faith was handed on at home, from one generation to the next, as the law commands (6:20–25).

The LORD’s portion is his people. When the Most High shared out the earth among the nations (the scattering of Genesis 10–11 is probably in view), he kept one people for himself. A portion or inheritance is what a man treasures and will not part with. Israel is God’s, not because she was great, but because he took her as his own (7:6–8). Peter gives the same title to the church: “a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

Textual note. Who are the “sons of God” (v. 8)? The standard Hebrew text reads “sons of Israel”; the ESV follows the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek translation, which read “sons of God”. The latter is most likely original. Many think the sense is that God set the nations under heavenly powers, while keeping Israel as “the LORD’s portion” (v. 9), and that such powers stand behind the gods the nations worshipped (v. 17; 1 Corinthians 10:20); others take the sons of God as angels appointed to serve. The details are debated. In Christ the nations are being reclaimed for their true King (Colossians 2:15).
verseByVerse.note: On the two readings, “sons of God” and “sons of Israel”, see above.

verseByVerse.quote: "He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him as the apple of his eye. Like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings, catching them, bearing them on its pinions, the LORD alone guided him, no foreign god was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God found Israel in the wilderness and carried her like an eagle; no other god had any part in it.

He found him in a desert land. How God came to have Israel is told in two images to be held together. The first is that God found Israel. He did not choose the best of the nations; he found him in a howling waste, where you find things nobody is looking for. Then he guards him as a man guards the pupil of his own eye.

Like an eagle that stirs up its nest. The second is the eagle, which stirs the nest deliberately. It makes the comfortable place uncomfortable so the young will fly, and then it hovers underneath, and when a fledgling drops, it goes below and takes the weight on its own back.

The LORD alone guided him. The last line of verse 12 is a hinge of the song. No foreign god was with Israel in the wilderness: no other god found her, carried her or fed her. That makes the turn to “strange gods” a few verses later (vv. 16–17) all the more senseless. Israel will thank gods who did nothing for her.

When life is unsettled. Any believer who has had a settled situation broken up and could not see why should read verse 11 slowly. The disturbance and the catching are done by the same bird.

verseByVerse.quote: He made him ride on the high places of the land, and he ate the produce of the field, and he suckled him with honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock. Curds from the herd, and milk from the flock, with fat of lambs, rams of Bashan and goats, with the very finest of the wheat— and you drank foaming wine made from the blood of the grape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Israel a feast from unlikely places, so that she could never call her wealth her own; the next verse is what she did with it.

Honey out of the rock. The pictures are of plenty from unlikely places: wild bees nested in clefts of the rock, and olive trees grow on stony hillsides where little else will. Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous for its cattle and rich pasture (Psalm 22:12; Amos 4:1), and “the blood of the grape” is a poet’s name for red wine. Every line is a gift, so that Israel could never say her wealth was her own doing (8:17–18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — Jeshurun Grew Fat, and Kicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel grew rich and turned on the God who made her, and his jealous anger answers her unfaithfulness. Jeshurun, God’s affectionate name for his people, grew fat and kicked, forsaking the Rock of salvation (v. 15). They provoked him with strange gods, sacrificing to demons and to new gods that had only recently arrived, and forgot the God who gave them birth (vv. 16–18). So God hides his face (vv. 19–20). Because they made him jealous with what is no god, he will make them jealous with those who are no people (v. 21). Fire, famine, plague, wild beasts and the sword follow (vv. 22–25).
verseByVerse.theology: Paul quotes v.21 — God provoking Israel to jealousy with those who are no people — to explain why the gospel went to the Gentiles (Rom. 10:19).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the nation called by a pet name grew sleek and kicked. Now: the danger is the same. Almost nobody is argued out of faith; a great many drift out of it through comfort and plenty.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him and scoffed at the Rock of his salvation. They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger. They sacrificed to demons that were not God, to gods they had never known, to new gods that had come recently, whom your fathers had never dreaded. You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Well fed, Israel kicked against the God who made her and forgot the Rock who gave her birth.

Jeshurun. A pet name for Israel, probably meaning “upright one”, used only four times in the Bible. God calls his people by a name of affection at the exact moment he describes their worst behaviour.

Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked. The image is a beast fed until it is sleek and strong, which then kicks the man with the bucket. Not oppressed, not deceived: well fed. It is the diagnosis of chapters 6, 8 and 31, and the repetition is the point: Deuteronomy’s great warning is not about persecution.

New gods that had come recently. There is a sneer in the phrase: they left the Rock, which is old and does not move, for gods that had only just arrived. And in the saddest line of the song the verb is a mother’s: God describes himself as the one who went through labour to give them birth, and says they forgot him, which is a thing you can do to a person without ever deciding to.

The newest gods. Few phrases describe a modern culture so well. We are trained to assume that the newest thing is the best, and every season brings a fresh saviour, a diet, a technique, a movement, promising what the last one failed to deliver. Luke says the Athenians of Paul’s day spent their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new (Acts 17:21), and he did not mean it as a compliment. Novelty thrills partly because it has not yet had time to fail us. The Rock has had time. He has been leaned on by every generation since Abraham, by slaves and kings, martyrs and the dying, and he has not given way. Yet the gospel is the newest thing in the world: “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). But that newness comes from the oldest Rock, not the latest arrival, and it lasts, because it is not a trend but a resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD saw it and spurned them, because of the provocation of his sons and his daughters. And he said, 'I will hide my face from them; I will see what their end will be, for they are a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness. They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation. For a fire is kindled by my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol, devours the earth and its increase, and sets on fire the foundations of the mountains. "'And I will heap disasters upon them; I will spend my arrows on them; they shall be wasted with hunger, and devoured by plague and poisonous pestilence; I will send the teeth of beasts against them, with the venom of things that crawl in the dust. Outdoors the sword shall bereave, and indoors terror, for young man and woman alike, the nursing child with the man of gray hairs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Israel’s idolatry in kind, and his judgment falls without flinching.

I will make them jealous. The punishment mirrors the crime exactly. They made God jealous with what is no god; he will make them jealous with those who are no people. Paul quotes this verse as the Old Testament’s own prediction that the gospel would go to the Gentiles: “First Moses says, ‘I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation’” (Romans 10:19). The church of the nations was in the Song of Moses before it was in anybody’s plan but God’s.

For a fire is kindled by my anger. The judgment itself is described without flinching. The song does not spare the reader, because the God who inspired it did not spare the nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — I Would Have Wiped Them Out, But…
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God judges his people but will not destroy them, and in the end he vindicates them and shows that he alone is God. He would have wiped them out, but he will not let their enemies boast that they did it (vv. 26–27). The nations lack understanding, their rock is not like Israel’s Rock, and their vine is the vine of Sodom (vv. 28–33). Vengeance belongs to the LORD; when his people’s strength is gone he will have compassion and expose their useless gods (vv. 34–38). The song climbs to God’s own words, “I kill and I make alive” (v. 39), his oath of judgment (vv. 40–42), and a call to the heavens to rejoice (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the section stands v.35, Vengeance is mine, and recompense, which the New Testament quotes twice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation was spared for the sake of God’s reputation rather than its own record. Now: that is still the only ground any of us stands on, and it is a far steadier one than merit.

verseByVerse.quote: I would have said, "I will cut them to pieces; I will wipe them from human memory," had I not feared provocation by the enemy, lest their adversaries should misunderstand, lest they should say, "Our hand is triumphant, it was not the LORD who did all this."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spares Israel, not for anything in her, but because he will not let his enemies take the credit.

Had I not feared provocation by the enemy. Two verses stop the judgment in mid-sentence, and they are the reason Israel survived: not her repentance (the song mentions none), not her value, but God’s concern for his own name.

A mercy from outside. That is a mercy whose reason lies entirely outside the one who receives it, and it is exactly the ground Moses had pleaded at Sinai (9:28). It looks like a lesser reason for sparing somebody, and is in fact the sturdiest, because it does not depend on the person spared.

verseByVerse.quote: "For they are a nation void of counsel, and there is no understanding in them. If they were wise, they would understand this; they would discern their latter end! How could one have chased a thousand, and two have put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had given them up? For their rock is not as our Rock; our enemies are by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s rout could only mean that her Rock had handed her over, for the nations’ gods are no match for him.

A nation void of counsel. Whom does this mean? Many take verses 28–29 of Israel, who would not learn from the covenant’s warnings. Others take them of the enemy just mentioned, who would misread Israel’s defeat as their own triumph (v. 27); if they were wise they would “discern their latter end”, the judgment awaiting them too (vv. 34–35). Either way, wisdom is seeing where a road ends.

How could one have chased a thousand? This reverses the covenant promise that a few of Israel would put many to flight (Leviticus 26:8; Joshua 23:10). When Israel is routed like that, the enemy’s strength cannot explain it. The only explanation is that “their Rock had sold them”, as a master sells a slave: the LORD himself had handed them over (Judges 2:14; 3:8).

Their rock is not as our Rock. The gods of the nations cannot be compared with Israel’s God, and the enemies themselves know it, as the Egyptians admitted at the sea (Exodus 14:25) and the Philistines before the ark (1 Samuel 4:7–8). Israel’s defeats were never a sign that her God was weak.

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 31, “our enemies are by themselves”, is obscure in Hebrew. It probably means “even our enemies being judges”: the enemies themselves must admit the difference between their gods and the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: For their vine comes from the vine of Sodom and from the fields of Gomorrah; their grapes are grapes of poison; their clusters are bitter; their wine is the poison of serpents and the cruel venom of asps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are no better than Israel: their vine grows from Sodom’s soil.

Grapes of poison. The picture answers verse 14, where Israel drank “the blood of the grape”. This vine is rooted, as it were, in the soil of Sodom and Gomorrah, and its wine is venom. Isaiah uses the same picture of Israel herself, the vineyard that yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7): what grows from a people shows what root it has.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Is not this laid up in store with me, sealed up in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine, and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip; for the day of their calamity is at hand, and their doom comes swiftly.' For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their power is gone and there is none remaining, bond or free. Then he will say, 'Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge, who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offering?
