Let them rise up and help you; let them be your protection!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vengeance belongs to God alone, and he will vindicate his people when their strength is gone.

Vengeance is mine. The New Testament uses these words twice, in two directions. Paul quotes them to forbid personal revenge: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). Not because the wrong does not matter, but because it matters too much to be left to us: vengeance belongs to one with perfect knowledge and justice. The God who will repay has already borne, in his Son, the wrongs we ourselves have done, and by his Spirit he enables the wronged to bless instead of curse (Romans 12:14, 21).

A warning to the church. Hebrews quotes the same words as a warning: “For we know him who said, ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay.’… It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:30–31). The same sentence comforts the wronged and warns the presumptuous, and both uses are right.

When he sees that their power is gone. Verse 36 is the turning point of the whole song, and its timing matters. God moves when their strength is gone: not while they still had options, reserves, or a plan. He waits until there is nothing left of them at all, and then he has compassion. That is his timing throughout Scripture. He is not slow; he is waiting for the point at which nobody, including you, will be able to credit the rescue to anyone but him.

Uncertain wording. “Bond or free” (v. 36) translates a Hebrew pair of words whose exact sense is unknown; it is probably an idiom for “everyone, without exception”: there is no one left.

verseByVerse.quote: "'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand. For I lift up my hand to heaven and swear, As I live forever, if I sharpen my flashing sword and my hand takes hold on judgment, I will take vengeance on my adversaries and will repay those who hate me. I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh— with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the long-haired heads of the enemy.' "Rejoice with him, O heavens; bow down to him, all gods, for he avenges the blood of his children and takes vengeance on his adversaries. He repays those who hate him and cleanses his people's land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone gives death and life, wounding and healing, and no one can escape his hand.

I kill and I make alive. The summit of the song is spoken by God himself, and few sentences in the Old Testament are more absolute. Two pairs, held in one hand: killing and making alive, wounding and healing. God does not divide the world between his sphere and somebody else’s. There is no rival deity operating the bad half, and no accident outside his reach.

A hard comfort. That is a hard doctrine and also the only real comfort available, and Job understood both halves of it at the worst hour of his life: “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10). A God who is sovereign only over the pleasant things could not be trusted with the rest.

None that can deliver out of my hand. It reads as a threat until you hear it in the mouth of the Son: “no one will snatch them out of my hand… and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:28–29). The same grip, which for those it holds is safety. And the God who makes alive raised Jesus from the dead.

Rejoice with him, O heavens. The New Testament keeps returning to the final call (v. 43). Paul quotes it to prove that the Gentiles were always meant to be included, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people” (Romans 15:10), and Hebrews takes the line about worship and applies it to Christ: “Let all God’s angels worship him” (Hebrews 1:6).

The song of the Lamb. The last time this song appears in Scripture, it is being sung beside a sea of glass: “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3). The piece God commissioned because he knew his people would forget him turns out to be one of the two songs of heaven.

Is God bloodthirsty? Lines about arrows drunk with blood are hard to read, and they should be. This is the poetry of judgment on enemies who persist against him, written so that wrong is not simply passed over. Revelation shows Christ coming in the same way, “clothed in a robe dipped in blood” (Revelation 19:13); the church leaves vengeance to him (Romans 12:19).

Uncertain wording. “The long-haired heads of the enemy” (v. 42) translates a rare Hebrew word that may mean long, loose hair or “leaders”. Either way it pictures the enemy’s fighting men brought down.

Textual note. The standard Hebrew text of verse 43 is shorter and lacks “bow down to him, all gods”; the ESV follows a longer form found in some ancient Hebrew and Greek copies, and Hebrews 1:6 quotes the Greek form.
verseByVerse.note: The Masoretic Hebrew text lacks “bow down to him, all gods” (ESV note); the longer wording is quoted in Hebrews.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–52 — The Song Taught, and the Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word of God is life itself, and Moses, who taught it faithfully, must still answer for his own sin. Moses recites the song to the people with Joshua beside him (v. 44). He urges them to take the words to heart and command them to their children, for “it is no empty word for you, but your very life” (vv. 45–47). That same day God tells him to climb Mount Nebo, view the land of Canaan, and die there as Aaron died on Mount Hor (vv. 48–50), because he broke faith at Meribah-kadesh; he will see the land but not enter it (vv. 51–52).
verseByVerse.theology: His last verdict on Scripture is that it is no empty word for you, but your very life. Then the sentence of Meribah is restated without softening (see 3:26).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man finished the song, handed over the book, and climbed a mountain to die outside the land. Now: the sentence was not the last word: Moses stood in the land at last, beside Christ (Luke 9:30–31).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses came and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun. And when Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel, he said to them, "Take to heart all the words by which I am warning you today, that you may command them to your children, that they may be careful to do all the words of this law. For it is no empty word for you, but your very life, and by this word you shall live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses teaches the song and tells Israel that God’s word is their very life.

He and Joshua the son of Nun. Moses recites the song with Joshua beside him. The song will outlive Moses, and the people see the man who will lead them into the land sharing in its teaching. The Hebrew here calls him Hoshea, the name he bore before Moses renamed him (Numbers 13:16).

That you may command them to your children. Taking the words to heart comes first, and then handing them on: a people that does not keep the word cannot teach it. The life promised is long life in the land, the covenant’s blessing (4:40; 30:20).

It is no empty word for you. This is Moses’ verdict on Scripture, given on the last day he will ever teach: not important, not helpful, not a resource, but life. The word is life because it comes from the God who redeemed them, and the same God would one day write it on the heart by his Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33).

verseByVerse.quote: That very day the LORD spoke to Moses, "Go up this mountain of the Abarim, Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel for a possession. And die on the mountain which you go up, and be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother died in Mount Hor and was gathered to his people, because you broke faith with me in the midst of the people of Israel at the waters of Meribah-kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, and because you did not treat me as holy in the midst of the people of Israel. For you shall see the land before you, but you shall not go there, into the land that I am giving to the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of Meribah, Moses must see the land from Nebo and die; yet he would stand in it at last beside Christ.

Go up this mountain of the Abarim. The same day God sends him up Nebo to die. The reason, his failure to treat God as holy at Meribah (v. 51), is restated in God’s own words, and Moses lets it stand without defence. He has asked once (3:25) and been told not to raise it again, and he does not. Like his brother Aaron on Mount Hor (v. 50), he dies outside the land. Then the last, aching clause: he will see the land but not go there.

You broke faith with me. At Meribah, when the people quarrelled for water, God told Moses to speak to the rock. Moses struck it twice and said, “Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?” (Numbers 20:10–12). He spoke as if the power were his and Aaron’s, and he did it in front of the whole people. A leader’s public sin is judged in public, and the greater the trust, the stricter the account (James 3:1).

He got there in the end. That is the sentence he lives under and dies under, and the book does not resolve it. It is resolved somewhere else entirely, on a different mountain, where two men appeared in glory and talked with Jesus about his departure, and one of them was Moses, standing on a mountain inside the land (Luke 9:30–31). He came in with the Christ he had been writing about, and by then crossing the Jordan no longer mattered.

keyVerse.quote: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he.
keyVerse.note: The song establishes who God is before it says a word about Israel’s sin, so that every accusation and every judgment is measured against his perfect faithfulness. He is the Rock that does not move when his people do, and Paul tells us that “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

32.reflection:
God is called “the Rock” again and again in this song (vv. 4, 15, 18, 30–31). What does that picture say about God, and where are you tempted to lean on something less stable?

“Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked” (v. 15). Why is prosperity so often more dangerous to faith than hardship? What “new gods that had come recently” (v. 17) compete for your heart?

God says, “Vengeance is mine” (v. 35), and acts when his people’s “power is gone” (v. 36). How do these verses help someone who has been wronged, or someone who has come to the end of their strength?

Moses calls the word “no empty word for you, but your very life” (v. 47). What would change in your week if you really treated Scripture that way?

33.title: The Blessing of Moses: The Eternal God Is Your Dwelling Place
33.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the people of Israel before his death.<sup>2</sup>He said, "The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon us; he shone forth from Mount Paran; he came from the ten thousands of holy ones, with flaming fire at his right hand.<sup>3</sup>Yes, he loved his people, all his holy ones were in his hand; so they followed in your steps, receiving direction from you,<sup>4</sup>when Moses commanded us a law, as a possession for the assembly of Jacob.<sup>5</sup>Thus the LORD became king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people were gathered, all the tribes of Israel together.<sup>6</sup>"Let Reuben live, and not die, but let his men be few."<sup>7</sup>And this he said of Judah: "Hear, O LORD, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people. With your hands contend for him, and be a help against his adversaries."<sup>8</sup>And of Levi he said, "Give to Levi your Thummim, and your Urim to your godly one, whom you tested at Massah, with whom you quarreled at the waters of Meribah;<sup>9</sup>who said of his father and mother, 'I regard them not'; he disowned his brothers and ignored his children. For they observed your word and kept your covenant.<sup>10</sup>They shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law; they shall put incense before you and whole burnt offerings on your altar.<sup>11</sup>Bless, O LORD, his substance, and accept the work of his hands; crush the loins of his adversaries, of those who hate him, that they rise not again."<sup>12</sup>Of Benjamin he said, "The beloved of the LORD dwells in safety. The High God surrounds him all day long, and dwells between his shoulders."<sup>13</sup>And of Joseph he said, "Blessed by the LORD be his land, with the choicest gifts of heaven above, and of the deep that crouches beneath,<sup>14</sup>with the choicest fruits of the sun and the rich yield of the months,<sup>15</sup>with the finest produce of the ancient mountains and the abundance of the everlasting hills,<sup>16</sup>with the best gifts of the earth and its fullness and the favor of him who dwells in the bush. May these rest on the head of Joseph, on the pate of him who is prince among his brothers.<sup>17</sup>A firstborn bull —he has majesty, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth; they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh."<sup>18</sup>And of Zebulun he said, "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents.<sup>19</sup>They shall call peoples to their mountain; there they offer right sacrifices; for they draw from the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand."<sup>20</sup>And of Gad he said, "Blessed be he who enlarges Gad! Gad crouches like a lion; he tears off arm and scalp.<sup>21</sup>He chose the best of the land for himself, for there a commander's portion was reserved; and he came with the heads of the people, with Israel he executed the justice of the LORD, and his judgments for Israel."<sup>22</sup>And of Dan he said, "Dan is a lion's cub that leaps from Bashan."<sup>23</sup>And of Naphtali he said, "O Naphtali, sated with favor, and full of the blessing of the LORD, possess the lake and the south."<sup>24</sup>And of Asher he said, "Most blessed of sons be Asher; let him be the favorite of his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil.<sup>25</sup>Your bars shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be.<sup>26</sup>"There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty.<sup>27</sup>The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms. And he thrust out the enemy before you and said, 'Destroy.'<sup>28</sup>So Israel lived in safety, Jacob lived alone, in a land of grain and wine, whose heavens drop down dew.<sup>29</sup>Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, and the sword of your triumph! Your enemies shall come fawning to you, and you shall tread upon their backs."
33.overview:
Where we are. Moses has finished his last sermon and taught Israel the song that will testify against them (chapter 32), and God has told him to climb Mount Nebo and die (32:48–52). Before he goes up, he does what Jacob did on his deathbed (Genesis 49): he blesses the family, tribe by tribe.

The message. Israel’s future rests not on Israel but on Israel’s God. The LORD came to them in fire because he loved them, made himself their King, and will give each tribe its place and its portion; above all he gives them himself: “The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (v. 27). After a song that exposed their unfaithfulness, the last word is a blessing: “Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD” (v. 29).

Why it was said. A nation about to cross the Jordan without its leader, into a land of walled cities, had every reason to fear, and chapter 32 had just told them they would fail (see the introduction). They needed to know that the God who had carried them would not put them down.

How the chapter makes its case. The blessing is framed by praise. It opens with the LORD coming from Sinai with his holy ones, giving the law because he loved his people, and reigning as King in Jeshurun (vv. 1–5). In the centre each tribe receives a word suited to its history and its future, from Reuben preserved and Levi entrusted with God’s word, to Joseph made fruitful and Asher promised strength for his days (vv. 6–25). It closes by turning from the tribes back to their God: none like him, the eternal refuge, the everlasting arms, the shield and sword of a saved people (vv. 26–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by revealing the character of God that Christ makes known, and partly by promise. The King of verse 5 came in person and was crucified as “the King of the Jews” (John 19:19); the prayer for Judah (v. 7) is answered in “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5); and Levi’s priesthood gives way to a priest from Judah, the tribe of which “Moses said nothing about priests” (Hebrews 7:14). The everlasting arms were never more plainly seen than when they were stretched out on the cross for “a people saved by the LORD”.

For us. A Christian’s security is not his record but his God, who has “blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3). Whatever your past, the God who turned Levi’s curse into a calling can use it; whatever your weakness, strength is given as your days require; and whatever you fall into, the everlasting arms are underneath.
33.theology:
The eternal God is our dwelling place. Our true home is not a place but a Person; the eternal God is our secure, unchanging refuge (cf. Ps 90:1), and there is none like him (33:26).

God's majesty and intimate love. The God who rides through the heavens (33:26) is the God who loved his people and holds them in his hand (33:3), carrying his beloved on his shoulders (33:12). Majesty far above us and tender, close love meet in the God who reigns as King over his people (33:5).

Strength proportioned to each day. God supplies grace sufficient for each day's need, mercies new every morning (33:25; Lam 3:23; 2 Cor 12:9).
33.examples: Our home is the eternal God himself, who upholds us beneath every weakness and fall, as he upheld the tribes Moses blessed. We trust his grace for each day as it comes, and rejoice that we are a people saved by the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The LORD Came from Sinai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s blessing rests on God’s love, not on Israel’s record. Moses, called here “the man of God”, begins his last words not with the tribes but with the LORD. He came from Sinai like the sunrise, blazing with fire and surrounded by holy ones (vv. 1–2). Then comes the reason for all that glory: “Yes, he loved his people” (v. 3). He gave them his law as their treasured possession (v. 4), and so reigned as King over Jeshurun, his upright people, when the tribes gathered as one (v. 5). Before a single tribe is blessed, Israel is told who their King is and why he came.
verseByVerse.theology: The blessing begins where Deuteronomy began, at the mountain, and states the ground of the covenant in five words. Verse 5 names what came of it: the LORD became king in Jeshurun.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation was told, before a single tribe was blessed, that the whole thing rested on God’s love for them. Now: the order is unchanged — we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the people of Israel before his death. He said, "The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon us; he shone forth from Mount Paran; he came from the ten thousands of holy ones, with flaming fire at his right hand. Yes, he loved his people, all his holy ones were in his hand; so they followed in your steps, receiving direction from you, when Moses commanded us a law, as a possession for the assembly of Jacob. Thus the LORD became king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people were gathered, all the tribes of Israel together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Moses blesses a single tribe, he reminds Israel what everything rests on: the LORD came to them in glory because he loved them, gave them his law, and became their King.

Moses the man of God. The title means one who belongs to God and speaks for him (compare Joshua 14:6). The last thing he does is bless them. After forty years of grumbling and rebellion, and a sentence on himself that they caused (3:26), the final act of his life is to go round the tribes one at a time and speak good over each of them.

The LORD came from Sinai. The verbs are sunrise verbs, dawned and shone forth: God rising over the horizon like the morning, from Sinai through Seir and Paran, the country Israel had travelled. He came with “ten thousands of holy ones”, the angels whom the New Testament also links with the giving of the law (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2).

Yes, he loved his people. Then, in the middle of all that fire, five plain words. That is the ground of everything that follows, stated before a single tribe is named: not their record, which the song of the previous chapter has just torn down, but his love (7:7–8). Even the law was love’s gift, “a possession for the assembly of Jacob” (v. 4).

Thus the LORD became king in Jeshurun. Jeshurun, “the upright one”, is an affectionate name for Israel (32:15; Isaiah 44:2). Verse 5 is Israel’s constitution in a line: God was king, and every human king afterwards ruled as a deputy under a law he had to copy out by hand (17:18). When Israel later asked for a king like the nations, God told Samuel exactly what had happened: “they have rejected me from being king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). This verse is what they gave up.

The King came back in person. The Son of David, who is also David’s Lord, rode into Jerusalem as its king and was crucified under the title “the King of the Jews” (John 19:19), and he now reigns over a people gathered from every tribe and nation. In him the LORD is king in Jeshurun again.

Uncertain wording. Verses 2 and 3 are among the hardest Hebrew in the book. The King James Version read “flaming fire” as “a fiery law”, but the word taken as law is otherwise found only in much later books, so most now read fire or lightning. Verse 3 is obscure, and “his holy ones” may be Israel or the angels. Verse 5 says literally “there was a king in Jeshurun”: most take the king to be the LORD, as the ESV does; some Jewish interpreters took it of Moses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–25 — The Tribes Blessed One by One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each tribe receives a word suited to its history and its calling, and in every one the blessing is God’s doing. Reuben, who lost the firstborn’s place, is kept alive (v. 6); Judah is promised God’s help in battle (v. 7); Levi, once cursed for violence, is entrusted with God’s word and altar (vv. 8–11). Benjamin is sheltered by the LORD, and Joseph receives the richest gifts of the land (vv. 12–17). Zebulun and Issachar will call peoples to worship (vv. 18–19). Gad, Dan, Naphtali and Asher are given strength, room and plenty, and Asher the promise that strength will match his days (vv. 20–25). Simeon alone is missing.
verseByVerse.theology: The blessings differ as the tribes differ: some are brief, one tribe is missing, and the fullest words go to Levi and Joseph.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dying man went round the family one by one and had something to say to each. Now: the God who turned Levi’s curse into a calling has not changed his habits with people whose history is against them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let Reuben live, and not die, but let his men be few."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben, the firstborn who forfeited his place, will survive as a tribe, though never great.

Let Reuben live, and not die. Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, lost the firstborn’s place for defiling his father’s bed (Genesis 49:3–4; 1 Chronicles 5:1). Moses prays not for greatness but for survival. Settled east of the Jordan, Reuben never led Israel as a firstborn should; in Deborah’s day his clans stayed among the sheepfolds while others fought (Judges 5:15–16). Yet mercy keeps him in the family.

Where is Simeon? Simeon is not mentioned at all, perhaps because the tribe was already fading: a Simeonite chief had sinned openly at Peor (Numbers 25:14), its numbers had fallen from 59,300 to 22,200 in a generation, and it would later be absorbed into Judah (Joshua 19:1, 9). Jacob had said Simeon would be scattered (Genesis 49:7), and so it was.

Uncertain wording. The second line may be a prayer that his men be few, as the ESV takes it, or, as many translations have it, that they not be few: the Hebrew line has no “not”, but the negative of the first line may carry over. Either way the prayer is for survival, not prominence.

verseByVerse.quote: And this he said of Judah: "Hear, O LORD, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people. With your hands contend for him, and be a help against his adversaries."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah, the tribe that will lead Israel into battle, is given a prayer: that God will hear its cry, fight for it and bring it home.

Hear, O LORD, the voice of Judah. Jacob had given Judah the sceptre (Genesis 49:8–10), and Judah would march first (Numbers 10:14; Judges 1:1–2). Moses asks that when Judah goes out to battle and cries to God, God will hear, fight for him with his own hands, and bring him home safe to his people. Judah’s strength is not its own; its blessing is that God hears it.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah. The prayer was answered in David, whose victories God gave, and beyond him in the Son of David, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, who “has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). He fought the decisive battle alone, and brings his people home with him.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Levi he said, "Give to Levi your Thummim, and your Urim to your godly one, whom you tested at Massah, with whom you quarreled at the waters of Meribah; who said of his father and mother, 'I regard them not'; he disowned his brothers and ignored his children. For they observed your word and kept your covenant. They shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law; they shall put incense before you and whole burnt offerings on your altar. Bless, O LORD, his substance, and accept the work of his hands; crush the loins of his adversaries, of those who hate him, that they rise not again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi, once cursed by its own father for violence, is now entrusted with God’s word and God’s altar, because at the decisive moment it chose God above its own kin.

Give to Levi your Thummim, and your Urim. These were the sacred lots kept in the high priest’s breastpiece, used to seek God’s decision (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21).

Whom you tested at Massah. At Massah and Meribah the people tested God by quarrelling over water (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:1–13); here God is said to have tested Levi there. Moses and Aaron, both Levites, stood at the centre of those quarrels, and the tribe is probably remembered in them.

Who said of his father and mother, ‘I regard them not’. At Sinai, when the people worshipped the golden calf, Moses cried, “Who is on the LORD’s side? Come to me”, and the Levites gathered and carried out judgment even on their own kin (Exodus 32:26–29). Loyalty to God came before family. Jesus asks the same of every disciple, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37), lived out now not with the sword but by putting him first.

They shall teach Jacob your rules. Levi’s calling is God’s word and God’s worship: to teach the law, and to stand at the altar with incense and burnt offerings (v. 10). The closing prayer asks God to accept their work and defend them, for those who serve at his altar will have enemies.

A sentence converted. On Jacob’s deathbed the same tribe heard this: “Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce … I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7), for a massacre at Shechem (Genesis 34). God did not cancel the sentence. He kept it and converted it. Levi was scattered, exactly as Jacob said, into forty-eight cities in every tribe (Joshua 21:41), which turned out to be how the whole nation got taught. The tribe with the worst family history carried the ark. Anybody whose past is genuinely against him should hold on to that.

A better priest. Levi’s priests died, and their sacrifices had to be repeated. The final priest came from Judah, the tribe of which “Moses said nothing about priests” (Hebrews 7:14): Christ, Teacher and Sacrifice in one, who offered himself once for all.

Uncertain wording. “Your godly one” (v. 8) may mean the tribe or its representative, Aaron or Moses, and no other passage says how God tested Levi at Massah; the plurals of verse 9 show the whole tribe is in view.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Benjamin he said, "The beloved of the LORD dwells in safety. The High God surrounds him all day long, and dwells between his shoulders." And of Joseph he said, "Blessed by the LORD be his land, with the choicest gifts of heaven above, and of the deep that crouches beneath, with the choicest fruits of the sun and the rich yield of the months, with the finest produce of the ancient mountains and the abundance of the everlasting hills, with the best gifts of the earth and its fullness and the favor of him who dwells in the bush. May these rest on the head of Joseph, on the pate of him who is prince among his brothers. A firstborn bull —he has majesty, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth; they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin will live safe under God’s protection, and Joseph will receive the richest gifts of the land, all flowing from the favour of the God of the burning bush.

The beloved of the LORD dwells in safety. Benjamin, Jacob’s youngest and best-loved son, is here the beloved of the LORD, sheltered by God all day long. God dwells between his shoulders, probably meaning on his slopes: Jerusalem, where the temple would stand, lay on Benjamin’s border (Joshua 18:16, 28).

Blessed by the LORD be his land. Joseph receives the richest blessing in the chapter, the best of sky, deep, sun, months and hills, echoing Jacob’s words (Genesis 49:25–26). Rain from above and springs beneath were the life of Canaan, and his two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, would hold the most fertile hill country in the land.

The favor of him who dwells in the bush. The phrase recalls the burning bush where God first called Moses (Exodus 3:2–4). Of all the gifts in the list this is the one that matters: the goodwill of the God who met a shepherd at a desert shrub.

A firstborn bull. Joseph’s strength is pictured as a young bull and a wild ox with its horns. Joseph received the double portion of the firstborn through his two sons (1 Chronicles 5:1–2), and the order of the last line, Ephraim’s ten thousands before Manasseh’s thousands, recalls Jacob crossing his hands to put the younger first (Genesis 48:13–20). “Prince among his brothers” remembers the brother who was sold and became their ruler.

The brother they rejected. Joseph, sold by his brothers and raised up to save them, is one of the clearest patterns of Christ in the Old Testament: the brother they rejected became the source of their bread.

Uncertain wording. “Between his shoulders” (v. 12) may mean that God dwells among Benjamin’s hills, or that he carries Benjamin on his back as a father carries a child (compare 1:31); both fit the tender tone.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Zebulun he said, "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents. They shall call peoples to their mountain; there they offer right sacrifices; for they draw from the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zebulun and Issachar will prosper abroad and at home, and use their prosperity to call others to worship the LORD.

Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents. Leah’s two youngest sons are blessed together: Zebulun in its going out, probably trade and travel toward the coast, and Issachar at home in its tents. Abroad or at home, both are told to rejoice.

They shall call peoples to their mountain. Their prosperity is not kept to themselves: they summon others to worship and offer “right sacrifices”, offered as God requires. The mountain may be Tabor, on their shared border (Joshua 19:12, 22). Wealth is blessed when it draws others to God.

Calling the peoples. This land became Jesus’ home country (see the note on v. 23), and from a mountain in Galilee he sent his disciples to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:16–19).

Uncertain wording. “The abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand” probably means the wealth of sea trade and of the shore. Some think of purple dye from shellfish or glass made from sand, but the exact sense is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Gad he said, "Blessed be he who enlarges Gad! Gad crouches like a lion; he tears off arm and scalp. He chose the best of the land for himself, for there a commander's portion was reserved; and he came with the heads of the people, with Israel he executed the justice of the LORD, and his judgments for Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gad, exposed on the eastern frontier, will be a fierce defender, and is honoured for keeping its word to fight alongside its brothers.

Blessed be he who enlarges Gad! The blessing begins by praising God, who gives Gad room. Gad lived east of the Jordan, open to raids from the desert, and had to be a fighter: it crouches like a lion.

He chose the best of the land for himself. Gad chose the best when it asked for the pastures of Gilead (Numbers 32:1–5), and Moses feared it was abandoning its brothers. Yet it kept its word and crossed the Jordan to fight for them before going home (Numbers 32:20–27; Joshua 22:1–4). That is how it “executed the justice of the LORD”: by doing what it had promised in the LORD’s war.

Uncertain wording. The words translated “a commander’s portion was reserved” are obscure. They probably mean a leader’s share of land set aside for Gad; the word for commander can also mean lawgiver, and some Jewish interpreters connected the line with Moses, buried east of the Jordan.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Dan he said, "Dan is a lion's cub that leaps from Bashan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dan is pictured as a young lion, small but strong and bold.

A lion’s cub that leaps from Bashan. Dan is a young lion springing from Bashan, the rich country east of the Sea of Galilee. The tribe was first allotted land near the coast but was pressed back into the hills (Judges 1:34), and later moved to the far north, where it took the city of Laish and renamed it Dan (Judges 18:29), not far from the country the picture names.

Strength is not faithfulness. Jacob’s word to Dan had carried a warning (Genesis 49:16–18); Moses gives it only strength. Yet in the north Dan set up its own idol (Judges 18:30–31): God’s gifts are no guarantee that we will use them for him.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Naphtali he said, "O Naphtali, sated with favor, and full of the blessing of the LORD, possess the lake and the south." And of Asher he said, "Most blessed of sons be Asher; let him be the favorite of his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil. Your bars shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naphtali and Asher are promised the fullness of God’s favour and the goodness of the land, and Asher the promise that strength will be given to match every day.

O Naphtali, sated with favor. Naphtali is filled to overflowing with the LORD’s favour and blessing, and told to possess the lake and the south. The lake is probably the Sea of Galilee, on whose western side Naphtali’s land lay.

Galilee of the nations. Isaiah later promised that “Galilee of the nations”, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2), and Matthew records that Jesus made his home in Capernaum, “in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali”, to fulfil it (Matthew 4:13–16). The tribes blessed with plenty were blessed far more with his presence.

Let him dip his foot in oil. Asher gets the most homely blessing: favoured by his brothers, with olive oil so plentiful you could paddle in it.

Your bars shall be iron and bronze. Asher held the coast in the north-west, a frontier toward Phoenicia. The bars are the bolts of city gates, made strong for defence.

As your days, so shall your strength be. This line has comforted more people than anything else in the chapter. The strength is issued to match the days, as they come. It is not a reservoir handed over in advance, which is what most of us would prefer and would certainly misuse; it is enough for today, and then enough for tomorrow when tomorrow arrives. It has never yet failed to arrive. That is the same arrangement as the manna, and the same as “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). Christ gives his grace on the same terms: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

What it does not mean. It does not promise that we will never feel weak; Paul’s thorn was not removed. It promises strength enough for what God sends.

Uncertain wording. “The lake” translates the common word for sea, which can also mean west, so some read “possess the west and the south”. The word rendered “strength” in verse 25 occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament; strength, rest and security have all been suggested, and each fits the sense.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–29 — Underneath Are the Everlasting Arms
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blessing ends where it began, with God, and names him as Israel’s true security. There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to help his people (v. 26). He is their home, and beneath them are arms that never tire; he drives out their enemies before them (v. 27). So Israel will live secure in a land of grain and wine, watered by dew (v. 28). Moses’ last words are a cry of wonder at their happiness: a people saved by the LORD, with God himself as their shield and sword (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: Three images in one breath: a God who rides to the rescue, a God who is himself the house they live in, and arms beneath them that do not tire.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation with no home of its own was told that God was the dwelling place. Now: the arms are still underneath, and in Christ the eternal God has shown how far they will reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty. The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms. And he thrust out the enemy before you and said, 'Destroy.' So Israel lived in safety, Jacob lived alone, in a land of grain and wine, whose heavens drop down dew. Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, and the sword of your triumph! Your enemies shall come fawning to you, and you shall tread upon their backs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s security is not in itself but in its incomparable God, who is its home, its support and its salvation; so Moses’ last word over them is “Happy are you”.

There is none like God, O Jeshurun. Moses calls them by the affectionate name one final time, the same name the Song used when it said “Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked” (32:15). Both are true, but the last time Moses uses it, God is riding through the heavens to their rescue.

The eternal God is your dwelling place. Verse 27’s two images work in opposite directions. God is the dwelling place, the house you live in, which is around you and over you; the psalm that bears Moses’ name says the same: “Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psalm 90:1). After forty years in tents, the men listening had never had an address; Moses tells them God is the house.

Underneath are the everlasting arms. And underneath are arms: the picture of a father carrying a child, the image of 1:31, “the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son”, returning at the very end. The arms are everlasting. Arms tire; a father carrying a sleeping child eventually has to put him down. These do not, which is why the verse has been read beside so many deathbeds.

Happy are you, O Israel! After all the curses and the song and the sentence on himself, the final word of the man who gave Israel the law is a blessing, not a warning. Not because of what they are, which the last thirty chapters have settled, but because of whose they are: “a people saved by the LORD”, with God their shield and sword. There is nothing in Moses’ last sentence about their achievements at all.

Arms stretched out for us. The arms beneath Israel were finally seen in Christ, whose name means “the LORD saves” (compare Matthew 1:21), whose arms were stretched out on the cross for his people, and who says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). In him the eternal God “dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

What it does not mean. The everlasting arms do not promise that God’s people will never fall or suffer, only that when we fall, we fall into his arms. Driving out and treading on enemies belonged to Israel’s unique wars in Canaan (see the introduction); the church’s enemies are sin, death and the devil, and the victory is Christ’s (Romans 16:20).

Uncertain wording. In verse 28, “Jacob lived alone” can also be read “the fountain of Jacob”, as in the King James Version, picturing Israel’s descendants flowing from their source. In verse 29, “their backs” can also mean “their high places” (so the King James Version).

keyVerse.quote: The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms.
keyVerse.note: Moses’ blessing turns at the end from the tribes to their God, and this line says what every tribe’s blessing depended on: God himself is his people’s home and their support, and his arms do not tire. It is the security the gospel gives every believer in Christ, from whose hand no one can snatch them (John 10:28).

33.reflection:
Moses says “Yes, he loved his people” (v. 3) before he blesses any tribe, straight after a song that exposed Israel’s unfaithfulness. Why must God’s love come first, and how does that change the way you hear his commands?

Levi, cursed by Jacob for violence (Genesis 49:5–7), became the tribe that taught Israel God’s law (vv. 8–11). What does this show about how God can use a past that is against us? Where do you need to believe that?

“As your days, so shall your strength be” (v. 25). Why does God give strength day by day rather than in advance? What day ahead are you dreading, and how might this promise meet it?

“The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (v. 27). Where do you tend to look for security instead, and how has Christ shown us what these arms will do?

34.title: The Death of Moses: The Law Could Not Bring Them In
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the LORD showed him all the land, Gilead as far as Dan,<sup>2</sup>all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the western sea,<sup>3</sup>the Negeb, and the Plain, that is, the Valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to him, "This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, 'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there."<sup>5</sup>So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows the place of his burial to this day.<sup>7</sup>Moses was 120 years old when he died. His eye was undimmed, and his vigor unabated.<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days. Then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were ended.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the people of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>10</sup>And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face,<sup>11</sup>none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land,<sup>12</sup>and for all the mighty power and all the great deeds of terror that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.
34.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of Deuteronomy and of the five books of Moses. Moses has blessed the tribes (chapter 33), and now he climbs Mount Nebo, as God told him (32:48–52), to see the land and die.

The message. God keeps his word, both his promise and his discipline. He shows Moses the whole land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, yet holds him to the sentence that he will not enter it. Moses dies at God’s word and is buried by God’s hand, Joshua takes up the work, and the book ends confessing that no prophet like Moses has yet arisen: Israel is left waiting for a greater one.

Why it was said. The generation about to cross the Jordan had to go on without the only leader most of them had ever known. The chapter tells them that God’s purpose had not died with his servant, and its closing epitaph, written after Moses’ death (see the introduction), kept later generations looking for the prophet God had promised (18:15).

How the chapter makes its case. First the view: from Pisgah God shows Moses the land, north, west and south, with his oath and his refusal (vv. 1–4). Then the death: Moses dies “according to the word of the LORD”, still strong, God buries him in a grave no one has found, and Israel mourns thirty days (vv. 5–8). Last the succession and the epitaph: Joshua, filled with wisdom through Moses’ laying on of hands, is obeyed, and Moses is honoured as the prophet whom the LORD knew face to face (vv. 9–12).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and by the need it exposes. Moses, the mediator of the law, could bring Israel to the border but not across it: “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, led them in, yet “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). The prophet like Moses has come. Moses himself stood with him on the mountain, and the Father said, “listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). Faithful over God’s house as a Son, not a servant (Hebrews 3:5–6), he does what Moses could not: he brings his people home.

For us. By our own record we all stand where Moses stood, short of the inheritance. The law can show us the land, but only Christ can take us in, and he does. And the death of God’s servants is never the end of God’s work: he buries his workers and carries on his work.
34.theology:
The law cannot bring us in; only the Savior can. Moses, the law-giver and mediator of the old covenant, sees the land but cannot enter it (34:4). The law shows us the inheritance and our inability to reach it, because none of us keeps it; Christ kept it perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted ours (Rom 5:19). Joshua leads the people in (34:9), for “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Where the law fails, Christ saves.

The servant of the LORD. Moses' deepest identity, even in death, was “the servant of the LORD” (34:5), faithful to the end. God's purposes did not die with his servant.

The Prophet greater than Moses. Moses himself foretold the Prophet to come (18:15), so the book ends in longing, pointing to Jesus, faithful over God's house as a Son (Heb 3:5–6), the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), everything Moses foreshadowed and more.
34.examples: The law brings us to the border and shows us the promise, but cannot carry us home; only Jesus, the Prophet greater than Moses, leads his people through death into the inheritance and the rest of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his oath and his discipline in the same moment. Moses climbs from the plains of Moab to the top of Pisgah on Mount Nebo, and the LORD shows him the whole land: Gilead and Dan in the north, Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, Judah as far as the western sea, the Negeb, and the Jordan valley down to Zoar (vv. 1–3). Then God names what Moses is seeing: the land he swore to give Abraham’s offspring, now in sight. Moses may see it with his own eyes, but he will not cross into it (v. 4). The sight is both a kindness and a sentence.
verseByVerse.theology: The tour is God’s own doing; he takes his servant up and points out the country he has been walking toward for forty years. Seeing is all he is given, and it is given as a kindness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man saw everything he had worked for and was told he would not enter it. Now: the sight was not a consolation prize — these all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb. 11:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the LORD showed him all the land, Gilead as far as Dan, all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the western sea, the Negeb, and the Plain, that is, the Valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar. And the LORD said to him, "This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, 'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lets Moses see the whole of the promised land before he dies, keeping both his promise to the patriarchs and his sentence that Moses will not enter it.

Then Moses went up. He climbs alone, at a hundred and twenty, and will not come down. Nebo is a summit in the mountains of Moab, and Pisgah its ridge, looking west across the Jordan valley to Jericho: the very view Moses had asked for and been granted (3:27).

The LORD showed him all the land. God gives him not a glance but a tour, region by region: north to Gilead and Dan, across Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, west to Judah and the sea, south to the Negeb, and down the valley to Jericho, “the city of palm trees”, and Zoar. Every place is somewhere Moses will never walk. Whether by unusually clear sight or by a sight God gave beyond the ordinary, Moses saw it all; the text says simply that the LORD showed him.

This is the land of which I swore. Both halves of verse 4 stand in one sentence, and neither cancels the other. The promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is being kept: Moses is looking at the evidence, the land Joseph died believing God would give (Genesis 50:24). And the crossing is refused to the man who brought them this far.

I have let you see it with your eyes. There is real kindness in the seeing. God did not have to show him anything; he could have let him die in his tent. Instead he took him up and let him look at what forty years had been for.

Seen from afar. Hebrews puts a whole company in this position and does not treat it as failure: “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). Seeing and greeting from a distance is not a lesser form of faith; it is what faith normally looks like while we are still living. And Moses did stand in the land at last, in glory on the mountain of the transfiguration, talking with Jesus about the “departure” (in Greek, the exodus) he would accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30–31), the exodus that brings God’s people into a better country than Canaan.

Why was Moses kept out? Because at Meribah he did not uphold God as holy before the people (Numbers 20:12; 32:51), and, as Moses himself said, “because of you” (3:26): the people’s provocation and their leader’s failure were bound together. He was disciplined, not rejected. God’s discipline of his children can be real and lasting in this life while his love for them is unshaken (Hebrews 12:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses’ death is God’s appointment, not the end of a slow decline. The servant of the LORD dies in Moab at God’s word (v. 5), and God himself buries him in a valley opposite Beth-peor, in a grave no one has ever found (v. 6). He was 120, his eyes still clear and his strength unabated (v. 7). Israel mourns him thirty days on the plains of Moab, and then the mourning ends (v. 8), for the people must go on with God.
verseByVerse.theology: The text says God buried him, which is said of nobody else in Scripture. The greatest man in Israel’s history has no tomb, no shrine and no site of pilgrimage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the man who spoke with God face to face was laid in unmarked ground by God’s own hands. Now: the grave that changes every other grave, including the ones we stand beside, is Christ’s, which was marked, guarded, and found empty.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD, and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows the place of his burial to this day. Moses was 120 years old when he died. His eye was undimmed, and his vigor unabated. And the people of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days. Then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses dies when and where God says, still strong, and God himself buries him in a grave no one can find; Israel mourns, and then must move on.

Moses the servant of the LORD. Not lawgiver, prophet or deliverer, but servant. It is among the highest titles the Old Testament gives anybody (Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2), and it is the title the book gives Moses at his death.

According to the word of the LORD. Literally “at the mouth of the LORD”, which later Jewish tradition tenderly read as death by God’s kiss. Moses did not die because his strength gave out: at 120 his eye was undimmed and his vigour unabated (v. 7). He did not fade away; God stopped him, so the mountain was God’s act and not the end of a decline.

He buried him. The Hebrew most naturally says God did. The Almighty attending to the body of his friend on a mountainside, alone, is tender beyond anything the ancient world imagined about its gods.

No one knows the place of his burial. Given what this nation did with a bronze snake, making offerings to it until Hezekiah smashed it (2 Kings 18:4), a known grave of Moses would have been a shrine within a generation. Israel was left his words, not his bones.

Wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days. The nation mourns thirty days, as it had for Aaron (Numbers 20:29; see mourning customs), and then the days of mourning end. Grief is honoured, and then the people move on, because the work God gave them is not finished.

Outside the land, outside the gate. Moses died outside the land for his own failure and the people’s provocation. Jesus “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12) for no sin of his own but for his people’s; he laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18) and took it up again, so that those he died for enter the inheritance Moses could only see.

Michael and the body. Jude says that Michael disputed with the devil over Moses’ body (Jude 9). Jude draws on a Jewish tradition not recorded in the Old Testament; one later form of it says the devil claimed the body because Moses had killed the Egyptian. Jude’s point is that even the archangel left judgment to God: “The Lord rebuke you.”

Textual note. The Hebrew text most naturally reads “he buried him”, that is, the LORD; the Greek and Samaritan texts read “they buried him”.
verseByVerse.note: On who wrote this closing account, see the question at vv. 9–12.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — There Has Not Arisen a Prophet Like Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s work goes on after his servant’s death, but the greatest prophet is still to come. Joshua, filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses laid his hands on him, is obeyed, and Israel does what the LORD commanded through Moses (v. 9). Then the book closes with Moses’ epitaph: no prophet has arisen in Israel like him, whom the LORD knew face to face (v. 10), and none has matched the signs and wonders done in Egypt or the mighty deeds done before all Israel (vv. 11–12). The five books end waiting for the prophet promised in 18:15.
verseByVerse.theology: The Pentateuch ends incomplete: the greatest prophet is dead, the land is unentered, and the epitaph (the closing tribute) is written in the negative, there has not arisen.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law ended with an open question and a fresh grave. Now: the Father has named the Prophet we were waiting for, and told us to listen to him (Matt. 17:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the people of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses. And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land, and for all the mighty power and all the great deeds of terror that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua takes up Moses’ work and the people follow him, yet the book ends confessing that no prophet like Moses has arisen: Israel is left waiting for the one God promised.

Full of the spirit of wisdom. The handover works. The man Moses commissioned in public (Numbers 27:18–23; 31:7) is followed, and the nation does not fall apart at the funeral, which is the best thing that can be said of any succession. The wisdom that fills Joshua is the Spirit’s gift, not his own store; the laying on of hands showed publicly that God had given it and that Moses’ authority now rested on him.

Whom the LORD knew face to face. Other prophets received visions and dreams; with Moses God spoke “mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8; compare Exodus 33:11). That nearness, with the signs in Egypt and the mighty deeds in the wilderness, set him apart from every prophet after him.

There has not arisen a prophet since. Because the epitaph is negative, the five books, from the creation of the world to this hillside, end on a note of waiting. Sixteen chapters earlier God had promised, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers” (18:15). The last paragraph of the book says, in effect: not yet. Nobody like him has come.

Listen to him. Centuries later, on a high mountain, Moses stood inside the land at last, in glory, talking with Jesus (Matthew 17:3), and he was not the point of the scene. A cloud came down, and a voice said the sentence Deuteronomy 18 had been waiting for: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). Peter and Stephen both preached that the prophet like Moses had come (Acts 3:22; 7:37). Moses knew God face to face as a servant; Jesus is “the only Son, who is at the Father’s side” (John 1:18), counted worthy of “more glory than Moses” (Hebrews 3:3).

Jesus only. When they looked up, “they saw no one but Jesus only” (Matthew 17:8). The law had led them as far as the bank of the river and stopped; the one who takes people across is not a law but a Person, named Jesus because “he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

Who wrote these verses? Most likely not Moses, and the text does not pretend he did. Phrases such as “to this day” (v. 6) and “there has not arisen a prophet since” (v. 10) read like the words of someone writing well after the event. An account of Moses’ death by another hand does not undercut the book’s claim that Moses wrote the law (31:9); it is what any book finished after its author died would contain.

Where Christians differ. Jewish tradition credited Joshua with these verses, while the ancient Jewish writers Philo and Josephus held that Moses wrote even this, by prophecy. Many Christians think a later inspired editor completed the book, and how much later is debated; many critical scholars date the whole of Deuteronomy centuries after Moses.

This commentary’s view. The substance of Deuteronomy is Moses’ own, as the book and our Lord say (31:9; Mark 10:3–5), and this closing account was added by a later inspired hand, perhaps Joshua’s (see the introduction).

keyVerse.quote: And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face
keyVerse.note: The five books of Moses end not with a triumph but with an admission: the prophet promised in 18:15 has not yet come. The verse leaves Israel looking forward, and the New Testament answers it with Jesus, the Son who knows the Father and makes him known, of whom the Father says, “listen to him” (Matthew 17:5).

34.reflection:
God showed Moses the whole land and then said, “you shall not go over there” (v. 4). Where do you see both God’s faithfulness and his discipline in this moment? Have you known his kindness and his discipline together?

Moses dies “according to the word of the LORD” and is buried by God in a grave no one can find (vv. 5–6). What does this teach about how God regards the death of his servants, and about the danger of venerating even the greatest of them?

Joshua carried on what Moses began, and the people followed him (v. 9). What does this chapter say to a church or family facing the loss of a faithful leader?

The book ends saying that no prophet like Moses has arisen (v. 10). In what ways does Jesus fulfil and surpass Moses, and what does it mean in practice to “listen to him” (Matthew 17:5)?
